holistic_analysis: Apple’s 2021 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, multi-dimensional threat that has already hurt the company and could materially worsen results.  The filing combines backward-looking evidence (store closures, supply shortages that affected worldwide sales in 2021, mandatory remote work) with forward-looking language (future supply-chain shocks, demand erosion, cost structure pressure, new virus variants).  The disclosures are specific – they name component shortages, manufacturing and logistics interruptions, retail shutdowns, labour displacement and even higher digital-content production costs – yet they stop short of assigning dollar figures.  Because the pandemic began in March 2020 and the filing date is October 2021, the event is well inside the 0-3-year “recent” window of the Time Decay Principle, allowing high severity scores.  Overall, the risk is direct and ongoing: actual adverse impacts have already materialised and management concedes that many key drivers remain outside its control.  Mitigation notes (store re-openings, continuous monitoring) modestly temper, but do not eliminate, the high risk profile.  Therefore, individual sentence scores cluster in the mid-to-upper range (≈2-8) depending on the depth, specificity and presence of mitigating language.

Apple’s 2022 Form 10-K positions COVID-19 as an active, multi-faceted threat that has already impaired the company’s performance and may continue to do so.  The disclosure shifts seamlessly from describing realised impacts (supply shortages that hurt worldwide sales, higher digital-content costs, prior adverse effects on stock price) to outlining forward-looking exposures across demand, supply-chain resilience, labour, retail operations and profitability.  The language is direct and company-specific—using phrases such as “materially adversely affected” and citing concrete operational disruptions—rather than vague boiler-plate.  Mitigating statements are sparse and largely limited to the company’s ongoing monitoring efforts, which do little to offset the gravity of the risks.  Because the filing date (28 Oct 2022) falls less than three years after the WHO’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Overall, the evidentiary set signals a high, persistent risk profile with tangible historic damage and substantial uncertainty going forward.

Apple’s 2023 Form 10-K continues to link the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective enterprise-wide risks.  The company explicitly states that the pandemic has already “adversely affected” operations and goes on to catalogue concrete channels of exposure—global demand shocks, supply-chain breakdowns, labor and freight constraints, and delays in product ramps.  These disclosures confirm that COVID-19 is not treated merely as a hypothetical but as a proven disruptor whose effects still linger across manufacturing, logistics and consumer demand.  However, the language remains largely qualitative and unquantified, suggesting Apple views the pandemic as a material but now better-understood, more diffuse risk than in 2020-2021.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, the event sits just beyond the three-year “recent” window (≈3.6 years at filing date), so evidentiary scores should fall in the mid-range (4-6).  Overall, the filing portrays COVID-19 as an ongoing, potentially material threat—especially to supply continuity and product launches—but no longer at the crisis peak that would warrant top-tier severity scores.

Apple’s 2024 Form 10-K still treats COVID-19 as a live, material risk rather than merely a historical event.  Although the initial outbreak began more than four years before the filing date, the disclosure makes clear that pandemic-related disruptions (supply chain bottlenecks, freight restrictions, employee travel curbs, depressed consumer demand and delays in new-product ramps) have already harmed the Company and could do so again.  This wording reflects both realised impacts (“have adversely affected”) and forward-looking threats (“could in the future materially adversely affect”), providing more than a boiler-plate reference.  Because the event is now in the 4-to-5-year window, the Time Decay Principle caps any single-sentence score in the moderate range (4-6).  No substantial mitigating language (e.g., alternative sourcing, remote-work efficiencies, pandemic playbooks) accompanies the statements, so the risk remains largely untempered.  Overall, the evidence supports a moderate-to-high residual risk assessment tied to COVID-19, consistent with Apple’s continued dependence on a globally concentrated supply chain and consumer sentiment that can shift quickly during public-health crises.

The filing was submitted less than a year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so time-decay does not diminish the evidentiary weight.  AbbVie’s disclosure mixes backward-looking facts ( lower new-patient starts, remote-work shift ) with forward-looking cautionary language ( possible material adverse impact, supply-chain uncertainty ).  The company explicitly references multiple enterprise functions—manufacturing, supply chain, sales & marketing, clinical trials—and acknowledges that, although the near-term effect has not been material, the outbreak "could continue to negatively impact results" and "could have a material adverse impact" overall.  The risk language is specific to AbbVie, cites concrete operational changes already taken, and identifies an observable earnings head-wind (lower patient starts), yet offers mitigating statements (impact “not been material,” proactive supply-chain management).  Balancing these aggravating and mitigating factors for a very recent event leads to generally moderate-to-high snippet scores (3-7 range).

ABBV’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly ties the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic to operational, financial and strategic risk.  The filing describes both realised and prospective effects: actual adjustments (remote-work shift, enhanced supply-chain monitoring) and measurable impacts (lower new-patient starts) show the threat is not hypothetical, while language about possible future adverse effects, uncertain duration, and dependence on external variables (variants, government measures) signals a forward-looking risk profile.  Although management stresses that the aggregate financial hit has ‘not been material’ so far and details mitigation steps, the disclosure nonetheless concedes that continued or re-implemented lockdowns, supply-chain strain and demand changes could still harm results of operations.  Given the filing date (Feb-2022) is less than two years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows relatively elevated scores.  Overall, the pandemic constitutes a moderate-to-high contemporary risk—significant enough to warrant specific board-level attention, but partially tempered by the company’s current resilience and mitigation efforts.

AbbVie’s 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an active, multifaceted source of operational and financial risk.  The company discloses that the pandemic has already forced concrete operational changes (e.g., modified business practices and lower new-patient starts) while simultaneously warning that future impacts remain highly uncertain and could extend across manufacturing, supply-chain stability, clinical trials, sales and overall financial condition.  Language is largely qualitative—AbbVie emphasizes uncertainty rather than quantified dollar impacts—but it still contains several aggravating signals: acknowledgement of past adverse effects, expectation of continuing pressure on results, and explicit reference to dependence on external variables such as government restrictions, new variants and supply-chain resilience.  Mitigating language (e.g., “impact … to date was not material” and descriptions of active supply-chain management) tempers but does not eliminate risk.  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is a recent, ongoing event (less than three years old at filing), so evidence can be scored in the upper range.  Overall, the risk profile is assessed as moderate-to-high: the company concedes real operational hits and sees potential for further deterioration, yet it has not reported material financial damage so far and is actively mitigating certain exposures.

COVID-19 first struck in early 2020, just four years prior to this 2024 filing, placing it solidly in the ‘medium-term’ window of the Time-Decay framework.  AbbVie’s disclosure cluster is concise but confirms that (1) the pandemic already forced concrete operational changes and (2) residual uncertainty persists around potential renewed lockdowns, supply-chain constraints and shifts in market behaviour (e-commerce, counterfeit risk).  The language is largely qualitative and un-quantified—there are no dollar figures, margin impacts, or specific capacity metrics—but it does acknowledge both historical impacts (“have had”) and forward-looking exposure (“could in the future have”).  On balance, the statements are more than boiler-plate yet fall short of a detailed, quantified assessment; therefore, risk severity is moderate.  Applying the Time-Decay Principle for a four-year-old event, individual snippet scores should cluster in the 1-6 range, with higher scores reserved for lines evidencing direct operational impact or strategic action, and lower scores for generic contextual remarks.

The filing is less than a year after the WHO’s March 11 2020 pandemic declaration, so COVID-19 is treated as a current, highly-salient threat.  ABNB repeatedly discloses that the pandemic has already produced material, quantified harm (declines in bookings, workforce reductions, lease impairments, extraordinary refund costs) and that the adverse effects will persist through 2021 and "beyond."  The company also details operational knock-ons—government lockdowns, depressed cross-border demand, remote-work frictions, privacy and fraud exposures—and admits it cannot predict the ultimate cumulative impact.  These statements are specific, forward-looking, and tied to financial metrics; there are few mitigating references beyond generic cost-cutting.  Given the timing (recent event), the breadth of impacts (revenue, costs, workforce, IT risk) and explicit language of materiality, individual snippets merit high risk scores (7-9) with moderate scores (4-6) for ancillary but still relevant operational exposures.  Time Decay does not reduce the assessments because the pandemic is ongoing and within three years of the filing date.

Airbnb’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as the single most significant near-term and continuing threat to its business model.  The filing—dated barely two years after the WHO declared the pandemic—provides plentiful, company-specific evidence of both realised damage and looming uncertainty, so time-decay does not meaningfully dilute severity.  Management discloses tangible financial hits (lease impairments, elevated refund outflows, host–earnings losses) and operational shifts (global remote-work, workforce reduction) already recorded in past results.  It also warns that new governmental travel curbs, shifting consumer behaviour and ongoing guest cancellations could keep depressing revenue, EBITDA, cash flow and even magnify other risk factors.  The language is explicit (“materially adversely impacted”, “continue to materially adversely impact”), recent, and directly ties the pandemic to core metrics—indicating a high, persistent risk profile.  Although some mitigants exist (e.g., business model adaptability), they do not outweigh the breadth of negative impacts identified.  Accordingly, individual snippets score in the upper mid-range (5-7) when they document concrete or quantified harm, and slightly lower (3-5) where the disclosure is broader or more speculative.  All scores sit within the 0-3-year window, so no time-decay reductions are applied.

Airbnb’s 2023 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as both an historical shock and a persisting, material threat.  The filing acknowledges that the pandemic already “materially adversely impacted” revenue through travel bans, quarantines and mass cancellations, and that it continues to influence host supply, guest demand, workforce deployment (remote work) and even cyber-security exposure.  Disclosures are largely qualitative but they go beyond boiler-plate: management cites concrete operational mechanisms—government travel restrictions, guests’ cancelled reservations under the extenuating-circumstances policy, long-lasting shifts in economic conditions, and heightened regulatory burdens—that can erode revenue and margins.  The statements are framed as existing impacts with potential for future amplification, using forceful language such as “materially adversely impacted” and “long-lasting adverse impact.”  Because the filing date (17 Feb 2023) is within three years of the WHO’s pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7-10) for direct, present-tense impacts and mid-range scores (3-6) for forward-looking or secondary effects.  No significant mitigating actions (e.g., hedging, insurance, or quantified recovery) are offered in the cited sentences, so deductions are minimal.  Taken together, the evidence depicts a high but not existential risk profile: the pandemic still shapes Airbnb’s operating environment and could quickly reignite revenue volatility should variants or regulations resurface.

Airbnb’s 2024 Form 10-K positions the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, medium-term risk that still meaningfully threatens demand, operations and the regulatory environment but no longer dominates the short-term outlook as it did in 2020-2022.  All references are forward-looking: management warns that future public-health crises—explicitly citing COVID-19—could suddenly depress travel demand, reduce listings, create cash-flow pressure and trigger new, restrictive laws.  The language is largely qualitative and speaks to potential material adverse effects (“would be materially adversely affected”) rather than disclosing fresh quantified impacts, reflecting that the acute phase has passed but uncertainty remains.  Because the filing date (Feb 2024) is just under four years from the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle places these disclosures in the 4-10-year ‘medium-term’ window, capping individual snippet scores around 4-6.  The sentences below collectively show (1) demand risk, (2) industry-wide travel disruption risk specifically naming COVID-19, and (3) continuing regulatory uncertainty stemming from pandemic-driven rules.  No meaningful mitigating factors (e.g., vaccinations, diversified geographies) are offered in these sentences.  Therefore each excerpt earns a moderate severity score, reflecting persistent but no longer acute exposure.

The 2021-02-19 Form 10-K explicitly ties Abbott’s risk profile to the still-unfolding COVID-19 pandemic.  Within Item 1A the company frames the pandemic as a live, enterprise-wide threat that can simultaneously erode demand, snarl supply chains, strain labour availability and unsettle capital markets.  The language combines both forward-looking uncertainty (e.g., EUAs could lapse; duration is unknown) and backward-looking evidence of realised impacts (e.g., lost procedure volumes, disrupted emerging-market drug sales).  Several passages also note operational counter-measures—business-continuity planning, remote work, travel bans—which partially mitigate, but do not eliminate, the exposure.  Under the Time Decay Principle the event is < 1 year old at filing, so high scores (up to 10) are permissible where impacts are direct and material.  Most statements are qualitative and unquantified, warranting mid-to-high single-digit scores; sentences that merely note mitigation or generic caution are scored lower or offset by negative points.

Across both the Risk Factors section and the MD&A, Abbott explicitly links the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic (declared March 2020) to a spectrum of operational, financial, and macro-economic threats. Because the Form 10-K was filed on 18 February 2022—well inside the 0-3-year ‘recent-event’ window—the Time Decay Principle permits elevated severity scores. The language shows a blend of realised impacts (e.g., higher costs, volatile test demand, past business challenges) and forward-looking uncertainties (e.g., unpredictable variants, potential inability to meet demand). Although most sentences remain qualitative and lack hard dollar figures, they describe concrete mechanisms—supply-chain disruption, labour/material shortages, demand volatility—that can materially erode revenue and margins. Mitigating statements exist (e.g., the firm has “been able to manage” disruptions so far), but these are hedged with “no assurance” caveats. Overall, the pandemic constitutes an active, evolving risk with medium-to-high severity for Abbott, warranting mid-to-upper-range snippet scores (4-7) under the scoring rubric.

Abbott’s 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly ties the 2020-23 COVID-19 pandemic to concrete, already-incurred disruptions and to forward-looking uncertainty.  The filing describes realised cost inflation and availability problems in raw materials and services, demand volatility for COVID-19 tests, procedure deferrals in device businesses, and volatile macro-economic conditions.  It also warns that the pandemic "may continue" to have a material effect on results, while acknowledging some mitigation (supply resilience so far, monitoring of regulatory changes, recovery in certain product lines).  Because the pandemic event is recent (within three years of the filing), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores where impacts are direct and material.  However, sentences that emphasise successful mitigation or recovery reduce the net score for that piece of evidence.  Overall, the risk remains elevated and ongoing, but partly offset by the company’s actions to manage supply chains, monitor regulations, and diversify its portfolio.

ABT’s 2024 Form 10-K makes it clear that COVID-19 remains a material but gradually receding driver of enterprise-wide risk.  Although the acute phase of the pandemic started nearly four years ago, the company still attributes demonstrable impacts to it: higher raw-material costs, supply-chain disruptions, labour availability problems, volatile testing demand, and procedure slow-downs in device businesses.  The language is not hypothetical; it cites realised consequences (“had a material effect…”, “negatively impacted…”, “adversely impacted cost and availability…”), quantified drops in testing revenue, and continuing unpredictability in 2024.  At the same time, ABT notes some mitigating dynamics—shift to an endemic state, recovery of certain volumes, and management’s ability to avoid “significant supply disruption.”  Applying the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 sits at the front edge of the 4-to-10-year ‘medium-term’ window (≈3.9 years since March 2020), so evidence can still score moderately high but should not exceed 6.  Consequently, the strongest sentences that link the pandemic to concrete operational or financial harm receive scores of 6, while more generic, macro-economic, or partially mitigated statements score 3-5.

Arch Capital Group Ltd.’s 2021 filing identifies COVID-19 as both an already-material and an evolving, forward-looking threat.  The language spans concrete, quantified impacts ($272 million of 2020 losses) and broad, prospective exposures—higher claim frequency, investment volatility, mortgage defaults, regulatory mandates, remote-work cyber risk and litigation.  The company repeatedly uses strong qualifiers such as “material” and “significant,” confirming that management sees the pandemic as a top-tier risk to results of operations, capital and liquidity.  Most disclosures are recent (less than one year after WHO’s pandemic declaration), so Time Decay does not dilute severity.  Although some mitigating references exist (e.g., capital strength, reinsurance), they are sparse and not sentence-specific.  Overall, the evidence portrays a high and multi-dimensional risk profile consistent with severity scores in the upper mid-to-high range (5-9) under the scoring framework.

ACGL’s 2022 Form 10-K openly frames COVID-19 as a current, high-severity threat across virtually every dimension of its global insurance, reinsurance and mortgage platforms.  The company does not treat the pandemic as a historical footnote; instead, it states that (i) the virus and an emerging “endemic” environment can still materially impair underwriting results, investment income and liquidity, (ii) regulatory, rating-agency and governmental responses could reshape coverage terms, pricing and capital needs, (iii) prolonged low-rate and volatile capital-market conditions tied to COVID-19 threaten investment returns, (iv) pandemic-driven economic stress is already pushing mortgage delinquencies higher and could spark future credit losses, and (v) the forced migration to remote work raises operating-risk and cyber-risk profiles.  Every disclosure is forward-looking or contemporaneous, couched in “material” or “significant” language, and linked to specific balance-sheet or operational vectors (claims frequency, premium volume, IT capacity, workforce stability, etc.).  Because the filing date (25 Feb 2022) falls within two years of the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  While many sentences use conditional verbs (“could,” “may”), ACGL also cites observed impacts (higher claims, defaults, IT strain).  Taken together, the statements evidence an acute, still-evolving risk environment with limited mitigation, justifying elevated micro-scores in the 7-9 range.

Arch Capital’s 2023 filing ties the COVID-19 pandemic to multiple, still-unfolding risk vectors that reach well beyond the initial health crisis.  The company acknowledges both realised effects (e.g., investment-portfolio hits in Q2-2020, regulatory mandates already ‘impacting’ operations) and prospective threats such as renewed variants, lingering mortgage forbearance, collateral calls, capital-market access, labour-model disruption and heightened claim frequency in specific lines (trade credit, travel, workers’ compensation, business interruption).  The language is largely specific and company-centred—using terms like “materially affect,” citing mortgage default mechanics, collateral triggers and rating-agency reactions—rather than generic boiler-plate.  Because the filing date (24-Feb-2023) is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores (up to 10).  Nonetheless, some sentences are forward-looking without quantified dollar impact or are partly mitigated by company actions (e.g., hybrid work model), warranting score modulation.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a direct, active and multi-faceted risk for ACGL, justifying high but differentiated micro-scores across the extracted evidence.

ACGL’s 2024 filing references the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an external macro-economic shock that can aggravate inflation, recessionary trends and large-loss scenarios, and secondarily as an operational disruptor that triggered hybrid-work arrangements and some claims activity.  Most language is prospective ("potential", "may", "could") rather than reporting quantified, realized losses; indeed, management notes that related claims have already fallen and that the company does not expect a significant ongoing impact.  Thus, the pandemic is framed as a lingering, but diminishing, risk driver—affecting investment markets, inflation, workforce patterns and the tail-risk of future pandemics—rather than a current material hit to earnings.  Because the filing date (Feb-2024) is almost four years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle places the event at the cusp of the recent/medium window, so individual sentence scores should sit in the mid-range (4-6) when the wording conveys meaningful adverse impact, and lower (1-3) when statements are generic or heavily mitigated.  No passage contains hard numbers or audited loss amounts; consequently, the overall evidence set indicates a moderate, forward-looking risk rather than an acute, quantified loss event.

All COVID-19 references occur a little more than one year before the filing date, so they fall squarely inside the 0-3-year ‘recent-event’ window; the Time Decay Principle therefore allows high scores (up to 10).  The filing describes both realized and prospective consequences: actual office closures, disrupted operations, employee-health strains and heightened cyber-threats are cited as impacts that have already occurred, while demand volatility, continued macro-economic uncertainty and the possibility that future variants or inadequate vaccines will hamper the firm’s ability to innovate represent forward-looking exposures.  Language is consistently explicit—using phrases such as “materially adversely impact,” “significantly negative,” or “disrupted our business”—but the document supplies no hard dollar amounts, so no snippet earns the absolute maximum.  Mitigating remarks (e.g., successful continuity procedures in India/Philippines) slightly temper some scores.  Overall, the evidence depicts a broad, multi-dimensional, still-evolving risk profile that is clearly material to ACN’s operations, warranting mid-to-high severity grades across the extracted sentences.

ACN’s 2022-10-12 Form 10-K places the COVID-19 pandemic squarely within its portfolio of material business threats. Because the filing date is barely thirty months after the WHO declaration (well inside the 0-3-year ‘recent event’ window), the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scoring.  The company explicitly acknowledges that COVID-19 has already harmed operations (“have had” impact) and could continue to do so.  The narrative, however, stays largely qualitative: it stresses volatile demand, impeded travel/communications, difficulty staffing projects, and supply-chain turbulence, but provides no quantified revenue, margin or cash-flow figures.  Risk language is strong (“significantly negative impacts”) yet is bundled with many other hazards, diluting specificity.  Overall, the evidence portrays a live, ongoing, but not precisely measured exposure—warranting mid-to-high severity marks for the most direct statements, and lower marks for generic or indirect references.

The filing discusses the COVID-19 pandemic as part of a broader set of disruptive “health emergencies or pandemics.”  Although the pandemic began more than three years before the October 2023 filing date, the text still frames COVID-19 as both a historic and forward-looking threat that can materially impair Accenture’s operations, client demand, workforce availability and technology infrastructure.  The language is largely qualitative and bundled with other catastrophe-type risks, so it lacks granular financial quantification; however, it identifies multiple concrete transmission channels—remote-work cyber-exposure, travel and communication breakdowns, labour shortages, and sudden shifts in economic activity.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic is now in the 4-to-10-year “medium-term” window, meaning evidence can merit moderate severity scores (≈4-6).  The extracted sentences therefore receive mid-range scores, reflecting explicit COVID-19 references, acknowledgement of past damage, and the possibility of significant future harm, but tempered by their generic, bundled presentation and absence of hard numbers.

The filing, dated October 10 2024, addresses the COVID-19 pandemic only in broad, catch-all language. Management groups ‘global health emergencies’ and ‘pandemics’ with other macro hazards and notes that these events have previously hurt demand and could do so again. The wording signals the company has already experienced some adverse impact (historical anchoring) while also treating the threat as an ongoing, forward-looking uncertainty. No dollar amounts, supply-chain statistics, or labor-force metrics are provided, and no specific mitigation steps (e.g., diversified sourcing, vaccination policies) are disclosed. Because the pandemic’s onset is now roughly 4½ years in the past, the Time Decay Principle requires that evidence be scored in the moderate range: the risk is still relevant but no longer at its peak. Consequently, individual snippet scores fall between 1 and 5, reflecting generic but still credible references to demand disruption and operational challenges such as prolonged remote work.

Adobe’s January 15 2021 filing discusses COVID-19 as an immediate, material and multifaceted threat.  Multiple passages confirm that the pandemic has already ‘materially affected’ operations—e.g., global office closures, mandatory remote-work, cancellation of in-person events and observable slow-downs in customer IT spending.  The company also highlights forward-looking uncertainties: potential long-term shifts in working patterns, supply-chain disruptions and delays in subscription renewals that might surface in later periods because of the firm’s ratable-revenue model.  The language is specific (naming concrete operational actions and financial exposure) and predominantly aggravating; very few mitigating actions are offered beyond generic monitoring and virtualisation of events.  Because the filing date is less than a year after the WHO declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores.  Overall, the evidence signals a high-severity, ongoing risk, warranting snippet scores clustered in the 4-to-9 range, with the strongest sentences receiving higher values where they show current, material impact on revenue or operations.

Adobe’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as a recent (≤3-year) event that has already produced material, multi-dimensional impacts and continues to pose significant uncertainty. The company discloses concrete, experienced disruptions – office closures, modified business practices, supply-chain delays, slowdowns in customer purchasing and IT spending – alongside forward-looking threats to workforce health, productivity, demand, real-estate strategy and partner performance. Language such as “materially affected,” “have seen,” and “are continuing to cause” confirms an existing, direct impact, while repeated references to uncertain duration, future variants and macroeconomic persistence highlight residual and potentially amplifying risk. Because the statements are recent, specific and describe both realized harm and ongoing vulnerability across operations, supply chain, labor and demand, the overall risk level is high under the Time Decay Principle. Mitigations are mentioned only tangentially (e.g., subscription model defers recognition), so they do little to offset severity. Consequently, individual sentence scores cluster in the upper-mid to high range (2-7), reflecting granular differences in specificity, materiality and conditionality, but all remain within the 0-10 bounds appropriate for a contemporary event.

All pandemic-related disclosures in the filing are clustered in the Risk Factors section and frame COVID-19 as both a realized and continuing threat.  Adobe acknowledges concrete impacts (e.g., supply-chain disruptions that have already occurred) as well as forward-looking uncertainties (e.g., acquisition delays, potential operational interruptions and macro-economic slow-downs).  The language is largely qualitative and precautionary—there are no dollar figures or quantified volume losses—yet it is specific enough to tie the pandemic to strategic functions such as M&A execution, hardware procurement for data-center continuity, and day-to-day customer operations.  Because the filing date (17 Jan 2023) is less than three years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  Nonetheless, the absence of quantified financial impact, coupled with mentions of only potential or un-sized adverse effects, moderates the severity assessment.  Overall, the pandemic presents a meaningful but not catastrophic risk to Adobe; corresponding snippet scores therefore fall in the mid-to-upper range (3-7) rather than the maximum level.

Adobe’s January 17 2024 Form 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a continuing but indeterminate source of operational and financial risk.  Nearly four years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic, the company frames COVID-19-related disruption as an event that “has had and may continue to have” adverse effects rather than providing any fresh, quantified impact.  The disclosures are forward-looking and largely generic—COVID-19 is bundled with other catastrophes, and management emphasises uncertainty (“will depend on many factors outside of our control”).  Nonetheless, Adobe does point to concrete vectors through which pandemic conditions could still hurt performance: employee productivity in a hybrid-work model, supply-chain and service-provider interruptions, and the possibility that a renewed global outbreak could magnify other risk factors.  Under the Time Decay Principle, an event that began in 2020 but remains relevant in 2024 warrants moderate severity: the immediacy of crisis has diminished, yet the company still sees material downside potential.  Accordingly, the individual evidence scores cluster in the low-to-mid range, with higher marks given to statements that explicitly link COVID-19 to adverse operating results and lower marks for broad, boiler-plate references.

Analog Devices, Inc. (ADI) provides an extensive and fairly candid discussion of COVID-19-related risks in its December 3 2021 Form 10-K.  Because the filing date is less than two years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits relatively high severity scores.  The disclosure spans both realized impacts (plant disruptions, remote-work transition, transportation bottlenecks and capital-market volatility) and forward-looking uncertainties (potential recession, future variants, liquidity stress and workforce illness).  Language is generally strong—using phrases such as “have adversely impacted,” “material adverse effect,” and “cannot assure”—indicating that management sees the pandemic as an active and continuing threat rather than a hypothetical contingency.  While no dollar amounts are provided, the breadth of operational areas cited (manufacturing, supply chain, labour, customer demand, liquidity) elevates the overall risk profile.  Mitigation references are limited (e.g., altered workplace practices), so downside exposure remains prominent.  In aggregate, the evidence supports upper-mid to high individual snippet scores (roughly 6-8), with lower scores for statements that are purely uncertain or generic.  The overall risk level is high for a recent, ongoing event with multi-faceted operational consequences, justifying robust snippet scoring within the allowed 0-10 range.

ADI’s 2022-11-22 Form 10-K repeatedly flags COVID-19 as both an already-felt and still-evolving threat.  Statements range from generic references in multi-factor risk lists to concrete descriptions of manufacturing slow-downs, supply-chain disturbances, remote-work complications, and potential liquidity strain if customers delay payments.  The company notes actual facility disruptions and work-practice changes that have already occurred, while also stressing that future impacts hinge on uncertain variables such as new variants and vaccination progress.  Because the filing date is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores.  However, many passages remain forward-looking and unquantified, or contain mitigating language (“could,” “uncertain,” contingency planning).  Accordingly, the evidence cluster warrants upper-mid but not maximum severity scores—generally 3-9—reflecting meaningful but mostly un-quantified, evolving risk rather than a precisely measured financial hit.

Analog Devices, Inc. (ADI) continues to treat the COVID-19 pandemic as a live, multi-dimensional risk even though the first global outbreak occurred more than three years before the 21 November 2023 filing date.  Across the Risk Factors section the company reiterates that COVID-19 has already disrupted its workforce, manufacturing footprint and supply chain, and that it can still trigger further production delays, customer-payment problems and heightened exposure to other listed risks.  The disclosures are largely qualitative—no dollar figures or quantified capacity losses are supplied—but they expressly link the pandemic to operational, financial and logistical stress points such as factory access restrictions, supply-chain interruptions and customer demand volatility.  Most sentences rely on conditional language (“may,” “could”), signalling forward-looking uncertainty rather than certain impact; however ADI also acknowledges historic, realised disruption, which elevates severity.  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 qualifies as a recent event (≤ 3 years), so evidence that shows direct or ongoing impact can attain moderately high scores (7-8), while generic, boiler-plate mentions stay lower.  No strong mitigating statements (e.g., detailed contingency plans or quantified cost controls) are provided, so deductions are mainly for conditional phrasing rather than offsetting actions.

ADI’s 2024 Form 10-K still flags the COVID-19 pandemic as a meaningful—though now medium-term—threat.  The filing does not cite any fresh, quantified losses; instead, management presents the pandemic in a forward-looking, contingency frame, grouping it with other catastrophic events.  Nonetheless, the language ties COVID-19 (and broader public-health emergencies) directly to core value-drivers: manufacturing continuity, supply-chain availability, and revenue predictability.  Because the pandemic’s official onset was in March 2020 and the filing date is November 2024 (~4¾ years later), Time-Decay shifts the evidence out of the “recent” band and into the 4-10 year window, capping potential severity at a moderate level.  The disclosures remain risk-elevating—mentioning global supply-chain constraints, possible factory shutdowns, and inventory disruptions—but they are entirely qualitative and embedded in long, catch-all sentences.  Taking these factors together, the overall risk signal is specific enough to matter (COVID-19 is named) yet lacks fresh, quantified impact, yielding a moderate aggregate risk posture in line with a medium-term event.

ADM’s 2021-02-18 Form 10-K openly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective risks across operations, supply chains, workforce availability, product demand, and working-capital requirements.  The filing was issued less than a year after the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), so Time-Decay permits high severity scoring.  ADM provides a layered disclosure: (1) broad, forward-looking statements that pandemics could disrupt operations; (2) specific contingencies—illness, quarantines, logistics breakdowns, higher costs—that could arise; and (3) concrete 2020 impacts already felt, such as volatile crushing margins, soft food-service demand, and the temporary idling of ethanol plants.  Although management mentions mitigation (monitoring, stakeholder coordination), it cannot yet quantify the ultimate effect and concedes the impact ‘could potentially be material.’  Overall, the risk is recent, multi-dimensional, partly realized, and only partially mitigated.  Consequently, individual sentence scores cluster in the mid-to-high range (4-7) when impacts are explicit, and lower (1-3) when language is generic or mitigation-heavy.

ADM’s 2022 filing discusses COVID-19 as both an already-felt and still-evolving enterprise risk.  Statements span three themes: (1) immediate operational pressure, such as manufacturing-labor shortages and higher input costs; (2) potential future shocks from harsher variants that could cripple contractual performance, supply chains, and product demand; and (3) observable demand volatility in specific business lines (oils, sweeteners, ethanol, animal nutrition).  The language is largely specific—naming supply-chain bottlenecks, working-capital strain, and product-channel exposure—yet most impacts are described qualitatively rather than with hard dollar figures.  Mitigating references (e.g., “ADM has effectively managed…”) temper but do not eliminate the threat, because management concedes that more severe variants could be “material.”  Given the filing date (February 2022), the disclosures fall inside the 0-to-3-year window of the Time Decay Principle, allowing higher scores.  However, because impacts are mostly potential or directional (rather than quantified losses already booked), the individual snippet scores peak in the mid-range, reflecting meaningful but not catastrophic risk evidence.

ADM’s 2023 Form 10-K continues to tie the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic to multiple operational and financial vulnerabilities.  The filing date (14 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO’s March 2020 declaration, so the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores.  The discussion is mostly forward-looking—management stresses that it “could be materially impacted” if a harsher variant or a new disease emerges—but it also cites already-observed strains, such as labour shortages in U.S. manufacturing.  Key impact channels are clearly laid out: (i) inability to meet contractual obligations, (ii) disruption of global supply-chain and logistics networks, (iii) unrecoverable cost inflation not covered by insurance, (iv) demand destruction for biofuels and food-service ingredients under lockdown scenarios, and (v) pandemic-induced labour constraints.  Mitigations are mentioned (the company “effectively managed” the initial COVID-19 wave and implemented mitigation actions), but these do not eliminate the residual risk.  Taken together, the language is specific, links directly to ADM’s core activities, and signals potentially material financial consequences, warranting moderate-to-high severity scores across the identified snippets.

ADM’s 2024 Form 10-K expressly acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a significant, near-term enterprise risk.  Although the company does not disclose historical dollar impacts, it frames the pandemic in concrete operational and financial terms—highlighting potential supply-chain breakdowns, inability to satisfy contracts, unrecoverable cost inflation, and sudden shifts in demand for biofuels and food-service ingredients.  The language is forward-looking but anchored in recent experience (“disruptions far more severe than previously experienced”), signalling that management views the threat as ongoing rather than purely hypothetical.  Because the filing date (March 2024) is within four years of the event’s onset, the Time Decay Principle places the evidence in the “recent” bucket, allowing high severity scores where warranted.  Overall, ADM’s disclosures combine specific channels of exposure (logistics, working-capital strain, product-demand volatility) with the prospect of material impact and limited insurance coverage—supporting elevated risk scores, though slightly tempered by the absence of quantified figures or concrete loss history.

ADP’s 2021-08-04 Form 10-K embeds COVID-19 across both backward-looking and forward-looking risk narratives.  Multiple sentences disclose that the pandemic has already produced tangible, adverse effects—most notably lower revenue and weaker new-business bookings—while also flagging continuing uncertainty around client employment levels, customer purchasing behaviour, remote-work logistics and workplace culture.  Although no hard dollar figure is provided, the company repeatedly characterises the impact as “significant” or “negative,” signalling materiality.  The document also outlines several plausible future pathways by which COVID-19 could further harm operations: delayed client decisions, pricing concessions, remote-work challenges, and broader macro-economic volatility.  Mitigating language is minimal and mostly reputational (e.g., “our priority is the safety of our associates”), so the overall tone remains cautionary.  Given that the filing date is only 17 months after the WHO declaration (well within the 0-3-year window), the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (7-10) where direct, company-specific impacts are stated, and moderate scores (4-6) where the discussion is broader or purely prospective.  No evidence is pre-event, so no mandatory zero scores apply.

ADP’s 2022 Form 10-K discusses the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, enterprise-wide uncertainty that can adversely impact virtually every facet of the company’s operations—from topline demand and per-employee transactional volumes to employee-productivity, remote-work logistics, and capital-market access. The disclosures are forward-looking in tone ("may", "depends on developments") but also acknowledge that the pandemic has already "created significant volatility and disruption," signalling that the risk is both realized and continuing. Although no dollar figures are provided, the narrative pinpoints concrete transmission channels (client decision delays, employment levels that change fee revenues, remote-work challenges, and supply-chain disruptions). Given the filing date of August 2022—well within three years of the March 2020 WHO declaration—the Time Decay Principle allows for elevated scores. However, because the language remains largely qualitative and un-quantified, the individual snippet scores stay in the mid-range rather than the maximum 9-10 bracket.

ADP’s 2023 Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic primarily to broad operational and macro-economic uncertainties rather than to a single, quantified hit to financial performance.  The filing acknowledges that the outbreak has already produced “significant volatility and uncertainty,” but most language is forward-looking or conditional (e.g., “may be adversely affected”).  The company highlights potential pressure points familiar to pandemic discourse—travel restrictions, business closures, remote-work arrangements, client payment risk, and talent retention challenges.  Only one sentence gives a hard dollar figure (a $26 million reversal of prior COVID-19 credit-loss reserves), suggesting the acute financial shock has eased.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is still a recent event (≈3 years old at the filing date), so risk evidence can score in the mid-to-upper range; however, the largely generic, unquantified, and partly mitigating tone warrants moderate—not maximum—severity scores for most snippets.

ADP’s 2024-08-07 Form 10-K positions the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, but now medium-term, macro‐hazard rather than an acute crisis.  The company acknowledges that the original 2020 outbreak already caused ‘significant volatility and uncertainty’ and that future public-health emergencies could again disrupt almost every facet of its business—from client demand and service delivery to capital-market access.  The narrative is largely forward-looking: management lists contingent variables (government actions, remote-work arrangements, client ability to pay, employment levels, pricing concessions) that could magnify or mitigate the impact.  Although no dollar figures are disclosed, the language is explicit about potential operational, financial, and labour-market consequences and repeatedly references COVID-19 by name.  Under the Time Decay Principle, a March 2020 event evaluated in August 2024 falls into the 4-to-10-year “medium-term” window, warranting moderate—not maximal—severity scores.  Overall, the risk is assessed as material but not existential: it is pervasive, detailed, and still relevant, yet tempered by its maturing temporal distance, the absence of quantified losses, and the company’s emphasis on uncertainty rather than current impairment.

Autodesk’s 2021 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective risks across operations, liquidity and customer demand.  The filing, dated March 19 2021, sits squarely within three years of the WHO-declared pandemic (11 Mar 2020), so the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores where warranted.  Language in the Risk Factors section confirms that COVID-19 has already disrupted normal business practice—forcing remote-work transitions, halting travel, postponing marketing events and altering customer payment behaviour—while simultaneously stressing that the ultimate magnitude on revenue, cash flow and renewal rates remains “uncertain.”  Several passages highlight concrete, near-term financial effects (e.g., cash-flow reduction from extended payment terms) and warn of possible “material adverse” outcomes if customer churn, economic downturns or supply-chain partners deteriorate further.  The company also outlines mitigating steps (payment extensions, deferred price increases, cost controls), which slightly temper but do not eliminate the risk.  Overall, the disclosures depict a recent, ongoing event with both present impacts and sizable downside potential, justifying elevated—but not maximal—severity scores (7-9 range) for the strongest evidence, with modest deductions where the company notes active mitigations.

Autodesk’s March 2022 Form 10-K situates COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, multi-faceted threat that is already disrupting the company’s operations while remaining highly unpredictable. Two years after the WHO declaration, management describes tangible, current impacts—mandatory remote-work arrangements, cancelled events, supply-chain bottlenecks, inflationary cost pressures and global labour shortages—that are directly weighing on the pace of recovery. At the same time, the filing frames a forward-looking risk profile in which new variants, renewed lockdowns and waning policy support could materially impair growth and cash flow. The language is specific (referencing supply-chain disruption and labour shortages) and portrays both realised and prospective effects, with only limited mitigating references to ongoing monitoring and operational adjustments. Given the recency of the pandemic (within three years of the filing date), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores; however, some moderation is warranted where the company evidences adaptive measures. Overall, the document supports a high but not maximal risk assessment, reflecting an event that is actively constraining operations and could deepen if adverse scenarios materialise.

Autodesk’s March 14 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly frames the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, multifaceted threat that could materially affect the company’s operations and financial performance.  The disclosures are largely forward-looking and couched in uncertainty, but they still identify a broad spectrum of concrete impact channels: global economic contraction, customer demand delays, supply-chain disruption, inflationary pressures, labour shortages, foreign-exchange volatility, cybersecurity exposure resulting from large-scale remote work, and the need to rationalise real-estate footprints.  Because the filing date is within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time-Decay Principle allows higher severity scores.  Nevertheless, the language is predominantly generic, lacks quantified dollar impacts, and is balanced at times by mitigating statements (e.g., the subscription model may defer or dampen revenue shocks).  Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the moderate range (2-7), reflecting meaningful but not yet fully crystallised risk.  Collectively, the evidence shows Autodesk treating COVID-19 as an enduring, systemic risk factor that permeates supply chains, workforce strategy, demand patterns and financial metrics, warranting continued investor scrutiny.

Autodesk’s 2024 Form 10-K treats the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, background macro-risk rather than a current acute crisis.  The filing does not quantify any recent financial hit, but it still frames COVID-19 as a potential disruptor of global operations, supply chains, labor availability, remote-work security, and foreign-exchange volatility.  All references are couched in forward-looking, conditional language (“could,” “may,” “continue to”), signalling residual but unmanaged exposure rather than imminent, measured damage.  Because the filing date (June 2024) is a little more than four years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle places the event in the 4-10-year “medium-term” window; therefore, individual snippet scores must land in the moderate range (≈ 4-6).  Overall, the company acknowledges persistent pandemic-related uncertainties across logistics, workforce practices, and FX markets, but offers no concrete mitigation plans or quantified impacts, leading to a risk level that is material yet not severe.

Ameren’s 2021 filing contains extensive, contemporaneous discussion of COVID-19 impacts covering realised 2020 effects and forward-looking exposures. The company reports concrete, already-incurred hits to sales volumes, cash collections and receivables, while also warning of continuing pressure on operations, liquidity and capital-market access. Many passages quantify past damage (e.g., $133 million group-wide past-due receivables) or cite specific operational metrics (commercial-industrial load declines), signalling a direct, material impact that is still unfolding. Others outline prospective vulnerabilities such as prolonged market disruption, labour illness, supply-chain delays and cyber-security issues created by remote work. The language is largely specific and anchored in actual experience rather than generic boilerplate, and nearly every risk dimension—revenues, liquidity, credit ratings, supply chain, workforce and technology—is touched. Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic sits firmly in the 0-3-year “recent event” window (Filing Date 2021-02-22, event start 2020-03-11), so high scores (up to 10) are permissible. Nevertheless, I moderate individual snippet scores where wording is conditional (“could”, “may”) or where mitigating factors (rate decoupling, offsets from residential load, cost-recovery riders) are cited. Quantified, realised impacts earn the highest scores; broad, speculative statements are scored lower. This calibrated approach reflects the event’s immediacy while weighting the quality and specificity of each disclosure.

Ameren’s 2022 filing discusses the COVID-19 pandemic as a recent (0-3 year) event with both realized and continuing implications for virtually every risk dimension the utility faces – revenue mix, cash collections, supply-chain reliability, labor availability, cyber-exposure from remote work, regulatory interventions and capital market uncertainty.  Statements are mostly qualitative but identify concrete operational changes (shifts from commercial / industrial to residential load, higher bad-debt, deferred customer payments) and give forward-looking warnings about employee illness, vaccine-mandate disruption and contractor non-performance.  The disclosure makes clear that impacts have already reduced cash from operations and altered sales patterns, yet the final magnitude hinges on the pandemic’s “severity and longevity,” so the risk remains open-ended.  Because the Form 10-K date (23 Feb 2022) is well within three years of the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high—though differentiated—scores.  Sentences that report present adverse effects and quantify operational channels earn higher micro-scores; broader, conditional or more generic statements are moderated but still material given the recency of the crisis.

Ameren’s 2023 filing shows that management still considers COVID-19 an active, material driver of both realised and prospective risk.  Three distinct impact channels are disclosed.  First, the company documents an observable, pandemic-driven demand shift: residential volumes are up while commercial-industrial volumes are down, raising concerns about long-term revenue recovery under existing rate-caps.  Second, the text flags COVID-related supply-chain and labour shortages that could disrupt generation projects, drive cost inflation and create reliability problems.  Third, pandemic-induced operating changes—especially large-scale remote work—are cited as new vectors for cyber-security and data-loss events.  All references are recent (2020-2023) and tied to the company’s core utility operations, but most are qualitative with limited quantification and, in several cases, are framed as potential rather than currently realised impacts.  Applying the Time Decay Principle (event ≤ 3 years old) these statements can score in the upper range, yet the absence of dollar figures or precise probability estimates moderates the overall severity.  Consequently, the extracted sentences cluster in the 1-6 range, indicating non-trivial but not catastrophic pandemic risk for Ameren at this stage.

COVID-19 is referenced in Ameren’s 2024 Form 10-K almost four years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  The filing no longer highlights acute, company-wide disruption; instead it frames the disease in two ways: (1) as an ongoing, but fairly generic, operational threat grouped with other low-frequency / high-impact catastrophes (‘pandemic health events’) and (2) as a tail-end financial clean-up item (refunds of over-recovered pandemic costs and CARES-Act tax credits).  There is also an explicit acknowledgment that remote-work arrangements—originally adopted because of the pandemic—create enduring cyber-security exposure.  The language is largely qualitative and forward-looking, with only one modest, quantified impact (a USD 4 million revenue reduction).  Given the filing date (Feb 2024) the pandemic sits at the edge of the 4-year “medium-term” window, so the Time Decay Principle limits the severity of any single snippet to the mid-range.  Overall, COVID-19–related risk for AEE is assessed as moderate: it is still present in corporate risk registers, but impacts are now either small, historical clean-ups or broad contingency planning rather than material, immediate threats.

AEP’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only limited but still explicit language linking its business risks to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company refers to “continued pandemic-related delays and cost increases,” positioning the pandemic as an ongoing disruptor of project schedules, supply-chain reliability and cost structures rather than as a one-time historical shock.  Elsewhere, management cites the possibility that “public health considerations” could suppress economic activity and electricity demand, again indicating a forward-looking posture.  None of the statements quantify financial impact, and they sit within broader, multi-factor risk lists, signalling a moderate—not acute—level of concern.  Because the filing date (Feb 2024) is roughly four years after the World Health Organization’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle caps any individual evidence score at a mid-range level.  Taken together, the disclosures show that COVID-19 remains a material but un-quantified head-wind, meriting moderate risk severity scores.

AES’ 2021 Form 10-K explicitly frames COVID-19 as both an already-manifested shock and a still-evolving, enterprise-wide threat.  Filed less than a year after the WHO declaration, the discussion combines statements of realised harm (lower global demand, operational disruptions) with a large catalogue of forward-looking contingencies spanning revenue compression, counter-party default, fuel logistics, construction delays, workforce health and capital-market access.  The language is highly specific (naming individual business lines such as Fluence energy-storage, renewables construction, fuel transport) and repeatedly labels the potential effects as “material” or “adverse,” signalling management’s acknowledgement of severity.  No quantified dollar amounts are given and most items are couched in conditional (“could,” “may”) phrasing, but the breadth, recency, and direct linkage to cash-flow fundamentals elevate the risk.  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 falls in the 0-3-year window, allowing high scores.  Overall, the disclosures represent detailed, multi-vector risk recognition with limited mitigation detail, warranting upper-tier severity ratings for the extracted evidence.

AES’ 2022 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-faceted threat that is already affecting— and could continue to affect— virtually every dimension of the company’s business.  The disclosure is framed as an existing, on-going impact rather than a purely hypothetical risk: management notes that the pandemic has “severely impacted” global economic activity and electricity demand, and then supplies a comprehensive catalogue of concrete ways in which AES could suffer— from customer non-payment and government moratoria, to construction delays, supply-chain blockages, workforce health problems, cybersecurity exposures from remote work, capital-market dislocations, and potential asset impairments.  The language is specific (naming utility customers, PPAs, fuel delivery, renewables construction, and credit-market access), forward-looking in scope, and explicitly links the event to material adverse effects on results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.  Because the filing date (28 Feb 2022) is less than three years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  None of the text offers meaningful mitigating language beyond acknowledging that future impacts depend on vaccination progress; therefore individual snippets are scored largely on the breadth and directness of the stated risk, generally ranging from 6-9, with the most sweeping statements receiving the upper bound.

AES’ 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly acknowledges COVID-19 as an active, multifaceted risk that is still influencing the company’s operating environment nearly three years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  The filing blends backward-looking statements about demonstrable, already-experienced impacts (e.g., depressed electricity demand, macro-economic slow-downs) with forward-looking language that frames COVID-19—and future pandemics—as ongoing threats to liquidity, supply chains, labour availability, construction schedules and overall credit quality.  While most disclosures remain qualitative and lack dollar quantification, the vocabulary is strong (“severely impacted”, “material and adverse effects”) and spans every major risk bucket the firm tracks (operations, finance, regulatory, supply-chain, human capital).  Given that the event window (2020-2023) is within the 0-3-year “recent” band of the Time Decay Principle, evidence can justifiably receive higher severity scores where it (i) links COVID-19 to concrete operational or financial stress already observed, or (ii) characterises foreseeable, material exposures.  Generic, laundry-list references to “pandemics” are scored lower because they provide little event-specific insight.  Overall, AES presents COVID-19 as an extant, enterprise-level risk with diverse pathways to value erosion, warranting moderate-to-high snippet scores between 3 and 7.

AES devotes a discrete risk-factor subsection to COVID-19, indicating that management continues to view pandemic disruptions as a strategically relevant, but now more chronic, threat.  The company acknowledges both (i) already-experienced impacts – e.g., the pandemic "has severely impacted global economic activity" – and (ii) a broad set of forward-looking vulnerabilities, ranging from demand destruction and customer non-payment to supply-chain delays, labor shortages, construction slippage, cyber-security exposures tied to remote work, and potential capital-market stress.  Language such as “material and adverse effects on our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows” and repeated references to utilities being unable to pay, force-majeure claims, or project impairments signal that management considers the risk potentially severe.  However, the disclosures are qualitative; no dollar amounts or probability estimates are provided, and several statements are prefaced with conditional words (“could,” “may”).  Because the filing date (Feb-2024) is almost four years after WHO declared the pandemic, Time-Decay tempers the weight of the evidence: the shock is no longer immediate, yet AES still treats the pandemic as an active medium-term risk driver.  Overall, the evidence merits mid-range severity (4-6) scores—higher than boiler-plate, but lower than acute, quantified impact statements.

The filing was prepared almost two years into the COVID-19 era, so management has had time to observe real impacts and still sees significant forward-looking uncertainty.  Throughout Item 1A and MD&A the company links the pandemic to concrete, already-experienced effects—lower U.S. sales, remote-work operational shifts, capital-market volatility—and to prospective threats such as supply-chain disruptions, elevated lapse rates and impaired investment performance.  Language such as “material adverse effect,” “unprecedented disruption,” and explicit references to multiple financial metrics (capital position, liquidity, profitability) show the risk is viewed as enterprise-wide and potentially severe.  Although management notes some stabilization and that 2021 claims were not materially affected, it repeatedly stresses that the duration and severity of COVID-19 (including variants) remain unpredictable.  Given the recency of the pandemic (well within the 0-3-year window) and the breadth of impacts cited, the overall risk level is high; any mitigating remarks do not outweigh the pervasive, multi-faceted exposure.  Therefore evidence snippets generally merit scores in the upper mid-to-high range (5-9), consistent with the Time Decay Principle for very recent events.

AFL’s 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-dimensional threat that remains squarely within the 0-3-year ‘recent-event’ window, so high residual risk is expected under the Time Decay Principle.  The filing repeatedly attributes current and prospective headwinds—in capital markets, inflation, supply-chain frictions, labor availability, face-to-face distribution, vendor reliability and actuarial pricing uncertainty—to the pandemic.  Language is generally forward-looking ("could continue to impact…", "may hinder sales…"), yet it is anchored by specific operational conduits (agent recruiting, small-business customers, remote-work transitions) and strong qualifiers such as “material adverse effect.”  No hard dollar figures are provided, but the statements are neither boiler-plate nor historic: they describe live exposures that management cannot fully quantify and for which no definitive mitigants are offered beyond adaptive measures.  Accordingly, the overall risk profile is elevated—material but unquantified—and the extracted sentences warrant upper-mid to high severity scores (6-9) after balancing aggravating factors (direct linkage, breadth of impact, severity wording) with minor mitigating factors (absence of hard loss data, expression of uncertainty).

The filing, dated February 22 2024, contains only limited, mostly macro-level language about COVID-19.  The company acknowledges that extraordinary fiscal support and supply-chain stresses that arose during the pandemic are now ‘normalizing,’ and it briefly flags public-health threats and U.S. labour-market tightness that could raise operating costs.  None of the passages quantify impacts or point to material, company-specific disruptions; instead they frame the pandemic as a past shock whose after-effects (inflation, labour shortages, supply-chain recovery) could still influence results.  Because the pandemic began four years ago, the Time-Decay Principle places any evidence in the medium-term window, capping plausible severity at a moderate level (4-6).  Overall, the residual pandemic risk for AFL appears modest: it is forward-looking, couched in broad economic terms and partially mitigated by language about recovery.  Consequently, individual snippets score in the low-to-mid range, reflecting acknowledgement of risk without concrete, ongoing damage.

AIG’s 2020 Form 10-K, filed in February 2021, provides an extensive, candid discussion of the COVID-19 pandemic’s impact. Because the filing date is well within three years of the World Health Organization’s March 2020 declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scoring.  The disclosure language is current-impact focussed ("is adversely affecting") and explicitly forward-looking ("expected to continue"), signalling that the risks are both realised and still evolving.  AIG identifies multiple vectors of stress: higher mortality claims, reduced demand for travel and other lines, premium refunds, credit-rating pressure, potential regulatory interventions, supply-chain and vendor outages, remote-work vulnerabilities, liquidity constraints and concentrated investment exposures (real estate, energy).  Although the narrative is largely qualitative, it ties the pandemic to concrete financial channels—cash-flow impairment, capital-ratio erosion, dividend restrictions, claim volume increases—demonstrating materiality.  The breadth, immediacy and persistence of these statements, coupled with limited mitigating language, warrant high individual snippet scores (7-9) under the recent-event rubric.

The filing, completed nearly two years after the official declaration of COVID-19 as a global pandemic, contains extensive, detailed and largely forward-looking statements that tie the pandemic to AIG’s specific lines of business, operating model and balance-sheet exposures.  The company discloses concrete channels of impact – capital-market volatility, labour-market disruption, supply-chain breakdowns, elevated mortality, suppressed consumer demand for travel products, remote-work strains, regulatory interventions and potential tax increases – and it repeatedly warns that many of these pressures are expected to continue through 2022 and beyond.  The language is company-specific (e.g., “we experienced an increase in mortality claims,” “we implemented work-from-home business continuity plans”) and acknowledges both realised losses (higher claims, lower premiums) and potential future deterioration.  Because the event is recent (within the 0-3-year window) and AIG provides granular, material and multi-faceted risk disclosures without offering strong offsetting mitigants, individual snippets warrant high severity scores (7-9), comfortably within the upper range permitted by the Time Decay Principle for recent events.

AIG’s 2023 risk-factor section leaves little doubt that the Covid-19 pandemic is a live, material threat.  Management describes both realised damage (higher mortality claims, reduced product demand, capital-market volatility) and forward-looking dangers (labour shortages, supply-chain disruption, reinsurance scarcity, inflationary pressure and cultural strain from prolonged remote work).  The language is direct and enterprise-wide, flagging impacts on liquidity, capital, underwriting results and operational resilience.  Because the filing date (17 Feb 2023) is within three years of the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  No meaningful mitigating actions are outlined in the cited sentences, so deductions are negligible.  Overall, the evidence points to a high, continuing risk profile rather than a historical footnote, justifying strong micro-scores in the 4-8 range and an aggregate risk assessment near the upper end of recent-event thresholds.

AIG’s 2024 Form 10-K contains multiple, explicit disclosures that COVID-19 has already produced material, adverse financial consequences and that the pandemic (and future variants or other health crises) remains a significant forward-looking risk.  The company cites concrete impacts such as higher claim volumes, premium reductions, lower premiums and deposits in Life & Retirement lines, valuation challenges in commercial real-estate exposed to remote-work trends, supply-chain disruption, labour-market dislocation and increased reinsurance costs.  The wording is strong (“materially and adversely affect,” “have had adverse economic impacts”) and the statements are specific to AIG’s operations, not merely generic.  Although the pandemic began in March 2020, the filing date (14-Feb-2024) is only slightly under four years later; under the Time Decay Principle this still falls at the edge of the “recent” window, permitting relatively high severity scores (mostly in the 6-8 range).  No meaningful mitigating language (e.g., controls, recoveries or reversals) accompanies the cited sentences, so deductions are minimal.  Overall, the evidence shows a live, direct risk with demonstrated financial impact, supporting elevated—but not maximal—severity scores.

AIZ’s 2021-02-19 Form 10-K discusses COVID-19 as an ongoing, recently-manifested risk that is already producing measurable financial, operational and strategic impacts across the company.  The filing pairs backward-looking evidence (lower investment yields, REO volume declines, higher mortality in Preneed, reinsurance cost increases, etc.) with forward-looking warnings (continued demand pressure, potential asset impairments, credit-market disruption, litigation exposure, etc.).  The language is detailed, naming concrete hit-points in revenues, expenses, capital access, workforce management, cybersecurity, and regulatory limits, showing the risk is direct and material rather than hypothetical.  Because the pandemic began less than a year before the filing, Time-Decay allows high severity scores.  Mitigation references (remote-work transition, monitoring, investments to counteract impacts) do appear, but they are outweighed by multiple, specific adverse effects already realized and the wide scope of possible future detriments.  Overall, COVID-19 represents a high-severity, multi-faceted threat with both realized losses and uncertain tail risk; the evidence therefore clusters in the upper mid- to high-severity range (scores 6-9).

AIZ’s 2022 filing contains an extensive, up-to-date discussion of COVID-19.  The company explicitly states that the pandemic has already disrupted its operations (“have been adversely affected”) and anticipates continued, potentially material impacts across almost every risk dimension – revenue, credit-market access, investment portfolio performance, workforce productivity, cybersecurity, litigation exposure and regulatory capital mobility.  The language is recent (within two years of the event), repeatedly characterises impacts as “material” and “continuing,” and itemises concrete transmission channels such as remote-work inefficiencies, client distress, fraudulent claims, capital-market volatility and mandatory vaccination costs.  No quantified dollar figures are provided and a few caveats (“may”, “could”) reduce certainty, but the breadth and specificity still signal a high-severity, forward-looking risk.  In line with the Time Decay Principle for events ≤3 years old, individual snippet scores cluster in the upper mid-range (3-7) with the most comprehensive sentences reaching 7 where multiple aggravating factors are named and no offsetting mitigations are offered.

Assurant’s 2023 Form 10-K was filed roughly three years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, placing the disclosure firmly in the “recent event” window (0-3 years) of the Time Decay Principle.  The filing acknowledges both historical and continuing impacts.  One sentence explicitly states that the pandemic already disrupted personnel availability, making the risk existing and realized rather than merely potential.  Elsewhere, the company folds COVID-19 into broader macro-economic and business-continuity risk language, signalling that management still views pandemic-driven volatility, supply-chain strain, labour shortages and remote-work pressures as material threats to operations, profitability and capital.  Several passages detail concrete actions or costs—such as a 2022 restructuring to support work-from-home arrangements—showing the firm is incurring real expenditures to adapt.  Other passages describe heightened competition for talent and possible productivity declines from remote or hybrid work.  Although the disclosures are largely qualitative, they link the pandemic to operational disruption, higher claims costs, and strategic adjustments, justifying moderate-to-high severity scores (5-8) under the scoring rubric for recent events.

AIZ’s 2024 filing still flags the COVID-19–type pandemic as a live, though now medium-term, enterprise-wide hazard. The references are largely forward-looking and qualitative: management discusses pandemics in the same breath as other ‘business-continuity events’ and macro shocks, emphasising potential disruptions to operations, labour availability, supply chains, workforce models and overall consumer demand. No direct dollar impacts are disclosed, indicating residual rather than acute financial stress. Yet several passages concede that earlier epidemics ‘have contributed’ to market volatility and that real costs have already been incurred through restructuring for remote work. Because the event is roughly four years old, Time-Decay dictates moderate severity scores (4-6). The language is specific enough to tie pandemic conditions to concrete risk channels—continuity planning, labour shortages, remote-work real-estate changes and supply-chain volatility—but is tempered by mention of mitigation plans and absence of quantified losses. AMD’s 2022-02-03 filing treats COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, enterprise-wide threat. AMD’s 2023 Form-10-K frames COVID-19 as a still-evolving, multi-faceted threat that is already disrupting operations while also posing sizeable forward-looking risks. Overall, the pandemic constitutes a high-severity, current risk for AME, justifying snippet scores that cluster in the upper mid-range (6-9) when quantified impacts are present, and moderate scores (2-5) where the language is more precautionary or partially offset by mitigants.

AME’s Form 10-K, filed in February 2023, presents COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that is still very much alive within the 0-to-3-year “recent” window dictated by the Time-Decay Principle. Given the filing date is only about three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, high—but not maximum—snippet scores (generally 6-9) are justified, reflecting direct, still-evolving risks without detailed quantified losses.
