Given the Time Decay Principle (event < 3 years old) the disclosures deserve moderately high severity grades—generally in the 6-8 range—because they describe current, not hypothetical, impacts and identify specific operational and financial mechanisms through which the pandemic may continue to pressure performance.  Mitigating language (e.g., describing actions already taken) is sparse and does little to offset the heightened risk narrative.

AVB’s 2023-02-24 filing squarely acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic, now within the 0-3-year ‘recent-event’ window, continues to pose both direct and secondary threats to virtually every facet of its multifamily business model.  The company frames the risk as ongoing and largely uncontrollable: public-health mandates can impair rent collection and eviction rights; shifting work-from-home patterns can drain demand; supply-chain blockages and labour illness can inflate costs and delay projects; and fee-waiver rules can immediately erode revenue.  Although the disclosure remains mostly qualitative (no dollar figures), the language is specific and granular, mapping the pandemic to concrete operational vectors—collections, construction, workforce, consumer demand and regulatory constraints.  Because these impacts are described as prospective, continuing and in some cases already observed (e.g., higher concessions during the pandemic), they represent live, non-remote risks.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, evidence from 2020-2023 can receive high scores (7-10) when the statement is specific and materially linked, while more generic or indirect references settle into the 4-6 range.  Mitigating language is minimal, so most snippets retain high net severity scores.

AVB’s 2024 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, medium-term threat that continues to influence cash-flows, development schedules, operating costs and demand patterns across its multifamily portfolio.  All language appears in the “Risk Factors” section, making it prospective rather than a disclosure of already-booked losses, yet the Company details concrete pathways by which another wave of pandemic conditions—or lingering after-effects—could hurt revenue (e.g., rent-collection restrictions, waived fees, foregone revenue), raise expenses (e.g., quarantine clean-up, supply-chain inflation) and delay value-creation projects (construction and redevelopment).  The wording is specific—naming supply-chain disruptions, labor force illness, remote-work migration and government moratoria—but remains largely unquantified.  Given that the initial WHO declaration occurred nearly four years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle requires that evidence be scored in the moderate band (4-6).  No mitigating actions (e.g., insurance coverage, contingency planning) are provided in the cited sentences, so scores are driven almost entirely by the severity and specificity of the identified exposures, capped for time decay.

AVGO’s December 2021 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic to a set of concrete, ongoing operational threats.  The filing describes an immediate and continuing impact rather than a hypothetical, future-only risk: actual shutdowns at suppliers, longer lead-times, price increases for wafers and substrates, transportation delays, and the forced shift to extended remote-work arrangements.  These statements are recent (within 0-3 years of the World Health Organization’s March 2020 declaration) and focus on hard-to-mitigate areas such as global supply-chain choke points and single-site dependencies (e.g., Fort Collins FBAR fab and Malaysia warehouse).  While a few mitigating references appear (e.g., the Malaysia warehouse remained operational, software segment little affected), the narrative overall is dominated by direct disruptions already experienced and the likelihood of further constraints.  Under the Time Decay Principle, evidence from this 2021 filing—less than two years after the pandemic’s onset—carries maximum weight, so most snippets receive high scores (7-9) when they provide specific operational details, quantified consequences (order lead-time extensions, product allocation), or emphasize critical dependencies; more generic or partially mitigated statements score in the mid-range (5-6).

AVGO’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to concrete and ongoing operational, supply-chain and workforce hazards.  The company discloses that the pandemic has already disrupted semiconductor sourcing, increased input costs, forced lengthened customer lead-times, triggered logistics delays and compelled a build-to-order production stance— all of which are direct, realized impacts, not merely hypothetical.  Forward-looking language stresses that these headwinds ‘may continue,’ could ‘recur,’ and remain subject to uncontrollable variables such as new variants and vaccine uptake, underscoring the persistence of risk.  Mitigating steps (employee safety measures) are acknowledged but portrayed as potentially inadequate.  Because the filing date (Dec-2022) is less than three years after the WHO declaration (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the pandemic is depicted as a recent, multifaceted risk with tangible operational consequences and only partial mitigations, meriting upper-tier risk scores across the extracted evidence.

AVGO’s 2023 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, forward-looking operational threat rather than as a source of currently measured damage.  The company embeds pandemic language in several risk-factor passages that cover supply-chain fragility, contract manufacturing, global logistics and potential plant shutdowns.  The statements are broad, contingency-oriented and bundled with other hazards (e.g., natural disasters, geopolitical turmoil).  Although COVID-19 is now almost four years old, the disclosure timeframe (Dec 2023 filing versus Mar 2020 WHO declaration) keeps the event inside the early edge of the “medium-term” window defined by the Time Decay Principle, so individual snippet scores should fall in the middle range (about 4-6).  No quantified losses, cost figures or concrete disruptions are supplied; instead, management warns that future pandemic flare-ups **could** materially harm operations, delay production or strain suppliers.  Therefore, the overall severity is moderate: the risk remains credible because it targets critical manufacturing and supply-chain nodes, yet the absence of specific impact data and the generic wording temper the score.

The filing, dated nearly five years after the official declaration of COVID-19, still acknowledges pandemic-related threats but only in broad, forward-looking terms. AVGO now treats pandemics as one of several disruptive forces—similar to natural disasters or geopolitical unrest—rather than as an acute, quantified shock. The text offers no fresh financial metrics or narratives of continuing COVID-19 impacts; instead, it warns of potential future supply-chain bottlenecks, facility shutdowns, or labor shortages should another medical epidemic arise. Under the Time Decay Principle, an event that is more than four but less than ten years old warrants a mid-range severity ceiling (scores around 4-6). Given the generic framing and absence of current-year cost figures, the overall pandemic risk is assessed as moderate but persistent: significant enough to merit mention, yet clearly diminished compared with disclosures made in 2020-2022.

The filing, dated less than one year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, presents COVID-19 as an ongoing and multifaceted risk to Avery Dennison (AVY).  Management discloses both realized impacts (2020 revenue declines, a quantified 15 % sales drop in Q2, credit-market disruption, manufacturing shutdowns and a 65 % jump in credit-loss reserves) and forward-looking uncertainties (supply-chain fragility, labor availability, remote-work resilience, liquidity access, macro-economic downturn and cost re-inflation).  While the narrative notes some sequential improvement and temporary cost savings, these are framed as partial and potentially reversible mitigation measures.  Because the pandemic’s effects are contemporaneous with the 2021 filing and many statements describe material, already-incurred losses as well as credible future exposure, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Individual sentence scores therefore reflect: (1) directness and specificity of the linkage to COVID-19, (2) presence of quantification or “material adverse” language, (3) breadth of impact (operations, supply chain, finance, workforce, demand), and (4) any explicit mitigating factors that moderate—though do not eliminate—the risk.

AVY’s 2022 Form 10-K describes COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, multifaceted threat that has already produced tangible harm (plant closures, $500 million emergency borrowing, negative 2020 results) and continues to cloud near-term outlooks.  The language is recent (within two years of filing) and mixes backward-looking impacts with forward-looking uncertainties about supply-chain reliability, labour availability, liquidity, and demand.  Although management highlights some mitigants (price increases, scenario planning, debt repayment), most statements emphasise unresolved risk and use strong material-adverse terminology.  Given the Time Decay Principle, evidence dated 2020-2022 qualifies for high—though not necessarily maximal—scores because the pandemic is ongoing and its future trajectory remains uncertain.  I therefore weight direct, quantified or operationally specific disclosures highest (scores 6-7) and assign moderate scores (3-5) to broader, more qualified or partially mitigated statements.

AVY’s 2023 Form 10-K shows that COVID-19 remains a high-salience, operational and strategic risk even three years after the WHO declaration.  The filing moves beyond generic cautionary language: it documents concrete production shutdowns in China, intermittent plant closures in Southeast Asia, supply-chain interruptions, labor-mobility constraints, and explicit references to demand deterioration tied to renewed outbreaks.  These disclosures span both realized impacts (2021–2022 closures, lower volumes, restructuring actions) and forward-looking uncertainty for 2023, e.g., unpredictable variants, vaccine efficacy, and further lockdowns.  While management notes partial recovery and facility re-openings, it does not provide quantified offsets, and continues scenario-planning for renewed disruptions.  Given the filing date (Feb-2023) falls inside the 0-3-year “recent event” window, the Time Decay Principle permits upper-range scores.  Overall risk is graded as high: the pandemic has already caused material operational hits and still threatens future earnings through supply-chain fragility, workforce limitations, and demand swings.  Mitigating statements (plants now open, scenario planning) temper but do not neutralize the severity because they are outweighed by evidence of direct past harm and uncertain outlook.

AVY’s 2024 filing continues to frame the COVID-19 pandemic and other epidemics as a material, multi-year enterprise-wide risk.  The company discloses both backward-looking impacts (e.g., supply-chain interruptions, facility closures, credit-loss reserves and head-count reductions that were “in response to the pandemic”) and forward-looking contingencies (e.g., the prospect that future outbreaks ‘could materially adversely impact our business’).  Language is mostly qualitative but uses strong modifiers such as “materially adversely affected” and “material adverse effect,” signalling management still sees the threat as significant.  Because the pandemic’s onset (March 2020) is roughly four years before the 2024-02-21 filing, the Time Decay Principle places the evidence in the medium-term window: scores should cluster in the 4-6 range where risk is actively monitored but no longer emergent.  Mitigating references (credit-loss allowances, completed restructurings) temper, but do not eliminate, residual exposure.  Overall, the pandemic remains a moderate strategic and operational risk rather than an acute crisis, justifying mid-level severity scoring for each sentence.

The 2021-02-24 Form 10-K shows that American Water Works (AWK) views COVID-19 as a live, multi-faceted enterprise risk.  The pandemic is treated as both an existing impact (documented cost increases, revenue shortfalls, liquidity actions and regulatory deferrals already booked for FY-2020) and a forward-looking exposure (uncertain customer demand, regulatory delays, capital-market access and supply-chain continuity).  The language is highly specific: the company identifies concrete financial consequences—higher uncollectible accounts, extra borrowing costs, incremental O&M, foregone late-fee revenue, and $30 million of pandemic-related regulatory assets—and it articulates contingent threats such as PUC moratoria, inability to obtain rate approvals, and potential service disruptions.  These statements tie directly to enterprise-level drivers (cash flow, capital recovery, liquidity and cost of capital) and reference real operational levers (vendor supply, workforce safety, customer disconnect bans).  Because the filing date is less than one year after the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time-Decay principle permits high severity scores.  Mitigating language (e.g., ‘has not experienced, and does not anticipate, any material negative impacts’ on supply chain) moderates some evidence, but overall the disclosures portray a materially elevated, near-term risk landscape; thus most snippets merit scores of 6-9, with the few quantified, realized impacts at the high end.

American Water Works (AWK) frames COVID-19 as both an already-felt shock and a continuing source of uncertainty.  Since the WHO declaration (March 2020) the company has booked tangible balance-sheet impacts (e.g., $36 million of regulatory assets) and lists several realised income statement hits such as foregone late-fee revenue, higher O&M, rising bad-debt expense and extra borrowing costs.  These are direct, recent and clearly attributable to the pandemic, so very little time-decay applies.  Beyond the numbers, AWK highlights regulatory interventions (disconnect moratoria, delayed rate cases) that can squeeze cash flow, plus potential effects on future permit approvals, liquidity access and customer demand—especially from large industrial accounts.  The language mixes backward-looking disclosures (“has experienced”) with forward-looking caution (“unable to predict the range of impacts”), signalling that management sees COVID-19 as an active, evolving risk.  Mitigants exist—e.g., recorded regulatory assets implying eventual recovery, and a statement that no major supply-chain disruptions have occurred—but these do not fully offset the breadth of exposure across revenue, expenses, capital projects and financing.  Given the filing date (Feb 2022) is within two years of the event trigger, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  Overall, the evidence paints a moderate-to-high severity risk posture (aggregate around 6-7 on a 10-point scale), combining concrete financial impact with ongoing regulatory, operational and demand-side uncertainty.

American Water Works (AWK) acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, material risk in its 2023 Form 10-K, filed less than three years after the World Health Organization declared the outbreak a global pandemic.  The disclosure is framed almost entirely in forward-looking, contingency language that groups COVID-19 with other extreme events (weather, epidemics, supply-chain interruptions).  AWK highlights three principal channels of exposure: (1) potential shortfalls in authorized returns if pandemic-driven emergencies change customer usage or raise costs, (2) service interruptions across its water and wastewater network if a pandemic impairs workforce or facility operability, and (3) health-related contamination risks from viruses such as COVID-19 entering water supplies.  None of the passages provide quantified dollar impacts, but they do explicitly tie COVID-19 to financial, operational, and regulatory outcomes.  Because the event remains recent (within the 0-3-year window) but the statements are largely generic and conditional, the evidentiary weight is moderate.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, individual snippets warrant mid-range scores (3-4), reflecting clear but unquantified, precautionary risk language rather than concrete, realized losses.

American Water (AWK) still frames the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a forward-looking, rather than a presently crippling, threat.  In its 2024 Form 10-K the company groups “pandemics and epidemics” with other natural or catastrophic events that could disrupt operations, curtail water supply, or drive unexpected capital spending.  The filing offers no quantified impacts, but it does acknowledge COVID-related cost deferrals that have required specific recovery in recent rate cases—a tacit admission that the pandemic has already imposed measurable financial pressure.  Management also flags supply-chain interruptions and labour shortages that could delay major capital projects—conditions strongly associated with the pandemic era—even though they are not explicitly tied to COVID-19 in the text.  Overall, the disclosures are broad and cautionary, lacking granular data or scenario analysis.  Given that the pandemic is within the 0-4-year “recent event” window but the language is largely generic and partially mitigated by approved cost recovery, the aggregate risk evidence merits only a moderate score.

AXON’s 10-K was filed less than twelve months after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, so the event is firmly within the ‘recent’ 0-3-year window of the Time-Decay Principle—allowing relatively high severity scores where warranted.  The filing moves from a broad macro description of the pandemic’s adverse effects on workforces and financial markets, to specific, company-level disclosures: (1) recognition that COVID-19 has already affected, and may continue to affect, AXON’s operations; (2) an explicit warning that business-disruption back-up plans may fail; (3) quantified disclosure of a $4.1 million cost impact in 2020; and (4) an expectation of further pandemic-driven costs.  The language is a blend of realised impacts (the $4.1 million expense) and forward-looking contingencies (possible operational and financial disruption).  Although management outlines mitigation efforts—monitoring, contingency planning, and travel-budget offsets—it simultaneously concedes that success is not assured.  Overall, the risks are direct, specific, and current, but only partially quantified; hence, individual snippet scores cluster in the mid-to-high range (5-9) under the recent-event allowance, weighted down where mitigating language appears.

Axon’s 2022 Form 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic as a still-unfolding, multi-faceted threat that has already created operational friction and could materially impair future performance.  The company cites concrete, present-tense impacts (business disruptions, supply-chain strain, and financial volatility) and admits that the duration and severity of the crisis are impossible to forecast.  Although Axon outlines mitigation efforts—continuous monitoring, employee-safety measures and contingency planning—it also concedes that such plans may prove insufficient.  The disclosure is therefore a blend of backward-looking impacts ("has adversely affected") and forward-looking uncertainty.  Because the filing date (25 Feb 2022) is less than three years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows for relatively high risk scores.  Nevertheless, the language is largely qualitative and unquantified, tempering the maximum severity assigned to any single sentence.  Overall, the risk level is assessed as material and continuing, with individual snippet scores ranging from 1–7 to reflect the mix of aggravating and mitigating factors.

AXON’s 2023-02-28 filing treats the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, but still potential, operational hazard rather than a presently quantified hit to results.  The company aggregates “pandemic” with other catastrophic or public-health crises that could disrupt sales, services, freight flows, labour availability and cyber-security.  Language is largely conditional (“could”, “may”) and no dollar impact or volume loss is attributed directly to COVID-19, signalling that management views the threat as continuing but not yet crystallised into material losses.  Nevertheless, the statements acknowledge concrete vectors—supply-chain delays, freight cost inflation, remote-work vulnerabilities—that have featured prominently in pandemic-era disruptions worldwide.  Because the event is recent (within three years) under the Time Decay Principle, references to pandemic-driven risks still merit meaningful scores, but the absence of specific metrics or evidence of realised damage tempers severity.  Overall, the risk profile is moderate: the company recognises multiple channels through which a global pandemic can hurt operations, yet frames them as contingencies rather than impacts already embedded in financials.

Axon’s Form 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a past event that demonstrated the company’s exposure to large-scale public-health disruptions, while also flagging that similar outbreaks could recur and again stress its workforce, customers, supply chain and demand environment. The language is mostly forward-looking and framed within broad ‘catastrophic-event’ or ‘public-health-crisis’ clauses, without dollar figures or detailed operational metrics. The pandemic is discussed as one driver—alongside natural disasters and cyber-attacks—that could hamper sales execution and business continuity; there is also a specific sentence noting that COVID-19 already “adversely affected” global workforces and economies. Because the filing date is almost four years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time Decay principle limits severity to a mid-range level: the risk remains relevant but no longer peaks. Disclosures are principally generic and precautionary, lacking company-specific quantification or evidence of current material impacts, yet they do reflect that COVID-19 previously impacted operations and could do so again. Consequently, individual snippets merit moderate scores (4-5 range for the strongest evidence, lower for boiler-plate references).

American Express (AXP) frames COVID-19 as both an already-realized shock and a continuing, hard-to-predict threat that could ripple through almost every major risk pillar: revenue, credit, liquidity, operations, workforce, litigation and reputation.  Management discloses concrete, quantified damage (e.g., airline-related billed business still 62 % below 2019 and large-corporate spending down 45 %), establishes that core drivers of its business—T&E volumes, corporate travel, consumer confidence—remain materially impaired, and warns that supply-chain bottlenecks, labor shortages, inflation and remote-work vulnerabilities may amplify the pandemic’s fallout.  These statements are recent (within two years of the March 2020 WHO declaration and within the filing’s February 2022 date) and describe both historical impacts and forward-looking uncertainties.  They provide granular metrics, acknowledge continuing volatility from variants such as Omicron, note potential regulatory and legal exposure, and recognize secondary effects such as cyber-risk escalation and workplace disruption.  Very few mitigating factors are offered beyond generic remarks about recovery; thus the overall COVID-19 risk profile is high.  Applying the Time Decay Principle (0–3 years window), individual evidence snippets can validly score in the 7-10 range when they contain quantified or clearly material effects; forward-looking but less quantified sentences merit mid-single-digit scores; any embedded mitigating language tempers scores slightly but does not outweigh the predominance of aggravating factors.

American Express’s 2022 Form 10-K (filed 10 Feb 2023) contains multiple, recent-event disclosures that tie the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and continuing risks.  The company acknowledges that the pandemic ‘had, and continues to have’ widespread, unpredictable effects that already cut into “a significant portion” of network volumes – a direct hit to its core revenue engine.  Management also warns that future impacts remain highly uncertain because of new variants, labour-market stress, supply-chain disruptions, inflationary pressures, potential re-imposition of containment measures, and the wind-down of government support programmes.  The filing highlights several concrete risk channels: depressed consumer and business spending, travel limitations (critical because ~25 % of billed business is T&E), operational challenges from remote/hybrid work, and a heightened threat of litigation and regulatory scrutiny.  All statements are forward-looking or contemporaneous (within three years of the pandemic’s onset), so the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  However, most disclosures are qualitative and lack hard quantification, which tempers peak severity.  Overall, the evidence portrays a material, still-developing risk landscape with direct revenue impacts already felt and multiple vectors for additional downside, warranting mid-to-high severity ratings (5-8 range) for individual snippets.

American Express (AXP) frames COVID-19 primarily as a macro-economic driver that has already produced material setbacks (e.g., a significant hit to network volumes) while still posing residual, forward-looking threats through labour-market frictions, supply-chain issues, inflation and the possibility of new variants.  Because the filing date (9 Feb 2024) is almost four years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the most acute phase of the crisis is treated as historical, yet the company explicitly acknowledges lingering impacts and continued uncertainty.  The disclosures are specific about past adverse volume effects and cite concrete transmission channels (consumer behaviour shifts, supply-chain disruption, labour shortages), signalling more than boiler-plate language.  Applying the Time-Decay Principle, evidence warrants moderate – not maximum – severity: the event sits at the threshold between recent and medium-term (≈4 years), so individual snippet scores are capped at 6, yielding an overall medium-high pandemic risk assessment for AXP.

AutoZone’s 2021-10-25 filing delivers a detailed, largely forward-looking but still partly realised assessment of COVID-19 risk.  The company confirms that the pandemic is ongoing, directly impacting operations, labour availability, supply chains, cyber-security exposure and customer demand patterns.  Statements repeatedly use strong qualifiers such as “material adverse effect” and cite specific financial data (e.g., $43 million in pandemic expenses) and operational metrics (e.g., unprecedented demand, same-store-sales surge), demonstrating that the risk is not merely hypothetical.  Narrative emphasis falls on continuing uncertainty—variants, government actions, labour shortages—underscoring that management cannot confidently forecast duration or magnitude.  Mitigating actions (cleaning protocols, safety measures) are referenced but are outweighed by admissions that such steps may prove insufficient if demand reverts, stores must close, or supply disruptions persist.  Because the event occurred within the last two years, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores; nevertheless, sentences that only mention COVID-19 generically or add significant caveats receive modest deductions.  Overall, the disclosures reveal a high but variably quantified risk profile, justifying snippet scores clustering in the 7-10 range for the most acute statements and tapering downward where mitigation or uncertainty language tempers the message.

The 2022-10-24 AutoZone filing acknowledges COVID-19 as both an historical and continuing risk that touches multiple operational fronts—supply-chain reliability, workforce availability/cost, cybersecurity exposure, and direct financial performance.  The risk language is mostly retrospective (describing impacts already felt in FY20-22) but remains forward-looking where the company notes that pandemic-driven disruptions ‘continue’ or could be ‘further exacerbated.’  One footnote quantifies more than $120 million of pandemic-related costs, elevating materiality.  Other passages tie COVID-19 to specific chokepoints (ports, rail, trucking) and to spikes in cyber-attacks stemming from remote-work practices.  No sentence claims the threat has fully abated; at best, AutoZone references temporary mitigations (e.g., reinstating share-repurchase activity).  Because the filing date is within three years of the WHO declaration (Time-Decay window for “recent” events), scores can be high where evidence is direct and quantified, and moderate where references are generic or diluted among other macro factors.  Overall, the filing shows a live but manageable risk profile: severe enough to record multi-million-dollar costs and to disrupt capital-allocation decisions, yet partially mitigated by resumed operations and declining pandemic expenses.

AZO’s 2023 Form 10-K contains several discrete references to the COVID-19 pandemic.  Taken together, the disclosures paint a picture of a risk that is no longer at the crisis peak of 2020-2021 but is still exerting meaningful pressure, especially through lingering supply-chain congestion, labour availability and macro-economic uncertainty.  Most of the language is qualitative and forward-looking (e.g., ports "have been further exacerbated"), signalling management’s view that pandemic–related disruptions could continue.  However, the only hard, quantified impact is historical: pandemic-related emergency time-off costs in fiscal 2020-2021.  This confirms that the pandemic has already produced material costs, yet the filing offers little numerical guidance for future exposure.  Because the filing date (24 Oct 2023) is roughly 3 ½ years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time-Decay Principle places these statements on the cusp between “recent” and “medium-term” evidence.  Consequently, the most direct, quantified sentence receives a high-moderate score, while broader, generic statements receive lower scores.  Overall, the pandemic remains a credible, but now moderated, risk factor for AZO.

AZO’s 2024-10-28 filing still ties multiple business vulnerabilities to the COVID-19 pandemic even though the initial outbreak occurred roughly 4½ years earlier (March 2020).  The document cites the pandemic as an aggravating factor for logistics congestion, acknowledges quantified pandemic-related expenses, and references a temporary suspension of share repurchases.  The company also groups “public health crises” with other disruptive events that could curtail store hours, hinder distribution networks, and dampen consumer demand.  These statements are largely forward-looking (supply-chain and operational warnings) but also contain backward-looking evidence of actual financial impact (millions in emergency time-off costs and capital-allocation changes).  Because the event now sits just beyond the 0-3-year “recent” window, the Time Decay Principle constrains individual snippet scores to the moderate 4-6 band for the strongest evidence and lower scores for generic or largely historical mentions.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a material—but no longer acute—risk driver for AZO, chiefly through lingering supply-chain fragility, labor cost pressures and macroeconomic uncertainty.

The filing, dated December 17 2021, speaks to the COVID-19 pandemic that erupted in March 2020—well within the 0-3-year “recent event” window, so the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Agilent repeatedly links COVID-19 to concrete, already-realized impacts: supply-chain interruptions, volatile customer demand, labour challenges, remote-work complications, installation delays, and financial-market uncertainty.  The language is largely specific (e.g., ‘disruptions or delays in shipments of certain materials,’ ‘significant and unpredictable reductions in demand’) and often phrased in the present tense, showing that effects are current and continuing.  Forward-looking clauses (e.g., “may continue,” “could reduce our ability to incur debt”) amplify risk persistence.  Mitigations (vaccination policies, remote-work protocols) are mentioned but framed as additional sources of risk rather than offsets, so they do little to dampen severity.  Because the statements describe direct, material impacts already experienced and forecast further adverse consequences, individual snippet scores cluster in the upper mid-range (4-7) and can legitimately reach as high as 7 without exceeding the 10-point cap for recent events.

Company A’s 2022-12-21 filing repeatedly ties the COVID-19 pandemic to concrete, continuing and material risks across virtually every dimension of its operations: supply-chain reliability, demand volatility, site closures, installation delays, service limitations, and capital-markets exposure.  Most statements describe direct impacts already felt (e.g., the 2Q-22 Shanghai shutdown) while also warning of further potential disruption. Mitigating language (customers returning, improved conditions) appears but is outweighed by emphasis on uncertainty and the company’s inability to forecast the pandemic’s full effect.  Overall, the pandemic is portrayed as an active, high-magnitude enterprise risk, justifying generally elevated snippet scores between 3 and 9.

The filing, dated December 20 2024, discusses COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, economy-wide hazard rather than as a one-time historical shock. Taken together, the disclosures show that the company still treats COVID-19 as an important, multi-faceted threat, but one whose severity is tempered by the passage of time and by the generic, non-quantified nature of the statements.

Bank of America’s 2021-02-24 filing links COVID-19 to a broad, material and continuing set of risks.  The disclosure acknowledges that the pandemic has already harmed 2020 earnings (e.g., higher loan-loss provisions and expenses) and states that management expects further adverse effects across revenues, credit quality, liquidity, capital and operations.  The company itemises concrete transmission channels – lower product demand, merchant charge-backs, prolonged low rates, deposit withdrawals, market volatility, remote-work disruptions and heightened litigation – illustrating a multi-faceted, enterprise-wide exposure.  Language such as “have adversely affected” and “material adverse effect” confirms realised damage, while extensive forward-looking qualifiers (“are expected to continue”, “highly uncertain”) signal persistent vulnerability.  Given the filing date is within one year of the WHO declaration, Time Decay permits high severity scores.  The statements are specific, cover several financial metrics and include few mitigating actions, leading to aggregated snippet scores mostly in the 7-9 range.

Bank of America’s 2022-02-22 filing shows that COVID-19 remains a front-line, multi-year risk across all of the bank’s major value drivers: revenue, expenses, credit quality, liquidity, capital and operational resilience.  The narrative repeatedly affirms that the pandemic has already produced measurable damage (e.g., higher allowances, elevated operating costs) and explicitly warns that these effects may recur or intensify through supply-chain fragility, labour shortages, remote-work vulnerabilities, inflation pressure and demand shifts.  The statements are therefore both backward-looking (actual adverse impact) and forward-looking (continued uncertainty).  Given that the filing date is within two years of the formal WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Language is specific – naming direct channels (deposit flight, lower trading revenue, uncollectible merchant charges) – rather than boiler-plate, signalling a meaningful, actively-monitored risk posture rather than generic disclosure.  There are few material mitigating factors offered beyond generic business-continuity references; consequently, most snippets warrant upper-mid to high scores (7-9/10), reflecting near-term, pervasive risk with quantifiable consequences.

Bank of America’s 2023 filing makes clear that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a live, material driver of risk across the franchise.  Management acknowledges that COVID-19 has already produced measurable, adverse effects – from supply-chain bottlenecks and labour shortages to direct hits on earnings – and warns that the ultimate trajectory of the virus, variants and policy responses will dictate further impacts.  The narrative spans both realised losses (e.g., compliance costs tied to rapid deployment of relief programmes) and forward-looking threats, such as elevated credit losses in sectors like office real-estate and shifts in consumer demand that could permanently reshape the loan book.  Operationally, the bank highlights stresses created by widespread remote work and reliance on digital channels. The language ties the pandemic to concrete, enterprise-level impacts: prior slow-downs in fund performance and fundraising, labour shortages, supply-chain breakdowns, remote-work and cyber-risk, stressed borrowers, tenant rent shortfalls, sector-specific pain (hospitality, travel, retail, office) and the risk of mass redemptions from semi-liquid vehicles that would hit management-fee income.  Although no precise dollar amounts are supplied, the text repeatedly uses material-impact phrasing (“adversely impact … materially”, “significant credit market contraction”, “decline in management fees”) and points to multiple transmission channels—operations, credit, liquidity and fee base.  Because the disclosure is contemporaneous with the pandemic (within three years of the 2020 event) and cites both realised damage and plausible future shocks, it carries high severity under the Time-Decay Principle.  Mitigations are sparse, largely noting that effects ‘may’ occur, so overall risk remains elevated.

Blackstone’s 2024 filing treats COVID-19 as an event with both a proven historical impact (2020-2022) and a continuing forward-looking threat.  The company explicitly catalogues how the pandemic produced labour shortages, supply-chain breakdowns, volatile capital markets and remote-work vulnerabilities, then projects that another large-scale outbreak would again depress portfolio-company revenues, impair asset sales, drive redemptions in semi-liquid vehicles, and strain internal operations.  These are direct, specific and material impacts rather than generic boiler-plate.  The disclosure is framed largely as an ongoing risk (i.e., “another pandemic or global health crisis”), but it leverages hard data from the recent COVID-19 experience to substantiate that risk.  Because the pandemic window (March 2020 onward) is less than four years from the 2024 filing date, the Time-Decay Principle allows relatively high severity scores.  Sentences that reference concrete operational or financial disruptions, name sensitive sectors (hospitality, travel, office, etc.), or flag liquidity/credit stress receive stronger scores.  More generic references to ‘pandemics’ without detail receive moderate scores.  No meaningful mitigating language (such as hedging, insurance or proven resilience) is offered, so downward adjustments are minor.  Overall, Blackstone portrays COVID-19 and future pandemics as a persistent, material, and largely un-mitigated enterprise risk.

CAG’s July 2021 Form 10-K repeatedly links the recent COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective enterprise risks.  Because the event sits squarely in the 0-to-3-year window, the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores.  The filing discloses a spectrum of impacts: (1) direct, quantified cost headwinds (e.g., $143 million of extra transportation, safety and labor expense in FY-2021 and $40 million in late FY-2020); (2) demand shocks—lower food-service volumes and extraordinary retail spikes that may normalize; (3) supply-chain fragility as global restrictions threaten ingredient availability and logistics; (4) workforce health/availability issues; and (5) broad uncertainty driven by variants, vaccine efficacy and government responses.  Some mitigating language appears—e.g., to-date liquidity remained intact, and specific task forces were created—but these do not neutralize the clearly material, multi-faceted risk profile.  Overall, the evidence shows both actual negative financial consequences and forward-looking vulnerability, warranting mid-to-high severity scores for individual snippets, with adjustments downward where mitigation or generic phrasing reduces immediacy.

CAG’s July-2022 filing squarely situates COVID-19 as both an experienced and an ongoing enterprise-level risk.  Pandemic impacts are described in three layers.  First, the company cites concrete, already-occurred effects (temporary plant closures, employee illnesses, supply-chain interruptions, reduced food-service demand and $69.8 million of incremental supply-chain cost in FY-22).  Second, management flags continuing operational pressure points—global ingredient shortages, inflationary raw-material prices, labour tightness, logistics cost spikes—and explicitly links them to pandemic restrictions.  Third, the narrative remains forward-looking, warning that new variants, vaccine efficacy or prolonged disruptions “could have a material adverse effect” and may amplify other risk factors.  Although the company notes that liquidity and overall results have not yet been materially harmed, that qualifier functions as a mitigation rather than elimination of risk.  Because the filing is within two and a half years of the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  Overall, I assess the disclosure as medium-to-high severity: significant realised costs and operational disruptions are already evident, while management concedes that further deterioration is plausible, albeit with some mitigating resilience in liquidity to date.

Conagra’s 2023 filing acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic as both a historical and continuing threat. The company states that its operations "have in the past been" adversely affected and "may continue" to be affected, explicitly naming COVID-19 alongside supply-chain challenges and labor shortages. It also warns that future pandemic waves could disrupt third-party manufacturing and transportation, impairing the firm’s ability to make or sell products. These references demonstrate that the pandemic has already had tangible, though un-quantified, impacts and remains a live operational risk. However, the language is largely embedded in sweeping, catch-all lists without any numeric disclosure of magnitude or duration, suggesting a standard, boiler-plate approach. Because the disclosure is slightly more than three years after the World Health Organization’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle suggests a moderate-to-high severity band: the event is still recent enough to matter materially, but some immediacy has faded. Consequently, evidence scores cluster in the 6-7 range—meaningful but not extreme.

CAG’s July 2024 Form 10-K retains several references to pandemic-driven risks, reflecting both realized impacts from COVID-19 since 2020 and the prospect of future disruption.  The narrative is largely generic—‘pandemics, epidemics, and disease’ are grouped with other macro headwinds—but it still links outbreaks to supply-chain breakdowns, labor shortages, commodity volatility, and impaired manufacturing or sales.  One sentence explicitly states that pandemics have *already* harmed results, signalling that COVID-19 effects were felt across the 2020-23 period.  Most other passages are forward-looking, outlining how another wave could hamper third-party partners or the company’s ability to make and move product.  Because the filing date is four-plus years after the pandemic’s declared onset, the Time-Decay Principle tempers severity from ‘acute’ to ‘moderate’; no quantified dollar figures or detailed contingency plans are given.  Overall, I assess pandemic risk disclosure as medium in intensity—material enough to merit attention but expressed in broad, catch-all language without fresh metrics—supporting snippet scores in the 1-5 range.

Carrier’s 2021 filing portrays COVID-19 as both a realised and continuing threat that permeates virtually every facet of the company’s risk profile—operations, supply chain, customer liquidity, labour availability, and macro-economic demand.  Statements repeatedly confirm that the pandemic has already impaired production and financial results (“have been adversely affected”) while warning that future waves, prolonged shutdowns, or delays in vaccination could further contract revenue, disrupt suppliers, and weaken customers’ ability to pay.  The language is concrete (plant shutdowns, order cancellations, supplier bankruptcy risk) and contemporaneous with the filing date (within one year of the WHO declaration), so Time Decay allows for high severity scores.  No meaningful quantitative mitigation is supplied beyond generic liquidity actions, and the forward-looking uncertainty around vaccines underscores residual exposure.  Overall, the evidence supports elevated risk scores (5-8 range) for individual snippets, reflecting a recent, direct and multi-dimensional impact that remains unresolved.

CAT’s 2021-02-17 Form 10-K squarely positions the COVID-19 pandemic as a near-term, high-severity enterprise risk.  The text blends backward-looking facts (actual drops in demand, supply-chain disruptions, workforce impacts) with forward-looking contingencies (uncertain duration, new strains, possible shutdowns, capital-market stress).  Although no numeric loss estimates are offered, the company repeatedly uses strong materiality language and lists multiple operational vectors—demand, supply chain, labor availability, logistics costs, financing capacity—through which the pandemic is already affecting or could further affect performance.  This makes the risk concrete rather than boilerplate.  Mitigating actions (health safeguards, cost controls, continued plant operations) are acknowledged, tempering but not eliminating severity.  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is well within the 0-3-year “recent” window, so scores can legitimately range toward the upper end.  Overall, the disclosures represent high but not maximal risk evidence because impacts are described qualitatively without hard financial quantification, and some mitigations are in place.

CAT’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly frames COVID-19 as a live, multi-dimensional threat that is already constraining operations while simultaneously clouding future performance.  The disclosures go beyond boiler-plate language: management cites concrete manifestations—material and component shortages, logistics bottlenecks, labour inefficiencies, transportation delays, supplier freight problems and inflationary cost pressure—and links them explicitly to CAT’s ability to meet demand and maintain financial health.  These references establish both present-day impacts (e.g., “have limited our ability to meet customer demand”) and forward-looking uncertainty (e.g., duration of new variants, credit-market disruption).  Because the filing date (16-Feb-2022) is less than two years after the WHO pandemic declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Most statements are specific (naming supply-chain choke points, workforce effects and customer-demand volatility) and use strong materiality qualifiers (“material adverse effect”).  A few sentences contain mitigating language—monitoring, contingency plans, safety protocols—which temper, but do not remove, risk.  Overall, the pandemic remains a critical, directly felt risk, justifying elevated scores in the 6-9 range for the strongest evidence and slightly lower where mitigation is emphasised.

The filing, issued less than three years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, treats the pandemic as an active, continuing threat rather than a historical footnote.  Throughout the Risk Factors section, Caterpillar states that COVID-19 has already produced material adverse effects—labour inefficiencies, component shortages, logistics constraints, customer-demand volatility and inflationary pressures—and that these impacts could persist or re-emerge.  The language is concrete ("has had, and continues to have, a significant impact") and repeatedly invokes the possibility of further material harm to sales, operations and credit quality.  Mitigation is mentioned only briefly (some restrictions have eased), so the disclosures remain predominantly aggravating.  Given the 2023 filing date, the Time Decay Principle classifies COVID-19 as a recent event (<3 years), allowing high per-sentence scores.  Consequently, evidence sentences generally score in the upper range (7-10), reflecting direct, ongoing and multi-dimensional risk to the company.

CAT’s 2023 Form 10-K situates COVID-19 within a broader “catastrophic events” risk category, but the company still describes concrete and ongoing vulnerabilities that stem from the pandemic.  Although the first global wave began four years ago, management continues to flag supply-chain bottlenecks, labor inefficiencies, logistics constraints and demand volatility that are either currently limiting production or could quickly recur.  The language is forward-looking (“could again impact”) yet grounded in prior experience (“had a significant impact”), signalling that COVID-related shocks remain part of the firm’s operational risk set.  These disclosures are moderately specific—linking pandemics to workforce availability, dealer networks, component shortages, financing demand and credit quality—without offering quantified dollar figures.  Given the filing date of February 2024, the event sits in the 4-year “medium-term” window, so the Time Decay Principle limits individual snippet scores to the mid-range.  Overall, the company treats pandemic risk as persistent and potentially material, but not as an acute crisis, warranting moderate severity assessments (scores 4-6).

CBOE’s 2021-02-19 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as both an already-experienced disruption and a continuing, high-uncertainty threat.  Because the filing date is less than one year after the WHO’s 11-Mar-2020 pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  The company discloses a concrete historical impact—the three-month suspension of open-outcry trading—and warns that further outbreaks or regulatory measures could again curb trading volumes, impede vendor performance, and raise legal-health liabilities.  Language such as “material adverse effect” signals management’s view that the risk is financially significant, while multiple forward-looking caveats (“depends on future developments”) highlight uncertainty rather than resolution.  Mitigation steps (remote work, communications, health protocols) are acknowledged but are not yet proven to neutralise volume-driven revenue risk.  Overall, the evidence describes a recent, enterprise-wide exposure with demonstrated operational shocks and the potential to erode demand for the company’s core products; thus, individual snippets warrant mid-to-high risk scores (5-8 range), tempered only slightly where the text stresses mitigations or lack of current disruptions.

Cboe’s 2022-02-18 Form 10-K ties COVID-19 squarely to multiple operational and financial threats that remain live less than two years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  The filing acknowledges both realised effects (e.g., forced remote-work migration, heightened employee turnover, prior suspension of open-outcry trading) and a spectrum of forward-looking possibilities— from supply-chain interruptions and labour shortages to trading-volume swings and litigation over workplace safety.  Although the company does not quantify dollar impacts, it repeatedly warns that further pandemic developments "could have a material adverse effect" on revenues, cash-flows and liquidity.  The disclosures are more than boiler-plate: they enumerate concrete pressure points such as cyber-security exposure from remote access, “great resignation” staffing risks, and potential disruption of technology-equipment vendors.  Given the recency of the pandemic (within the 0-3-year high-severity window) and the breadth of identified impact channels, the overall risk profile is high, albeit mitigated somewhat by the lack of specific lost-revenue figures or probability estimates.  Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the 4-8 range, reflecting significant but largely un-quantified, still-evolving threats that conform to the Time Decay Principle for a recent event.

CBOE’s 2023 filing situates COVID-19 as an ongoing, forward-looking risk that could materially affect virtually every facet of its business model—from trading volumes and market-data demand to workforce availability and legal exposure.  All references are couched as potential, not yet realized, impacts; however, the company explicitly lists multiple operational vectors (supply-chain disruptions, remote-work complications, regulatory shutdowns, shifts in trading behaviour) and repeatedly warns that these could have a “material adverse effect” on revenues, cash-flows and liquidity.  Because the filing date (February 2023) is fewer than three years after the pandemic’s declared onset, the Time-Decay Principle permits relatively high severity scores.  The language is largely qualitative and precautionary—there are no quantified dollar amounts—but the breadth of functions cited and the admission of possible material harm elevate the risk beyond boiler-plate.  Overall, I assess the disclosure as a moderately high (but not maximal) severity signal: specific operational channels are identified, the threat is active and proximate, yet the narrative remains un-quantified and partly generic, which tempers the ultimate scoring.

CBOE’s filing, submitted roughly four years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, acknowledges that pandemic-related disruptions remain a meaningful, though now largely prospective, threat.  The company frames COVID-19 as part of a broader “pandemic” risk category that could trigger renewed government lockdowns, supply-chain breakdowns, labour-force constraints, remote-work frictions, legal liabilities, and—most critically for an exchange operator—shifts in trading behaviour and volumes.  All statements are forward-looking and unquantified, signalling potential rather than current damage; yet CBOE repeatedly uses strong language such as “material adverse effect,” tying the hazard directly to revenues, cash flows and operations.  Under the Time Decay Principle, an event that began in 2020 is now in the 4-to-10-year window, warranting mid-range severity scores (4-6).  The evidence therefore indicates a moderate but persistent risk that could resurface if new variants or policy responses emerge, affecting both the company’s operational infrastructure and demand for its products.

CBRE’s 2021 filing depicts COVID-19 as a pervasive, multi-dimensional threat that is both already impairing results and likely to reshape the company’s risk profile for years.  The narrative combines facts (2020 revenue-line declines, emergency remote-work deployment, essential-worker exposure) with forward-looking warnings about credit-market dislocations, structural demand changes from work-from-home, and possible litigation over workplace infections.  The company uses forceful language—“material adverse effect,” “significant economic and societal disruption,” “decline in real estate sales, financing, construction and leasing activity”—that goes far beyond boiler-plate.  Most of the statements refer to impacts that have already happened or are expected to persist through 2021, positioning them in the 0-3-year window where Time Decay permits high scores.  Only limited mitigating language (e.g., mention of best-practice safeguards) appears, and it is outweighed by extensive detailing of revenue, liquidity, operational and reputational vulnerabilities.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, specific, and enterprise-wide, justifying elevated severity scores across the extracted sentences.

CBRE’s 2022 Form 10-K ties COVID-19 directly to both historical financial damage and to material, ongoing uncertainty.  The filing was made less than two years after the WHO declared the pandemic, so—under the Time Decay Principle—the disclosures are evaluated as ‘recent’.  Management identifies concrete past impacts (sharp drops in sales, financing, construction and leasing volumes) and explains how remote-work adoption, shifting tenant demand and variant-driven outbreaks could further erode core fee streams.  At the same time, they note pockets of benefit (e.g., booming logistics demand) but warn these may not offset broader losses, stressing that mitigation is uncertain.  The language is company-specific, operational and forward-looking, not boiler-plate: it cites client rent collections, staff health and retention, office closures, vaccine efficacy, and the possibility that pandemic stress will amplify other listed risks.  Overall, the pandemic is framed as an immediate, multi-dimensional threat with lingering trajectory unknowns.  Because the event window is well within three years of the filing date, high (but not maximum) severity scores are justified, with deductions applied where management points to offsetting benefits or resilience initiatives.

CBRE’s 2022 Form 10-K reveals that management still sees COVID-19 as a material, live risk only three years after the WHO declared a pandemic.  The filing links the virus to an historic collapse in commercial real-estate activity, describes structural shifts in space utilisation (a proxy for the remote-work pivot and evolved tenant demand), and warns of continuing uncertainty that makes forecasting difficult.  All of these comments are forward-looking rather than purely retrospective, so the risk remains present rather than merely historical.  The company also acknowledges margin pressure and the need for contingency cost cutting, but pairs these acknowledgements with mitigating factors such as variable compensation and active expense management, which temper – though do not eliminate – severity.  Because the disclosure occurs within three years of the event, the Time-Decay Principle allows for relatively high scores (up to 10); however, mitigating language and the absence of precise, quantified losses mean most sentences fall in the moderate-to-high range rather than the maximum.  Overall, COVID-19 continues to represent a strategic and operational threat to CBRE, particularly through lasting changes in space demand and the volatility of capital markets, albeit partly offset by management’s flexible cost structure.

CBRE’s 2024 filing treats COVID-19 as an event whose acute phase has passed but whose commercial-real-estate after-shocks remain material. The risk language is forward-looking, describing both continuing macro headwinds (e.g., lower leasing volumes) and fundamental, longer-lived shifts in space utilisation caused by the pandemic-driven rise of remote work. None of the disclosures quantify dollar impacts, but they expressly acknowledge structural change, persistent demand weakness, and the possibility of further adverse effects. Four years have elapsed since the World Health Organization declared the pandemic; therefore, under the Time Decay Principle the evidence warrants moderate—rather than maximal—severity scores, capped at 6. Overall, the statements are specific enough to show material relevance (ongoing repercussions, altered demand patterns) yet sufficiently seasoned in time to merit middle-range risk ratings.

CB’s 2021-02-25 filing embeds an extensive discussion of COVID-19 as both an already-realised shock and a continuing, forward-looking threat.  The company expressly quantifies pandemic-driven losses (US$1.4 billion pre-tax, 4.5 points on the combined ratio) and revenue erosion (1.9 % fall in global consumer-line premiums), demonstrating direct, material impact on current financial results.  Beyond hard numbers, the text outlines multiple transmission channels—higher claims frequency and severity, investment portfolio stress, credit & collateral strain, premium base contraction, and operational challenges from large-scale remote work—that could amplify future volatility.  Language ranges from factual (“has had a significant effect”) to conditional (“could adversely impact”), signalling both incurred and contingent exposures.  Given the filing date lies well within three years of the WHO pandemic declaration, time-decay is minimal; therefore, evidence scores can lie toward the upper end of the 7-10 band when quantitative and toward the mid-range when qualitative.  Overall, the risk level is assessed as high because impacts are already material, diversified across financial, operational and strategic dimensions, and remain highly uncertain in trajectory.

The filing, submitted in early 2022, squarely addresses COVID-19 as both an event that has already produced measurable impacts and an ongoing source of uncertainty for Chubb (CB).  Management acknowledges concrete disruptions experienced to-date—ranging from operational upheaval to higher claims and investment-portfolio volatility—while emphasising that future waves, policy responses and economic after-shocks could continue to erode premiums, strain capital, and stress information-technology infrastructure.  The language is specific (naming premium suppression, collateral calls, remote-work stress and investment losses) and forward-looking, signalling that material downside remains.  Because the pandemic is still within the 0-3-year “recent event” window, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores.  Overall, the risk is judged high: it is multi-faceted, presently manifest, and described in terms that go beyond boiler-plate by linking COVID-19 to distinct financial channels (claims inflation, asset impairments, credit risk, operational resilience and workforce disruption).

Chubb’s 2023 filing makes it clear that the company still faces material, forward-looking exposure from the COVID-19 pandemic even though acute impacts have eased.  The pandemic is explicitly framed as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that can raise claims severity, depress premium volumes if commercial activity again stalls, erode investment portfolio values through financial-market stress, and strain collateral requirements.  All disclosures are recent (within three years of the WHO declaration) so the Time-Decay principle allows elevated scoring.  The language is mixed: it admits that vaccines and loosened restrictions have helped (a mitigating element) yet emphasises that new variants or renewed lockdowns may continue to hit earnings, capital and liquidity.  Impacts are not quantified but are described in several concrete business channels—loss ratios, premiums, invested-asset quality—indicating more than generic boiler-plate.  Overall, the risk level is significant but not at the “quantified crisis” extreme; therefore individual snippet scores cluster in the mid-to-upper range (4-8), with a single generic pandemic reference scoring very low.

COVID-19 is referenced by CB primarily as part of its broader catastrophe-management narrative rather than as an isolated, quantified loss driver.  The 10-K recognises that a global or other wide-impact pandemic can generate material volatility in claims and can disrupt operations, yet the language is forward-looking and largely generic – the company speaks in terms of potential exposure and severity rather than booked losses or hard numbers.  This framing indicates that management views pandemic risk as an ongoing, but now better-understood, medium-term threat that sits alongside terrorism, cyber and natural peril risk pools.  Statements point to (i) ‘substantial exposure’ on existing books, (ii) the possibility that ultimate claims could exceed carried reserves if pandemic-related litigation or regulation expands coverage, and (iii) operational ramifications for employees, brokers and insureds.  No new mitigation tools beyond customary catastrophe modelling and reinsurance are disclosed, nor are remote-work, supply-chain or labour-shortage themes explored, suggesting residual uncertainty remains.  Because the WHO declaration occurred in March 2020, the references fall in the 4-year (medium-term) window; under the Time Decay Principle, individual evidence scores should therefore be moderate (typically 4-6) when language is specific and risk-enhancing, and lower (≤3) when it is merely generic.

All COVID-19 references appear inside a dedicated risk-factor section dated February 2021, less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration; therefore the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  The company acknowledges that, although 2020 results were not materially hit, COVID-19 could still trigger material adverse effects through several pathways: supply-chain failure, reduced demand for communications infrastructure, permitting delays, labour/operational disruptions, and restricted access to capital.  The narrative mixes current observations (they already changed business practices) with forward-looking uncertainty, using largely qualitative language (‘could’, ‘might’, ‘difficult to predict’).  Mitigating language (no 2020 impact, modifications already implemented) tempers but does not eliminate the risk.  Overall, the disclosures show moderate-to-high severity: they are company-specific, enumerate concrete channels of impact, and stress potential materiality, yet remain unquantified and contingent.  Consequently, individual snippet scores range from  -3 (explicit mitigation) to +7 (detailed, company-specific material risks), and the aggregate picture supports a meaningful but not maximum COVID-19 risk assessment for CCI within the recent-event window.

CCI’s 2022 filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad spectrum of potential operational and financial threats.  The company acknowledges only limited historical impact, yet it details numerous forward-looking vulnerabilities—supplier delays, labor shortages, permitting slow-downs, shifts in tenant demand, and higher capital-market costs.  Because the filing date (Feb 2022) is less than three years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic (Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits relatively high risk scores.  Most statements are prospective rather than reporting realised losses, but the language repeatedly uses strong qualifiers such as “materially affect,” “adversely affect,” and “volatility,” indicating that management views the pandemic as a continuing, material uncertainty.  Mitigating language (“no material impact in 2021”) tempers some risk, but the overall disclosure points to a still-elevated exposure driven by ongoing supply-chain and demand-side pressures.  Accordingly, individual sentence scores concentrate in the mid-to-upper range (4-9), with deductions where the company asserts past immateriality or highlights mitigation efforts.

The filing, made almost exactly three years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, shows that CCI still attributes tangible, present-day operational and cost pressures to the pandemic. The disclosures focus on two main vectors: (1) a persistently tight labour market with elevated turnover directly “stemming from the COVID-19 pandemic,” which is driving higher compensation and hiring costs; and (2) a rebound in travel and facilities expenses as the company transitions from pandemic-era remote work back to a hybrid/office setting. These statements are recent, explicit and describe realised cost increases rather than merely hypothetical future risks, placing them high on the severity scale under the Time Decay Principle (the event lies within the 0-3-year window). At the same time, the impacts are limited to cost inflation and workforce management rather than core revenue loss or large-scale supply chain collapse, keeping the overall risk below the maximum. Consequently, the pandemic is assessed as a meaningful, ongoing operational and cost risk with high relevance but not an existential threat.

The filing contains only one explicit reference to pandemic-style disruptions: management warns that supply-chain breakdowns and labour shortages could delay projects and raise costs by limiting the availability of materials, equipment and contractors.  Although the company never names COVID-19, these very disruptions are emblematic of the post-2020 pandemic environment, so the sentence functions as a forward-looking disclosure that such conditions could persist or recur.  Because the language is conditional ("may experience") and un-quantified, the identified risk is potential rather than a currently booked impact, which tempers severity.  Nevertheless, the acknowledgement of concrete operational consequences—delays and cost inflation— elevates the importance above a boiler-plate mention.  Given that the pandemic began less than four years before the February 2024 filing and continues to influence global logistics and labour markets, the Time Decay Principle allows a mid-to-high score; overall, the evidence supports a moderate-high risk rating.

CCL’s filing clearly ties continuing risk exposure to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company acknowledges that the 2020 outbreak forced a total pause of guest cruise operations, drove the accumulation of substantial new debt, and could still trigger renewed shutdowns if another outbreak occurs.  While parts of the narrative are retrospective, most language is forward-looking, listing concrete ways a future pandemic wave could again suppress demand, disrupt itineraries, inflate costs, and damage reputation.  The discussion is specific to core operating metrics—occupancy, ship deployment, fleet impairments—and cites the debt overhang created by the prior suspension.  Because the pandemic began less than four years before the 10-K date, the Time Decay Principle allows relatively high scores, but the absence of precise dollar quantification tempers maximum severity.  Overall, the evidence depicts a live, material risk that could quickly re-escalate, justifying mid-to-high severity ratings in the 5-7 range for the strongest sentences and lower scores where statements are generic or reputational in nature.

CDNS’s February 22 2021 Form 10-K repeatedly links the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic to operational, financial, supply-chain and macro-economic threats.  Because the filing date is only eleven months after the WHO declared the pandemic (well within the 0-3-year “recent” window), time-decay does not materially diminish severity scores.  The disclosures mix statements of FACT (e.g., delivery delays, remote-work arrangements, customer requests to defer payments) with forward-looking CAUTION (e.g., possible capital-market constraints, prolonged downturn).  Language is mostly qualitative but is concrete enough—citing specific business processes, collections risk, laboratory access, and hardware lead-times—to evidence real, continuing exposure.  Some mitigating comments appear (e.g., liquidity confidence; no material adverse impact in FY-2020), but they do not erase the documented disruptions.  Overall, the pandemic risk profile is elevated, with individual snippets scoring from 1–7 depending on specificity, immediacy, and presence of mitigating language.

CDNS’ 2022-02-22 filing links the still-unfolding COVID-19 pandemic (under two years old at the report date) to a broad spectrum of operational, financial and strategic threats. The company moves beyond boiler-plate language by detailing concrete, present-day consequences—remote-work arrangements covering a “vast majority” of employees, volatility in hardware deliveries caused by limited access to customer sites, laboratory shut-downs, higher freight and raw-material costs, potential bad-debt exposure, and the risk that vaccine mandates could hamper talent retention. While some passages are forward-looking (“could”, “may”), others confirm impacts already felt (e.g., delivery delays and work-from-home). Mitigating notes exist—management states fiscal-2021 results were not materially hurt and a pilot office-return program has begun—but these do not erase the breadth of continuing exposure. Because the pandemic falls inside the 0-3-year “recent event” window, Time-Decay allows high scores; however, credit is subtracted where the company emphasises uncertainty or cites offsetting factors. Overall, the risk evidence is specific, multi-dimensional and current, warranting generally elevated snippet scores, though none reach the maximum because quantitative dollar impacts are absent and some mitigating language is present.

CDNS’s February 13 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as a still-present, multi-faceted risk.  Because the pandemic is less than three years old, the Time-Decay principle allows high risk scores where warranted.  The filing blends forward-looking cautions with acknowledgements of concrete, albeit un-quantified, impacts that the company has already felt—inefficiencies, delivery delays, extra costs and volatile demand.  It also warns of broader macro-economic knock-on effects such as extended downturns, inflation and credit-collection issues.  However, management simultaneously discloses that, to date, COVID-19 “has not had a material, adverse impact” and that mitigation measures (remote-work protocols, policy adaptations) have sustained operations.  Overall, the evidence supports a medium-high residual risk: the pandemic is ongoing and continues to threaten supply chains, labour availability and customer demand, but the absence of material financial damage thus far, plus stated mitigation actions, temper the severity.  Scores therefore cluster in the 3-6 range rather than the extreme upper bound allowed for recent events.

CDNS’s 2024 filing references the COVID-19 pandemic only in broad, macro-risk passages. The company positions the pandemic as one example of a wider class of “public-health emergencies,” stressing that it has already curtailed economic activity and could still disrupt global markets, international travel, supply chains and, indirectly, its stock price. The wording is forward-looking and largely hypothetical—there are no quantified dollar figures, no disclosures of recent operational hits, and no pandemic-specific mitigation plans beyond general monitoring. Because the initial outbreak is now four years old, the Time Decay Principle places these statements in the medium-term window (4-10 years), capping severity in the mid-range. Overall, the risk is acknowledged but generic: COVID-19 remains a potentially disruptive backdrop rather than an acute, company-specific crisis. Therefore, individual snippets merit moderate scores, generally between 4 and 5, with minor mentions scoring lower.

CDW’s 2021-02-26 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as a present-day, multi-faceted threat that is already eroding performance and may intensify.  The filing repeatedly confirms actual adverse effects—supply-chain bottlenecks, vendor product constraints, labour and facility disruptions, slower customer payments, and higher credit-loss reserves—while also warning of future demand contractions and budgetary pressures across key end-markets.  Although most disclosures remain qualitative, they are company-specific (e.g., inability to meet customer demand, temporary distribution-centre closures, heightened credit-loss provisioning) and describe concrete operational chokepoints.  Few numerical impacts are supplied, so the language stops short of a “quantified materiality” tier, but the narrative clearly links recent-to-current losses with additional downside scenarios.  Because the filing date is less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (up to 10).  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, direct, and ongoing, meriting mid-to-high severities across the extracted sentences; only modest downward adjustments are applied for generality or embedded mitigations.

CDW’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as both an already-realized shock and an enduring, forward-looking threat across every major operational dimension—supply chain continuity, labour availability, customer demand, logistics, cost inflation and liquidity.  The company states that it has “experienced” concrete disruptions (e.g., supply shortages, facility closures, delivery bottlenecks) and cost increases, while simultaneously warning that resurgences, new variants and government mandates could intensify these pressures.  Language is specific (naming supply chain partners, facilities and labour functions), repeatedly uses “materially” and “adversely,” and links the pandemic to fundamental metrics such as cash flows, results of operations and liquidity.  Because the filing date (28 Feb 2022) falls less than three years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores; no mitigating statements of equal weight (e.g., comprehensive risk controls or quantified offsets) are provided.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, direct and multi-faceted, warranting upper-tier scores in the 6-9 range for individual snippets.

CDW’s 2023 Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad array of concrete and continuing risks that have already affected – and are expected to keep affecting – the company’s operations, finances and supply chain.  The filing describes direct, realised impacts (e.g., supply-chain bottlenecks, labour disruptions, rising logistics costs and inflation) alongside forward-looking uncertainties (resurgences, new variants, macro-economic recession, government budget cuts).
