Because the filing date (24 Feb 2023) is within three years of the WHO pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Overall, the disclosure depicts an elevated, multi-faceted risk landscape that remains current; none of the sentences offer meaningful mitigation offsets, so individual evidence pieces receive robust positive scores (generally 4-9, capped at 10) to reflect the recent timing, specificity and already-realised impacts.

CDW’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to acknowledge the COVID-19 pandemic as a meaningful—but now moderating—enterprise-wide threat. References to the pandemic appear in the Macroeconomic & Industry, Supply-Chain, and Logistics risk sections. The language is predominantly forward-looking (“could”) and clusters COVID-19 with other disruptive forces, signalling that management now views it as one of several potential shock factors rather than a singular crisis. Nonetheless, the filing records a concrete historical impact—surges in delivery-service demand experienced “during the COVID-19 pandemic”—confirming that the virus has had real operational consequences. Given that the pandemic’s official onset is nearly four years old, the Time Decay Principle caps severity in the mid-range. Overall evidence supports a moderate residual risk level: the company recognises continuing vulnerabilities in supply-chain reliability, shipping capacity and macro-economic demand, but provides no quantified losses or highly specific contingencies. Accordingly, snippet scores fall in the 4-6 band, reflecting medium-term but still relevant pandemic exposure.

The filing occurs in February 2022, less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic on 11 March 2020, so the Time-Decay Principle permits high scores where warranted.  CEG discloses both realized and prospective pandemic impacts.  The risk narrative is two-fold: (i) a backward-looking, quantified hit of roughly $170 million to 2020 net income that the company explicitly attributes to pandemic-driven economic weakness, and (ii) multiple forward-looking statements that continued uncertainty over vaccination progress, customer-demand recovery, workforce availability and new pandemic waves could hinder operations and demand.  These statements are direct and company-specific—e.g., potential inability to run generation assets and deliver power—rather than boiler-plate.  At the same time, management cites a series of concrete mitigations (remote-work protocols, travel limits, cybersecurity hardening, pandemic response plans) and notes that 2021 financial impacts were “not material,” indicating partial risk abatement.  Consequently, the overall pandemic risk for CEG is material but not existential: a mid-to-upper-range risk score is justified (roughly 6-7 on a 10-point scale), tempered by observable mitigation efforts and an improving 2021 financial trend.

The filing was made only three years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so under the Time Decay Principle the pandemic remains a ‘recent’ risk whose disclosures can score toward the high end of the scale.  CEG’s narrative shows a mixed profile: it confirms a real, quantified hit to 2020 net income (-$170 million), acknowledges that the drag largely disappeared by 2021-22, yet warns that any renewed or future pandemic could again suppress customer demand and impair plant operations by constraining labour and other resources.  The language is somewhat specific—citing the financial hit and naming concrete operational vulnerabilities—but becomes more generic when grouped with other catastrophes.  The company also flags a partial mitigation (“plans in place to respond”), which tempers overall severity.  Taking these factors together, I view the pandemic risk to CEG as material but moderating, with evidence scores clustering in the mid-to-upper range (3-7) rather than at the maximum.  This calibration honours the Time Decay window (0-3 yrs allows high scores) while recognising the company’s assertion that recent impacts have been “not material,” and its stated contingency planning.

COVID-19 is portrayed as both an already-material and an ongoing systemic threat to Celanese (CE).  Multiple passages disclose that 2020 results were “significantly and adversely” hit, with specific reference to depressed customer demand, plant run-rate reductions, supply-chain interruptions and segment-level profit deterioration.  At the same time, the company enumerates forward-looking uncertainties—potential renewed lockdowns, raw-material shortages, liquidity pressure, IT vulnerabilities from remote work, and the unknown duration of demand disruption.  Although management cites mitigation steps (inventory management, cost control, health protocols and hopes for vaccine roll-out), these are conditional and do not eliminate risk.  Because the Form 10-K was filed on 11 Feb 2021—well within three years of the 11 Mar 2020 pandemic declaration—the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  The language is highly specific, links directly to operational and financial metrics, and distinguishes multiple impact channels (demand, supply chain, labour/remote work, IT, liquidity).  Overall, the risk level is elevated and immediate, warranting high aggregate severity scores, tempered only modestly where explicit mitigation or recovery expectations are stated.

The filing was made less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, so any language about the virus represents a ‘recent-event’ risk under the Time Decay Principle and can be scored at the upper end of the scale.  Celanese (CE) repeatedly states that COVID-19 has already had a “significant and adverse” effect on operations and financial results (realised risk) and also details a wide array of forward-looking exposures: supply-chain interruptions, raw-material shortages, labour tightness, remote-work cyber-security gaps, and future demand swings tied to potential variants.  Although the company does not quantify dollar impacts, it does acknowledge broad geographic reach (“substantially all locations”) and explicitly links the pandemic to past production slow-downs and continuing uncertainty about compliance costs, logistics and workforce availability.  A few mitigating notes appear—plants are “now operating at more normalised levels,” and the firm refers to cost pass-through efforts—but these do not materially offset the breadth of the identified threats.  Taken together, the disclosures constitute specific, recent, and still-unfolding risks rather than generic boiler-plate, warranting mid-to-high individual snippet scores (5-7) with downward adjustments where impacts are merely potential or partially mitigated.

Celanese’s 2023 filing repeatedly references the COVID-19 pandemic as an active, continuing source of operational, cost, supply-chain and cybersecurity risk.  All mentions appear in a forward-looking risk-factor context and the MD&A discussion, signalling that management now treats the pandemic less as a one-off shock and more as a persistent threat embedded in its risk landscape.  The company does not quantify financial effects, but it ties COVID-19 (and its variants) to specific exposures: (i) significant raw-material and logistics price volatility, (ii) potential shutdowns of manufacturing facilities, (iii) heightened cybersecurity vulnerabilities created by long-term remote-work arrangements, and (iv) demand uncertainty caused by lockdowns.  Because the pandemic timeframe (2020-03-11 onward) is within three years of the 2023-02-24 filing, the Time Decay Principle allows relatively elevated scores.  Nevertheless, most statements remain generic and bundled with other macro-risks, which tempers severity.  Only the remote-work cybersecurity disclosure offers a concrete, direct linkage between COVID-19 and a specific operational vulnerability.  Overall, the evidence supports moderate-to-high but not maximal risk scores, reflecting a live but largely unquantified threat profile.

Celanese’s 2024 filing references the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, broad-based operational hazard rather than a currently crippling threat. The company situates pandemic risk within long enumerations of potential disruptions—supply chain interruptions, labor issues, price volatility, IT security vulnerabilities—all couched in largely forward-looking language. Only one sentence attributes concrete, already-incurred impacts (supply disruptions and higher input costs in 2021-2022), and it does so without explicitly naming COVID-19. Given that the pandemic’s onset was March 2020—just under four years before the filing—the Time Decay Principle places this evidence at the cusp between “recent” and “medium-term.” Accordingly, direct but unquantified historical impacts merit a mid-level score, while generic, prospective mentions are scored lower. No sentence offers quantified financial damage, and several are diluted by long lists of other hazards, tempering overall severity. The aggregate risk signal is therefore moderate: the pandemic remains material enough to warrant disclosure, yet its incremental threat is now comparable to other macro uncertainties rather than an acute, stand-alone crisis.

COVID-19 is treated by CFG as a still-live, multi-layered threat whose effects have already been felt (higher credit-loss provisions, lower non-interest income) and whose future trajectory remains highly uncertain.  Nearly three years after the WHO declaration, the company continues to frame the pandemic as both an historic impact ("has in the past negatively affected") and a forward-looking, potentially material risk.  The wording is more than boiler-plate: management links the pandemic to concrete banking fundamentals—deposit stability, borrower repayment capacity, collateral values, credit-loss provisioning and the volatility of capital markets that feed fee income.  While no hard numbers are disclosed, the risk language is specific to core income statement and balance-sheet drivers and recognises second-order effects (e.g., pandemic heightening other listed risks).  Because the filing date (17 Feb 2023) falls within three years of the event’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores; however, absence of quantified dollar impacts or current operating disruptions keeps individual snippet scores below the absolute maximum.  Overall, the evidence portrays a recent, still-evolving external shock with material but un-quantified consequences, meriting upper-moderate to elevated severity assessments (4-7 range for most sentences, top end capped at 7 given the qualitative nature of disclosures).

CFG’s 2024 filing contains only brief, forward-looking references to pandemic risk.  The company now treats COVID-19 as one element within a broader category of ‘catastrophic events,’ noting that while the U.S. economy has largely recovered, a renewed outbreak could again hurt earnings, liquidity and capital.  There is no quantified effect, no discussion of specific operational disruptions (e.g., remote-work costs or supply-chain stress), and the language is largely precautionary.  Because nearly four years have passed since the March 2020 declaration of the pandemic, the Time Decay Principle requires we view these disclosures as mid-term, warranting moderate—not high—severity.  Consequently, individual snippets score in the 4-5 range, reflecting acknowledgement of ongoing exposure but tempered by generic wording and references to post-COVID recovery.

CF’s 2021 Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad spectrum of operational and financial threats.  Because the filing date (24 Feb 2021) falls only eleven months after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), Time-Decay allows elevated risk scores.  The disclosure blends (a) concrete, already-experienced impacts – e.g., reduced industrial nitrogen demand, disrupted food supply chains and transportation bottlenecks – with (b) forward-looking contingencies such as large-scale workforce illness, supply-chain failures, heightened feed-stock price volatility and customer default.  Language is mostly specific (naming labour shortages, logistics choke-points, energy-demand shocks and corn / ethanol linkages) and repeatedly flags “material adverse effect,” signalling management’s acknowledgement of severity.  Mitigation is mentioned (critical-infrastructure status, no 2020 earnings hit yet), but these caveats are outweighed by the breadth and depth of potential impacts described.  Overall, the risk profile is high and current, justifying snippet scores in the 6-9 range under the Time-Decay Principle.

COVID-19 is discussed in the 2022 Form 10-K primarily as a continuing, enterprise-wide threat that can materially disrupt CF’s supply chain, labor force, input-cost environment and customer demand profile.  Although the filing date (24 Feb 2022) is almost two years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the pandemic is still ongoing, so Time-Decay allows relatively high scores.  The company frames the risk in both realised (e.g., prior demand reductions for energy, prior food-chain disruptions) and prospective terms (e.g., potential workforce outages, supply-chain bottlenecks).  Language such as “material and adverse effect” signals high severity, and multiple corporate value drivers (prices, costs, margins, contract performance) are explicitly referenced, raising the overall risk level.  No significant mitigating controls are offered beyond an admission of uncertainty; instead the narrative stresses limited visibility and inability to predict the ultimate impact.  Therefore the evidence skews toward aggravating factors, justifying mid-to-high micro-scores (5-8) for the most detailed statements, with smaller scores for generic or indirect references, all within the 0-3-year time-band permitted range.

The filing makes only a passing but still relevant reference to COVID-19.  Instead of detailing direct operational disruptions (e.g., plant shutdowns, remote-work transitions or labour shortages), CF frames the pandemic as one among several factors that could depress ethanol demand by reducing vehicle miles travelled.  Because corn‐based ethanol consumption is a major driver of U.S. corn acreage – and thus of nitrogen-fertiliser demand – the company implicitly recognises that lingering or renewed pandemic-related mobility restrictions could weaken its end-market.  The statement is forward-looking and couched in conditional language ("may put pressure"), signalling a potential rather than an existing impact.  Nevertheless, the event remains within the 0-3-year ‘recent’ window, so time decay does not materially dilute the score.  Overall, the disclosure evidences a moderate, second-order risk: COVID-19 could indirectly depress fertiliser demand through the ethanol channel, but the company provides no quantification or concrete mitigation steps, keeping the severity in the mid-range.

The filing, dated February 22 2024, contains only one substantive reference to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company frames the virus as a demand-side risk: pandemic-era reductions in travel can depress gasoline consumption, which then squeezes ethanol margins; lower ethanol production would shrink U.S. corn acreage and thereby dampen nitrogen-fertilizer demand.  This is a forward-looking, indirect linkage rather than a disclosure of current operational disruption (e.g., supply chain, labour or remote-work costs).  No dollar amounts or concrete probability estimates are supplied, but the narrative does map out a clear causal chain from pandemic travel patterns to CF’s end-market volumes.  Because the pandemic onset (March 2020) is roughly four years in the past, the Time Decay Principle calls for mid-range severity scores.  Overall, the risk is specific enough to merit attention yet is only moderately material given its indirect nature and lack of quantification.

CHD’s 2021 filing presents COVID-19 as a recent, ongoing, enterprise-wide threat that is already distorting demand patterns, disrupting the supply chain and retail channels, and pressuring both manufacturing continuity and working capital.  The language is largely specific – citing store closures, employee absenteeism, freight bottlenecks, and demand spikes or collapses by brand – and blends descriptions of realised impacts (e.g., lost personal-care sales, higher manufacturing costs) with forward-looking warnings (e.g., potential facility shutdowns, inability to source materials).  Because the pandemic began less than one year before the filing date, Time Decay is negligible, so evidence can be scored near the top of the 0-10 scale.  None of the excerpts provide hard dollar figures, but several reference “significant” or “material” impacts, global scale, or direct operational penalties, warranting high severity ratings.  Mitigating language (e.g., monitoring, capacity investments) appears but is limited, so most net scores remain firmly positive.  Overall, COVID-19 represents a high-severity, still-unfolding risk for CHD, with most individual snippets justifying scores in the 4-7 range and the strongest statements approaching, but not reaching, the maximum due to lack of precise quantification.

Church & Dwight’s 2022 filing paints COVID-19 as an active, multi-dimensional threat that is already eroding operational efficiency and could further depress revenue and margins.  The company cites concrete, present-day impacts—labour shortages, factory and logistics bottlenecks, retail shutdowns, inflationary cost spikes—as well as structural, longer-term changes such as a permanent shift to e-commerce and volatile category demand.  Risk language is largely specific (naming facilities, labour, transportation, and demand mix) and couched in both current-impact (‘continues to impact most of our businesses’) and forward-looking conditional terms (‘could face,’ ‘may continue’).  No exact dollar figures are disclosed, but the breadth of business functions affected (supply chain, production, customer orders, pricing, and competitive dynamics) signals high severity.  Because the pandemic is well within the 0-3-year “recent event” window, time-decay does not materially diminish scores; instead, recency amplifies them.  Mitigations (price increases, added capacity) are mentioned elsewhere but not in the extracted sentences, so they do little to offset the overall risk profile.  Consequently, the evidence supports medium-to-high snippet scores (3-8), reflecting substantial, ongoing exposure without quantified magnitude.

Church & Dwight’s 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly ties material, continuing and multi-dimensional threats to the 2020-present COVID-19 pandemic.  The disclosures span demand volatility, channel mix upheaval, raw-material shortages, labour and transportation constraints, retail store closures, and uneven category performance (e.g., vitamins spike then soften).  Most references are not hypothetical: management cites concrete disruptions already experienced—factory fill-rate shortfalls, customer shutdowns, strain on the supply network, and brand-level sales/profit declines.  The company also warns that future government restrictions or new variants could prolong or intensify these effects.  Because the filing date (16-Feb-2023) is less than three years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  No meaningful mitigating language (e.g., fully effective hedges, robust alternative sourcing, or quantified offsets) accompanies the pandemic statements.  Accordingly, the overall pandemic-related risk profile is assessed as high, recent, and still evolving, warranting elevated snippet scores in the 6-9 range depending on the directness and specificity of the impact described.

CHD’s 2024 Form 10-K makes repeated, explicit references to the COVID-19 pandemic as a driver of both historical damage and continuing uncertainty.  Management discloses concrete operational consequences that have already materialised – e.g., supply-chain strain and demand volatility – and warns that these effects "could continue" despite the official end of the public-health emergency.  The wording is mostly qualitative (no dollar figures) but it is specific: it cites disruptions to raw-material availability, labour shortages, transportation bottlenecks and swings in consumer purchasing patterns as pandemic-linked hazards.  The company also layers pandemic risk together with other macro shocks (inflation, wars), showing it is embedded in CHD’s overall risk landscape.  Because the filing date (15 Feb 2024) is almost four years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), Time-Decay downgrades the severity from “acute” to “medium-term.”  Accordingly, snippet scores are capped in the mid-range (≈4-6).

CHRW’s 2021-02-19 filing contains numerous, recent-dated statements that tie the March-2020 COVID-19 pandemic directly to observable operational, financial and strategic stresses. The language spans both backward-looking impacts (e.g., 8 % freight-volume decline, carrier capacity shortages, 12 % drop in small-business customers, 7 % furlough of U.S./Canadian staff) and forward-looking uncertainty (possible material adverse effects, inability to estimate 2021 impact). These disclosures are specific, data-supported and framed as material threats to margins, volumes, labour availability and supply-chain continuity. Because the event is less than a year old at filing date, Time-Decay allows scores in the upper range. Mitigating language (temporary expectation, cost-cutting actions, remote-work success) modestly tempers but does not eliminate severity. Overall, COVID-19 represents a high-severity, still-evolving risk for CHRW, warranting mostly 7-10 scores per sentence with downward adjustments where the company notes mitigation or uncertainty rather than realised loss.

CHRW’s 2022 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as an ongoing, high-salience threat that has already produced concrete operational and financial consequences while remaining highly unpredictable.  Multiple sections—Risk Factors, MD&A market commentary, segment discussions and liquidity analysis—link the pandemic to supply-chain congestion, capacity shortages, volatile pricing, customer volume swings, labour and equipment constraints, remote-work transitions, working-capital pressure and even capital-allocation decisions.  The disclosures are largely backward-looking (actual declines in air capacity, 12 % customer loss, negative margins) but also forward-looking, stressing uncertainty around variants and duration.  Although the company notes certain mitigations (work-from-home, charter flights, continued customer service), these do not neutralise the material exposure described.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic is well within the 0-3-year window, so evidence can carry high severity scores (up to 10).  Overall, the risk is assessed as medium-high because impacts are already realised and quantitatively significant, yet some adaptive measures and recovery in 2021 temper the absolute severity.

CHRW’s Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and prospective risks that could materially affect performance. Management notes that the pandemic has already disrupted global supply chains, dampened demand in certain industries, created volatile pricing, and constrained carrier capacity—demonstrating direct operational impact. At the same time, the filing stresses that future effects remain "highly uncertain," pointing to the possibility of new variants and shifting government responses that could influence 2023 results. The narrative therefore blends backward-looking evidence of concrete harm with forward-looking contingency language. Specific operational channels—supply-chain disruption, labour and equipment shortages, travel restrictions, and shifts in freight rates—are identified, although no precise dollar figures are offered. Some mitigating language appears (e.g., “continuously monitoring,” improving air-freight capacity), which partially offsets severity. Applying the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic falls within the recent (0-3 year) window relative to the 17 Feb 2023 filing date, permitting higher risk scores; however, the lack of quantification and the presence of mitigation mean most snippets merit moderate-to-high rather than maximum scores.

COVID-19 is within the recent-to-medium window (≈4 years) for CHRW’s 2024 filing, so pandemic-related statements could still indicate elevated risk under the Time Decay Principle.  However, the Form 10-K offers only brief, umbrella language: the pandemic is grouped with other catastrophic events as a hypothetical future disruption, with no reference to specific lessons learned from 2020-2023, no metrics, and no continuing supply-chain, labour, remote-work or demand shocks.  The disclosure therefore frames the pandemic mainly as a contingent, forward-looking risk rather than an ongoing material impact.  The generic wording, lack of quantification and presence of multiple other hazards dilute the severity, so the overall evidence supports a low-to-moderate risk score despite the relative recency of the event.

Charter (CHTR) acknowledges COVID-19 as both an already-material and an ongoing, uncertain risk.  Because the filing is dated January 29 2021—well within one year of the WHO declaration on 11 March 2020—the pandemic is a recent event under the Time Decay Principle, so evidence can receive high severity scores.  The disclosure set contains two layers: (1) forward-looking risk language in Item 1A that highlights possible future churn, bad-debt, supply-chain disruption, vendor performance and workforce safety; and (2) backward-looking, quantified impacts in MD&A that reveal concrete financial effects in 2020 such as a $102 million receivable write-off, $163 million programming cost reductions, $217 million timing shifts, $218 million forthcoming customer credits, reduced advertising revenue, and higher labour expenses.  The company also details operational shifts like remote work, network capacity upgrades and safety protocols.  While management notes some mitigants (service continuity, improved collections, expected re-normalisation of bad-debt), the overall tone remains cautious, stressing that the ultimate impact “cannot be predicted.”  Given the specific, quantified losses and continuing uncertainty, the aggregate risk exposure is high (upper-mid range), justifying strong but differentiated snippet scores that reflect both the immediacy of realised impacts and the still-evolving nature of the threat.

Charter’s 2022 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 as a live, multi-faceted threat whose effects have already materialised and may intensify.  The disclosure blends backward-looking evidence (actual supply-chain interruptions, altered customer usage patterns, labour-force constraints and reduced service transactions) with forward-looking contingencies (unknown duration, vaccine uptake, further government restrictions).  Language such as “has caused economic disruption,” “significantly impacted,” and “materially affect our financial condition” indicates present, tangible exposure, even though no precise dollar amounts are supplied.  The company also details specific operational pinch-points—vendors, port congestion, employee health, on-site repairs—showing that the risk penetrates day-to-day operations rather than remaining abstract.  Mitigating language centres on uncertainty and the inability to forecast ultimate outcomes, but no concrete counter-measures are offered, so mitigation is weak.  Because the filing date (January 2022) falls within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high but not maximum severity scores; evidence justifies scores mostly in the 4-7 range, with direct, realised impacts scoring higher and purely speculative or heavily caveated statements scoring lower.

Charter’s 2023 filing contains only limited—but still relevant—references to pandemic-related pressures.  The clearest disclosure lies in the supply-chain section, where the company states that third-party vendors “have been disrupted” over the past three years by quarantines, factory shutdowns, port congestion and other health-related restrictions.  This language points to a direct and already-realized operational exposure: vendor delays could impede Charter’s ability to deploy network equipment and complete its rural build-outs.  The disclosure is recent (within three years of the March 2020 WHO declaration) and specific about the mechanisms of impact, so time-decay allows a fairly high severity score.  A second, more marginal sentence attributes a $191 million year-over-year swing in content costs to the NBA season’s COVID-19 delay.  While quantified, the effect is backward-looking and actually reduced costs, making it a weaker indicator of ongoing risk.  Overall, the pandemic is portrayed as a continuing but largely indirect threat—affecting Charter through suppliers and occasional content-timing quirks rather than through catastrophic revenue loss—so the aggregate risk is material but not extreme.

After a meticulous review of every sentence in the provided Risk Factors and MD&A sections, no passage explicitly or implicitly references COVID-19, pandemics, public-health emergencies, or the commonly associated business impacts (such as pandemic-driven supply-chain disruptions, workforce illness/shortages, office‐closure or remote-work transitions, or pandemic-induced changes in consumer demand). Although the filing does discuss generic competitive pressures, supply-chain dependencies, labor retention challenges, and economic downturn scenarios, none of those statements are framed in the context of a global pandemic or any lingering COVID-19 effects. Because the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores for recent events (0-3 years) only when the text links the risk directly to that event, and here there is no such linkage, every potential snippet scores 0. Accordingly, there is no qualifying evidence to micro-score, leading to a null evidence list.

Cincinnati Financial’s 2020 Form 10-K, filed in February 2021, conveys that the COVID-19 pandemic is a recent, already-manifesting source of material risk.  Multiple disclosures describe both realised impacts (an $85 million hit to earnings and specific legal-defence costs) and forward-looking threats (potentially material business-interruption verdicts, premium shrinkage, investment-portfolio shocks, liquidity strains from delayed receipts, and distribution-channel disruption).  The language is generally specific – it quantifies losses, names exposed business lines (commercial property, business interruption, investments), and details operational stressors such as agent shutdowns and remote-work transitions.  Some mitigation is noted (rapid shift to work-from-home, strong capital, reinsurance programmes), but these statements are modest compared with the breadth of adverse scenarios.  Given the filing date (within one year of the pandemic’s declaration), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the risk is immediate, multi-faceted and explicitly labelled as potentially “material,” warranting high micro-scores for the most critical evidence while still recognising occasional mitigating language where present.

Cincinnati Financial’s 2021-10-K (filed February 2022) presents COVID-19 as a live, multifaceted threat that intersects directly with the company’s core insurance activities, capital markets exposure and day-to-day operations.  The filing is contemporaneous with the pandemic (within two years) so Time-Decay allows high scores.  The disclosure palette ranges from concrete, quantified figures (e.g., $85 million of 2020 pandemic losses; specific reserve adjustments in 2021) to forward-looking warnings about potentially ‘material’ impacts from litigation, legislation, macro-economic instability and labour/operational disruption.  The most acute risk is legal: the company is already a defendant in COVID-19 business-interruption lawsuits and fears adverse court or legislative outcomes that could compel it to honour claims for which no premium was collected—an exposure explicitly described as ‘material’ to financial condition and cash-flows.  Second-order but still significant are reserve-estimation uncertainties and the prospect of further loss development as the pandemic evolves.  The company also acknowledges capital-market volatility, remote-work operational shifts and earlier premium-growth dampening, but partially mitigates these with statements about successful work-from-home transitions and limited 2021 premium impact.  Overall, the risk is recent, active, explicitly linked to the company and partially quantified, producing high but not maximal severity evidence scores.

Cincinnati Financial’s 2022-10-K positions COVID-19 as a still-material, evolving threat that is both backward-looking (actual claims and litigation already on the books) and forward-looking (legislative, judicial and macro-economic uncertainty).  Although management notes minimal premium impact in 2022 and cites current reserve adequacy, the filing repeatedly acknowledges open-ended litigation over business-interruption coverage, potential for reserve shocks, and broader capital-market volatility.  Quantified data are provided ($85 million 2020 pandemic losses; small 2021 reserve tweaks), but the company concedes that future adverse court rulings could be “material” to results and cash-flows.  Because the pandemic began less than three years before the 2023 filing date, Time-Decay allows high severity scores.  Mitigating language (current reserve adequacy, modest 2022 premium impact) slightly tempers the risk, but overall the disclosure reflects an ongoing, significant exposure that could rapidly escalate, warranting upper-mid severity for most evidence.

CI’s 2021-02-25 filing was prepared less than one year after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  The risk discussion is extensive and multi-layered: management states that COVID-19 has already produced material adverse effects (e.g., testing and treatment costs that exceeded savings from deferred care) and warns that the final impact could remain material because the scale, scope and duration of the crisis are still unknown.  The company enumerates concrete transmission channels—supply-chain breakdowns, labor shortages from quarantines, remote-work productivity issues, spikes in medical claims, revenue pressure from premium relief, regulatory volatility around tele-health and vaccination mandates, and macro-economic weakness that erodes customer volumes.  Although the filing describes a few mitigating actions (tele-health expansion, support programmes), those are sparse and largely qualitative; the narrative is dominated by direct, specific and forward-looking threats.  Given the recency of the event, the specificity of the disclosures and the fact that some impacts are already being felt, the overall pandemic risk exposure for CI is assessed as high, meriting individual snippet scores chiefly in the 5-8 range.

CI’s 2022-02-24 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as a present, multi-dimensional and potentially material threat that has already disrupted its operations and could continue to erode earnings, cash-flows and liquidity.  The disclosures are largely contemporaneous (within two years of the WHO declaration) and describe both realised impacts (higher testing and treatment costs, deferral-of-care distortions, labour and supply-chain friction, remote-work cyber-risk) and forward-looking uncertainties (variant emergence, regulatory mandates, vaccination efficacy).  Language is concrete—using terms such as “material adverse effect,” “has adversely affected,” and enumerating specific operational pinch-points—yet generally un-quantified.  The company also acknowledges limits to its forecasting ability (“cannot estimate the full impact”) and highlights that many drivers are outside management’s control, reinforcing residual risk.  Mitigating references (e.g., vaccine promotion, supply-chain optimisation) temper but do not eliminate exposure.  Given the recency (0-3 yrs), breadth, and demonstrated financial effects, the individual snippet severities cluster in the upper-mid range (6–9), consistent with the Time-Decay Principle.

CI’s 2023 filing describes COVID-19 as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat that is already affecting performance and could do so further.  Nearly three years after the WHO declaration the company still reports material adverse impacts on cash-flow and earnings and explicitly warns that scale, scope and duration remain unknown.  The narrative links the pandemic to multiple concrete risk channels – higher medical costs, revenue pressure, workforce illness, supply-chain interruptions, cybersecurity exposure created by remote work, and macro-economic weakness. Individual sentence scores below reflect this balance of aggravating versus mitigating factors, capped according to recent-event guidelines.

CLX’s 2023 filing frames COVID-19 as both an historical shock that has already disrupted performance and a continuing, forward-looking threat. These disclosures are recent (within three years of the 2020 onset), attribute realised harm directly to COVID-19 and signal that management still views the risk as live. CLX explicitly acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic has already harmed, and may still harm, its business through supply-chain breakdowns, labor shortages, vendor failures and broader macro-economic stress.  The wording blends backward-looking language ("has had") with forward-looking qualifiers ("could continue to"), indicating that management sees the pandemic’s effects as both realized and still developing. Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the 4-6 range, reflecting a live but moderating threat.

CL’s 2021-02-18 filing describes the COVID-19 pandemic as both an already-experienced shock and an ongoing, forward-looking risk that permeates every layer of its operating model—demand, supply chain, workforce, logistics, capital markets and strategic outlook. Therefore, most snippets receive scores in the 6-9 range, reflecting significant, current and specifically articulated pandemic exposure.

Colgate-Palmolive’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as a current, multi-faceted threat that is already influencing operations and will continue to do so for the foreseeable future. COVID-19 is portrayed by Colgate-Palmolive (CL) as a recent, multi-dimensional threat that has already disrupted – and may still disrupt – virtually every pillar of its global value chain. COVID-19 is treated by Colgate-Palmolive (CL) as a still-relevant, but gradually moderating, enterprise-wide risk. Overall, the pandemic remains a meaningful, though diminishing, risk driver for CL’s operations, and the extracted snippets below are scored accordingly.

CMCSA’s 2021-02-04 filing contains extensive, concrete disclosures that COVID-19 is both an already-realised and a continuing, material threat to virtually every line of business. Comcast’s 2022 Form 10-K squarely acknowledges that COVID-19 is an ongoing, material, enterprise-wide risk. Although the company cites no precise dollar figures, it repeatedly uses “material” and “material adverse effect,” signalling high severity. Under the Time-Decay Principle, a March 2020 event discussed in a February 2022 filing qualifies as “recent,” so snippet scores may justifiably fall in the 7-10 range for unequivocal, enterprise-level impacts, and somewhat lower (3-6) where the discussion is narrower, less quantified, or partially mitigated.

COVID-19 is prominently acknowledged across the 2023 CMCSA filing as both a realized and an ongoing risk driver. CMCSA’s 2024 filing presents COVID-19 primarily as a medium-term, lingering operational threat rather than an acute financial crisis. CME’s 2021 Form 10-K squarely links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and forward-looking threats across operations, revenues and strategic execution. The narrative contains (i) direct statements of actual impacts already felt—most notably a fall in trading volume and the closure of the open-outcry floor; (ii) detailed enumerations of potential continuing impacts such as labour shortages, remote-work productivity drag, supplier-side disruption, market-access limits and shifts in product demand; and (iii) acknowledgement that such effects could be “material” and persist “for a significant period of time”. Mitigating language is minimal (no firm counter-measures quantified), so snippet scores cluster in the 5-9 range, consistent with a recent event displaying tangible but mostly un-quantified impacts.

CME’s 2022 Form 10-K positions COVID-19 as a recent, already-material threat that simultaneously introduces acute operational shocks and lingering strategic uncertainties. The filing makes clear that the pandemic has *already* disrupted CME’s markets, employees, clients and suppliers (direct impact) while also warning that the *ultimate* duration and magnitude remain unknowable (forward-looking risk).  The narrative is highly specific: it cites labour shortages, employee attrition, remote-work productivity drag, supply-chain interruptions, vendor failure, clearing-member stress, market-access restrictions and even heightened cyber risk.  These references are not abstract—they connect directly to revenue drivers such as trading volume, product demand and expansion initiatives.  Because the disclosure is made within two years of the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high per-snippet scores (up to 10).  Nevertheless, scores are tempered when the language is generic, when impacts are only potential, or when the company notes mitigation steps (e.g., work-from-home protocols).  Overall, the risk is severe, recent, multi-faceted and largely unmitigated, justifying a cluster of high but differentiated snippet scores.

CME’s 2023-02-27 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a live, multi-faceted threat that has already disrupted the firm while still holding the potential for further material damage.  The disclosure sits in the Risk Factors section, uses present-tense verbs ("has disrupted," "continues to cause"), and enumerates concrete operational channels of impact – labour shortages, supply-chain interruptions, remote-work vulnerabilities, declining trading volumes, stress on clearing members, and cybersecurity exposure. Overall, the risk evidence is recent, specific and ongoing, warranting upper-moderate to high snippet scores (5-8) with no snippet exceeding 8 due to absence of quantified losses.

Only one passage in CME’s 2023 Form 10-K explicitly references pandemic exposure.  It places pandemics alongside a long list of exogenous factors that can dampen or shift trading volumes. CMG’s 2021 filing provides abundant, current-period evidence that the COVID-19 pandemic is exerting a material, multi-faceted strain on the company.  The disclosure spans already-incurred impacts (restaurant closures, higher operating costs, reduced guest traffic, delayed capital projects) and forward-looking uncertainties (future supply-chain shortfalls, labour availability, demand recovery timelines).  Language is explicit—using terms such as “has adversely affected,” “materially,” and “could continue”—and ties the pandemic to core financial metrics like liquidity, sales and growth capacity.  Because the filing date (February 2021) sits well within three years of the WHO’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  While CMG notes certain mitigating actions (e.g., safety protocols, supplier communication), these are outweighed by the breadth of direct disruptions and the company’s own admission that it cannot forecast the pandemic’s duration or ultimate financial toll.  Overall, the risk profile is acute and ongoing, warranting elevated scores across most extracted sentences.

CMG’s Form 10-K makes it clear that COVID-19 is not merely a hypothetical threat but an event that has already disrupted virtually every facet of the company’s business and will likely continue to do so.  The filing, dated only two years after the WHO declaration, describes concrete historical impacts—mandatory dining-room closures, supply-chain bottlenecks, labour shortages during the “great resignation,” inflationary pressure on commodities, and even higher construction costs for new stores. Most of the language is specific and rooted in observed operational or financial outcomes, with only limited mitigating statements (e.g., “no significant disruptions to date”).  Given the recency of the pandemic (well within the 0–3-year window), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores; nonetheless, individual sentences are calibrated according to the degree of detail, directness, quantification, and presence of mitigating factors.  Overall, COVID-19 presents a high, multi-dimensional and continuing risk to CMG’s revenue growth, margins, labour model and supply chain integrity.

COVID-19 is addressed in CMG’s February 2023 10-K primarily as an ongoing, recently-experienced driver of cost inflation, supply-chain disruption, labour tightness and shifting customer behaviour. Overall, the evidence portrays a moderate-to-high residual risk: the pandemic has already affected costs and growth, and management warns those impacts could continue, but the disclosures stop short of providing quantified dollar figures, tempering maximum severity.

CMG’s 2024 filing contains only broad, forward-looking references to pandemics rather than detailed, COVID-19-specific disclosures. CMI’s 2021 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as an acute, multi-dimensional threat that is already depressing revenues and could further erode operations, cash flow and liquidity. Overall, the disclosure evidences a high, continuing risk (recent, direct, already impacting results), moderated only slightly by references to facility re-openings and vaccine roll-out. CMI’s 2022 10-K paints COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-dimensional risk that has already dented financial results and could further erode performance. CMI’s 2024 Form 10-K refers to the COVID-19 pandemic only in umbrella phrases such as “pandemic restrictions,” “public health crises (epidemics or pandemics)” and “future pandemics.”  The references are embedded in broader risk narratives about supply-chain delays, multinational operations and catastrophic‐event planning. CNC’s 2021 filing ties the still-unfolding COVID-19 pandemic to a broad set of operational, financial and strategic risks. Accordingly, snippet scores cluster between 4 and 8, reflecting recent timing, detailed linkage to core value drivers, and limited mitigating language.

Centene’s 2022-02-22 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a highly salient, still-unfolding threat. Consequently, the extracted evidence warrants elevated—but not always maximum—severity scores, with modest downward adjustments where impacts to date have been favourable (e.g., membership gains).

Because the filing date (February 2024) is four years after the pandemic was declared but the impacts are still current, the Time Decay Principle places COVID-19 in the medium-term window; therefore, individual evidence scores are capped in the 4-6 range.
