CenterPoint Energy’s 2021 Form 10-K was filed less than one year after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  The filing contains numerous, detailed disclosures tying COVID-19 to tangible, present-day impacts across almost every business line: (i) direct financial hits such as goodwill and equity-method impairments, higher bad-debt reserves, and lower cash distributions; (ii) operational pressures including lower commercial-industrial load, moratoria on disconnections, potential supply-chain delays, remote-work cyber-security threats and workforce‐availability concerns; and (iii) regulatory and liquidity risks such as delayed rate cases, possible rate restrictions and the need for additional external financing.  Importantly, management concedes that it “expects the COVID-19 pandemic to adversely impact us in future quarters” but cannot predict the magnitude, underscoring forward-looking uncertainty.  Although the company notes some mitigating factors (no major supply-chain disruption to date, regulatory deferral mechanisms, continued monitoring), these are outweighed by the breadth, immediacy and quantification of adverse effects already experienced.  Consequently, most evidence snippets merit high but differentiated scores: sentences citing actual impairments or measurable financial strain receive 8-9 points; those describing ongoing but unquantified exposures receive 6-7; and statements dominated by generic uncertainty or limited mitigation receive 4-5.  No snippet is scored the maximum 10 because the impacts, while material, are not portrayed as existential threats to solvency, and several mitigating mechanisms are acknowledged.

CNP’s 2022-02-22 10-K shows COVID-19 is a live, multifaceted enterprise-wide threat.  The filing comes less than two years after WHO declared the pandemic, so under the Time Decay Principle a high severity band (up to 10) is permissible.  Management discloses both realised and prospective impacts: (i) actual and continuing supply-chain disruptions that have already forced a down-sizing of a large solar project and have raised input costs, (ii) weakened counter-party credit quality and higher bad-debt risk as economic conditions deteriorated, (iii) regulatory and compliance friction from evolving health mandates, (iv) labour-force and remote-work strain that could impair operations and heighten cyber-exposure, and (v) potential demand destruction for electricity and gas if commercial/industrial customers remain shuttered.  Although no dollar amounts are attached, the language ties the pandemic directly to material adverse effects on cash flow, liquidity, capital execution and rate recovery.  Mitigation language is limited and largely conditional (e.g., “may”, “could”).  Therefore individual sentences warrant mid-to-high single-digit scores (4-8), reflecting significant but mostly un-quantified, still-developing risks within the 0-3 year window.

CenterPoint Energy’s 2022 Form 10-K openly recognizes COVID-19 as an ongoing, enterprise-wide risk that has already produced tangible effects (e.g., supply-chain delays, labor shortages and liquidity strain on retail electric providers) and could continue to depress revenue, inflate costs and disrupt operations.  The language is largely qualitative—no dollar amounts are cited—but it expressly links the pandemic to specific operational areas: receivables collection, materials procurement, workforce availability, project timing and regulatory processes.  Management frames COVID-19 both retrospectively (the company has already ‘experienced’ impacts) and prospectively (future variants and prolonged disruptions ‘could’ further affect demand, capital plans and customer payments).  Because the filing date (17 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO declaration of the pandemic, the Time Decay Principle permits relatively high severity scores.  However, the absence of quantified losses, the sharing of blame with other macro factors (inflation, weather, etc.) and the lack of detailed mitigation language temper the overall risk rating, leading to moderate-to-high—but not maximum—scores for the extracted evidence.

COVID-19 is referenced throughout the 2024 filing as a continuing but now-evolving business risk.  Because the pandemic began almost four years before the filing date, the comments are framed less as acute crisis effects and more as medium-term economic, credit-quality and supply-chain uncertainties that could still impair cash flow, capital execution and labor availability.  The company points to (1) weakened retail-electric-provider liquidity that could delay collections, (2) pandemic-driven global supply-chain bottlenecks that raise costs for critical materials, and (3) the broader possibility that future variants or health emergencies will amplify other listed risks (workforce, regulatory timelines, customer demand).  All disclosures are qualitative and un-quantified, yet they tie COVID-19 directly to cash-flow, operational and strategic execution threats that remain “ongoing” or “future” oriented.  Given the Time-Decay principle, evidence scores are capped in the mid-range (4-6) to reflect that the pandemic is now a medium-term rather than immediate event, even though the company still describes specific financial and operational exposures.

Capital One’s 2021 filing depicts COVID-19 as the single most pervasive near-term threat to the firm’s earnings, liquidity and capital.  The text confirms that the pandemic is already producing material adverse effects – lower purchase volume, suppressed loan growth, multi-billion-dollar credit-loss builds, branch re-configurations, remote-work costs and suspended share-repurchases – and that these pressures could intensify if public-health or macro conditions deteriorate.  Management repeatedly characterises the risk as both existing (observed 2020 impact on net income, capital and operations) and prospective (future credit losses, recession, regulatory actions).  The disclosures are specific: they cite a “substantial build” in reserves during the first two quarters of 2020, higher capital costs, operational strain from work-from-home, and participation in government relief programmes that entail compliance and litigation exposure.  Because the filing date (25 Feb 2021) is less than one year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7-10).  The company’s language is largely un-mitigated – noting uncertainty rather than offsetting actions – so most snippets warrant scores in the 8-9 range, with modest deductions where mitigation or uncertainty tempers the immediacy of harm.

Capital One’s 2022 Form 10-K shows that, two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, management still views the virus and its knock-on effects as a high-severity, near-term risk driver.  The filing links COVID-19 to concrete, business-relevant threats: labour shortages, global supply-chain disruptions, higher inflation, suppressed purchase volumes, elevated credit losses, operational challenges from extensive remote-work arrangements, and exposure to litigation and compliance risk stemming from government relief programmes.  These statements are forward-looking but grounded in the company’s lived experience (e.g., Omicron, prior forbearance actions, Federal Reserve capital restrictions).  They remain largely unquantified, yet they repeatedly signal the possibility of “material” or “significant” adverse impacts across revenue, credit costs, operations and capital.  Given the filing date (February 2022) falls within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, COF discloses a current, multifaceted, and systemic risk profile; the breadth of potential impacts and the persistence of uncertainty justify high, though not maximal, evidence scores.

Capital One’s 2023 Form 10-K explicitly acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic, although entering a recovery phase, still represents a live and multi-faceted enterprise risk.  The filing describes tangible, continuing headwinds—labour shortages, supply-chain disruption, inflationary pressure—and links them to concrete financial exposures such as lower purchase volumes, higher credit losses, liquidity strain, increased capital costs and incremental operating expense from a post-pandemic hybrid-work model.  Disclosures are largely forward-looking ("may", "could") yet provide specific channels of transmission that elevate credibility (credit losses, purchase volume, allowance builds, supply-chain issues).  Because the filing date (24 Feb 2023) sits almost exactly three years after the WHO declaration of a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high—but no longer peak—severity scoring; risks are still current but beginning to normalize.  The overall picture is one of persistent, material operational and financial exposure tempered only modestly by mitigants such as monitoring procedures and potential management actions.  Consequently, evidence snippets generally earn upper-mid scores (4-8) rather than the absolute maximum, reflecting a residual, not unprecedented, threat profile.

Capital One’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only limited, largely forward-looking references to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company places the pandemic in a broader bucket of “catastrophic events” and “disease outbreaks” that could disrupt operations, damage infrastructure, and hurt financial results.  No quantified dollar impacts or detailed post-2020 lessons are provided, indicating that management now views COVID-19 primarily as a residual, medium-term macro-operating risk rather than an acute crisis.  The filing does, however, highlight second-order effects that were first triggered or magnified by the pandemic—labour shortages, global supply-chain disruptions, hybrid/remote work challenges, and shifts in consumer behaviour that could depress credit-card demand or commercial real-estate values.  Because the pandemic began four years before the filing, the Time-Decay Principle caps maximum evidentiary scores in the mid-range (4-6) even for explicit pandemic language, while more generic, indirect references merit lower scores.  Overall, COVID-19 is portrayed as a potential, forward-looking risk backdrop rather than a current material drag, yielding a moderate risk assessment.

The filing, dated December 10 2021, repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective harm across virtually every facet of the COO Group’s operations.  Statements describe (i) already-experienced declines in sales, increased costs and operational inefficiencies, (ii) continuing supply-chain, manufacturing, liquidity and workforce challenges, (iii) macro-economic uncertainty and sector-specific disruptions (e.g., clinic closures, remote-work cyber-risk) and (iv) an open-ended horizon of possible further deterioration tied to virus variants and governmental responses.  Because the pandemic is well within the 0-3-year “recent-event” window, the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  The disclosures are mostly qualitative but very specific (facility shutdowns, cost inflation, covenant breaches, inventory write-offs, etc.) and often framed as material or already-incurred impacts, indicating an elevated, ongoing threat.  Mitigating remarks are scarce (one note of no ‘significant disruption’ to raw-material access), so overall risk remains high, warranting upper-mid-range snippet scores (5-7) for direct, detailed impacts and lower (1-3) where language is more generic or conditional.

COVID-19 erupted in early 2020, so by the December 2024 filing date the outbreak is roughly four-and-a-half years old—squarely in the Time-Decay “medium-term” window (4-10 years).  The filing still cites pandemics (often grouped with supply-chain disruptions, labour shortages and macro-economic volatility) as a continuing enterprise-wide hazard.  The disclosures, however, are high-level and qualitative: they flag uncertainty and potential adverse effects but give no quantified dollar impacts and cite no current operational shut-downs.  This indicates that management views pandemic fallout as an ongoing, but now more background, risk rather than an acute crisis.  Accordingly, individual snippets warrant moderate scores (4-6).  Sentences that name “pandemic conditions” or explicitly bind pandemics to supply-chain and labour issues receive higher marks; generic references to inflationary pressures tied to logistics constraints are scored slightly lower because the link to COVID-19 is only implicit.  No meaningful mitigating actions (e.g., robust contingency planning or quantified hedging) are provided in these passages, so there are few negative offsets.

COVID-19 is addressed throughout COR’s November 2021 filing as both an already-realised shock and a continuing, multi-faceted threat.  Management describes concrete impacts that have already occurred—temporary shutdowns of distribution centres after employee infections, higher cold-chain volumes for vaccine logistics, and customer liquidity stress stemming from capital-market volatility.  They also flag forward-looking exposures: possible manufacturer shutdowns, labour retention problems tied to vaccine mandates, further supply-chain disruptions, demand weakness if prescriptions fall, and higher financing costs.  The language is mostly specific (naming supply chains, cold-chain capacity, customer credit, employee health and WBA reliance) and repeatedly uses materiality qualifiers (“material adverse effect”).  Because the filing date (23-Nov-2021) is well within three years of the WHO pandemic declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle permits elevated severity scores (up to 10).  I therefore rate realised, quantified or operationally granular statements in the upper mid-range (7-9), while purely contingent or generic remarks score lower (4-6).  No pre-event discounting is necessary.

AmerisourceBergen’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that is already depressing operations while still carrying unpredictable forward-looking consequences.  Several passages confirm realised damage—supply-chain bottlenecks, higher cold-chain volumes, volatility in credit markets, and reductions in sales of certain pandemic-related therapies—establishing that the pandemic is not merely hypothetical.  The company also itemises forward risks: continued product shortages, labour retention problems tied to vaccine mandates, additional legal exposure, and knock-on effects on customer liquidity and prescription volumes.  Although a few mitigating actions are noted (business-continuity protocols, employee-safety measures), most language is precautionary and non-quantified, using modal verbs like “could,” “may,” and “expect.”  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is a very recent event (within three years of the 2022 filing), so elevated scores are warranted; however, the absence of precise dollar figures or hard probability estimates tempers the severity.  Overall, the disclosure set signals a moderate-to-high risk profile (upper-mid single-digit micro-scores) that is both current and evolving, rather than a legacy or purely contingent concern.

Cencora’s 2023 filing still links the 2020-era COVID-19 pandemic to material business risks, but the tone has clearly shifted from crisis-mode to a more residual, scenario-planning posture.  The Risk Factors section explicitly catalogues forward-looking threats – supply-chain breakdowns, labour constraints tied to vaccination mandates, demand volatility, and cascading effects on key partners such as WBA – while the MD&A quantifies an actual $1 billion year-over-year drop in COVID-19-related product revenue.  These disclosures show both realised impacts (lost sales) and persisting uncertainties (future pandemics or renewed outbreaks).  Language remains largely conditional (“could”, “may”) but is supported by concrete references to prior pandemic disruptions, signalling that management views the threat as credible.  Because the pandemic began in March 2020, the evidence sits just under four years old; under the Time Decay Principle, snippets may still score in the upper-mid range (roughly 6–8) but not the absolute maximum reserved for brand-new shocks.  Mitigating measures are scarcely detailed, so most statements remain aggravating.  Overall, pandemic-related risk for COR is assessed as moderate-to-high owing to demonstrated revenue impacts and continued exposure across supply chain, labour, and customer demand channels.

COR’s 2024 filing still flags pandemic-related challenges, but the tone has clearly shifted from acute crisis management to an ongoing, background operational risk.  Nearly five years after WHO’s declaration (March 2020), management now frames COVID-19 and future pandemics mainly as potential disruptors to key partners’ distribution facilities and to the broader supply chain rather than as a current, quantifiable hit to COR’s own facilities.  The disclosures are forward-looking and largely generic ("if operations are disrupted … whether by a pandemic or otherwise").  They acknowledge that a pandemic could hinder the Walgreens Boots Alliance (WBA) relationship—material because WBA drives a large share of revenue—and could hamper COR through wider “public health issues.”  At the same time, the MD&A shows that pandemic-linked products (COVID-19 therapies and vaccines) actually boosted 2024 revenue, signaling that the company has partly benefited from the pandemic’s demand shifts.  Applying the Time Decay Principle (event ≈ 4 ½ years old), these statements warrant moderate, not high, severity scores: they remain relevant but are neither quantified nor unique, and mitigating language is prevalent.  Overall pandemic risk therefore sits in the mid-range (scores 3-5), reflecting residual but not immediate threat.

Costco’s 2021-10-06 filing contains numerous, recent and forward-looking disclosures that explicitly connect the COVID-19 pandemic to material operational, financial and strategic risks.  Because the pandemic began in March 2020—well within the 0-3-year “recent” window—the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  The language is largely specific: it cites concrete channels of impact such as supply-chain bottlenecks, labour shortages, inflation in certain merchandise categories, cyber-exposure from remote work, fulfilment delays from online order spikes, and potential facility closures.  Costco also acknowledges cascading effects (e.g., reputational damage, litigation, heightened exposure to other risk categories).  While many sentences use probabilistic phrasing (“may,” “could”), the filing simultaneously states that COVID-19 “continues to affect” current performance—asserting both realised and potential impacts.  No meaningful mitigating language (such as insurance recoveries or quantified cost offsets) is offered.  Accordingly, individual snippets receive high but differentiated scores: sentences documenting broad, multi-faceted and already-manifest impacts score near the top of the scale (8-9), whereas more peripheral or generic mentions are scored moderately (4-6).

COST’s filing contains multiple, recent-period acknowledgements that the COVID-19 pandemic is exerting both ongoing and potential future pressure across virtually every operational dimension—supply chain reliability, labour availability and cost, inflation, remote-work cyber-exposure, and overall consumer demand.  Most disclosures appear in the mandatory Risk Factors section, so they are forward-looking in tone, yet several passages explicitly concede already-incurred effects such as supply-chain interruptions and category-specific inflation.  The language is largely qualitative—no dollar figures are supplied—but it is unequivocal in describing actual disruptions and in warning that COVID-19 could amplify other enumerated risks.  Because the event is well inside the 0-3-year “recent” window and COST openly states continuing adverse impacts with no firm end-point, the overall risk profile is assessed as elevated.  Some mitigating references (e.g., expectation that facilities will stay open) appear, but they are outweighed by the breadth and immediacy of cited vulnerabilities, supporting generally high—but not maximal—severity scores in the micro-scorecards that follow.

Costco’s 2023-10-11 filing acknowledges COVID-19 as an ongoing, but now medium-term, enterprise-wide risk.  Management no longer describes the pandemic as an acute disruption; instead, it is framed as a forward-looking uncertainty that can still influence supply-chain reliability, labour availability, consumer demand, litigation exposure and overall financial performance.  The narrative is qualitative and does not quantify impacts, yet it does single out specific operating vectors (inventory in-stock positions, cost of doing business, access to inventory, etc.), showing that management still perceives material exposure even 3½ years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  Because the disclosure is current (within four years) but not accompanied by hard numbers or evidence of realised losses, the Time Decay Principle places the risk in the “medium-term” bucket, capping appropriate snippet scores in the 4-6 range.  Overall, the language is specific enough to demonstrate continuing vigilance, but its conditional phrasing (“could affect”, “uncertain”, “may result”) and absence of quantified impacts moderate the severity assessment.

The filing, dated nearly five years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, positions pandemic-related disclosures as forward-looking yet still salient.  COST repeatedly acknowledges pandemics as an on-going risk driver that can disrupt operations, squeeze supply chains, create labour shortages, alter consumer demand, and impair financial performance.  The language is mostly qualitative and un-quantified, signalling that management views pandemic effects as material but not readily measurable.  No new, quantified impact data are given, yet the company enumerates concrete operational pinch-points—warehouse delays, inventory shortages, labour availability, litigation exposure—which elevates the discussion above a boiler-plate recitation.  Under the Time Decay Principle, a 2020-origin event analysed in a 2024 filing falls into the 4–10-year “medium-term” window, capping individual snippet scores in the mid-range.  Overall, the risk is ongoing, broad-based, and somewhat specific, warranting moderate severity scores (4-6) for the strongest passages, with lower scores for generic uncertainty statements.

CPAY’s 2021-02-26 filing provides an extensive, contemporaneous discussion of COVID-19.  The company discloses both realised 2020 impacts and forward-looking exposures: an actual, material drop in transaction volumes and revenue; workforce disruptions from remote-work mandates; credit-loss events; and broad macro-economic pressures that can contract demand for fuel, lodging and cross-border payments.  The language is firm (“significant decrease”, “materially adverse”) and repeatedly links the pandemic to specific financial drivers—volume, liquidity, credit defaults and capital-market access—rather than using boiler-plate phrasing.  Several passages emphasise the persistence of these pressures even after the health crisis abates, suggesting structural demand shifts.  Mitigating actions (cost controls, work-from-home transition, tightening credit lines) are mentioned but are framed as uncertain in effectiveness.  Given that the filing is less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores; however, snippets that merely reference generic uncertainty or include explicit mitigation receive modest deductions.  Overall, COVID-19 constitutes a live, material enterprise risk with multi-faceted operational and financial consequences for CPAY.

COVID-19 is presented as a recent (≤ 3 yrs) and still-unfolding external shock with both realised and prospective consequences for CPAY.  The filing explicitly discloses that the pandemic already reduced transaction volumes in 2020, forced operating changes (remote work, travel curbs) and tightened labour availability.  Management also links COVID-19 to wider macro-financial stresses—capital-market volatility, inflation, energy prices and continuing global-supply-chain disruption—each of which could cascade into revenue, credit-loss and liquidity pressures.  The narrative balances current impacts (depressed spending, workforce modifications, decreased volumes) with forward-looking uncertainty, repeatedly stressing that future developments (variants, vaccine uptake, regulatory measures) remain “highly uncertain.”  Although no dollar figures are provided, the language is specific to CPAY’s operations and cites material adverse effects on results of operations, liquidity and access to capital.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic falls in the 0-3 year window, permitting high scores.  However, because most disclosures are qualitative and unquantified—and some contain mitigating notes about recovery in 2021—individual sentence scores are capped in the mid-to-high range (5-9) rather than the maximum 10.

COVID-19 is framed by CPAY (FLEETCOR) as both a realized and continuing enterprise-wide hazard.  Management concedes that the pandemic already “negatively impacted” operating results, liquidity, consumer demand, labour availability and day-to-day practices (e.g., forced remote work and travel bans).  At the same time, the filing stresses that future variants or lingering macroeconomic knock-ons (inflation, fuel-price volatility, capital-market dislocation, supply-chain stress) could further harm revenue, credit access and workforce stability.  The language is largely qualitative—there is no dollar quantification—but it is detailed, covers multiple risk vectors (demand, supply chain, labour, finance) and notes that some effects have already occurred.  Given the February-2023 filing date, the pandemic still falls in the Time-Decay “recent (0-3 yrs)” window, permitting high severity scores where warranted.  However, several passages also highlight uncertainty, easing of restrictions and mitigation efforts, which temper scores.  Overall, the disclosures signal a material but not existential risk: strong evidence of past disruption with cautious, forward-looking warnings rather than precise financial impact statements.

CPAY’s 2024 Form 10-K places pandemic risk primarily in the forward-looking, macroeconomic bucket rather than citing direct, quantified damage already incurred.  References to COVID-19 appear as illustrative parentheticals inside broader risk factors—e.g., travel bans, credit deterioration, and operational disruption—that could hurt transaction volumes or increase customer defaults.  The language is mostly conditional ("could", "may") and bundled with other catastrophes, signalling management views the pandemic as a continuing but diminishing external threat rather than an acute crisis.  Because the filing date is almost four years after the WHO declaration (medium-term under the Time-Decay Principle), maximum severity is capped at a moderate level.  The absence of specific dollar impacts or novel mitigation steps further tempers the assessment.  Overall, the pandemic remains a material but generalized risk, meriting mid-range scores (≈5 for direct COVID-19 mentions; ≈2-3 for generic pandemic clauses).

Campbell Soup Company’s 2021-09-23 filing provides a dense, multi-layered discussion of how the COVID-19 pandemic has already affected—and may continue to affect—the business.  The disclosure blends backward-looking facts (e.g., experienced workforce and trucking shortages, a surge in at-home consumption) with forward-looking contingencies (e.g., possible plant shutdowns, commodity volatility, channel shifts).  The language is specific, listing concrete operational pinch-points such as manufacturing closures, labor absenteeism, third-party failures, logistics bottlenecks, IT stress from remote work, and heightened commodity costs.  Although the company notes certain mitigating factors—vaccines, cost-saving initiatives, hedging and safety protocols—these are largely conditional and do not eliminate the residual risk.  Because the pandemic’s onset (03-11-2020) is well within three years of the filing, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  However, the absence of hard dollar quantification and the presence of some mitigating statements keep most individual sentences below the absolute maximum of 10.  Overall, the evidence reflects a high, but not catastrophic, risk profile that is both current and evolving.

Campbell Soup Company’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as both an already-realized and still-evolving enterprise risk.  Multiple passages document tangible, recent impacts—commodity cost spikes, workforce disruptions, and altered innovation timelines—demonstrating that the pandemic is not merely theoretical.  Other statements are forward-looking, warning of future outbreaks, labor shortages, and possible facility shutdowns.  The language ranges from hard evidence ("we have experienced temporary workforce disruptions") to broader cautions ("could heighten many other risk factors").  Because the filing date is within three years of the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores for direct, quantified, or multi-dimensional impacts, while more generic or partially mitigated statements merit moderate or low scores.  Overall, the risk level is material: COVID-19 has already increased costs and disrupted operations and remains capable of amplifying supply-chain, labor, and demand-pattern volatility for CPB.

COVID-19 is treated in CPB’s 2023 filing primarily as an ongoing external threat that can destabilise input costs, disrupt supply chains, constrain labour, alter consumer demand, and heighten IT-system vulnerability through a sustained remote-work environment.  The company frames most statements in a forward-looking, contingency style (“could,” “may”), yet one passage explicitly concedes that CPB “has been, and may continue to be, adversely affected” by pandemic-related macro-economic conditions—an acknowledgement of realised impact.  No sentence quantifies dollar effects, so the risk evidence is qualitative but still material because (i) the pandemic began in 2020, placing it well inside the 0-3-year ‘recent’ window; (ii) the disclosures tie COVID-19 to core cost drivers (commodities, labour, logistics) and to foundational consumer-behaviour shifts; and (iii) none of the passages identify strong mitigants beyond routine hedging and price actions.  Under the Time Decay Principle the pandemic remains highly relevant, but the lack of numeric detail and the largely conditional language temper maximum scoring.  Overall, the evidence warrants moderate-to-elevated snippet scores ranging from 2-7, reflecting real but unquantified impacts within a still-recent horizon.

Copart’s 2021-09-27 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a recent, still-evolving threat with both realized and prospective impacts.  The filing states that the pandemic already caused “substantial declines” in vehicle assignments and lower processed volumes, explicitly connecting these effects to the March 2020 onset and subsequent shelter-in-place orders.  Management also warns of forward-looking risks—continued miles-driven reductions, government restrictions, supply-chain disruptions, staffing outbreaks, title-processing delays, and cost inefficiencies—that could depress revenues or raise operating expenses.  While the company notes certain mitigants (essential-business status, on-line auctions, higher average selling prices, and process adjustments that avoided material cost spikes), these are framed as conditional and potentially temporary.  Given the filing date (≈18 months after the WHO declaration) the Time-Decay Principle places the pandemic in the 0-3 year “recent” bucket, allowing elevated scores.  Nevertheless, the language is a mix of concrete historical data (actual volume drops) and probabilistic qualifiers (“may,” “could”), so per-sentence severity ranges from moderate to high.  Overall, COVID-19 represents a significant ongoing risk, with downside amplified by uncertain duration and global reach but partially offset by Copart’s resilient digital model and essential-service designation.

Copart’s 2022-09-27 10-K explicitly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and still-emerging risks.  The filing moves well beyond boiler-plate: management discloses concrete, historical impacts (e.g., lower processed-vehicle volumes, depressed assignment levels) and provides a balanced view of partially offsetting benefits (higher average selling prices).  The company also flags a suite of forward-looking uncertainties—future shelter-in-place orders, labour-process inefficiencies, supply-chain distortions, and demand shifts tied to miles-driven trends.  Because the pandemic event is less than three years old at the filing date, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  However, some passages are purely generic list items, warranting only minimal credit, whereas sentences that describe actual operational or financial effects deserve materially higher scores, tempered where the company notes mitigating offsets (e.g., price increases).  The resulting evidence portfolio thus ranges from very low (generic bullet-point mentions) to high (specific statements of adverse volume impacts), with final snippet scores spanning 2–7.

The 2023-09-28 Copart (CPRT) Form 10-K places COVID-19 in the filing’s risk landscape, but only at a generic, forward-looking level. The company flags the pandemic as one of many ‘public-health issues’ that could disturb international operations or overall results, and the MD&A boiler-plate notes that forward-looking statements cover possible COVID-19 impacts. There is no quantified disclosure of past financial damage, nor any detailed discussion of supply-chain interruptions, labour shortages, or remote-work challenges. Consequently, the risk is presented as a continuing but largely contingent threat rather than an observed material impact. Given that the pandemic event is recent (≈3.5 years old) under the Time-Decay Principle, a moderate score is still warranted, yet the absence of specificity or metrics tempers severity. Overall, the COVID-19 risk appears acknowledged but not deeply analysed, suggesting a medium-level concern (roughly mid-single-digit scoring across snippets).

CPRT’s Form 10-K continues to flag the COVID-19 pandemic only in sweeping, boiler-plate bullet lists that group it with a host of other macro hazards. The language is forward-looking (“will continue to subject us to…”) but offers no concrete figures, operational anecdotes, or mitigation measures. As the filing date (30 Sep 2024) is roughly 4½ years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows for a mid-range score, yet the highly generic phrasing tempers severity. Overall, the disclosures indicate that management still perceives pandemic-related disruptions (labour, supply chain, travel, etc.) as possible future headwinds, but the absence of specificity or evidence of current material impact points to a moderate residual risk—credible enough to warrant attention, though clearly reduced from peak-pandemic levels.

CPT’s 10-K describes COVID-19 as an active, multi-faceted threat that is already eroding rent collections, inflating operating costs and jeopardising growth projects.  The language is mostly present-tense and uses strong qualifiers such as “material adverse effect.”  Management quantifies direct hits to 2020 earnings (≈ $14.8 million of lost revenue and extra costs) and foresees additional pressure on rent levels, occupancy, construction schedules, liquidity and cyber-security as the pandemic persists.  Mitigations (remote work, resident-rent restructurings, relief funds) are mentioned but are minor relative to the scale and uncertainty of the risk.  Because the filing date (18-Feb-2021) is well within three years of the pandemic’s March-2020 declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, COVID-19 represents a recent, direct, and quantitatively significant risk to CPT, warranting upper-tier scores for the most explicit and quantified disclosures and moderate scores where impacts are indirect, generic, or partly mitigated.

CPT’s 2022-02-17 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as a still-evolving, multifaceted threat that has already produced measurable financial harm and could intensify.  The filing blends backward-looking evidence (e.g., $9.1 million in rent abatements and $4.5 million in pandemic expenses) with forward-looking language that stresses continuing uncertainty around variants, government moratoria, tenant solvency, and operational constraints such as leasing disruptions.  Risk statements are largely specific—naming rent collection bans, employee access limitations, and potential occupancy declines—yet generally lack precise future dollar quantification.  Because the pandemic began less than two years before the filing, Time Decay allows high scores (up to 10).  Taken together, the disclosures indicate a material, ongoing risk that is only partially mitigated by recent market “signs of improvement,” warranting moderate-to-high severity scores across the evidence set.

CPT’s 2023-02-23 Form 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, forward-looking threat rather than as a quantified, already-realised hit to results. The language appears in the Risk Factors section, framed hypothetically (“could negatively impact”) and stresses exposure points typical for a multifamily REIT: residents’ ability to pay rent, occupancy levels, market rents and the enforceability of leases during eviction moratoria. While no dollar amounts, time-series metrics or supply-chain cost descriptions are provided, the discussion does map the pandemic to core revenue drivers and identifies possible regulatory constraints. Given that the filing date is within three years of the World Health Organization’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits moderately high scores; however, the generic, unquantified and largely contingency-based wording keeps individual snippet scores in the middle range rather than the upper extreme. Overall, the risk evidence is specific enough to be material but not severe enough—due to lack of metrics or realised losses—to merit top-tier scores.

CPT’s 2024 Form 10-K acknowledges the continuing possibility that pandemics—explicitly framed as “global or locally-targeted”—could materially interfere with its core apartment-rental model by limiting the company’s legal ability to collect rent. The disclosure is presented in the Risk Factors section as a forward-looking contingency rather than a report of current, quantified harm. Although COVID-19’s initial shock occurred nearly four years prior to the filing date, eviction moratoria and public-health mandates remain plausible re-emerging constraints on revenue. The statement therefore reflects a still-credible but decaying threat: it is specific enough to tie the health crisis to an operational mechanism (enforcement of contractual rental obligations) yet generic in magnitude and timing. Language such as “could negatively impact,” “has significantly impacted,” and quantified examples of currency effects show that part of the impact is already observable, while much is framed as forward-looking contingency planning. Applying the Time Decay Principle for a very recent event, evidence can be scored in the upper range; however, generic wording and the presence of mitigations temper individual sentence scores.  Overall, the pandemic represents a high, actively monitored risk with broad operational and financial implications for Corteva.

Corteva’s 2022 filing was prepared almost two years into the declared COVID-19 pandemic, so any pandemic-related language must be weighed as a recent-event disclosure under the Time Decay Principle.  The company repeatedly frames COVID-19 as both an existing and forward-looking threat, citing concrete disruptions that have already happened (e.g., lockdowns limiting operations, shortages of manufacturing inputs) and a spectrum of potential future consequences (supply-chain bottlenecks, higher distribution costs, labour shortages, credit risk, asset impairments). Given the recency of the pandemic (within three years of the filing date), the specificity of the operational channels described, and the acknowledgement of impacts already experienced, the overall risk evidence sits in the upper-medium to high severity band (roughly 7–9 out of 10 after time-decay adjustments).

CTVAs 2023-02-09 Form 10-K treats the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat that can quickly disrupt operations, supply chains and market demand. Under the Time-Decay Principle, COVID-19 remains a ‘recent event’ (0–3 yrs) so evidence can legitimately score in the upper range (7-10) when statements are direct and granular; more generic or illustrative references warrant mid-range scores. Corteva’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 and future pandemics as an ongoing, medium-term enterprise risk. Overall, the narrative evidences a live but un-quantified threat that management is monitoring rather than an acute balance-sheet shock, justifying mid-range scores across the extracted sentences.

CVS’s 2021 Form-10-K presents COVID-19 as a proximate, multifaceted, and still-evolving threat that could materially affect every major operating segment.  The filing moves well beyond boiler-plate: management links the pandemic to concrete channels of impact – utilisation swings, mandated benefit expansions, operating-expense spikes, supply-chain and labour disruptions, remote-work vulnerabilities, liquidity strain on customers, and fundamental shifts in consumer traffic patterns.  Most disclosures are forward-looking but anchored in already-observed 2020 experience (e.g., elective-procedure deferrals, remote work transitions and diagnostic-testing surges).  Language such as “material and adverse,” “could materially and adversely impact,” and enumerated financial pressure points signals senior-level recognition of severe downside risk.  Mitigation references (e.g., cost-savings initiatives, vaccine roll-outs) exist but are clearly outweighed by the breadth of potential harm.  Given the filing date (Feb-2021) is less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the COVID-19 pandemic represents a recent, direct, and pervasive enterprise risk with limited offsetting factors, justifying elevated snippet scores clustered in the 6-9 range.

COVID-19 is framed by CVS as both an active and a continuing enterprise-wide threat. Accordingly, the risk evidence is high-severity but not quite maximal: most snippets warrant scores in the 5-9 range after applying the Time Decay Principle for a < 3-year-old event and subtracting modest points where wording is purely forward-looking or where the Company references mitigation.

CVS’s 2023 Form 10-K positions COVID-19 as one of the most material and still-unfolding enterprise-wide threats.  The disclosures frame the pandemic as both a realised shock (past negative impacts on utilisation, customer traffic, medical cost volatility and retail sales) and an ongoing, forward-looking risk that could flare again with new variants.  Management highlights multiple operational pressure points: supply-chain disruption, labour shortages, higher medical-service utilisation, remote-work re-adoption, and potential facility closures – all of which could directly erode margins, cash-flows and competitive positioning. Because the filing date (8 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores (7-10).  Some mitigation is noted – prior support programmes and easing restrictions – yet management concedes continuing uncertainty and the possibility of reinstating costly measures.  Overall, the pandemic remains a high-impact, recently manifest risk, warranting upper-range snippet scores that nevertheless recognise the partial mitigation and uncertainty disclosed.

CVS’s 2024-02-07 10-K portrays COVID-19 as a still-active, enterprise-wide hazard that complicates actuarial forecasting, provider behavior, consumer demand and overall economic conditions. Because the disclosure concerns an event that is less than four years old, the Time Decay Principle permits high—though not maximal—scores; most evidence merits 5-7 points. Mitigating factors are minimal: there is no claim that the risks have been fully resolved, only acknowledgement of uncertainty. Overall, COVID-19 remains a significant, contemporaneous risk with operational and financial ramifications for CVS.

CZR’s 2021-03-01 filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to both immediate and continuing threats across virtually every dimension of the company’s casino-hospitality business. CZR’s 2022 filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and continuing risks that cut across operations, finances and strategic outlook. CZR’s 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly characterises COVID-19 as both a realised and continuing enterprise-level threat. Overall, the pandemic remains an elevated (but partially stabilising) risk, justifying high but not maximal snippet scores where concrete impacts are described, and moderate scores where language is broader or more contingent.

CZR’s 2024 Form 10-K positions the COVID-19 pandemic as an already-experienced shock with lingering, hard-to-measure consequences that remain material almost four years after the March 2020 declaration. Delta’s 2020 Form 10-K, filed only eleven months after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, paints a picture of an immediate, deep and still-evolving threat.  The disclosure moves well beyond generic caution: it chronicles demand collapse, capacity cuts, liquidity strain, debt build-up, partner insolvencies, labour and cyber exposures, and the spectre of a lasting structural decline in business travel. Because the filing date (12 Feb 2021) falls squarely within three years of the onset of the pandemic, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Overall, the risk is direct, already crystallised, and still expanding, warranting elevated snippet scores that cluster between 6 and 9, with minor downward adjustments where mitigation or uncertainty temper the immediate impact.

Delta’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to severe, ongoing and still-evolving threats across every pillar of the airline’s business model: core passenger demand, operational continuity, labour availability, liquidity and long-term shifts in customer behaviour.  Unlike generic boiler-plate, the filing provides concrete cause-and-effect language—government travel bans, testing mandates, employee quarantines, and the possibility of permanent business-travel contraction—together with an explicit admission that cost-cutting actions cannot offset lost revenue.  The disclosures characterise COVID-19 as both a realised loss ('material adverse effect on our business, results of operations and financial condition') and a continuing forward-looking risk (‘will continue to have’, ‘may be reinstituted’, ‘could have a material impact’).  Because the filing date (11-Feb-2022) sits less than two years after the pandemic onset, the Time Decay principle allows high severity scores.  No material mitigating language (e.g., successful hedges or full insurance recovery) offsets the pervasive downside; even references to vaccines are tempered by warnings about new variants.  Accordingly, individual evidence snippets register in the upper-mid to high range (5-9/10), reflecting specific, current, and company-wide exposure to pandemic-related hazards.

Delta’s 2022 Form 10-K places COVID-19 at the core of its current and forward-looking risk profile.  Multiple sections state that the pandemic has already produced material, quantified damage—new leverage, multi-billion-dollar impairments, and a prolonged collapse in demand—and that several of these effects (e.g., elevated debt service, weakened partner airlines, labour shortages, customer-behaviour shifts) will linger. The wording is typically strong (“material adverse effect”, “significant impairment”, “could negatively affect”), and the link to cash flow, liquidity and network strategy is explicit.  Because the filing date (10 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows relatively high severity scores.  However, some passages are generic or discuss recovery trends, warranting moderate deductions.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a high-severity, contemporaneous risk whose financial and operational repercussions are only partially mitigated by the ongoing recovery.

Delta’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 as both a recently realised shock and an ongoing strategic hazard. DAY’s 2021 filing discusses COVID-19 as a recent (within 12 months) and still-evolving threat that is already depressing revenue and operations while also posing additional forward-looking uncertainties. DAY’s 2023 Form 10-K positions COVID-19 as both a recently-realised shock and an ongoing, potentially material threat. COVID-19 is framed in DuPont’s 2021 Form 10-K as both an already-material shock and a continuing source of uncertainty. Overall, DuPont’s disclosure reflects a high—and still evolving—risk profile, so recent, specific and quantified statements receive the highest micro-scores, generic or mitigated statements receive mid-level scores, and no evidence is scored above 10, in line with the recency window.

Because this Form 10-K was filed on 15 Dec 2022—less than three years after the WHO’s March 2020 declaration—the COVID-19 pandemic is a very recent event for Deere & Company (DE).
