DLTR’s 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted risk that is already eroding profitability and could further destabilise operations if new variants or renewed restrictions materialise.  Management emphasises both realised impacts—higher store and distribution-center operating costs, supply-chain bottlenecks, labour-market tightness, altered traffic patterns—and prospective threats such as future shutdowns, facility closures and added compliance costs.  Language is largely specific (e.g., ‘significant increases in the cost of operating our stores’, ‘pandemic-related port closings’) and repeatedly classifies the consequences as “material” or “adverse.”  Because the filing date (10 Mar 2023) sits less than three years after the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high risk scores.  While the company mentions limited mitigating actions (e.g., an Instacart partnership), these are minor relative to the breadth of vulnerabilities disclosed.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a high-severity, contemporaneous risk driver for DLTR’s margins, supply chain, labour availability and consumer-demand mix, warranting elevated evidence scores in the 7-10 range.

DLTR’s 2024 Form 10-K still attributes parts of its supply-chain vulnerability and macro-demand uncertainty to the COVID-19 pandemic and to the possibility of future epidemics. The filing describes having already "experienced" pandemic–related port closures as well as lingering shocks in freight and labor markets; these are presented as factual, historical impacts rather than hypothetical ones. At the same time, any forward-looking discussion is high-level and unquantified, couched among many other external hazards. Four years have elapsed since the WHO pandemic declaration, so the Time-Decay Principle places the evidence in the medium-term band, warranting only moderate severity scores. Overall, the company acknowledges that pandemic disruptions have materially affected shipping and could continue to do so, but it offers no fresh numerical estimates or detailed mitigation strategies, signalling an ongoing—but now less acute—risk profile.

DOC’s 2021 filing portrays COVID-19 as the single most material, near-term threat to its operating model.  The disclosures blend backward-looking data (e.g., 2020 occupancy collapsing by 8-10 percentage points and immediate project shutdowns) with forward-looking warnings (cash-flow erosion, continued rent deferrals, labour shortages, re-suspension of construction).  Language is unequivocal—“material cost increases”, “significant decrease in cash receipts”, “adversely affected”—and repeatedly ties those impacts directly to pandemic-related health measures.  Quantified evidence (occupancy drop from 83.2 % to 75.3 %) and explicit references to development halts demonstrate real, already-incurred harm, not merely hypothetical risk.  Because the filing date (Feb-2021) is well within three years of the event’s onset (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  No meaningful mitigating offsets (such as insurance coverage or permanent rent-escalators) are offered; most statements emphasise uncertainty and continued deterioration.  Accordingly, individual sentences score in the upper range (7-9), collectively signalling a high, persistent pandemic risk profile for DOC.

DOC’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as a recent, already-material event with continuing repercussions.  The company discloses both backward-looking damage (e.g., double-digit occupancy erosion in senior housing and sharp labour-cost escalation) and forward-looking uncertainties (persistently higher expenses, supply-chain delays, potential rent deferrals).  The narrative is specific to core revenue drivers—occupancy, net operating income, development timing—and repeatedly links those metrics to the pandemic.  Quantified data (occupancy dropping from 85.6 % to 79.1 %) and language such as “direct and immediate impact” elevate severity.  Mitigations are scarce; the company largely acknowledges that many higher costs will outlive the pandemic and that it “does not yet know” when demand will recover.  Because the filing date (Feb-2022) is within two years of the World Health Organization’s March-2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores (7-10) for direct, quantified effects, with slightly lower scores (5-7) for more generic or purely prospective statements.  The evidence set therefore skews toward the upper half of the scale, reflecting both immediacy and materiality.

DOC’s 2023 filing repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to heightened, continuing risk across its healthcare-focused real-estate platform.  The disclosures mix backward-looking evidence (2020–22 revenue pressure and operational disruption) with forward-looking warnings that new variants, renewed public-health measures or persistent macro-aftershocks could still depress occupancy, raise operating costs, slow development timetables and weaken tenants’ ability to pay.  The company points out structural vulnerabilities—sector concentration, lack of pandemic business-interruption insurance, and potential regulatory constraints such as eviction moratoria—that would amplify any fresh pandemic wave.  While no single sentence quantifies the dollar impact, several explicitly use “material adverse effect” language and enumerate concrete transmission channels (rent defaults, supply-chain inflation, labour shortages, construction delays).  Because the filing date (Feb-2023) is less than three years after WHO’s March-2020 pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Overall, the risk is assessed as high but unquantified: COVID has already impaired results and remains a live, multi-dimensional threat without full mitigation, warranting evidence scores in the 4-8 range.

DOC’s 2024 filing situates COVID-19 within a cluster of continuing macro-risks rather than as an isolated, historical crisis.  Several sentences link the pandemic to ongoing cost inflation, tenant revenue pressure, insurance gaps and potentially severe operational disruptions.  The company repeatedly uses mixed tenses—“have been” and “may continue”—showing that impacts already materialised (e.g., reduced senior-housing revenues, higher costs) while also remaining forward-looking.  No dollar figures are offered, and the language is largely qualitative, but the disclosures go beyond boiler-plate: they specify concrete channels (move-outs, delayed move-ins, supply-chain inflation, absence of business-interruption insurance).  Because the pandemic’s official declaration (March 2020) is just under four years before the filing date (February 2024), the Time-Decay principle places it at the cusp of the “recent” and “medium-term” bands; therefore snippet scores are kept in the moderate-high range (4-6).  Overall, COVID-19 remains a live, multi-faceted risk driver for DOC, but the absence of quantified impacts tempers severity.

Dover’s February 2021 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as an acute, multi-dimensional, and still-evolving threat.  Because the filing date is within one year of the WHO-declared pandemic, time-decay does not dilute severity.  The company discloses both concrete 2020 damage (e.g., a 6.6 % organic revenue decline worth roughly $0.5 billion, plant-level capacity cuts, and restructuring costs) and forward-looking exposures (future facility closures, furloughs, supply-chain fragility, and uncertain demand recovery).  Language is largely specific—naming disrupted end-markets, quantified revenue erosion, workforce restrictions, and international pressure—though some passages highlight uncertainty and mitigation efforts.  Net, the text shows an event that is already materially hurting earnings, cash flow, labour availability and logistics, with management unable to bound the downside.  Mitigations (health protocols, supply procurement successes) exist but are clearly portrayed as insufficient guarantees.  Under the Time Decay Principle, scores can be high (recent event), but are tempered when statements emphasise uncertainty or describe partial mitigation.  The evidence therefore receives mostly upper-mid to high micro-scores, topping out where the filing quantifies material financial harm.

Dow’s 2021-02-05 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat that has already produced material, quantified damage (e.g., 10 % sales decline, idled assets) and is expected to keep disrupting manufacturing, supply chains, labour availability and market demand.  The language blends backward-looking impacts (plants idled, 18 % sales drop in 1H-20, remote-work cybersecurity risks) with forward-looking uncertainty (“could continue to have a substantial negative impact”), signalling that management views the pandemic as both a realised loss driver and a continuing hazard.  Disclosures are highly specific—listing impaired assets, logistics bottlenecks, labour shortages and heightened cyber-risk—and frequently reference effects on results of operations, cash flows and liquidity, which elevates severity.  Some passages mention mitigating factors (essential-site exemptions, contingency plans, strong liquidity), but these are outweighed by the breadth and depth of identified exposures.  Because the filing date is less than one year after the declared pandemic (within the 0-3-year “recent” window), the Time Decay Principle permits high scores (7-10) for the strongest evidence; moderately phrased or partially mitigated statements receive mid-range scores (3-6).  Purely mitigating or weak generic sentences earn low scores or point deductions.

Dow’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as both an already-realized and still-evolving enterprise-wide threat.  The Risk-Factors section documents material impacts that have *already occurred* (e.g., demand destruction, supply-chain disruptions, labor shortages, asset impairments) while warning they can ‘continue’ and remain un-quantified because the duration and severity of the pandemic are unknown.  The company stresses that the virus has touched **all geographic regions** in which it operates and could ‘substantially’ harm results, cash-flow and liquidity, thereby elevating financial-statement risk.  Sentences are generally specific—listing concrete operational, financial and workforce impacts—yet remain partly generic regarding magnitude.  Management discussion later in the filing offers partial mitigation (plants largely kept running, strong liquidity, re-opened sites), but these statements do not eliminate the forward-looking exposure.  Considering the Time-Decay principle, COVID-19 is < 2 years old on the filing date, so high severity scores (7-10) are warranted for the most direct, material disclosures; sentences dominated by mitigation receive offsets.  The combined evidence confirms a high but actively managed risk profile.

Dow’s 2023 Form 10-K continues to treat COVID-19 as an acute, enterprise-level risk that remains highly relevant less than three years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  The filing’s pandemic-related language is concentrated in a dedicated “Pandemic-Related Risks” subsection but is also woven into climate, operational and macro-economic discussions, underscoring that the virus can amplify many other risk factors.  Most statements are forward-looking ("could") yet repeatedly acknowledge that several of the cited impacts have already occurred (“has resulted,” “has included”), demonstrating both realized and prospective exposure.  Although no impacts are quantified, the risk descriptions are expansive—covering supply-chain disruption, labor shortages, cyber threats from remote work, asset impairments and demand shocks—indicating materiality across operational, financial and strategic dimensions.  Because the filing date (1 Feb 2023) is well within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scores; however, the absence of precise dollar figures or probability estimates tempers scores below the absolute maximum.  Overall, the evidence supports a high but not extreme risk assessment, reflecting a live threat with broad but un-quantified consequences.

Dow’s 2024 filing treats COVID-19 as an ongoing but no longer acute hazard: language has shifted from describing immediate shocks (2020-21) to framing a standing catalogue of operational, financial and supply-chain vulnerabilities that "could" or "in the past has" materialised.  All references are forward-looking, unquantified and mostly conditional, yet they remain detailed – naming labour shortages, remote-work cybersecurity, facility shutdowns, raw-material scarcity and demand swings.  Because the pandemic began almost four years prior to the filing date, the Time Decay Principle pushes the evidence into the medium-term band; scores must therefore be moderate even though the disclosures enumerate many serious impacts and cite some historical experience.  No meaningful mitigating language (e.g., insurance coverage, contingency buffers or cost estimates) is offered, so the net risk posture is still material but no longer critical, warranting mid-range severity scores (3-6) for individual sentences.

Domino’s 2021 Form 10-K explicitly and repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to material, continuing and multi-faceted risks.  Because the filing date (25 Feb 2021) is well inside the 0-3-year “recent-event” window, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  The text combines (a) concrete, already-realised impacts—store closures, supply-chain interruptions, work-from-home shifts, borrowing for liquidity and specific revenue declines—with (b) forward-looking uncertainties such as unknown pandemic duration, customer-demand volatility, labour shortages, rising costs and cyber-exposure.  Most statements are detailed, event-specific and tied directly to operational, financial and strategic consequences, although some mitigation measures (contact-less delivery, safety spend, repayments of borrowings) modestly temper the overall risk.  Taken together, the disclosure presents a high but not maximal risk profile: COVID-19 has already affected results and could intensify numerous other risk factors.  My snippet scores therefore range mainly from 4-8, reflecting directness, specificity, quantification and evidence of realised disruption, with downward adjustments where mitigating language or positive offsets appear.

DPZ’s 2022 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-dimensional threat that is already reshaping operations and could materially erode future performance.  The filing moves well beyond boiler-plate language: it cites realized impacts—labour shortages, temporary store closures, volatility in ingredient costs, and supply-chain disruptions—while also mapping forward-looking exposures such as vaccine mandate compliance costs, prolonged macro-economic uncertainty, and heightened cyber-risk from remote work.  Numerous passages link the pandemic directly to adverse movements in sales, service levels and customer experience, explicitly stating that these factors have already hindered growth initiatives like new-store openings and promotions.  Taken together, the disclosures reflect both (i) concrete, quantifiable operational hits already booked and (ii) amplified tail-risks whose magnitude is “ultimately unknown.”  Because the filing date (March 2022) is less than three years after the WHO’s March 2020 declaration, the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores; the pandemic remains a live, evolving stressor rather than a historical footnote.  Overall, the risk profile is elevated: most statements are specific, company-focused and describe cascading effects across supply chain, labour, consumer demand and strategic growth plans, justifying scores clustered in the upper mid-to-high range (4-9).

DPZ’s 2023 filing frames COVID-19 as both an historical and still-active threat with direct operational, financial, labour and supply-chain consequences. Multiple sentences document concrete impacts that have already materialised—store hour reductions, delayed openings, temporary closures, supply-chain interruptions and foregone promotions—all explicitly attributed to the ongoing pandemic. These retrospective disclosures elevate the severity because they confirm realised losses, not merely hypothetical risks. At the same time, the company layers forward-looking language about continued or future disruptions to labour availability, consumer demand, inflationary pressures and global economic uncertainty, signalling that management expects COVID-related volatility to persist. The statements are fairly specific (naming lost sales drivers, supply-chain breakdowns, compliance costs), though most are qualitative rather than quantified. Given the filing date (February 2023) sits inside the 0-to-3-year “recent event” window, the Time Decay Principle allows high risk scores. Overall, the pandemic represents a high but not existential risk: impacts are material and ongoing, yet the company also notes some offsetting sales benefits from delivery reliance. This context underpins the individual micro-scores below.

DPZ’s 2024 filing frames COVID-19 as an event that produced tangible operational disruptions between 2020 and 2023 and that still presents a meaningful, though moderating, threat.  The company describes concrete historical impacts—labour shortages, elevated turnover, supply-chain interruptions and delayed store openings—while also warning that macro-demand, consumer behaviour, and growth trajectories remain unpredictable as the pandemic’s after-effects unwind.  These are largely factual, backward-looking statements coupled with forward-looking cautions; they reference real operating changes already taken, but do not quantify hard dollar amounts.  Because the event is now four years old, the Time Decay Principle places the evidence in the “medium-term” bucket; scores therefore sit in the 4-6 range depending on the immediacy and severity of each disclosure.  Overall, the language is specific to COVID-19, acknowledges material adverse possibilities and cites direct operational consequences, warranting a moderate risk assessment rather than either a negligible or extreme one.

DRI’s July 2021 Form 10-K depicts COVID-19 as a current, material and multi-faceted threat.  The filing chronicles actual disruptions—complete dining-room shutdowns, capacity caps, guest-traffic declines, same-restaurant sales drops, a US$390 million impairment charge, supply interruptions, and acute labor shortages—as well as forward-looking exposures should cases rise again.  Although the company notes partial mitigation through vaccine roll-outs, eased restrictions and operational adjustments (to-go service, menu simplification, technology upgrades), these steps do not eliminate the underlying volatility.  Because the pandemic began only 16 months before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores; the risk is both contemporaneous and continuing.  Overall, the disclosure language is specific (naming closures, capacity limits, financial effects) and mostly un-quantified except for the impairment figure, warranting generally high but sub-maximum scores, tempered where meaningful mitigations are described.

Darden’s 2022-07-22 filing depicts COVID-19 as a still-present, multilateral threat that has already produced tangible harm and could intensify.  The company explicitly states that the pandemic “has disrupted” operations, citing significant guest-traffic declines, mandatory dining-room closures, labour quarantines, supply-chain interruptions and higher input inflation.  These impacts are not hypothetical; they are recent (FY-2021-2022), directly tied to the Omicron wave, and labelled “material.”  At the same time, management warns that variants could re-impose capacity limits, exacerbate wage inflation and further strain procurement.  Although some mitigating signals appear (e.g., easing restrictions after vaccine roll-out), the narrative is predominantly aggravating and forward-looking.  Because the disclosure occurs less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores (up to 10).  However, the text offers few hard numbers, so most sentences merit mid-to-high—but not maximum—severity ratings.  Overall, the risk profile is high, immediate and multifaceted, justifying a set of snippet scores clustered in the 4-7 range.

The filing, dated July 21 2023, repeatedly links COVID-19 to both realized and forward-looking pressures across Darden’s operations.  The disclosures confirm that the pandemic is not merely historic; it has produced measurable adverse effects within the last 18 months (e.g., Omicron-driven restaurant restrictions) and is expected to keep influencing labor availability, supply chain continuity, commodity inflation and consumer dining patterns.  Language such as “significantly impacted our restaurants,” “adversely affected our results of operations,” and detailed references to wage, product-cost and staffing disruptions demonstrate direct, company-specific exposure rather than boiler-plate generalities.  Although no precise dollar amounts are provided, the statements are recent (within 0-3 years), specific to Darden’s core value drivers and acknowledge multiple impact channels, elevating the risk severity under the Time Decay Principle.  The overall risk profile therefore sits in the upper-moderate to high range, warranting snippet scores between 2 and 7, with the highest marks reserved for sentences that describe concrete operational disruptions during fiscal 2022 and identify multiple concurrent risk vectors (labor, supply chain, inflation).

DRI’s 2024 filing continues to flag the COVID-19 pandemic under a broader “food-related pandemics” risk.  All disclosures are forward-looking rather than post-mortem, signalling that management views pandemic disruption as a persisting threat rather than a one-off shock.  The language identifies multiple operational pressure points – supply-chain cost/availability, labour shortages, forced closures, guest-traffic declines, and the lasting consumer pivot toward off-premise dining – but gives no quantified dollar impact or timeframe.  Because the pandemic’s onset (March 2020) is now a little over four years behind the filing date, the Time Decay Principle places these statements in the medium-term window (scores should cluster in the 4-6 range).  The evidence is moderately strong: it explicitly cites COVID-19, specifies several business channels that could be hit, and references observed changes in consumer behaviour, yet remains largely conditional (“may”, “could”) and unquantified.  Overall, the risk is live and material but not described with the immediacy or precision that would merit a high-severity score.

COVID-19 is portrayed in the 2021-02-25 filing as both an already-realised and a still-evolving source of risk for Duke Energy (DUK).  The company discloses numerous direct effects that occurred during 2020 – e.g., a 2 % drop in retail electricity sales, higher bad-debt expense, shifting 18 000 employees to remote work and cost-cutting of $400-$450 million – but simultaneously emphasises that the aggregate financial hit was “not material as of this filing date.”  The narrative therefore contains a mixture of definitely-incurred impacts (demand destruction, operational disruptions, extraordinary customer relief measures) and contingent, forward-looking exposures (supply-chain shortages, labour availability, financing constraints, asset impairments, tighter regulation).  The statements are mostly specific (naming cost buckets, percentages and operational choke-points) and are very recent (within one year of the World Health Organisation’s 11 March 2020 declaration).  Under the Time-Decay Principle, evidence can be scored in the upper range (7-10) where the company cites concrete or highly plausible impacts; moderately where the company hedges with qualifiers; and lower where it stresses successful mitigation.  Mitigating factors (e.g., cost recovery mechanisms, O&M savings, continued service reliability) appropriately reduce some individual scores but do not erase the overall conclusion that COVID-19 is a significant, near-term operational and financial risk for DUK.

COVID-19 is acknowledged in the filing as a still-evolving, recent (≤ 3 years) external threat that has already touched Duke Energy’s operations yet remains largely a prospective, scenario-driven risk.  Management states that impacts to-date have been "immaterial," but then lists a concrete set of potential future pressure points that map directly to the pandemic-related vectors requested in the prompt: labour shortages, equipment delays, fuel procurement difficulties, and delays in regulatory proceedings.  These statements are forward-looking, qualitative and largely un-quantified, signalling uncertainty rather than booked losses, but they nonetheless recognise enterprise-wide exposure.  The company tempers the threat with mitigating language—e.g., cost-containment actions that yielded roughly $200 million of O&M savings—and a self-declared record of successfully navigating supply-chain challenges.  Taken together, the disclosure reflects a moderate recent-event risk: it is specific enough to identify operational choke points, yet it downplays severity and pairs each risk with at least one mitigation.  Under the Time Decay Principle, a 2020-era pandemic discussed in a 2022 filing is “recent,” allowing high theoretical scores, but the self-labelled immateriality and mitigation efforts justify mid-range severity for individual snippets rather than the maximum.

COVID-19 is expressly framed as both an already-felt and still-evolving enterprise-wide threat for Duke Energy (DUK).  The filing, made less than three years after the pandemic was declared, therefore falls in the recent-event window, so any evidence can carry a relatively high risk weight under the Time Decay Principle.  The company acknowledges concrete, present-day disruptions to customers and vendors and flags a spectrum of forward-looking vulnerabilities—rate-case delays, construction slow-downs, supply-chain bottlenecks, labour shortages and personnel health.  While the disclosures are qualitative and lack dollar quantification, they are more than boiler-plate: they connect the pandemic to specific operational choke-points and to core financial metrics (strategy, earnings, cash-flow).  Because the language is not accompanied by hard numbers or definitive impairment charges, the overall severity is assessed as high-moderate rather than catastrophic, yielding snippet scores clustered in the 5-7 range.  No mitigating statements (e.g., pandemic tailwinds, insurance coverage, or fully executed contingency plans) are offered, so downward adjustments are minimal.

COVID-19 first emerged nearly four years before the February 2024 filing, placing it in the Time-Decay window where ongoing effects are still material but naturally moderating. Duke Energy no longer frames the pandemic as an acute crisis; however, the Risk Factors confirm that management continues to view pandemic health events—especially a prolonged or resurging COVID-19 wave—as a non-trivial threat. The language is forward-looking and scenario-based, yet it also references concrete historical impacts (suspension of customer disconnections, broad economic disruption) that have already manifested. Importantly, the company specifies multiple operational transmission channels—delays in regulatory proceedings, labour and equipment shortages, fuel procurement constraints, and workforce availability—that map directly to the typical pandemic-related vectors our mandate requires (supply chain, labour, remote-work/health). No dollar figures are provided, and the tone is largely generic, so the disclosures are moderate rather than severe; nonetheless they show that pandemic risk remains part of Duke’s strategic risk register. Applying the Time Decay Principle (event≈4 yrs old), the maximum justified severity sits in the 4-6 range. The evidence sentences below therefore cluster between 1 and 5, reflecting realised but unquantified impacts, detailed causal pathways, and some mitigating actions already in place.

DVA’s 2021 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as a recent, acute and multi-faceted threat that is already reshaping its economics and operations.  The company discloses both realized impacts—lower treatment volumes, higher mortality, increased PPE and labor costs—and forward-looking exposures such as adverse shifts in payer mix, supply-chain pressures, workforce shortages, and heightened cyber-risk from large-scale remote work.  The language is largely concrete (“have experienced,” “continue to have,” “substantial resources,” “materially reduced share”) and ties each effect directly to the pandemic rather than speaking in vague hypotheticals.  Because the filing date (12 Feb 2021) is well within three years of the pandemic’s onset (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the disclosure signals a high-level, continuing risk with measurable financial and operational consequences, warranting elevated snippet scores that cluster in the upper-mid range of the 7-10 band for direct, realized impacts and slightly lower scores for indirect or prospective risks.

DVA’s 2022 filing portrays COVID-19 as an acute, multi-dimensional threat that is already depressing revenue and growth and is expected to persist.  The company links the pandemic directly to lower treatment volumes driven by excess patient mortality, labour shortages that raise wages and threaten clinic closures, surging PPE and other supply-chain costs, new compliance mandates, a forced shift to remote work with cybersecurity exposure, and fundamental pressure on its high-margin commercial-payor mix.  These statements are concrete (e.g., “have experienced” impacts and “substantially increased” costs), reference materiality, and describe both realised and forward-looking risk.  Because the Form 10-K is filed less than two years after the WHO declaration (within the ≤3-year “recent” window), Time-Decay permits high severity scores.  Few mitigating actions are cited; where mitigation is mentioned (e.g., dedicating resources), it does not offset the scale or duration of the described harms.  Overall, the disclosures evidence a high, continuing enterprise-level risk from the COVID-19 pandemic.

DVA’s 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an on-going, material and multi-dimensional threat that continues to reshape the company’s risk landscape nearly three years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  The filing chronicles hard, present-day impacts—lower treatment volumes, higher patient mortality, labour shortages, wage inflation, supply-chain disruptions and direct cost increases—while also stressing substantial forward-looking uncertainty surrounding new variants, government policy shifts and the May 2023 sunset of U.S. public-health emergency declarations.  The disclosures go beyond boiler-plate language: they explicitly link COVID-19 to revenue contraction, margin pressure, commercial-payor mix erosion and heightened legal / compliance exposure.  Because the pandemic event remains within the 0-3 year “recent” window, the Time Decay Principle permits scores toward the high end of the scale.  Nevertheless, the company also notes mitigation efforts (cost-savings initiatives, vaccination progress, etc.), so final snippet scores are calibrated to reflect both aggravating and offsetting factors, generally ranging from 3-9, but never exceeding 10.

The filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to DaVita’s operating risk profile as a still-active, enterprise-level threat.  Although the World Health Organization declared the pandemic in 2020 (now four years in the past), management states that COVID-19 continues to suppress treatment volumes, raise patient-mortality-driven census losses, and dampen new-admission growth.  These disclosures identify concrete business levers—revenue, non-acquired growth, missed-treatment rates—showing that the virus has moved from an acute external shock to a persistent, structural headwind.  The language is mostly qualitative and forward-looking (“expect to continue,” “likely to continue”) rather than fully quantified, which tempers severity.  Under the Time Decay Principle, a 2020 event evaluated in a 2024 filing falls in the 4-to-10-year ‘medium-term’ band, so scores should land in the mid-range (4-6) unless statements are weak or heavily hedged.  Overall, the risk is moderate-to-elevated because impacts are direct, recurrent and tied to core revenue drivers, but still lack hard dollar figures and are partially conditional.

Dexcom’s 2021 Form-10-K discloses wide-ranging, still-unfolding risks tied to the COVID-19 pandemic. Because the filing date (11 Feb 2021) is less than a year after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), Time-Decay is minimal and evidence merits high severity scores. The company links the pandemic to nearly every operational layer: supply-chain interruptions, factory access limits, higher component costs, labour shortages, remote-work and sales-force constraints, clinical-trial delays, loss of customer insurance, pricing pressure, and volatility in capital markets. Most statements are forward-looking but framed as “material adverse impact,” indicating management sees a clear, significant threat rather than a remote possibility. No hard dollar figures are given, but multiple passages cite concrete mechanisms (e.g., shelter-in-place orders blocking plant access, global shortages already affecting next-gen product manufacture). Dexcom does note mitigation actions (virtual sales, hospital use, employee safety measures), yet repeatedly concedes uncertainty over the “ultimate impact.” Balancing the breadth of specific operational vulnerabilities against the absence of quantified loss, the overall pandemic risk profile is assessed as high-to-severe in the 8–9 range under the Time Decay Principle.

DXCM’s 2022 filing discusses the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that could materially harm the company’s near-term operations and financial performance.  The text repeatedly links the pandemic to concrete operational stressors—higher manufacturing costs, global supply-chain disruption, labor constraints caused by shelter-in-place orders, delays in FDA reviews and clinical trials, sales-force restrictions, possible loss of patient insurance coverage, and downward pricing pressure if a recession deepens.  Although most passages remain qualitative (no dollar amounts), they consistently characterize the impact as “material,” “pronounced,” and already experienced in areas such as supply‐chain shortages and delayed next-generation product timelines.  These are forward-looking risks but anchored in present-day experience, making them direct and recent.  Mitigating language (e.g., essential-infrastructure exemptions, remote-work shifts) is mentioned but does not outweigh the breadth of vulnerabilities.  Because the filing date (14-Feb-2022) is inside three years of the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the pandemic disclosures signal elevated continuing risk—generally unquantified yet operationally specific—meriting high, though not maximum, snippet scores.

DXCM’s 2023 filing repeatedly links the still-active COVID-19 pandemic to a broad spectrum of operational and financial threats.  Management discloses that the company has already experienced concrete effects—supply-chain interruptions, higher manufacturing costs, clinical-trial delays, customer insurance losses, and downward pricing pressure—while also warning of additional, forward-looking impacts such as further production shortfalls, lower demand and margin compression.  The language is largely specific (e.g., citing delays in pivotal trials and supply disruption for next-generation CGM products) and acknowledges both realised and potential damage.  Because the pandemic began less than three years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows relatively high scores; however, many statements remain unquantified and partially mitigated by their conditional nature, so the evidence is severe but not maximal.  Overall, the risk is assessed as high, recent, and only partially within management’s control, warranting mid-to-upper severity scores for individual sentences.

Dexcom’s 2024 filing still carries explicit, though largely forward-looking, warnings about the lingering repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company links a broad range of operational vulnerabilities—global plant or supplier shutdowns, logistics bottlenecks, labour shortages, shifts in patient demand and insurance coverage—to any future resurgence of COVID-19–type public-health crises.  The language is mostly conditional ("may", "could") rather than describing current impairment and no dollar figures are supplied, so the risk is characterised as potential rather than already-realised.  Because the filing date is almost four years after the WHO declaration (placing the pandemic at the start of the medium-term 4-to-10-year window), the Time Decay Principle tempers the severity that otherwise strong phrasing such as “material adverse effect” might command.  Overall, the disclosures indicate a moderate, persisting exposure that management believes is still material enough to highlight, but the absence of quantified impacts or present-tense losses limits the final scores to the mid-range.

COVID-19 is treated in the filing as an ongoing, externally-driven threat whose disruptive force has already been experienced and is expected to persist.  Although the pandemic’s peak occurred four years prior to the 2024 filing date, the company still highlights concrete channels of exposure—supply-chain bottlenecks, labor shortages, demand destruction, construction delays, collection moratoria and capital-market stress.  All references are couched as forward-looking contingencies rather than quantified historical hits, indicating the risk is viewed as continuing but largely manageable.  Because the outbreak is now just beyond the three-year ‘recent’ window, the Time Decay Principle tempers severity from “acute” to “moderate”; thus individual sentence scores are capped in the 4-6 range.  Overall, the disclosures are specific enough to be meaningful (naming supply chains, labor, customer demand, etc.) yet remain unquantified and partly mitigated by their conditional wording ("could," "may").  Consequently, each snippet is assigned a mid-level risk score that collectively reflects a material but not crisis-level exposure.

Electronic Arts’ 2021 Form 10-K repeatedly frames COVID-19 as a material, multi-dimensional risk that is both current (already disrupting operations) and prospective (could worsen).  The filing cites concrete, realized impacts—sports-season cancellations that impair the timing of key franchise launches, forced retail-store closures, office shutdowns, and a global shift to distributed development teams.  It also highlights systemic uncertainties such as employee fatigue, reduced productivity, quality lapses, and possible delays or cancellations of titles. The aggregate picture is a high but nuanced COVID-19 risk profile that EA must continue to monitor and manage.

EA’s 2022 filing portrays COVID-19 as an ongoing, multifaceted threat that is already disrupting day-to-day operations while simultaneously creating longer-term strategic uncertainty.  The company cites concrete, realised impacts—such as delayed game launches, diminished workforce productivity in a distributed environment, and hit-to-date operating results—showing that the pandemic is not merely theoretical but a present, material factor. Given the filing date (May 2022) sits well inside the 0-3-year window of the Time Decay Principle, high scores are justified for sentences that evidence direct, quantified or operational impacts, while more generic or mitigated statements warrant moderate or low scores.  Overall, the disclosure signals a substantial and continuing pandemic-related risk profile for EA.

EA’s Form 10-K devotes a discrete risk-factor subsection to the COVID-19 pandemic, establishing that the virus has already had a “significant” adverse effect on the company’s operations, workforce productivity and product launch timing, while also emphasizing that these pressures could persist or intensify.  The language is largely qualitative, but it is specific, recent (within three years of the filing) and cites concrete operational consequences—e.g., delayed launches, remote-work productivity erosion, and heightened talent-retention risk—rather than generic boiler-plate.  Mitigating references (office re-openings, flexible work models) temper but do not neutralize the seriousness. Taken together, the disclosures reveal a material, ongoing operational risk whose magnitude is meaningful but not yet quantified in dollars, warranting an overall elevated—but not maximum—risk assessment.

EA’s 2024 Form 10-K only references pandemic exposure in a broad, catch-all ‘catastrophic events’ paragraph rather than in a stand-alone COVID-19 discussion. eBay’s 2021-02-04 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic to multiple, concrete risk vectors that could materially disrupt the firm in the near-term.  The disclosures sit squarely within the 0-3 year “recent-event” window, so Time Decay does not diminish severity.  Management frames COVID-19 as both an existing impact (traffic shifts, mobility restrictions, mandated remote work) and a forward-looking threat (consumer-spending declines, shipping slow-downs, liquidity pressure, higher borrowing costs).  While some language notes short-term upside from increased on-line shopping, these mitigating remarks are outweighed by repeated warnings of potential material harm to operations, supply-chain throughput, workforce productivity and capital access.  Overall, the filing provides specific operational channels through which the pandemic could strike—consumer demand volatility, delivery delays, remote-work friction, and funding constraints—raising the aggregate risk profile to moderately-high.  Consequently, individual snippets that spell out tangible mechanisms of harm score between 5-8, whereas generic or mitigating statements fall into the 0-3 range, consistent with the micro-scorecard rules and recent-event Time Decay ceiling of 10.

eBay’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as both an already-felt and a still-evolving threat.  The filing acknowledges concrete impacts that have already materialised—such as lower consumer spending, forced remote-work arrangements, traffic volatility and tightening logistics—while also warning of forward-looking exposures in financing, liquidity and supply-chain stability.  Most statements are qualitative, but several explicitly link the pandemic to measurable business drivers (traffic, GMV, borrowing costs).  The tone is largely cautionary, using verbs like “created,” “has resulted,” and “may experience,” indicating both realised losses and prospective downside.  Because the filing date (24 Feb 2022) sits well within three years of the pandemic’s onset (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores; the disclosures are recent, directly tied to the event, and outline multiple operational vectors of risk.  Mitigating notes—such as prior traffic spikes—temper but do not eliminate the overall risk narrative, which remains elevated due to continuing uncertainty around variants, consumer behaviour and supply-chain friction.

eBay’s 2023 Form 10-K shows that management still views COVID-19 as a live, multifaceted threat, even though the acute phase of the pandemic is fading.  The filing moves beyond generic boiler-plate by citing concrete operational realities: shifting consumer demand, potential supply-chain bottlenecks (e.g., China’s former “zero-COVID” policy and shipping delays), labor-model disruption caused by prolonged remote and hybrid work, and an observed decline in 2022 net revenues and GMV as mobility restrictions eased.  All of these disclosures are forward-looking or presently unfolding, rather than purely historical, which places them in the “recent-event” bracket (0-3 years) under the Time Decay Principle.  No quantified dollar impact is given, but management explicitly warns of possible “material” harm and admits to already-realized revenue softness.  Accordingly, overall pandemic risk is assessed as moderate-to-high: the evidence is specific, connects directly to core metrics, and is temporally fresh, but lacks precise financial quantification, keeping individual snippet scores mostly in the mid-to-upper range rather than at the absolute maximum.

Across its 2024 Form 10-K, eBay still frames the COVID-19 pandemic principally as a potential, forward-looking head-wind rather than an immediate, quantified impairment.  References to “a pandemic” or “pandemics” appear inside longer catalogues of macro-economic threats that could weaken discretionary demand or disrupt international operations and user engagement.  The company links a pandemic to reduced customer spending and lower site traffic—factors that would directly hit GMV and fee revenues—yet gives no numerical ranges or examples from the 2020-2023 period.  Four years have elapsed since the WHO declaration (March 2020), so under the Time Decay Principle the pandemic is now a medium-term (4-year-old) risk: still relevant, but partly normalized.  Because disclosures are high-level, conditional (“may”, “could”), and embedded among many other risks, the evidence merits moderate severity scores (4-6).  No snippet reaches the threshold for a high (7-10) score, but the continued acknowledgement of pandemic-driven demand and operational impacts prevents scores from dropping to very low levels.

ECL’s 2021-02-26 Form 10-K offers abundant, recent and company-specific discussion of the COVID-19 pandemic. Given the filing date is within one year of the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Most evidence sentences therefore receive scores in the 4-9 range, calibrated to their specificity, directness, quantification and any mitigating context.

ECL’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as a recent, still-evolving threat that has already produced material, measurable damage to the company’s revenues, margins and supply chain, while simultaneously creating forward-looking uncertainty.  Multiple sentences state that the pandemic ‘materially and adversely’ affected results beginning in March 2020, especially through demand destruction in hospitality, foodservice and travel—core markets for ECL.  Beyond demand, the filing highlights systemic pressures such as labour shortages, logistics bottlenecks, rising delivered-product costs, capital-market volatility and talent-retention challenges.  The narrative blends historical fact (realised margin/volume hits, disrupted supply chains) with prospective risk (future variants, renewed lockdowns, lingering macro instability).  Language strength is high (‘material adverse effect’, ‘significant supply chain disruptions’) and specificity includes named sectors, timing markers, and causal mechanisms.  Because the filing date (25-Feb-2022) sits less than three years after the 11-Mar-2020 WHO declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows elevated scores.  However, not every sentence carries equal weight: some merely note evolved labour expectations or possible future lockdowns.  Overall, the risk level is high but heterogeneous; the micro-scorecards therefore range from 2/10 to 9/10, reflecting each sentence’s directness, severity descriptors, quantified or sector-specific detail, and any mitigating language.

The filing, dated February 24 2023, contains multiple, recent-vintage disclosures (2020-2023) tying the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and ongoing adverse effects on ECL’s operations.  The company explicitly cites material impacts already felt in core end-markets (food-service, hospitality, travel) as well as broad macro-pressures such as supply-chain disruption, inflation and labour-market shifts.  Several passages move beyond generic cautionary language: they acknowledge concrete demand declines, supply-chain bottlenecks and workforce productivity constraints that have already “materially and adversely” affected results.  Other statements are forward-looking, flagging continued uncertainty, potential resurgence of variants and evolving labour expectations.  Because the pandemic period is within the 0-3-year “recent” window, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores where impacts are direct and quantified; nonetheless, mitigating phrases (e.g., future uncertainty, conditional wording) temper some snippets.  Overall, the risk profile is high: the firm has faced actual financial harm and foresees continuing exposure across supply chain, labour, demand and operational continuity.

ECL’s 2024 filing repeatedly references the COVID-19 pandemic as both a historical shock and a continuing source of vulnerability. Management acknowledges that the pandemic directly depressed demand in core end-markets (foodservice, hospitality, travel) and created broader macro-pressures such as supply-chain disruption, inflation and currency volatility. No quantified dollar amounts are offered, but the language is specific about affected sectors, demand shortfalls and operational challenges. Four years have elapsed since the WHO declaration, placing the event in the Time-Decay medium window (4-10 years); therefore risk evidence should be scored in a moderate range. Overall, COVID-19 remains a material, though diminishing, risk driver for ECL—its severity is tempered by time but maintained by the company’s dependence on still-recovering customer segments and potential recurrence of public-health restrictions.

ED’s 2021-02-18 filing discusses COVID-19 as an active and evolving threat only 11 months after the WHO declaration, so no time-decay discount applies.  The narrative spans actual, quantified hits (e.g., $61 million in foregone revenue), operational stresses (remote-work cyber exposure, supply-chain vigilance, suspended collections), and forward-looking uncertainty over liquidity and demand.  Language is mostly specific—linking the pandemic to lower billed sales, higher uncollectibles, slower cash recovery and potential increases in bad-debt expense—yet it also notes partial offsets such as revenue-decoupling mechanisms.  Because the disclosures combine realised financial pain with continuing, not-fully-quantifiable exposures, overall risk is assessed as elevated but not catastrophic: high severity, medium-high likelihood, tempered by some structural mitigants.

Consolidated Edison (ED) acknowledges COVID-19 as a recent and still-evolving hazard that is already eroding cash flow, hampering supply chains, and introducing labour-force and regulatory complications.  The disclosure spans both realised impacts (e.g., quadrupling of bad-debt reserves, concrete supply-chain cost inflation, liquidity pressure) and forward-looking uncertainty (rapidly changing variants, vaccine mandates, unknowable future regulations).  Language is generally specific—quantifying receivable deterioration and itemising shortages of microchips and raw materials—rather than boiler-plate.  Although some mitigating factors are noted (revenue-decoupling mechanisms, ongoing monitoring, vaccination-compliance plans), they do not neutralise the breadth of the threats.  Given the 2022 filing date, the pandemic falls well inside the 0-3-year “recent” window of the Time Decay Principle, so individual sentence scores may legitimately reach the upper range when impacts are both direct and quantified.  Overall, the risk profile is high because the pandemic is simultaneously stressing liquidity, operations, and human capital with few certainties about duration or magnitude.

COVID-19 is treated by ED (Con Edison and its utility subsidiaries) as a live, multi-year threat that is still exerting measurable pressure on operations as of the February 2023 filing.  The disclosure moves well beyond boiler-plate: management cites concrete, realized impacts—cash collection delays, swollen customer receivables and liquidity strain—and explains clear causal pathways (economic slowdown, customer hardship, supply-chain disturbances, workforce disruption).  Although no dollar figures are attached, the language uses past-tense confirmations ("has resulted") as well as forward-looking warnings ("could continue to impact").  Mitigations such as revenue-decoupling are acknowledged but do not fully offset the exposure.  Because the pandemic is within the 0-3-year window of the Time Decay Principle, recent, operationally specific statements can attract high scores (7–10) depending on directness and materiality; generic or mitigated remarks receive lower scores.  Overall, the risk profile is significant and ongoing, underpinning liquidity, credit-quality, labor availability and service reliability concerns.

ED’s 2024 filing treats COVID-19 as both an historical shock and a still-material, yet fading, operational and financial risk.  The company frames the pandemic chiefly in two ways: (i) an ongoing contingency that could again disrupt workforce availability and essential utility operations, and (ii) a realised regulatory/collections shock that has already lengthened cash-conversion cycles and strained liquidity through mounting aged receivables.  The language is mostly qualitative—there are no dollar figures—but it is concrete, tying pandemic illness to service-continuity threats and tracing specific regulatory actions (state-mandated moratoriums on disconnections) back to COVID-19.  Because the pandemic’s onset is now roughly four years old, the immediacy of the threat has decayed; however, the disclosure makes clear that certain impacts (slower receivable recovery and potential liquidity pressure) are still unfolding.  Under the Time Decay Principle, that places the evidence in a mid-range severity band: higher than generic boiler-plate, lower than a freshly quantified loss.  Overall, I view ED’s pandemic exposure as moderate-to-elevated, warranting snippet scores between 2-7, with direct, causal statements about regulatory actions scoring highest and generic statements about “health epidemics” scoring lowest.

Equifax’s 2021 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a clear, present, and continuing enterprise-wide threat.  Because the filing date (25 Feb 2021) falls well inside the "recent" window of the Time-Decay Principle, any evidence of direct impact can justifiably receive high severity scores.  The disclosure set contains both backward-looking facts (e.g., ‘significant revenue declines’, worldwide vertical-market contraction, accelerated remote-work shift) and forward-looking warnings (persistent revenue pressure, liquidity risk, heightened cyber-exposure, possible asset impairments).  Some mitigation—cost controls, cloud migration progress, no internal-control disruption—is acknowledged, but management repeatedly stresses uncertainty and the potential for “material adverse” effects.  Importantly, Equifax links COVID-19 not only to lost revenue but to secondary risks such as financing constraints and amplified cybersecurity exposure from a remote workforce.  Given the immediacy of the pandemic, the magnitude of realized revenue declines, and the breadth of operational and financial vulnerabilities identified, overall risk is assessed as high (7–10 range for the strongest excerpts).  Where the company cites mitigations or expresses confidence (e.g., work-from-home protocols working well), downward score adjustments are applied in the micro-scorecards.

EFX’s 2022 Form 10-K candidly acknowledges both realized and continuing threats from the COVID-19 pandemic.  The filing cites concrete, historical impacts—such as “significant revenue declines,” early-2020 hits to consolidated results, and acute damage to international markets—demonstrating that the pandemic is not merely hypothetical but an existing drag on performance.  It then layers forward-looking warnings: management expects revenue pressure to persist, flags labour shortages, states that worsening macro-conditions could materially harm cash-flow and leverage metrics, and stresses the heightened uncertainty posed by new variants and government responses.  Although the company describes mitigation steps (stakeholder engagement, continuity plans, remote-work success), it concedes that these measures may fail and that COVID-19 could have a “material adverse effect.”  Because the event is recent (within the 0-3-year band of the Time Decay Principle) and the disclosure blends realised financial harm with ongoing, potentially material exposure, the evidence merits mid-to-high risk scores (generally 3-7).  Sentences that report experienced revenue losses or explicitly foresee material adverse effects score highest, while generic acknowledgements or purely mitigating statements receive lower or zero scores.

EFX’s 2023-02-23 Form 10-K squarely acknowledges that COVID-19 has already hurt the firm and can still do so. The filing cites concrete, realized impacts (e.g., “significant revenue declines in several of our markets”) and points to continuing vulnerabilities such as weakened consumer lending, lingering labour shortages, and the possibility that similar pandemics could recur. Although the language is largely qualitative and lacks precise dollar figures, it explicitly ties the pandemic to adverse demand shocks and operational strain, confirming that the risk is both historical and forward-looking. Because the pandemic’s onset (March 2020) is less than three years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows relatively high severity scores. Overall, the disclosures reveal a material but un-quantified risk that remains live; mitigation language is sparse and mainly limited to noting some recovery in unemployment-related revenue, so the net risk assessment stays elevated.

EFX’s 10-K acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic is both a historical and an ongoing risk driver.  The filing states that the company “experienced significant revenue declines” in several markets because of the pandemic, demonstrating a direct, realised impact on its financial performance. Although the narrative stops short of providing dollar figures or detailed operational disruptions (e.g., remote-work costs, supply-chain interruptions), it still elevates risk by expressly linking pandemic conditions to revenue shortfalls.  Given that COVID-19’s peak disruption began less than four years before the 2024 filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows moderately high scores (7-10) for direct, unquantified impacts and mid-range scores (3-6) for generic or background references.  Overall, the language reflects a material, recently-experienced risk that remains relevant, but the absence of precise metrics or granular operational details tempers the severity slightly below the maximum range.

EG’s 2021-03-01 filing contains multiple, recent and company-specific disclosures that tie the COVID-19 pandemic (declared 11-Mar-2020) to both realised 2020 impacts and forward-looking threats. Management reports a concrete, quantified hit to underwriting results (USD 511 million of pandemic losses) and acknowledges adverse effects already felt on results of operations, investment values and liquidity. Sentences that quantify or confirm actual losses score highest; purely contingent or generic statements score lower; any embedded mitigation (e.g., operational resiliency) would reduce a score, but such offsets are minimal here. Overall, the filing evidences a high but varied pandemic risk profile, requiring a sentence-by-sentence scoring spectrum roughly between 1 and 9.

EG’s 2022-02-28 filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad spectrum of risks that are both already impacting the company and expected to remain material over the next several years.  The disclosure is dominated by direct, contemporaneous effects (e.g., adverse operating results, claim reserves, premium reductions) and forward-looking uncertainties around legislative actions, capital markets volatility, credit stress and operational continuity.  The language goes well beyond generic boiler-plate: it cites concrete mechanisms—loss-reserve volatility, premium give-backs, remote-work cyber-exposures—and repeatedly labels the potential impact as “material.”  Because the pandemic began in March 2020, less than three years before the filing date, Time Decay is minimal and high severity scores are permissible.  However, most statements remain qualitative and some include mitigating elements (existing reserves, remote-work implementation).  Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the 4-8 range rather than the absolute maximum of 10.  Overall, the pandemic constitutes an elevated, multi-dimensional, continuing risk for EG with limited decay and high strategic relevance.

The filing, dated February 28 2024, contains only a brief reference to pandemic risk within a broader disclosure on business-continuity threats. I therefore assess the evidence at the lower end of the medium-term band, reflecting acknowledgement of an ongoing pandemic threat but little specificity or immediacy.

ELV’s 2021-02-18 Form 10-K repeatedly frames COVID-19 as a recent, still-evolving hazard that is already disrupting operations and could inflict further, material damage on virtually every financial metric the company tracks.  The filing contains both backward-looking evidence (higher 2020 costs, accelerated fourth-quarter expense, membership shifts) and forward-looking warnings (possible cash-flow shortfalls, supply-chain interruptions, labour challenges, investment losses, cost-of-capital spikes).  Language is highly specific—identifying remote-work inefficiencies, vendor failures, cyber-risk, delayed customer payments, and supply-chain breakdowns—and explicitly states that impacts “could be material.”  No quantitative dollar figure is supplied, so the disclosures fall short of a maximum-severity, but the breadth of identified channels (claims volatility, rate unpredictability, capital-market access, infrastructure disruption) and the fact that the pandemic began less than a year before the filing date justify high risk scores under the Time Decay Principle.  While the company notes monitoring efforts and some mitigating actions (e.g., expanded benefits, remote work), these do not materially offset the magnitude or uncertainty of the threat.  Overall, COVID-19 represents a live, enterprise-wide risk with high severity potential, warranting strong (7-9) scores for the most acute statements and moderate (4-6) scores where specificity or directness is weaker or partial mitigants are cited.

The filing, dated February 16 2022, shows Anthem/ELV describing COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that has already produced measurable adverse impacts and remains highly uncertain.  Disclosures span direct cost pressure (surging utilisation, testing, treatment, vaccine administration), operational friction (remote-work productivity loss, heightened cyber-risk), supply-chain and third-party vendor disruptions, volatility in enrolment mix and cash-flows, and retroactive rate adjustments by regulators.  Language is largely present-tense (“are adversely affecting”, “continues to evolve”), indicating active impacts rather than hypothetical future risks, and repeatedly flags the possibility of “material” effects.  Because the 10-K is filed within two years of the WHO pandemic declaration (March 11 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7-10).  Nevertheless, statements vary in specificity; some provide broad, qualitative warnings while others tie COVID-19 to concrete cost categories or operational problems.  The overall risk level is assessed as high: the pandemic has already affected claims, cash-flows and workforce arrangements, and management cites numerous paths through which further deterioration could occur, with limited mitigating language beyond ongoing monitoring.  Consequently, the evidence snippets earn scores clustered in the upper-mid to high range, reflecting immediacy, breadth of impact and explicit materiality references, tempered slightly where descriptions are generic or list potential rather than realised effects.

ELV’s 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly frames COVID-19 as a live, material, and multi-dimensional threat. Overall, the risk profile is acute, recent, and enterprise-wide, justifying upper-mid to high micro-scores across the extracted evidence.

ELV’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 as a live, albeit moderating, enterprise-wide threat. EL’s 2021-08-27 filing acknowledges that COVID-19 is both an ongoing and a highly uncertain threat that is already eroding revenue drivers (brick-and-mortar traffic, travel retail, makeup demand) while simultaneously creating forward-looking exposure (future variants, consumer behaviour shifts, retailer bankruptcies). Because the filing date is well within three years of the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores. The micro-scores below reflect this mix, with direct, quantified or operationally specific impacts scoring highest and purely cautionary or mitigated statements scoring lower.

COVID-19 remains a dominant, multi-dimensional risk for Estée Lauder (EL) in its 2022-08-24 filing. Because the event window (March 2020 onward) is well within the 0-3-year “recent” band, time-decay does little to diminish severity.  Most disclosures are forward-looking but are anchored in concrete, realised impacts and dollar figures, elevating credibility.  Overall, EL faces a high residual pandemic risk (≈ 8/10 average across snippets) that is only partially offset by mitigation efforts such as digital pivoting and gradual travel recovery.

The filing, dated February 25 2022, repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized 2020–2021 financial impacts and to continuing, forward-looking uncertainties.  Several passages quantify the operational harm in qualitative terms—lower capacity utilization, reduced sales volumes, unfavorable product mix and EBIT pressure—while the risk section projects that ongoing pandemic-driven disruptions in demand, supply chains, labor markets and capital markets "may adversely impact" liquidity and future results. EMN’s 2023 filing treats COVID-19 as an ongoing, recently experienced risk rather than a closed historical issue.  The company explicitly states that the “continuing COVID-19 pandemic” has already affected demand, costs, cash flows, and supply-chain reliability and could further constrain access to capital, worsen liquidity, and raise raw-material and energy prices. The risk discussion combines (a) forward-looking language about recurring waves and future pandemics, (b) current-state disclosures on eviction moratoria and rent-collection limits that remain in force in several jurisdictions, and (c) hard data quantifying elevated cash delinquencies (1.9 % in 2021; 1.2 % in 2022 versus a pre-pandemic norm of 0.3-0.4 %).  These statements show both direct realised impacts (higher delinquencies, statutory constraints) and continuing potential exposures (renewed moratoria, restructuring of tenant obligations, reduced liquidity for mezzanine borrowers).  Because the filing date (Feb-2023) is less than three years after the initial event window, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores where impacts are direct or quantified.  Nevertheless, some passages are framed as contingencies (“could,” “may”) or even as partial mitigants (e.g., ability to access funding), and these are scored lower or net-negative.  Overall, the company’s language signals a significant but partially stabilising risk: operational effects are still evident, but severity has eased from early-pandemic peaks, and management notes certain offsets such as government rental assistance and continued capital-market access.  This mixed picture is reflected in the individual micro-scores below.

ESS’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to flag the COVID-19 pandemic as a material but now medium-term risk.  Nearly four years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), management’s language has shifted from emergency triage to managing lingering structural consequences: elevated cash delinquencies, tenant attitude changes toward rent payment, ongoing rent-control-style legislation, and broader macro knock-ons such as remote-work demand shifts, labor and material shortages, and supply-chain cost inflation.  The company still records quantifiable impacts (e.g., delinquency rates ~5× pre-pandemic and specific Emergency Rental Assistance inflows) while simultaneously noting that it is “emerging from restrictions,” signalling partial mitigation.  Because the filing date (Feb 2024) sits just beyond the 3-year “recent” window, the Time-Decay Principle limits severity to a moderate band; the evidence therefore warrants scores between 4-6, capturing continued but no longer peak risk exposure.  The disclosures are generally forward-looking but anchored by observed financial effects, making the overall pandemic risk profile meaningful, un-mitigated in several key areas, yet not catastrophic.

Eversource’s February 2021 filing devotes an extensive, detailed section to COVID-19.  The company recognises both realised and prospective impacts across financing, operations, supply chain, labour and customer demand.  Several passages describe concrete effects already experienced—such as rapid deterioration of commercial-paper liquidity, moderate schedule slippage on offshore-wind permits, and observable drops in C&I energy demand—while others highlight still-uncertain exposures (e.g., potential future work restrictions, unquantified workforce impacts, unknown cost of receivables).  Language is mostly specific and anchored in the company’s own circumstances, not generic boiler-plate, and it ties the pandemic directly to material financial metrics (cash flow, results of operations, capital programmes).  Mitigating actions—remote work, supply-chain measures, capital-market access to date—are also disclosed, tempering but not eliminating risk.  Because the filing date is less than one year after the WHO declaration (Time Decay window 0-3 years), evidence can receive high severity scores where warranted.  Overall, the disclosure reflects a significant, current risk profile with a mix of realised hits and sizeable residual uncertainty, justifying mid-to-high snippet scores (4-7 range) under the scoring framework.

Eversource’s February 2022 filing repeatedly links the 2020-onward COVID-19 pandemic to material and still-evolving enterprise risks.  The language is forward-looking but rooted in already-incurred impacts such as higher bad-debt reserves and incremental pandemic costs; therefore the disclosures merge present impact with potential escalation.  Core risk vectors identified include (1) global supply-chain delays and price inflation for critical materials, (2) labour market stress and potential loss of key staff, (3) greater cybersecurity exposure because of pandemic operating conditions, (4) elevated uncollectible receivables following moratoria on customer shut-offs, and (5) regulatory uncertainty over cost recovery of pandemic-related expenses.  No single figure threatens solvency, yet the company quantifies millions of dollars in 2021 COVID-related charges while simultaneously admitting it “cannot estimate” the full financial effect.  The statements are detailed, recent (within two years of filing) and span multiple operational pillars, giving them moderate-to-high severity under the Time-Decay Principle.  Because most impacts are described qualitatively or at low-eight-figure scale without long-term projections, scores cluster in the 4-7 range rather than the maximum 9-10 reserved for quantified, transformative losses.

COVID-19 appears in the 2023-02-15 Form 10-K almost exclusively in the context of customer receivable risk.  Management states that the pandemic’s chief impact has been a rise in uncollectible accounts, quantifies the amounts still embedded in reserves ($50.9 million company-wide, down from $55.3 million the year before) and explains that most of these amounts have been deferred for probable recovery in future rates.  No other pandemic-era pressure points—such as supply-chain delays, site shutdowns, remote-work inefficiencies or labour shortages—are identified as material.  Thus, the disclosure is recent (inside the three-year Time-Decay window) and quantified, but the company simultaneously emphasises mitigation: explicit cost deferrals, declining balances and strong confidence in eventual regulatory recovery.  Accordingly, while the statements merit scoring in the upper-middle range because they document a direct, measured financial exposure that is still live, the heavy presence of offsetting language tempers the severity; overall the risk evidence sits in the 4-6 band rather than the 7-10 band that would attach to an unmitigated, wide-ranging pandemic threat.

After a meticulous, sentence-by-sentence review of the entire filing, no passages explicitly or implicitly connect the Company’s risks to the COVID-19 pandemic or to pandemic-specific consequences such as lockdown-driven demand shifts, mandated remote work, workforce illness, or pandemic-related supply-chain breakdowns. Although the document discusses generic supply-chain volatility, labor availability, and other operational uncertainties, none of those statements attribute the cause—or even a contributory role—to COVID-19. Under the methodology, if no language ties the described risk to the stated event, there is no qualifying evidence. Consequently, all potential snippet scores must be zero, and no micro-scorecards are produced. The Company therefore provides no discernible disclosure of pandemic-related risk, implying either that management now considers pandemic impacts immaterial or that such impacts are fully embedded in broader risk categories without event attribution.

The filing, dated only eleven months after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, presents COVID-19 as both an already-materialized threat and an ongoing, highly uncertain risk. Eaton explicitly discloses that the outbreak has *already* “negatively impacted” its operations and financial results, making the risk current rather than hypothetical. The company then details the mechanisms of impact—government lockdowns, travel bans, shifting consumer demand, and potential production-facility disruptions—while stressing that future consequences remain unpredictable. The language is largely qualitative (no dollar figures), but it is direct, specific and tied to operational and financial performance, so under the Time Decay Principle (0-3-year window) high but not maximum scores are warranted. No meaningful mitigating actions are described, so aggravating factors dominate the scoring.

The filing, dated February 23, 2022—less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic—contains multiple, company-authored sentences that link the pandemic to both realized and potential future impacts. The language is primarily qualitative and unquantified, yet it is specific about operational pinch points such as plant closures, cost inflation, and supply-chain strain. Because the event is recent, the Time Decay Principle allows higher severity scores, but the absence of hard numbers or outright declarations of material financial loss moderates the ceilings. Overall, the narrative signals a meaningful, ongoing risk that is already manifesting in day-to-day operations, with some mitigating notes (e.g., essential-business designations). The evidence therefore merits mid-to-upper-range scores (3-6) rather than the absolute maximum.

ETN’s 2023 Form 10-K shows that COVID-19 remains a live, material, yet partially mitigated risk.  The filing, dated less than three years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), repeatedly links the pandemic to both historical disruptions (mandatory shutdowns, restricted operations, supply-chain congestion, price inflation, labour scarcity) and to forward-looking uncertainty (possible renewed closures, continued supply-chain stress, amplification of other risk factors).  The language mixes fact (‘we were restricted’) with conditional statements (‘could further disrupt’, ‘no assurance’), indicating that some impacts have already occurred while management still sees material potential downside.  Mitigating statements—essential-business exemptions, subsiding disruptions—temper but do not eliminate the risk.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, evidence dated within three years of the event permits high but not maximal scores; unquantified, largely qualitative disclosures place most snippets in the 3-6 range, with lower scores for generic or heavily mitigated statements and higher scores for company-specific, direct impact sentences.

Eaton (ETN) presents COVID-19 as a still-relevant but now partially abating operational threat. The filing, dated February 29 2024—almost four years after the WHO declared the pandemic—frames the virus as both an historical source of proven disruption (facility shutdowns, employee restrictions, supply-chain interruptions) and a continuing, forward-looking uncertainty (possibility of future closures, further supply-chain stress, exacerbation of other risks). The language is mostly qualitative and cautionary, with no hard dollar figures, and it is tempered by acknowledgements that many disruptions "have subsided" and that essential-business classifications previously mitigated impacts. This context underpins the individual micro-scores below.

Entergy’s 2022 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad spectrum of operational, financial, workforce and supply-chain threats. The language is both backward-looking (citing realised drops in sales and rising arrearages) and forward-looking (warning of renewed shutdowns, credit-market turmoil, labour shortages, and supply-chain bottlenecks).  Some mitigating themes appear—partial sales recovery, vaccine roll-outs, reconnection of delinquent customers, and active regulatory engagement—but management repeatedly stresses “highly uncertain” outcomes across liquidity, capital access, and strategic execution.  Overall, the disclosure signals an elevated, continuing risk profile with several realised pain points and numerous unresolved contingencies, justifying mid-to-upper‐range scores for individual snippets.
