The filing discusses the COVID-19 pandemic only in the broader category of “public health crises,” but the accompanying language maps directly onto the classic pandemic stress points: supply-chain bottlenecks, labor shortages from infections, telecommuting-driven cyber-risk, liquidity strain, regulatory delays, and potential government mandates.  Because the pandemic began in March 2020 and this Form 10-K is dated February 2024, we are four years removed from the event’s onset; under the Time-Decay Principle this places the evidence in the medium-term window (4-10 years), capping realistic severity in the mid-single digits.  The text is forward-looking and conditional (“could be adversely affected”) rather than reporting concrete 2023 losses, so it represents potential ongoing exposure rather than a realised hit.  Nevertheless, the company enumerates multiple operational and financial vectors that remain vulnerable, signalling a still-material but moderated risk posture. COVID-19 is treated throughout the filing as a current, multi-faceted and material threat. Because the Form 10-K was filed less than one year after the WHO declaration (within the 0-3-year ‘recent event’ window), the Time-Decay Principle allows scores up to the high range. Overall, the risk profile is high, direct and still evolving, warranting elevated—but not peak—severity scores.

EVRG’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as both an already-experienced shock and a continuing, multi-faceted threat. Overall, the disclosures reflect a material, continuing, but largely un-quantified enterprise risk driven by the pandemic.

The filing, made nearly four years after the formal declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic, frames pandemic exposure as a continuing, forward-looking enterprise-wide threat rather than as a recently realised shock.  EVRG clusters pandemic language under a dedicated risk factor, positioning the hazard alongside other systemic perils (e.g., supply-chain upheaval, inflation, labour shortages). This generic, ‘could/may’ phrasing signals that management views the pandemic more as an ongoing contingency than as an acute impact already embedded in the accounts.  Because the disclosure window (Feb-2024) falls just beyond the three-year “recent” band, the Time-Decay Principle caps severity in the mid-range; nonetheless, EVRG still links COVID-19 to material operational and financial vectors (capital projects, liquidity access, supply-chain cost escalation).  Overall, the risk evidence is moderate: it is direct and multi-dimensional but unquantified and highly conditional, yielding snippet scores that cluster between 4-5, with downward adjustments for the generic caveats and lack of specificity.

COVID-19 is an extremely recent event relative to the February 12 2021 filing date, so any disclosed effects carry maximum time-relevance. Because the disclosures combine (i) direct, realised impacts from 2020, (ii) quantified or explicitly qualified language like “material” and “significant,” and (iii) broad forward-looking uncertainty, the overall pandemic risk for EW merits an elevated severity assessment in the 7-10 range under the Time Decay Principle, tempered slightly only where the firm demonstrates specific mitigations.

EW’s 2022-02-14 filing repeatedly acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic has already produced material, broad-based disruptions and that these pressures remain highly uncertain going forward.  The language spans both Risk Factors and MD&A, documenting concrete historical impacts (e.g., “procedure volumes dropped significantly,” “sales were negatively impacted”) and identifying future exposure to supply-chain constraints, clinical-trial delays, labour and hospital-capacity shortages, and volatile product demand. Mitigating disclosures (inventory management, resumed trials, monitoring) temper, but do not erase, the severity.  Given the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is a very recent, ongoing event (<3 years), so individual snippet scores can reasonably range up to 10; none are fully quantified, so the highest evidence tops out at 7. Overall, COVID-19 represents a significant, ongoing operational and financial risk for EW with moderate mitigation, justifying elevated—though not maximum—severity scores across the extracted evidence.

I therefore expect individual snippet scores to range from low-single digits for purely mitigative or de-emphasising sentences, up to the high-single digits where a direct, quantified 2022 impairment is disclosed.

Expedia’s 2024 Form 10-K repeatedly ties the COVID-19 pandemic to both historical damage and ongoing risk vectors. Management states that the pandemic “severely restricted” economic activity, produced an “unprecedented negative impact” on global travel, and “materially impacted” the firm’s business, liquidity and those of its partners. Although demand has largely recovered by 2023, the filing still invokes the pandemic as the reference scenario for liquidity strain, working-capital pressure and industry demand shocks, signalling that a similar health event remains a material forward-looking threat. The language is largely specific and fact-based (e.g., liquidity squeeze, merchant hotel cash flows), not boiler-plate, yet most impacts are framed in the past tense or as illustrative stress cases. Because the event occurred four years ago, Time-Decay dictates that per-sentence scores fall in the moderate range (4-6) even when wording is severe; mitigating statements that “lingering impacts did not have a significant impact” further dampen some evidence. Overall, COVID-19 remains a meaningful but now moderated risk factor whose severity has attenuated since peak disruption, justifying mid-level severity scores for the extracted evidence.

EXR’s 2021 Form 10-K squarely acknowledges COVID-19 as both an already-realized and an ongoing threat.  The filing date (26 Feb 2021) is less than one year after the WHO declared the pandemic (11 Mar 2020), putting the disclosure in the “recent event” window where high scores are justified under the Time-Decay Principle.  The company does more than offer boiler-plate language: it details concrete, historical impacts (lower rental rates, reduced new rentals, higher bad-debt, etc.) and flags continued macro-economic uncertainty that could materially hurt future results.  At the same time, it outlines multiple mitigating responses—work-from-home, contactless rentals, PPE, online interaction—which temper, but do not eliminate, the risk.  Because the narrative combines (1) specific, already-observed operational hits, (2) a forward-looking warning of potentially “significant” future effects, and (3) explicit mitigation efforts, the overall risk profile is high but not existential.  The strongest evidence sentences therefore score in the 6-8 range, with mitigation-heavy sentences receiving low or zero scores, and purely generic references receiving only modest points.  All scores are constrained to the 0-10 band appropriate for a sub-3-year-old event.

EXR’s 2022 filing places COVID-19 squarely in the “recent event” category (less than three years old), so the Time Decay Principle allows high scores where warranted.  The company discloses both backward-looking, realized impacts (e.g., lower rental rates, frozen auctions, higher bad-debt expense in 2020) and forward-looking uncertainties (possible future economic shocks, new variants, continuing emergency orders, and heightened cyber-risk tied to remote work).  The narrative is mixed: management documents a measurable hit to operating metrics in 2020, partial recovery in 2021, and lays out mitigation steps (safety protocols, monitoring emergency orders).  Because the text stops short of quantifying dollar figures, the risk evidence is strong but not maximal.  Overall, I assess COVID-19 as a material, continuing risk that could re-intensify; the realized 2020 effects justify higher mid-to-upper scores for the most specific sentences, while mitigation language and partial normalization temper—but do not negate—the risk profile.

EXR’s 2023-02-28 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as a still-relevant, recently manifest threat rather than a closed historical episode. Management discloses that the pandemic already hurt 2020 performance and could "materially and adversely" affect future operations through multiple channels—chiefly demand destruction (lower rental rates, higher bad-debt, inhibited auctions), capital-markets impairment, and broader economic shock. The wording is largely qualitative and forward-looking, with no dollar figures, but it is specific on operational mechanics and acknowledges a past, direct hit. Because the filing date is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, Time Decay does not significantly soften severity. Therefore, individual evidence snippets merit mid-to-high scores (4-6) when they articulate concrete pathways or note actual past impact, with lower scores for generic or heavily mitigated statements.

EXR’s 2024 Form 10-K discusses COVID-19–type threats primarily under the broader heading of “public health emergencies.”  The company frames the pandemic risk as forward-looking: it does not cite any quantified, historical hit to revenue or cash flow, but it does spell out several clear operational transmission channels—lower demand from stay-at-home orders, reduced late-fee collections, difficulty holding lien-sale auctions, higher bad-debt expense, and impaired capital-raising capacity.  The language is somewhat generic (no dollar figures or probability estimates) yet still uses strong qualifiers such as “materially and adversely” and “significant.”  Because the filing date (29 Feb 2024) is less than four years after the WHO declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows relatively high scores.  Overall, the disclosure signals a real but unquantified, continuing exposure; therefore the individual snippets generally fall in the moderate-to-elevated range (4-6), with modest downward adjustments where the company cites industry resilience or expresses uncertainty.

FAST’s 2021-02-08 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and prospective business risks.  Across the filing the company describes concrete, recent impacts: sharp reductions in fastener demand, emergency purchases through non-optimised supply chains, labour-force and branch closures, and an immediate mix-shift toward low-margin PPE that compressed gross margin.  It also warns of continuing and possibly material adverse effects stemming from further government lockdowns, staffing shortages, customer liquidity problems, and supplier/manufacturer disruptions.  The disclosures mix backward-looking data (e.g., 2020 spending declines, gross-profit hits) with forward-looking uncertainty (“may continue”, “could be material and last for an extended period”).  Language such as “material adverse effect”, “sharply reduced”, and precise operational channels (supply chain, staffing, liquidity) underscores severity.  Because the filing date is less than a year after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7-10) where statements show direct, recent impact; moderately lower scores (4-6) are applied where the impact is secondary or partially mitigated; sentences that emphasise safeguards or ongoing operational effectiveness carry negative points to reflect mitigation.  This calibrated approach yields an evidence set that consistently portrays COVID-19 as a major, active risk driver for FAST.

FAST’s 2022 Form 10-K positions COVID-19 as both an already-realized and still-evolving threat.  Numerous passages describe concrete damage the pandemic inflicted in 2020-2021— missed Onsite and FMI sign-up targets, labour shortages, supply-chain congestion and sharply higher freight costs—showing the risk is not merely hypothetical but has materially hit growth drivers and margins.  Other statements expand the risk horizon by warning that future outbreaks could force facility shutdowns, remote-work transitions or further customer slow-downs, and that management cannot yet quantify the eventual financial toll.  The language is mostly specific, tying the virus to identifiable business levers (customer access, shipping lanes, product mix, head-count), and repeatedly labels the effect as “material.”  Because the filing date (7 Feb 2022) falls less than two years after the initial WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Still, some mitigating notes—ongoing mitigations, lack of precise dollar figures, inclusion of broader macro factors—temper the maximum scores.  Overall, the disclosure set signals a high but not existential level of pandemic risk, justifying snippet scores largely in the 5-9 range.

FAST’s 2023 filing shows that COVID-19 remains a live, though moderating, enterprise-wide risk.  Management references both realised consequences (2020-22 facility closures, weakened Chinese revenues, supply-chain bottlenecks, labour shortages, inflation and lower Onsite/FMI signings) and a continuing cloud of uncertainty (potential future outbreaks, variants, demand swings and product-availability issues).  The disclosures therefore mix backward-looking facts that have already eroded sales growth with forward-looking language that keeps the threat active.  Because the pandemic erupted less than three years before the filing, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores; however, the company also notes offsetting positives (PPE sales) and even states 2022 results were not “meaningfully” affected, which tempers the overall risk assessment.  Collectively, I rate COVID-19 risk for FAST as moderate-to-high: the event has demonstrably harmed operations and still carries material downside, but its incremental impact appears to be easing relative to the initial shock of 2020-21.

FAST’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to acknowledge the COVID-19 pandemic (and any future widespread public-health crisis) as a material, though now moderating, enterprise risk.  The filing does not cite new, quantified dollar impacts; instead, it frames the pandemic largely as a prospective threat that could again disrupt demand, supply chains, labour availability, and workplace practices.  The language is mostly conditional (“could”, “may”), signalling that management views the pandemic’s acute phase as past, but still sees residual vulnerability should another wave or comparable pathogen emerge.  References to earlier revenue swings in safety and janitorial products confirm that the company has already experienced real pandemic-driven volatility, yet these are historical observations rather than forward-looking forecasts.  Given that the initial WHO declaration occurred in March 2020—just under four years before this February 2024 filing—the Time-Decay Principle places the event at the cusp of the 0-3 and 4-10-year bands; accordingly, individual snippet scores are capped in the mid-range (4-6 for the most specific, multi-impact disclosures, 2-3 for generic or historical mentions).  Overall, the disclosure set indicates a moderate, still-relevant risk that warrants ongoing monitoring but no longer rises to crisis-level severity.

FDS’s 10-K, filed in October 2021, addresses COVID-19 risks in detail.  Because the filing date is well inside the 0-3-year window following the WHO’s 11 March 2020 pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores where language shows direct or potentially material impact.  The company mostly frames the pandemic as an ongoing and forward-looking threat—citing possible client spending cuts, operational hurdles from government restrictions, remote-work productivity risks, medical-cost exposure, and management distraction.  Importantly, it also discloses that operations have already been “affected,” and that wide-ranging mobility limits were imposed on staff, evidencing present-tense impact rather than pure hypotheticals.  Mitigating statements—e.g., that financial results have not yet been materially harmed and that remote work has “had relatively little impact”—temper some severity, but do not erase the substantive risk factors.  Overall, the document presents a moderate-to-high risk profile (individual snippets range roughly 1-7) with no sign of long-term time decay discounting, because the pandemic remains acute and its duration unknown.

FDS acknowledges COVID-19 primarily as a potentially severe but still largely emergent operational and financial threat.  Although the company notes that, up to the October 2022 filing date, the pandemic has not yet produced a “material negative impact,” management nonetheless describes multiple channels through which future damage could arise: (i) government counter-measures such as travel restrictions, quarantines and site closures; (ii) productivity losses among employees, vendors and data-suppliers, especially in remote-work settings that heighten dependence on video-conferencing and cloud services; (iii) higher medical-insurance costs; and (iv) knock-on amplification of other disclosed risks.  The language is forward-looking and conditional, but it repeatedly uses strong qualifiers such as “materially and adversely affected,” “substantial negative impact,” and “may interfere with the ability of our employees… to perform,” indicating that the company views the risk as significant even if not yet realised.  Because the filing date falls only 2½ years after the WHO declaration (within the 0–3 year window), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores; however, the company’s explicit statement of *no* current material impact and its description of active mitigation efforts partially offset that severity.  Overall, the pandemic presents a medium-to-high residual risk (roughly mid-single-digit scores), with the most acute vulnerability tied to workforce productivity and supply-side content gathering rather than immediate revenue contraction.

FDS’ 2023-10-27 Form 10-K positions the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, but largely potential, threat rather than a presently quantified drag on performance.  All references appear in the Risk-Factors section, signalling management’s acknowledgement that the pandemic has altered operating conditions (remote-work infrastructure, reliance on video-conferencing vendors, and possible supply-chain or data-collection constraints) and could again disrupt demand or internal processes.  The language is forward-looking and largely generic—there are no dollar figures, probability estimates, or time-bound scenarios—yet it repeatedly uses high-impact terms such as “materially and adversely affected,” “widespread health crisis,” and “interfere with the ability of our employees, vendors, and data suppliers,” implying the consequences could be severe.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, the event is still within the recent window (COVID-19 declared March 2020; filing October 2023 = ~3 ½ years), so evidence can be scored in the upper-mid range.  Because the disclosures describe broad operational and financial exposure without specific loss data, I assess the overall pandemic risk disclosure as moderate-to-high: serious enough to merit investor attention (scores 6-8) but tempered by its contingency-based framing and lack of quantification.

FDS acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat, even though the initial outbreak occurred more than four years before this 2024 filing.  The company frames the pandemic primarily as a forward-looking, continuing risk rather than a past, quantified loss: language such as “could be materially and adversely affected” and “may interfere” signals potential rather than realized impact.  Nevertheless, the disclosure explicitly cites COVID-19 and details multiple pathways of harm—macroeconomic slow-downs, reduced client demand, employee and vendor disruption, and heightened remote-work-related vulnerabilities.  These statements are specific enough to identify operational chokepoints (e.g., travel restrictions, site closures, dependence on video-conferencing providers) but remain largely un-quantified and generic in timing.  Under the Time Decay Principle, a 4-plus-year-old event should receive moderate severity scores (4-6 range) when the filer still sees material exposure.  Therefore, evidence that links COVID-19 to material adverse effects and concrete operational friction is scored toward the upper mid-range, while more generic or indirect references (e.g., remote-work cybersecurity concerns) receive lower mid-range scores.  No sentence is scored higher than 6 because the pandemic is no longer a “recent” (0-3 year) event, and no sentence is scored below 0 because the filing date is after the event began.

FedEx’s 2021 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an acute, still-evolving threat that is already reshaping every major driver of the company’s performance: demand mix (surging residential volumes, volatile commercial traffic), operating cost structure (labour, PPE, cleaning, security), network efficiency (need to ‘flex’ assets amid constrained air-freight capacity and disrupted global supply chains) and enterprise-wide risk profile (cyber-exposure from remote work, heightened exposure to partners such as the USPS).  The disclosure is not merely cautionary; it cites concrete, realised impacts—"unprecedented" peak-level residential volumes, “increased costs” and “lower composite yields”—as well as forward-looking uncertainties tied to variant outbreaks, government restrictions and labour shortages.  Language is company-specific and repeatedly links the pandemic to material financial metrics, but remains largely unquantified.  Given the filing date (July 2021), the pandemic sits well inside the 0-3-year ‘recent’ window, so time-decay allows high risk scores.  Overall, the text evidences a high-severity, continuing risk, tempered only by the absence of exact dollar figures or probability estimates.

FedEx’s 2022 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and still-evolving threats across every major risk vector the prompt asks us to track.  Because the filing date (18-Jul-2022) is within 30 months of the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), Time-Decay permits high scores.  The company discloses concrete, already-incurred impacts—lower 2022 operating results, reduced shipping demand, network disruptions, higher labour and PPE costs—while also warning that fresh variants, remote-work vulnerabilities and uncertain government restrictions could further erode margins and heighten other disclosed risks.  The language is mostly specific (naming cost categories, business lines and operational choke-points such as FedEx Express) and sometimes quantified qualitatively (“higher costs,” “reduced shipping demand”), but does not give precise dollar amounts.  No meaningful mitigating language (e.g., insurance recoveries, firm cost-savings) offsets these statements.  Therefore the evidence set warrants mid-to-high severity scores (4-9 range), with sentences describing concrete 2022 detriments at the upper end and more generic forward-looking cautions at the lower end.

FDX’s 2023-07-17 filing references COVID-19 and broader public-health crises across both the Risk Factors and MD&A sections.  The text acknowledges a mix of realised and prospective impacts: (i) concrete, recent effects—e.g., lower volumes, Asian lockdown-related disruptions, shifts in consumer behaviour and elevated safety costs—and (ii) forward-looking uncertainties such as further variants, supply-chain instability and heightened exposure to other disclosed risks.  Language is mostly qualitative but does tie the pandemic to specific operational pain points (supply-chain bottlenecks, labour/fuel cost pressures, network agility).  Because the statements come only a little over three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle places them at the cusp of “recent” and “medium-term.”  Accordingly, I weight direct, continuing impact sentences in the 6-7 range, while more generic or mitigated references score lower.  No sentence merits the absolute maximum because none quantifies dollar materiality, yet multiple snippets still signal material continuing exposure, justifying moderate-to-high risk scores overall.

FDX continues to frame the COVID-19 pandemic and future public-health crises as material, but now largely prospective, enterprise-wide threats.  The 2024 filing no longer cites specific dollar impacts; instead management stresses the pandemic’s enduring ability to disrupt demand profiles, supply-chain fluidity, labor availability, cost structure and regulatory posture.  The language is broad and conditional ("could," "may"), signalling that the most acute financial pain has passed, yet the company still sees a meaningful possibility of renewed volatility—especially through new variants, travel or lockdown restrictions, and heightened compliance costs.  These statements therefore represent forward-looking, unquantified risk disclosures rather than confirmations of current impairment.  Given that the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic more than four years ago (March 2020) and the filing date is July 2024, the Time-Decay Principle places this in the medium-term window (4-10 years).  Consistent with that framework, individual evidence snippets warrant moderate scores (4-6) that acknowledge ongoing but diminished severity.  Mitigating specifics such as successful network agility programs or quantified cost offsets are largely absent, so no material downward adjustments apply beyond generic wording penalties.

FFIV’s 2021-11-16 filing squarely acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic remains an active, enterprise-level threat.  Although management says fiscal-year 2021 results were not yet materially hit, they concede that pandemic-driven supply-chain shortages are already reducing visibility into component lead-times and that a broad set of downstream effects— from customer-spending slow-downs to remote-work disruptions—could still impair revenue, operations and margins.  The language is recent (within two years of the March 2020 WHO declaration), mixes concrete present-tense impacts (ongoing supply-chain constraints) with forward-looking contingencies (possible demand declines, cash-collection delays, workforce challenges), and generally avoids quantification.  Taken together, this yields a moderate-to-high risk profile: specific operational pain points have emerged, but the company also notes mitigation efforts and reports no significant historical hit yet.  Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the 2-8 range, with higher marks where the filing ties direct, ongoing impacts to COVID-19 and lower marks where management highlights mitigation or uncertainty without evidence of current damage.  All scores comply with the Time Decay Principle for a recent event (0-3 years, scores may reach up to 10).

FFIV’s November 2022 Form 10-K ties multiple, still-developing operational and financial threats directly to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The firm confirms present-day, tangible impacts—chiefly global supply-chain constraints that extend lead-times, raise component costs, and delay hardware deliveries—while also conceding broad uncertainty around future customer demand, collections, and workforce logistics.  Statements are largely specific, describing concrete bottlenecks and cost pressure rather than generic boiler-plate, and they reference on-going mitigation efforts that partially offset but do not eliminate the risks.  Because the disclosures address an event that is less than three years old, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores where the language demonstrates immediate, material effects.  Overall, the risk profile is elevated: the pandemic is not merely a hypothetical future concern but an active drag on visibility, revenue timing, and cost structure, although lack of precise quantification and mention of mitigation temper a few scores.

FFIV’s Form 10-K continues to acknowledge COVID-19 as a live, but now mostly macro-level, risk driver.  The company no longer speaks of factory shutdowns or office closures; instead, it frames the pandemic’s effects in terms of lingering supply-chain constraints, component cost inflation, and broader macroeconomic volatility that can dampen customer demand and squeeze gross margins.  The wording is largely forward-looking ("could" or "may" adversely affect), yet it also concedes that pandemic-linked disruptions "have led" to slower global growth, signalling that some impact is already embedded in current results.  Because the filing date (14 Nov 2023) is roughly 3.5 years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle calls for mid-range severity: the pandemic is neither brand-new nor remote history, but a persisting medium-term threat.  The extracted sentences are mostly qualitative and unquantified; nevertheless, they explicitly link COVID-19 to supply-chain problems, cost pressures, and profitability.  Accordingly, individual snippet scores fall in the 4-6 band, and no evidence exceeds that range.

The company’s 2024 Form 10-K does not dwell on COVID-19 by name, but its Risk Factors still embed pandemic-type vulnerabilities—supply-chain fragility, labor shortages and macro-demand shocks—under broader ‘macroeconomic uncertainties.’  The single explicit reference to “outbreaks of pandemic diseases” appears in a sentence that also bundles supply-chain disruptions, labor shortages and softer demand as potential hits to profitability.  This framing is forward-looking and largely qualitative: it warns that the same systemic stresses seen during COVID-19 could recur, but provides no fresh quantitative evidence that the firm is currently suffering.  Because the filing date is November 2024—roughly 4 years after the initial March 2020 outbreak—the Time-Decay principle places the event in the medium-term window; therefore, individual snippet scores should land in the moderate range (≈4-6 when pandemic is explicit, ≈2-3 when only indirect supply-chain exposure is cited).  Overall, the disclosures confirm the company remains exposed, but the language is generic and anticipatory rather than describing acute, ongoing damage, leading to an overall moderate risk assessment.

FICO’s 2021 Form 10-K shows that COVID-19 is a live, multi-faceted risk spanning operations, workforce strategy, customer demand and even cybersecurity.  The company discloses events that have already occurred—temporary office closures, permanent real-estate reductions, head-count cuts and lower product-origination volumes—demonstrating that the pandemic is not merely hypothetical.  At the same time, management highlights forward-looking exposures such as prolonged sales cycles, payment defaults, supply-chain interruptions, and heightened cyber-threats, all of which could materially affect revenue, liquidity and cash-flows.  The language is detailed and recent (within two years of the filing date), satisfying the Time-Decay Principle’s allowance for high scores.  However, the disclosures remain largely qualitative; no dollar figures are attached, and management notes it has “not experienced material disruptions” so far.  Consequently, I assess the overall pandemic risk as elevated but not maximal—sufficient to justify strong (but not perfect) snippet scores, with downward adjustments where mitigation or uncertainty tempers severity.

FICO’s 2022 filing acknowledges COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, high-impact threat that spans macro-economic shock, customer demand uncertainty, supply-chain disruption and fundamental changes to its own labour model.  The company cites both historic damage (global economic contraction, reduced lending) and forward-looking vulnerabilities (future revenue pressure, longer sales cycles, payment defaults, productivity risk from hybrid work).  While the discussion is largely qualitative and avoids concrete dollar figures, it explicitly links the pandemic to core financial metrics—revenues, operating results, liquidity and cash flows—and describes multiple operational channels of exposure such as supply chains and remote-work productivity.  No counter-measures or offsets are detailed beyond mentioning new workplace policies, so mitigation is minimal.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is well within the 0-3-year “recent-event” window for this November-2022 filing, justifying upper-mid to high severity scores (5-8 range) for the individual snippets depending on their specificity and materiality.

FICO’s 2023-11-08 Form 10-K frames the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, macro-level threat that can dampen customer demand, elongate sales cycles, increase credit defaults, and complicate internal workforce arrangements.  The discussion is almost entirely forward-looking—phrased with “may” and “could”—and does not quantify concrete dollar impacts, indicating that management views the pandemic more as a continuing risk factor than a currently crippling loss driver.  Nonetheless, because the filing date is within three years of the World Health Organization’s March-2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits moderately high scores where language directly links COVID-19 to material financial or operational harm.  The strongest evidence appears in the Risk Factors section, where management details multiple transmission channels (customer spending reductions, payment defaults, remote-work productivity risks) and explicitly states that financial performance could suffer.  Mitigating language is sparse; outside of mentioning new remote-work policies, the company offers few concrete counter-measures.  Consequently, the overall risk profile is assessed as moderate-to-elevated (scores in the 5-7 range for the best sentences), reflecting a live but largely unquantified exposure whose severity is tempered only by its conditional wording rather than by elapsed time.

FICO’s 2024-11-06 filing continues to flag the COVID-19 era as a material, albeit no longer acute, enterprise risk. All references are framed in forward-looking, precautionary terms—e.g., potential drops in customer spending, elongated sales cycles, or operational outages—rather than citing a quantified, historical hit from the 2020-2022 period. Four to five years have elapsed since the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle moderates any severity scores. Nevertheless, management still links large-scale health epidemics to revenue, cash-flow and IT-continuity threats, and explicitly pairs “pandemics” with supply-chain and labor-availability disruptions. The language is specific enough to show continuing vigilance (e.g., enumerating delayed purchasing decisions and payment defaults) but remains unquantified and largely hypothetical. Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the mid-range (1-5), reflecting credible but generic, medium-term risk awareness rather than acute, quantified damage.

FIS acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a forward-looking, ongoing macro-risk that can disrupt operations, depress transaction volumes and strain its global workforce. Nonetheless, the disclosure is more than boiler-plate: it identifies concrete vectors of harm (workforce illness, travel restrictions, increased costs to serve clients, reduced consumer and corporate spending, heightened exposure in weaker-health-care jurisdictions) that tie directly to the firm’s core revenue streams from transaction processing and outsourcing. Because the filing date (February 2024) is roughly four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time Decay Principle limits maximum snippet scores to the mid-range; the pandemic’s acute shock has passed, but systemic risks—variant flare-ups, lingering labour and supply-chain frictions, and shifts in demand—remain relevant. Accordingly, individual sentences are scored between 2 and 5, producing an overall moderate-to-elevated risk profile for FIS on pandemic-related factors.

Fifth Third’s 2021-02-26 Form 10-K contains extensive, specific and contemporaneous discussion of COVID-19.  The disclosures cut across credit, liquidity, capital and operational dimensions, demonstrating that the pandemic is already exerting a measurable, adverse impact while also presenting material forward-looking uncertainty.  Management cites concrete manifestations—rating-agency outlook downgrades, programme-driven dividend / buy-back restrictions, industry-specific borrower distress, workforce-disruption threats, and revenue compression tied to payment-deferral programmes. No meaningful mitigating language offsets these threats.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, COVID-19 is a “recent event,” so scores in the upper range (≈7-10) are justified where disclosures show direct or quantified impacts; generic or highly contingent statements receive moderate scores.

Fifth Third’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly acknowledges COVID-19 as a major, still-evolving risk driver. Overall, the risk profile is significant and recent, but largely described in broad, forward-looking terms, with only one sentence confirming concrete financial impact to date.

Alphabet’s 2024 Form 10-K still links the COVID-19 pandemic to several operational and strategic vulnerabilities, but the framing has shifted from an acute, near-term shock to an ongoing, albeit moderating, source of risk.  The company now discusses the pandemic mostly in tandem with other disruptive forces (natural disasters, geopolitical conflicts, climate events), signalling that management views COVID-19 as one of several external stressors rather than the singular driver it was in 2020-2021.  Nonetheless, the filing acknowledges both (i) tangible past impacts (e.g., supply shortages already experienced; outsized but temporary advertising growth) and (ii) forward-looking exposures (possible IT outages, weakened incident-response, cultural/HR strains).  Because the pandemic began almost four years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle caps severity in the mid-range; evidence points to credible, company-specific risks, but they are largely unquantified and blended with broader contingency language.  Overall, the risk profile merits moderate scoring (4-6 range) rather than the high urgency of recent-event disclosures.

Genuine Parts Company’s 2021-02-19 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad suite of material, near-term threats.  Management acknowledges that the virus is already depressing sales, inflating costs, disrupting supply chains, tightening labour markets, straining liquidity routes, and forcing large-scale remote-work arrangements—each of which erodes margin or operational resilience.  Although some passages are forward-looking, many describe current, realised effects (e.g., higher protective-health costs, actual supply-chain delays, slowed Q2 sales).  No precise dollar figures are offered, but the repeated use of “materially adversely impacted” and explicit references to inventory shortages, credit deterioration, and impairment charges signal severity.  Because the filing date is less than one year after WHO’s March 2020 pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high risk scores.  Mitigating language is sparse and largely generic (e.g., creation of a task-force, continued supplier “support”), so most snippets remain strongly aggravating.  Overall, the disclosure evidences a live, high-impact, multi-faceted risk environment consistent with upper-tier severity ratings (7-9 range), with modest downward adjustments where the company cites mitigation or notes immaterial impact to-date.

COVID-19 is still within the 0-3-year “recent-event” window at the February 17 2022 filing date, so any reliable statement that the pandemic is currently harming GPC, or could materially harm it, commands a high risk weighting.  The filing repeatedly acknowledges that the company has already suffered supply-chain disruption, labour shortages and heightened cyber-risk; it also flags the possibility of future store closures, demand volatility and credit/liquidity stress.  None of the disclosures are quantified, but many use strong language such as “materially impacted” or describe concrete operational effects (e.g., global labour shortages, spikes in cyber-attacks).  Mitigating remarks—open facilities, supportive suppliers, safety measures—temper but do not eliminate the risk.  Overall, the narrative depicts an existing, multi-faceted, only partly controllable threat whose ultimate cost “cannot be reasonably estimated.”  Given recency, breadth and admitted materiality, individual sentence scores cluster in the 4-8 range, with downward adjustments where management highlights successful mitigation.  No score is time-decayed below this range because the pandemic is ongoing and squarely within the Time Decay Principle’s “recent” band.

GPC’s 2023 Form 10-K squarely acknowledges that the 2020-onward COVID-19 pandemic has created both realized and continuing risks across multiple operational fronts.  The filing confirms that the company has already suffered supply-chain friction—specifically global labour shortages and delays on internationally-sourced inventory—directly attributed to the pandemic.  Although management notes that these particular disruptions have not yet been “material,” it concedes that future impacts could become material and adverse, signalling an unresolved, forward-looking threat.  The text also ties the pandemic-driven shift to remote work to a measurable spike in cyber-security attacks, introducing a second, distinct risk vector.  A further, more generic sentence folds pandemics into the firm’s macro-economic risk framework, underscoring that health crises remain a standing consideration in demand and operations planning.  All statements are recent (within three years of the event) and refer to either experienced impacts or credible future exposures; therefore, under the Time Decay Principle, scores can range into the higher band (7–10) for the strongest evidence.  Mitigating language (“not material to date”) tempers, but does not eliminate, severity.  Overall, the pandemic presents a moderate-to-high risk profile for GPC, with supply-chain continuity and cyber-security as the most acute pressure points.

GPC’s 2024 Form 10-K still links a portion of its risk profile to the COVID-19 pandemic, but the language reflects a maturing, medium-term threat rather than an acute crisis. The filing acknowledges that pandemic-related pressures—most notably supply-chain disruptions, global labor shortages and expanded remote-work practices—have already been felt and could persist. The company concedes that it has “experienced” pandemic-driven disruptions and that they may “continue,” yet it also specifies that those impacts have not been material to date, signalling effective mitigation or reduced severity as time passes. References are largely qualitative and embedded among other macro-risks (geopolitical conflicts, weather, etc.), showing a shift from specific COVID-19 shock language toward a more integrated, multi-factor risk narrative. Applying the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is now almost four years old; therefore, individual evidence scores should land in the moderate band (4-6) only when the statement shows a clear, on-going impact. Generic or strongly mitigated references warrant lower scores. Overall, the filing depicts COVID-related risk as real but moderated, with the dominant exposure centred on supply-chain resilience and cyber vulnerabilities linked to sustained remote-work models.

GPN’s 2022 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad spectrum of operational and financial threats.  Because the filing date (18 Feb 2022) falls within two years of the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  The company makes multiple statements that the pandemic has already reduced transaction volumes and revenue, and that negative impacts ‘will likely continue.’  Disclosures go beyond generic force-majeure language: they enumerate concrete channels of risk—merchant insolvency, supply-chain delays, labor shortages, remote-work vulnerabilities, cyber-fraud spikes, financing constraints, and potential impairment of M&A strategy.  Several passages also acknowledge persistent macro-economic drag and uncertain long-term effects, underscoring that the threat is both existing and forward-looking.  Mitigating notes (e.g., accelerated digital payments and partial recovery in 2021) appear, but they do not neutralise the pervasive, detailed risk narrative.  Accordingly, individual sentence scores cluster in the 4-8 range, reflecting recent timing, specificity, and evidence of realized harm, tempered where the company cites contingencies or offsetting trends.

GPN’s 2023-02-17 filing presents COVID-19 as both an historical shock and a continuing, multifaceted risk.  Several passages acknowledge that the pandemic has already produced measurable harm—slowing economic activity in the company’s markets and weakening merchant viability—while warning that further disruptions remain plausible via new variants, persistent macro-economic after-effects, continuing supply-chain bottlenecks, labour-cost pressures and tighter capital markets.  The disclosures are largely qualitative; no dollar amounts are attached, but management repeatedly uses strong language such as “materially adversely affected” and notes specific operational domains at risk (merchant credit, M&A pipeline, supply-chain for hardware, financing access).  Because the filing date is less than three years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high but not automatic maximum scores: evidence describing concrete, already-realised impacts earns upper-mid scores (7-8), while generic or merely potential statements rank lower (2-5).  Overall, the pandemic remains a significant and active risk factor for GPN, with limited mitigation noted beyond general monitoring; hence the aggregate risk profile is elevated but not catastrophic.

COVID-19 is now almost four years old relative to the 14 Feb 2024 filing, placing it in the early ‘medium-term’ band where Time-Decay calls for mid-range scores.  The Form 10-K repeatedly references the pandemic as a continuing external threat rather than a closed, historical matter.  The company frames the risk largely in macro-economic terms—slow-downs, consumer-spending shifts and supply-chain disruption—rather than specific quantified dollar impacts.  Language such as “materially adversely affected,” “economic slowdown,” and “effects may persist for an indefinite period” underscores that management still sees meaningful downside.  At the same time, several mitigating cues appear: the pandemic is described as having “subsided,” and management stresses that it is “continuing to evaluate” the situation.  Taken together, the disclosures point to a live but generalized risk: direct impacts have already been felt (and could recur), but the discussion is qualitative and forward-looking with no fresh, company-specific figures.  Accordingly, evidence snippets score in the 3–5 range, never exceeding 6, in line with Time-Decay for a ~4-year-old event and the absence of precise financial quantification.

GRMN’s 2021-02-17 Form 10-K repeatedly acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic is already exerting material, multi-faceted pressure on the company.  Language such as “have had” and “continues to result in” confirms that impacts are not merely hypothetical—they are current and measurable, especially in reduced demand, supply-chain friction, higher per-unit manufacturing costs, and segment-level profit deterioration (auto and aviation).  The disclosure also enumerates operational complications: office and factory closures, remote-work inefficiencies, rising employee-safety costs and potential write-downs of assets.  Although the filing lists a robust set of mitigation tactics (direct-to-consumer fulfilment, inventory buffers, vertical integration, etc.), these actions do not eliminate the risk; they merely temper it.  Given that the event window (March 2020 onward) is less than one year before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (7-10) for sentences evidencing realised or imminent effects, with modest deductions where the company presents concrete offsets.  Overall, COVID-19 represents an elevated, ongoing risk to GRMN’s demand, cost structure and supply chain, warranting high—but not maximum—severity assessments across most snippets.

GRMN’s 2022 Form 10-K presents the COVID-19 pandemic as a current, multi-faceted threat that is already depressing sales in some segments, distorting demand patterns, raising component and freight costs, impairing production capacity, and eroding operating efficiency.  The language is concrete and largely backward-looking (“have experienced”, “has resulted in”), confirming an existing material impact, but it also projects continued uncertainty and possible deterioration (“may continue”, “could intensify”), so the risk is both realized and forward-looking.  The disclosure spans supply-chain bottlenecks, labor disruption, remote-work productivity, liquidity risks from customers and partners, and margin pressure—touching virtually every element of the value chain.  No quantitative dollar figure is provided, yet the breadth and persistence, combined with management’s admission of limited visibility and control, indicate a high-severity, enterprise-wide exposure.  Because the filing date (Feb 2022) falls within three years of the WHO declaration (Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores (7-10).  Mitigating actions are mentioned only tangentially (e.g., benefits for employees), so risk-reductions are minimal.  Overall, the evidence supports high but not maximum severity scores, generally in the 7–8 range for the most specific operational impacts and 5–6 for broader but less detailed statements.

Garmin’s 2023 Form-10-K frames COVID-19 as an event that has already produced tangible disruptions and remains a live, evolving threat across demand, supply-chain, manufacturing, workforce and financial dimensions.  The company repeatedly uses past-tense verbs ("have had") to confirm realized impacts while pairing them with forward-looking verbs ("will continue," "may continue") that extend risk into the future.  Specific operational touch-points—component shortages, logistics constraints, manufacturing shutdowns, remote-work efficiency losses, inventory obsolescence and gross-margin pressure—are enumerated, demonstrating that the risk is concrete rather than generic.  No quantified dollar amounts or probability metrics are supplied, and limited mitigating language appears, so the disclosures are largely aggravating.  Because the filing date (Feb 2023) sits less than three years after the World Health Organization’s March 2020 pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the evidence indicates a high but unquantified risk profile, warranting upper-mid to high snippet scores (5–7 range) with modest downward adjustments when statements are purely conditional or lack specificity.

The filing recognizes the COVID-19 pandemic as both a historical and continuing source of enterprise-level disruption. Management explicitly states that the pandemic has already "significantly affected" the company through lower demand, operational and supply-chain interruptions, and government restrictions, and they warn these impacts could persist. The discussion is largely qualitative—no dollar figures or quantified volume effects are provided—yet it describes multiple functional areas that could be hit simultaneously (margin volatility, foreign-exchange swings, product development delays, talent constraints, and sole-source supplier exposure). Because the pandemic began in March 2020 and the 10-K is dated February 2024, the disclosure falls just into the “medium-term” (4-year) window of the Time Decay Principle; therefore, maximum snippet scores must be moderate (≈4-6) rather than very high. Overall, the language is specific to COVID-19, cites realized impacts, and remains forward-looking, so the aggregate risk is material but not acute enough—four years on—to warrant top-tier severity scores.

Goldman Sachs’ 2020 Form 10-K was filed only eleven months after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, so virtually the entire discussion is contemporaneous with – and in places already reflects – realised impacts.  Multiple risk-factor sentences show that COVID-19 has already affected the firm’s liquidity (e.g., March 2020 revolver draws), capital policies (share-repurchase suspension), client demand (muted business activity, reduced M&A certainty, product-mix shift toward low-fee liquidity products) and operational profile (work-from-home cyber-risk).  They also outline forward-looking threats such as prolonged market dislocation, defaults, valuation disputes and further credit-line utilisation.  The disclosures are recent (inside the 0–3-year window) and provide concrete channels of transmission, several citing actual historical figures or events (e.g., March 2020 liquidity spike).  Although most statements remain qualitative and unquantified, they go well beyond boiler-plate, demonstrate firm-specific impacts already incurred and map clearly onto the pandemic’s systemic features (market volatility, consumer weakness, remote-work pressures).  Accordingly, individual evidence snippets merit upper-mid to high scores (6-8), capped at 10 by the Time Decay Principle for a very recent event but reduced where wording is broad or purely anticipatory.

Goldman Sachs’ 2021 Form 10-K, filed in February 2022, provides a multi-faceted picture of COVID-19–related risk that is both retrospective and forward-looking.  The firm explicitly states that the pandemic has already hurt client activity, liquidity, funding, capital distributions and operational resilience, and then maps out numerous channels through which future waves or variants could further damage earnings—equity- and debt-underwriting volumes, M&A pipelines, asset-management fee bases, borrower credit quality, hedging effectiveness, market valuations and collateral disputes.  Several disclosures are concrete and time-stamped (e.g., the March 2020 liquidity draw-downs), demonstrating direct realised impacts; others enumerate specific potential stresses that would materialise under prolonged or renewed outbreaks.  These statements are recent (within two years of the event start), company-specific and go beyond boiler-plate by quantifying mechanisms (draw-downs, fee compression, loan defaults, liquidity drains) even if they stop short of monetary figures.  Under the Time Decay Principle, high severity scores (7-10) are warranted for sentences showing direct impacts or detailed forward-looking pathways, moderate scores (4-6) for generic or primarily operational remarks, and only low scores for vague, catch-all pandemic references.

Goldman Sachs’ 2023 Form 10-K contains several explicit references to the continuing impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.  The firm acknowledges that the pandemic has already produced concrete, adverse effects – notably March 2020 liquidity strains and documented declines in client activity – and warns that similar stresses could recur.  The disclosures are recent (within three years of the March 2020 outbreak), directly link COVID-19 to past and potential future hits to liquidity, profitability and operations, and give specific examples (e.g., corporate clients drawing down revolving credit facilities).  They are, however, largely qualitative and un-quantified: the company does not disclose dollar figures, precise margin impacts, or detailed supply-chain or workforce cost data.  The language is a mix of backward-looking evidence (“have been adversely affected”) and forward-looking caution (“may in the future”), with only minimal mitigating language.  Applying the Time Decay Principle (high relevance for 0-3-year events), the strongest sentences merit high scores (7-8/10) because they show a direct, realized impact; moderately strong statements that cite actual but less materialised effects score mid-range (5-6/10); and generic “pandemic” boiler-plate receives only low weight (≤2/10).

Goldman Sachs’ 2024 Form 10-K continues to acknowledge the COVID-19 pandemic as a material but now medium-term risk.  The filing confirms that the firm endured a concrete liquidity shock in March 2020, when corporate clients drew down revolving credit lines, and it uses that episode as a live stress reference for future liquidity planning.  Beyond that specific example, the document treats pandemics in general as a standing source of market, operational and macro-economic disruption that can impair asset values, curtail client activity and tighten funding conditions.  The language is largely qualitative and forward-looking—no numerical impacts or scenario ranges are disclosed—yet it makes clear that pandemic-driven liquidity and earnings pressure “have been and may in the future be” significant.  Because the COVID-19 outbreak began four years before the filing date, the Time-Decay Principle places the risk in the 4-10-year “medium-term” bucket, warranting moderate (not maximal) severity scores.  Overall, the company flags both a historical, realized impact on liquidity and an ongoing exposure to renewed waves or future pandemics, but mitigation steps such as enlarged liquidity buffers and stress testing are only implied, not detailed.  Consequently, evidence snippets earn scores between 2 and 6, reflecting moderate current relevance without quantified losses.

The filing was made less than a year after the WHO’s March-2020 pandemic declaration, so COVID-19 is a very recent, still-evolving threat; the Time Decay Principle therefore allows high severity scores.  Grainger’s disclosure language is detailed and largely backward-looking, citing concrete disruptions already experienced (customer demand shifts, supplier breakdowns, PPE shortages, lower gross margins, facility restrictions) while also outlining forward-looking uncertainties (duration of the outbreak, macro-recession risk, capital-market access, cyber-vulnerabilities from remote work).  The narrative links the pandemic to every major risk bucket—sales, supply chain, workforce, IT security, liquidity—using strong qualifiers such as “material adverse effect,” “has disrupted,” and “unprecedented demand.”  Although some mitigating steps are acknowledged (maintaining liquidity, remote-work enablement, inventory management), the text stresses that many variables remain “highly uncertain.”  Given the immediacy of the event, the breadth of impacts, the presence of realized losses (lower margin mix, demand declines) and the absence of firm quantitative caps on exposure, the evidence supports high—but not maximum—risk scores (generally 6-8), consistent with recent, multifaceted, partly-quantified harm.

The filing, submitted less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, provides a dense, multi-faceted discussion of how the outbreak has already hurt, and could continue to hurt, Grainger (GWW).  The narrative goes well beyond generic boiler-plate: management cites concrete past disruptions (customer demand swings, inventory write-downs, labour shortages, increased freight costs), identifies operating‐level pain points (shipping delays, excess stock, cybersecurity exposure from remote work) and repeatedly labels the impacts as “material.”  Although no exact dollar amounts are disclosed, the company explicitly references below-cost inventory sell-offs and higher wages/health-care costs, signalling realised financial damage.  The risks are therefore both realised (back-looking) and prospective (forward-looking), with several statements warning that the effects “may continue” or “could materially adversely affect” future performance.  Because the disclosure date (23-Feb-2022) is within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores; nonetheless, individual sentence scores are moderated when wording is contingent (“could,” “may”) or when mitigating actions (inventory management, diligence with new suppliers) are noted.  Overall, the tenor is of a high, persistent risk that touches supply chain integrity, workforce availability, customer demand and even regulatory compliance (vaccine mandates), justifying elevated—but not always maximal—snippet scores.

Grainger’s 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to concrete pressures on supply-chain continuity, customer demand, inventory management, labour availability, transportation costs and even capital-market access.  The company discloses both realised impacts (e.g., “have been adversely affected”) and forward-looking uncertainties (“could materially adversely affect”), signalling that pandemic-driven risks are not fully in the rear-view mirror.  None of the disclosures quantify dollar amounts, but the language is specific, multi-dimensional, and in several places labelled “material.”  Because the filing date (21 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the World Health Organization’s 11 Mar 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scores.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, ongoing and operationally fundamental, warranting mid-to-high severity scores that cluster in the 4-8 range depending on how direct, concrete and mitigated each statement is.

The filing, dated February 22 2024, treats pandemic-related disruption as an ongoing but now normalized business risk. Although COVID-19 first emerged almost four years ago, Grainger continues to flag “pandemic diseases or viral contagions” in multiple risk-factor categories—including supply-chain continuity, customer demand, supplier reliability, freight costs, market volatility and cybersecurity vulnerabilities tied to remote work. The language is primarily forward-looking and couched in conditional terms (“could be disrupted,” “may continue”), and there is no quantified impact or reference to specific COVID-19 financial losses. Nonetheless, the company repeatedly links pandemic conditions to core operational pillars such as same-day shipping, supplier delivery, inventory costs and remote-work security. Under the Time Decay Principle, a March 2020 event is now in the 4-year “medium-term” window, so maximum evidence scores must be moderate (4-6). The overall risk profile is therefore assessed as moderate: COVID-19 no longer represents an acute shock, but it remains a material contingent threat embedded in Grainger’s supply-chain, cost and demand architecture.

Halliburton’s 2020 Form 10-K, filed on 5 Feb 2021, paints COVID-19 as a recent, already-manifesting threat with the potential to intensify.  The company explicitly discloses that the pandemic has already produced a “material adverse effect” on virtually every financial dimension—revenue, liquidity, operating results and balance-sheet health—making the risk direct and present rather than merely speculative.  Beyond this headline statement, the filing details numerous operating vectors through which the virus is disrupting or could further disrupt performance: border closures, travel restrictions, work-site inaccessibility, remote-work inefficiencies, supply-chain interruptions, labour availability, contract force-majeure claims, customer bankruptcies, liquidity strain, and even a possible long-term structural decline in oil demand as working and travel patterns evolve.  These points are largely specific, contemporaneous and, in many cases, already observable inside the 2020 numbers (e.g., 36 % revenue drop and $3.8 bn of impairments).  Given the filing date is less than a year after the official pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7–10) where disclosures show current, quantified or clearly material impacts; moderate scores (4–6) where impacts are plausible but less concrete; and lower scores (≤3) where the language is general or heavily caveated.  Mitigating language (e.g., liquidity cushion, cost control) is minimal in the COVID passages, so few point deductions are warranted.  Overall, the pandemic constitutes an acute, high-severity enterprise risk for Halliburton in this time frame.

COVID-19 is a very recent (≤ 3-year) event relative to the February 4 2022 filing date, so Time-Decay does not materially erode severity scores.  HAL’s Form 10-K contains numerous, candid disclosures that the pandemic already caused concrete financial harm (e.g., a USD 3.8 billion impairment and 2020 operating loss), depressed oil demand, disrupted logistics, and forced remote-work travel restrictions.  The company also flags continuing, forward-looking exposures—supply-chain inflation, labour availability, liquidity squeezes, force-majeure claims, structural shifts in energy demand, and potential renewed lockdowns.  Language such as “material adverse effect,” “significant volatility, uncertainty, and turmoil,” and the detailed bullet list of ten separate impact channels indicates a high level of specificity and acknowledgement of both realised and prospective risk.  While management notes some recovery signs (e.g., demand improvement, vaccination progress), those mitigating comments are sporadic and do not outweigh the breadth and depth of the risk narrative.  Consequently, individual snippet scores cluster in the upper mid- to high-range (5-10) when impacts are quantified or clearly realised, and in the low- to mid-range (2-5) where statements are more speculative or partially mitigated.  Overall, the pandemic represents a live, multi-faceted threat with material financial and operational ramifications for HAL, justifying elevated risk ratings under the Time Decay Principle.

HAL’s 2023 Form 10-K confirms that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a live, material risk for the company.  The filing links the pandemic to three distinct exposure channels: (i) continued volatility in global oil-and-gas prices, (ii) ongoing supply-chain shortages and logistics delays that directly affect HAL’s ability to source raw materials, and (iii) depressed customer drilling activity that is still running below pre-pandemic levels.  Most references are couched as present-tense, already-occurring impacts (“we are being impacted”), not merely hypothetical threats, indicating the risk is direct and current.  However, the language is largely qualitative and unquantified; there is no dollar amount assigned to pandemic impacts, and some phrasing is generic (e.g., COVID-19 listed among other ‘health issues’).  Because the event began in March 2020—less than three years before the 7 Feb 2023 filing—the Time Decay Principle allows high scores, but the absence of precise financial metrics tempers them.  Overall, the pandemic represents a meaningful, continuing operational and market risk for HAL, but the disclosures stop short of emphatic, quantified materiality, so the individual sentence scores fall in the moderate-to-high range (2-7).

COVID-19 is mentioned only twice in HAL’s 2023 Form 10-K (filed February 2024).  Both references frame the pandemic as a broad macro driver—first as one of many potential factors that can sway oil and gas prices, and second as a historical cause of the severe price volatility that began in early 2020.  The company does not quantify specific financial damage, nor does it describe lingering operational constraints such as labor shortages or remote-work impacts; instead, the pandemic is treated as a background condition that has already flowed through commodity markets.  Because nearly four years have passed since the WHO declaration (placing the event at the front edge of the 4-to-10-year “medium-term” window), the Time Decay Principle limits severity to the mid-range.  Overall, the disclosure signals a moderate, largely indirect risk—important enough to acknowledge but evidently no longer viewed as a primary threat to HAL’s operations or liquidity.

HAS’s February 2021 10-K presents COVID-19 as a recent, already-material threat that cuts across every link of the company’s value chain.  Language throughout Item 1A attributes concrete 2020 damage—factory shutdowns, delayed film releases, and lower sales—to the pandemic, so the disclosures are not merely hypothetical; they evidence realized impacts.  At the same time, many sentences describe continuing or future-looking vulnerabilities: prolonged supply-chain interruptions, labour constraints, ongoing theatre and retail closures, liquidity pressures and shifts toward e-commerce and direct-to-streaming models.  These statements are specific as to operational mechanisms (e.g., production delays, accounts-receivable risk), cover multiple geographies, and in several cases explicitly characterise the effect as “significant” or “adverse.”  No meaningful mitigating actions or offsets are offered beyond generic acknowledgements of e-commerce growth, so the net risk remains high.  Because the filing date (24-Feb-2021) is less than one year after the WHO declared the pandemic (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores; most evidence warrants scores in the 6-8 range, with slight reductions where the wording is more generic or partly mitigated.

HAS’s 2022-02-23 filing repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to concrete, continuing operational and financial threats.  Unlike generic boiler-plate, the language describes actual disruptions already experienced (plant shutdowns, delayed entertainment releases, higher freight and material costs) and warns that many of these pressures are still unfolding into 2022.  The statements span multiple vectors—production, logistics, workforce, retail channel shift, and consumer demand—demonstrating an enterprise-wide exposure.  None of the passages provide dollar quantification, but they do specify real-world effects (e.g., supply-chain bottlenecks, ecommerce spike, manufacturing stoppages) and explicitly state adverse impacts on sales, margins and profitability.  Because the pandemic event began in March 2020 and the filing date is February 2022, the disclosures fall in the 0-3-year “recent” window, so elevated severities (≈7-9) are appropriate under the Time-Decay Principle.  Mitigations (remote-work protocols, alternative ports, air-freight, etc.) are mentioned elsewhere but not in the extracted sentences; therefore only minor downward adjustments apply.  Overall, the evidence paints a high but not existential risk profile: sustained, widespread, and already material, yet still partly manageable—justifying snippet scores largely in the 6-8 range.

HAS’s 2023 filing treats COVID-19 as an ongoing, material threat that has already affected multiple parts of the enterprise and may continue to do so.  The language spans (i) confirmed, realized impacts – higher freight and material costs, manufacturing shutdowns, disrupted film releases, lost sales – and (ii) forward-looking exposures – continued supply-chain fragility, changing consumer demand, remote-work labour dynamics and entertainment monetisation risk.  Statements are largely specific (naming factories in China/Vietnam, port congestion, box-office reliance) and use strong qualifiers such as “significant disruption”, “substantially harm” and “lost sales”, evidencing a high-severity posture.  Because the WHO declaration (March 2020) is less than three years before the 22-Feb-2023 filing, the Time-Decay Principle allows elevated scores (up to 10).  Nevertheless, most disclosures remain un-quantified and partly forward-looking, so individual snippet scores fall in the moderate-to-high 4-6 range rather than the maximum.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a contemporaneous, direct risk driver across HAS’s supply chain, cost structure and revenue channels, warranting sustained investor attention.

HAS’s 2024-02-28 filing frames COVID-19 as both a proven and continuing enterprise-wide threat.  Management cites concrete, already-realised impacts—factory shutdowns, higher material costs, logistics bottlenecks, and entertainment-production delays—showing the pandemic has materially affected margins and revenue streams since 2020.  They also describe forward-looking exposures: future outbreaks could still disrupt third-party manufacturing, shipping lanes, labour availability, consumer demand, and remote-work productivity.  The language is a mix of retrospective (“has resulted in”) and prospective (“could substantially harm”), with multiple specific operational channels identified.  Because the event is now almost four years old, the Time Decay Principle tempers severity: the pandemic is no longer an acute shock, but its knock-on effects remain embedded in supply-chain, labour and demand patterns.  Accordingly, individual sentence scores fall in a moderate-to-high band (3-6), reflecting tangible past damage and ongoing vulnerability, yet recognising that COVID-19’s peak immediacy has begun to wane.

HBAN’s 2023 Form 10-K touches on pandemic risk only in broad, forward-looking terms.  The company still cites “disease pandemics” – and explicitly “the COVID-19 pandemic and related variants” – as events that could disrupt operations, harm the economy, and adversely affect financial performance.  The disclosures sit in catch-all risk lists (Operational Risk and Forward-Looking Statement cautionary language) rather than in focused discussions of supply-chain breakdowns, labour disruptions, or remote-work costs.  No quantified impacts, reserve builds, or strategic adaptations are provided.  Because the COVID-19 outbreak began four years before the filing date, the TIME DECAY principle classifies it as a medium-term event: the pandemic is no longer an emergent shock but remains a plausible stressor.  Accordingly, the risk evidence warrants only moderate severity scores (4-5 range).  The statements aggravate risk by naming the pandemic explicitly and tying it to potential material impacts, yet they are generic, un-quantified, and clearly prospective, which tempers the final scoring.

HCA’s 2021 filing presents COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-dimensional threat that is already eroding operating performance and could further destabilise the company.  The disclosures combine (a) hard-evidence of realised damage—cancelled elective procedures, reduced patient volumes, higher costs, supply-chain delays—and (b) forward-looking warnings about liquidity, labour shortages, payer-mix deterioration and long-term demand shifts (e.g., tele-health).  Language such as “significantly affecting,” “resulting in significantly reduced… revenues,” and “we have experienced… supply chain disruptions” show that the pandemic is more than a hypothetical; it is a current, material drag on cash flow, margins and control processes.  Because the Form 10-K is dated February 2021—well within three years of the pandemic’s declared start (11 March 2020)—the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Mitigating details (e.g., ongoing monitoring, business-continuity plans) are mentioned only briefly and do not offset the overall gravity or uncertainty.  Accordingly, individual snippets that evidence direct, quantified or enterprise-wide impacts receive scores in the 7-9 range, while broader, less-specific or conditional statements score mid-range. The filing, dated December 6 2023, addresses pandemic-related threats primarily through a short cluster of sentences that explicitly cite COVID-19 and remote-work-driven vulnerabilities.
