Nevertheless, the text enumerates broad areas of exposure—global demand, supply chain, co-manufacturers, labour availability, and financial results—indicating management still considers pandemic shocks material almost four years after WHO’s declaration.  Mitigation is acknowledged (contingency plans), but the firm tempers this with a disclaimer that “no assurance” can be given that such plans will work, leaving residual risk.  Under the Time Decay principle, COVID-19 falls on the edge of the 0-3-year “recent” band (≈3.75 years), so moderately elevated scores are appropriate; the lack of quantification and the presence of mitigation dilute severity, keeping individual snippet scores mostly in the 4-6 range rather than the upper 8-10 tier.

HRL’s 2024 filing treats COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, forward-looking threat rather than describing specific historical damage.  The company explicitly links a potential or recurring pandemic to broad operational and financial exposures—global economy deterioration, demand shocks, supply-chain breakdowns and workforce shortages—which mirror the classic COVID-19 risk profile.  However, the language is mostly conditional (“may”, “could”), suggesting recognition of persistent vulnerability rather than reporting of realised losses.  The disclosure also outlines mitigation via contingency planning, but immediately tempers this with a caveat that such plans may prove ineffective, leaving residual uncertainty.  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 falls in the medium-term window (~4.5 years since March 2020), so individual snippet scores should sit in the moderate range (≈4-6) when aggravating elements dominate and be pulled lower where strong mitigating language appears.  Overall, the evidence indicates a material yet unquantified and somewhat speculative risk, landing at a moderate severity level for each core statement.

HSIC’s 2021-02-17 filing discusses COVID-19 in unusually direct, detailed and contemporaneous terms. Management states that the pandemic has already produced material adverse effects on revenue, cash-flow and liquidity and could do so again. The disclosure is not merely generic—specific operational mechanisms are identified: mass closure of dental practices in March–April 2020, continuing sub-pre-COVID patient volumes, volatile demand for core products, acute PPE supply-chain shortages, labour and remote-work challenges, credit-risk spikes, and third-party failures due to travel bans and border closures. These statements blend backward-looking evidence of actual losses with forward-looking scenarios, indicating both realised and potential risk. Given the filing date is less than one year after the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10). The language repeatedly uses “material adverse effect,” “severely impacted,” and “unprecedented,” signalling magnitude. Mitigating language is limited to brief mentions of partial recovery, so overall risk remains elevated. Therefore, individual snippets that show realised, quantified or operationally specific impacts receive scores in the 7-9 range, while broader, less quantified statements or those with offsetting mitigants score in the mid range (4-6).

Henry Schein’s 2022-02-15 Form 10-K devotes an unusually large and detailed section to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company repeatedly discloses both historical damage (lost sales during office closures, inventory write-downs, margin pressure) and a wide spectrum of forward-looking threats (supply-chain failures, customer credit stress, remote-work frictions, labour shortages from vaccine mandates, renewed lockdowns).  The language is forceful—“material adverse effect,” “significant volatility,” “unprecedented impact”—and ties the pandemic explicitly to every major financial metric: revenue, margins, cash-flow, liquidity and leverage covenants.  Because the event window (March 2020-present) is well within three years of the filing date, Time Decay allows high severity scores.  Most statements describe current conditions that are still unfolding or can recur, so the risk is classified as both existing and persisting rather than purely hypothetical.  No meaningful mitigating language (such as hedging, insurance or contractual protections) accompanies these disclosures.  Consequently, the overall risk profile is high; individual snippets cluster in the 5-9 range, reflecting directness, specificity, and whether they describe realised impacts or only potential downsides.

HSIC’s 2023 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as both an historical shock and an ongoing, material enterprise risk.  The company states that the pandemic already “had” a material adverse impact on 2020–2022 results (e.g., $17 million inventory write-offs) and cautions that many of those pressures—volatile PPE pricing, remote-work disruptions, potential dental-office shutdowns, political restrictions, and capital-market instability—“may again” recur.  The text moves beyond generic language by naming concrete operational channels (supply-chain shortages, labour realignment, demand suppression, inventory obsolescence) and, in one instance, quantifies a specific charge.  Most disclosures are prospective or continuing, signalling that management sees COVID-19 as an unresolved threat rather than a closed historical matter.  Because the filing date (Feb-2023) is within three years of the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle permits high scores (up to 10) for direct, quantified and recent impacts.  Nevertheless, certain mitigating notes (e.g., adequate PPE supply, normalising demand) and the passage of peak crisis conditions temper some severity scores.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, specific and multi-dimensional, warranting mid-to-high micro-scores across the extracted sentences.

HSIC’s 2024 Form 10-K openly acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic has already caused material, quantifiable harm and could continue to do so.  The company discloses a dual reality: (i) realised negative impacts – for example, a US-$532 million (-42.7 %) drop in global PPE/COVID-19-test-kit revenue and a US-$422 million (-52.9 %) decline within the medical segment – and (ii) forward-looking exposure to renewed pandemic waves or other public-health emergencies.  The language is largely specific (naming concrete product categories, supply-chain interruptions, demand destruction, volatility in pricing, and operational adaptations) and repeatedly labelled “material.”  Although almost four years have elapsed since the WHO’s March-2020 declaration, the pandemic is still within the early edge of the Time-Decay medium window; therefore, individual snippet scores are capped in the mid-range (≈2-7).  No substantial mitigating actions are outlined in the cited sentences; hence the net risk remains moderately high.  Overall, HSIC continues to face meaningful pandemic-related risk through reduced demand for elective care, distorted PPE markets, supply-chain fragility, and possible future resurges, justifying aggregate evidence scores in the 2-7 range.

The filing, dated February 25 2021, portrays COVID-19 as the single most acute and immediate risk to HST.  Because the pandemic was declared less than a year before the balance-sheet date, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  The narrative repeatedly states that the pandemic has already produced material, quantifiable harm—sharp revenue declines, very low occupancy, liquidity stress and negative rating outlooks—while also highlighting prospective threats such as prolonged demand weakness, disrupted supply chains and staffing shortages.  Language is specific (e.g., “materially and adversely impacted,” “sharp decline in revenues,” “may be required to raise additional capital”) rather than boiler-plate, and it spans multiple risk dimensions: operational, financial, competitive and strategic.  Although some clauses use conditional verbs (“may”), the overarching tone is one of realised damage with continued uncertainty, not purely hypothetical exposure.  Consequently, most snippets warrant upper-mid to high scores (5-9), reflecting direct impact, recency and breadth, with modest deductions where wording is forward-looking or un-quantified.

HST’s 2022 filing portrays COVID-19 as an acute and continuing threat that has already eroded fundamentals and may further strain the REIT’s liquidity, capital structure and demand profile.  Disclosures move well beyond generic caution: they cite concrete business damage (occupancy well below 2019, sharp revenue declines, 40 % cost cuts, negative outlook from rating agencies) and detail multiple transmission channels—travel curbs, event cancellations, labour-pool shrinkage, incremental cleaning costs, and competitive shifts toward hygiene standards.  The language is consistently definitive (“materially and adversely impacted”, “continues to have a material negative impact”) and, because the pandemic began less than two years before the filing date, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Several sentences also flag forward-looking exposure (possible long-term cost creep, capital-raising needs) while offering few true mitigants, underscoring that risk remains elevated.  Taken together, the narrative indicates a live, enterprise-wide risk with both realised and prospective financial consequences; therefore individual snippets generally warrant upper-mid to high scores (5-9) after minor deductions for conditional phrasing or partial mitigation.

Host Hotels & Resorts (HST) places COVID-19 firmly at the centre of its current risk landscape.  The 2023 filing is well within the Time-Decay window for a high-severity score (the pandemic began in 2020 and its operational and financial effects are ongoing).  Management discloses both backward-looking evidence of material damage—-historic revenue collapse, labour disruption, and a forced draw-down of its revolver—-and forward-looking threats, such as new variants, lasting demand shifts (e.g., virtual meetings), and inflationary cost pressures resulting from heightened cleaning protocols.  The language is repeatedly specific (“materially and adversely”, “significantly increased our indebtedness”) and links the pandemic to concrete balance-sheet items (debt), P&L categories (cleaning costs, bookings) and geographic vulnerabilities (urban markets).  Some mitigation is acknowledged—-repayment of revolver borrowings and a partial return to pre-pandemic operating levels—-but these are presented as conditional and reversible should new variants emerge.  Taken together, the disclosures constitute high-grade, recent, multi-dimensional risk evidence; therefore individual snippets generally warrant scores in the 6-9 range, with modest deductions where the company cites offsetting improvements.

HST’s 2024 filing treats the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a medium-term, ongoing risk that has already demonstrated material impacts and could continue to suppress lodging demand. The company’s disclosures combine backward-looking evidence—large urban hotels were “disproportionately impacted” by pandemic-era restrictions—with forward-looking language that pandemics and related public-health crises can still curb occupancy and demand. Although the most acute phase of COVID-19 passed more than three years ago, management still frames the virus as a core driver of business-travel weakness and of the structural shift toward virtual meetings. The language is specific (linking pandemics directly to occupancy, demand and geography) but not quantified, and it contains no mitigating actions beyond general awareness. Applying the Time Decay Principle (event ≈4 years old), the severity of each disclosure warrants moderate scores—high enough to capture continuing exposure but capped below ‘recent-event’ levels.

COVID-19 is reflected in the filing as both a realized and a continuing source of material risk for Hershey (HSY).  The Risk Factors section lays out multiple, concrete channels—demand volatility, supply-chain breakdowns, labor availability, and third-party failures—through which the pandemic could damage operating results.  Several of these channels are described as having already produced "unfavorable" effects, satisfying the criterion for an existing, not merely hypothetical, threat.  The MD&A then corroborates this with hard evidence: double-digit sales declines in Mexico and China, higher plant costs for PPE and sanitation, and ERP delays.  These statements are recent (less than 12 months after the WHO declaration) and sufficiently specific, some even quantified, so the Time Decay principle allows high severity scores.  Mitigating language—e.g., facilities remain open, supply-chain disruptions have been minimal to date—tempers but does not neutralize the overall risk because management itself concedes that conditions remain “dynamic” and “subject to rapid and possibly material change.”  Taken together, the disclosure indicates a high, ongoing operational and financial risk profile, warranting elevated but differentiated snippet scores (3-9 range) depending on the degree of specificity, magnitude, and presence of mitigants.

The filing was made in February 2022, less than two years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  HSY’s disclosure set contains both forward-looking risk factor language and backward-looking MD&A discussion of actual 2020-2021 impacts.  The company flags multiple threat vectors—demand volatility, supply-chain breakdowns, labor shortages, manufacturing interruptions, incremental PPE and sanitation costs, and gross-margin pressure—demonstrating that COVID-19 is not just a hypothetical but an experienced, ongoing risk.  While HSY notes some mitigating factors (e.g., “minimal disruption” to its network and active management efforts), it concedes that conditions remain “dynamic,” costs have already risen, and future volatility is likely.  The mix of concrete 2021 impacts and explicit warnings about uncontrollable future developments supports a generally high but not maximum risk severity.  Mitigating statements temper but do not outweigh the materially adverse effects already recorded, so most evidence snippets cluster in the 4-7 range, with one negative-scoring snippet reflecting the company’s own mitigating claim.

HSY’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 both as a still-relevant external threat and as a recently realised cost/operational shock.  The risk language spans two categories.  First, forward-looking statements warn that another pandemic wave could disrupt manufacturing, supply chains and macro-demand – positioning COVID-19 alongside other systemic shocks.  Second, the filing cites concrete, recent impacts: mandated retail shutdowns in 2020 and higher 2021 insurance costs tied to delayed medical care.  The disclosures remain largely qualitative and unquantified, but they do connect the pandemic to material areas (production ability, revenues, corporate expenses).  Because the filing date (Feb-2023) falls within three years of the pandemic’s declared onset, the Time Decay Principle permits moderately high scores.  However, the absence of fresh 2023 impacts, the presence of mitigation wording, and the generic ‘could’ phrasing temper severity.  Overall, COVID-19 is treated as an ongoing but now better-managed risk, warranting mid-to-upper-medium evidence scores.

The filing discusses COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing external hazard that could disrupt Hershey’s supply chain, manufacturing footprint and consumer demand rather than as a currently quantifiable loss.  All references are forward-looking (“could result”, “may impact”), indicating potential rather than already-incurred damage.  Although the company explicitly names the coronavirus pandemic and links it to operational and financial exposures (factory interruptions, revenue declines), the language remains broad and bundled with other disruptive forces such as natural disasters and inflation.  Mitigating language (“we believe we take adequate precautions”) tempers the severity, signalling management believes the risk is manageable.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is now four years old, placing it in the medium-term window (4-10 years); therefore snippet scores must be moderate.  Collectively, the evidence shows a material but not acute risk: COVID-19 is still treated as a meaningful threat to operations and profitability, yet without fresh, quantified impacts, so overall severity sits in the mid-range.

Hubbell’s 10-K, filed eleven months after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, paints a picture of an event with both already-incurred and still-evolving consequences.  The company reports concrete, quantified damage for 2020 (e.g., a $418 million organic sales decline) and describes specific operational disruptions such as shutdown-driven supply-chain downtime, work-stoppages across three countries, and halted smart-meter installations.  These are present-tense, realized impacts—not merely hypothetical—and they span multiple classic pandemic vectors: labour availability, supply chain interruptions, demand destruction and incremental cost pressures.  At the same time, management stresses forward-looking uncertainty—citing possible resurgences, new strains and lingering macro-economic weakness—and concedes that even ongoing mitigation efforts may fail, with the potential for „material adverse effects“.  Because the filing date (February 2021) is well within three years of the event onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the risk level is assessed as high: Hubbell is already absorbing material financial hits and foresees continued exposure, while only limited, largely cost-focused mitigations are identified.

Hubbell’s 2022 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a continuing, multi-dimensional threat that already has produced tangible adverse effects (supply-chain shortages, transportation cost spikes, operating-margin pressure) and that could further disrupt operations through renewed outbreaks, regulatory mandates, labour attrition and macro-economic weakness.  The disclosure blends backward-looking evidence of realized impacts with forward-looking warnings, signalling both present and potential severity.  Language such as “material adverse effect,” “significant global supply chain shortages,” and “affected our operating margin in 2021” elevates the risk while the Company’s acknowledgement of mitigation efforts (revised SOPs, monitoring guidelines) only partially offsets it, since management concedes such actions may not prevent further disruption.  Because the filing date (11-Feb-2022) is less than three years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high scores (up to 10).  Overall, the pandemic risk to Hubbell is assessed as high: it is current, multi-faceted, and already impacting financial performance, though uncertainty about duration and regulatory responses remains a key variable.

Hubbell’s 2023 filing treats COVID-19 as an active, multifaceted risk that is still shaping the company’s cost structure, supply-chain reliability, workforce logistics and customer demand nearly three years after the WHO declaration.  The language repeatedly states that the pandemic “has had” concrete adverse effects (e.g., higher freight, labor, commodity and transportation costs) and “continues” to disrupt every region in which Hubbell operates, while also projecting that shortages, inflation and demand volatility “could escalate” in coming quarters.  Although management notes some easing of restrictions, no quantitative dollar impact is provided, and uncertainty around the durability of the economic recovery is emphasized.  Because the filing date (9 Feb 2023) is within three years of the event’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the disclosures are recent, specific (supply-chain shortages, semiconductor scarcity, shipping delays, accounts-receivable deterioration) and describe both realized and forward-looking impacts, pointing to a risk level in the upper mid-to-high range (roughly 6-8 per sentence), rather than the absolute maximum, due to the absence of precise financial quantification or covenant breaches.

Hubbell’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only one explicit reference to the COVID-19 pandemic, embedded in a broader paragraph that groups pandemics with other catastrophic events. The company frames the pandemic chiefly as a potential, ongoing source of economic uncertainty and operational disruption rather than as an already-quantified or isolated impact. No specific dollar amounts, supply-chain metrics, labour statistics, or remote-work references are provided, and the statement is written in conditional language ("could in the future"). Because the initial shock of COVID-19 is now almost four years old, the Time Decay Principle dictates a moderate severity band (4-6). Overall, the disclosure signals that Hubbell still recognises pandemic-related uncertainty but treats it as one risk among many, with no new, concrete impact data offered. Accordingly, the overall risk evidence is moderate and forward-looking, meriting mid-range scoring for any supporting sentences.

HUM’s 2021-02-18 filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to multiple, material and ongoing business risks.  Because the event is recent (within one year of the report date), Time-Decay allows high severity scores.  The disclosure moves well beyond generic wording: management spells out concrete channels of impact – premium adequacy, higher medical utilisation, mandatory benefit expansions, regulatory uncertainty, supply-chain and labour interruptions, remote-work vulnerabilities, liquidity pressure, and macro-economic demand shocks.  Most statements are forward-looking (‘may’, ‘could’) but they describe direct financial exposure rather than abstract possibilities.  Only limited mitigating language (e.g., actions already taken) appears, so adjustments for mitigation are small.  Overall, the pandemic is portrayed as a live, multi-front threat with potential to erode profitability and operational continuity.  Accordingly, evidence snippets generally score in the upper-mid range (4-7), reflecting serious but not yet quantified impacts, consistent with a very recent event under the Time Decay Principle.

HUM’s 2022 filing provides a multifaceted, largely contemporaneous depiction of COVID-19 risk.  The company cites both realised and forward-looking impacts: suppressed non-COVID utilisation, spikes in treatment/testing costs, mandated benefit expansions, and higher mortality shifting claims trends.  Beyond pure claims volatility, HUM flags operational hazards—labour shortages, facility closures, remote-work cyber-exposures, and supply-chain or infrastructure disruptions—showing that the pandemic threatens core service delivery as well as cost structure and cash-flows.  Language such as “material and adverse” and explicit references to profitability, cash-flow and ability to operate indicate severity.  Because the disclosure date (17-Feb-2022) is within two years of the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores.  The statements are specific, enumerate causal mechanisms, and in several cases describe impacts already experienced, justifying elevated risk ratings (7-9/10).  No significant mitigating language (e.g., hedges, insurance, or offsetting gains) is offered, so deductions are minimal.

HUM’s 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as both a still-unfolding operational head-wind and a source of realised financial stress.  Because the filing date (16 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the disclosures sit in the “recent‐event” window of the Time-Decay Principle, allowing elevated severity scores.  The narrative moves beyond generic boiler-plate: management cites concrete, already-experienced effects (e.g., lower 2022 utilisation, disrupted 2021 Medicare risk-adjustment revenue) and itemises forward-looking exposures such as labour shortages, facility closures, remote-work cyber-risk, mandated benefit expansions and volatility in premium adequacy.  These statements show a blend of retrospective impact (realised revenue hits, utilisation swings) and prospective uncertainty (possible premium insufficiency, supply-side constraints).  The company’s language is largely qualitative (few dollar figures) but contains strong “material adverse effect” phrasing and explicit links to core earnings levers, signalling a medium-to-high overall risk posture.  Given the recency and the specificity of operational and financial channels, individual snippets score in the 5-8 range, with modest downward adjustments where mitigation or generality reduces severity.

COVID-19 is portrayed by HUM as both a historical shock and a still-relevant operational risk.  The filing repeats traditional, forward-looking boiler-plate (e.g., pandemics listed with other catastrophes) but, crucially, also provides concrete backward-looking evidence of material impacts: utilisation swings, increased treatment/testing costs, disruption of clinical initiatives, adverse effects on 2021 revenue under Medicare risk-adjustment, altered cash-flow timing, and supply-chain pressure in the pharmacy channel.  These statements show that the pandemic has already affected profitability, reserves and liquidity, and could continue to do so if variants re-emerge or future public-health emergencies arise.  Because the filing date (Feb-2024) is only just under four years after the WHO declaration (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows relatively high—but not maximal—severity scores: the event is moving from “recent” toward “medium-term,” so top-end scores (>8) are unwarranted, yet a solid 5-7 range is justified wherever HUM discloses direct, quantifiable or strategically significant effects.  Generic references or clear indications that the emergency phase has ended are scored lower or neutralised.  Overall, the risk profile is moderate-to-high (≈6/10), driven by demonstrated financial impacts and lingering uncertainty, tempered by the official end of the national and public-health emergencies.

HWM’s 2021 filing was drafted less than a year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so all disclosures sit firmly in the “recent-event” window under the Time Decay Principle and can carry high scores.  The company repeatedly states that COVID-19 is already reducing sales, shutting down plants, depressing demand in its core aerospace and commercial-transportation markets, and jeopardising liquidity.  The language is unambiguous—using phrases such as “have been and could continue to be materially adversely affected,” and it offers specific, quantified customer exposure (e.g., Boeing 8 %, GE 11 %).  The discussion spans multiple classic pandemic-risk vectors: supply-chain interruptions, labour shortages, production shutdowns, contractual non-performance, credit stress, and potential asset impairments.  Although HWM lists some mitigating actions (cost cuts, safety protocols, dividend suspension), those steps are framed as insufficient to offset the uncertain, possibly prolonged damage.  Given the immediacy (February 2021 filing), the specificity of described impacts, and the breadth of risk channels, the evidence merits generally high per-sentence scores in the 7-10 range when impacts are direct and already realised, and moderate scores where statements are more contingent or mitigated.

HWM’s 2022-02-14 filing presents COVID-19 as a recent, still-evolving threat that has already produced measurable harm and could intensify.  The company discloses both backward-looking evidence—e.g., a 5 % ($287 m) sales decline, site shutdowns, customer production suspensions—and forward-looking uncertainties around new variants, supply-chain fragility, labour availability, liquidity pressure and possible asset impairments.  The language is specific (identifies key customers and percentages of sales, references aircraft platform slow-downs, spells out pension-funding and EBITDA risks) and explicitly labels the impact “material.”  Because the pandemic began less than three years before the filing, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  While management notes that it “continues to monitor” guidance, no strong mitigating actions are described that would offset the breadth of operational, demand and financial exposures.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, direct and in several instances quantified, warranting elevated snippet scores that cluster in the 4-8 range, with the highest evidence tied to the quantified revenue drop.

HWM’s 10-K presents COVID-19 as a still-evolving, high-severity risk that began in 2020 but remains materially relevant in the 2023 filing.  The company discloses both realized impacts—such as the collapse of air-travel demand that cut aerospace sales, continuing labor and supply-chain bottlenecks, and the prospect of asset impairments—and forward-looking uncertainty tied to new variants, vaccination uptake and travel restrictions.  The language is concrete (e.g., ‘material adverse effect,’ ‘adversely affected demand’) and explicitly links the pandemic to revenue, customer production rates, cost pressures and product-mix shifts.  Some mitigating signals appear: U.S. domestic travel has mostly rebounded and management expects narrow-body growth, but wide-body recovery lags and China and international traffic remain below 2019 levels.  In line with the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is within the 0-3-year “recent” window, so high scores (up to 10) are appropriate for direct, quantified, or highly material statements, while sentences that emphasise recovery or uncertainty temper the scoring.  Overall, the disclosure reflects a significant, ongoing enterprise risk that is only partially offset by early signs of market normalization.

Within Howmet’s 2024 Form 10-K, explicit pandemic-related language appears primarily in the Risk Factors and MD&A sections.  The firm continues to frame COVID-19 mostly as an ongoing, but now generalized, operational hazard – grouping it with “public health crises” and “pandemic events” that can disrupt factories and global supply chains.  These statements are forward-looking and largely qualitative, signalling potential future shocks rather than describing acute current dislocations.  Nevertheless, the MD&A provides one concrete, quantified datapoint: commercial-aerospace revenue mix remains 11 percentage-points below the 2019 (pre-pandemic) level, confirming a lingering financial drag almost four years after WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic.  Because the filing date (13 Feb 2024) is just under four years from the event trigger (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places the material in the high-to-moderate zone; strong, quantified disclosures can still merit scores in the 7–10 range, while generic boiler-plate language should land mid-scale.  No passage demonstrates a fully quantified, presently material loss directly tied to COVID-19, nor do we see robust mitigation language (e.g., remote-work systems or insurance recoveries) that would offset risk.  Accordingly, the evidence set receives mid-to-upper-range scores, with the highest mark reserved for the MD&A sentence that quantifies the continuing revenue gap attributable to pre-pandemic baselines.

IBM’s 2021 Form 10-K repeatedly ties the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic (declared March 11 2020) to material business risks across demand, operations, supply chain, service delivery, liquidity, currency exposure, accounting estimates and cybersecurity. The disclosures are largely forward-looking (“could,” “may”) yet they also acknowledge realized disruption (“has created significant volatility, uncertainty and economic disruption”), signalling that the threat is already manifesting. While no dollar amounts are provided, the language pinpoints multiple core value drivers—revenue, profit, transaction execution and remote-work security—indicating a broad, enterprise-level exposure. Because the filing date (23 Feb 2021) is well within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores, though absence of quantification and the presence of conditional wording temper the severity. Overall, the risk evidence is recent, multi-faceted and significant but remains mostly qualitative, justifying mid-to-high individual sentence scores in the 3-6 range rather than the absolute maximum.

The 2022 IBM filing repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic—declared only two years before this report—to multiple, material risk vectors: demand contraction, supply-chain disruption, remote-work cyber exposure, macro-economic volatility, accounting uncertainty and currency/credit pressures.  Most statements are forward-looking conditionals ("could" or "may"), yet IBM also concedes that the pandemic "has created volatility, uncertainty and economic disruption," signalling that impacts are already being felt.  The company offers few quantitative figures or detailed mitigation plans, so the disclosures remain qualitative, but the breadth of functions potentially affected elevates the overall risk profile.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is a recent (0-3 yrs) event, permitting higher scores; however, the largely generic tone and absence of hard dollar amounts temper severity.  Consequently, individual snippet scores cluster in the mid-range (3-6), reflecting meaningful but not maximally evidenced risk.

IBM’s February 28 2023 Form 10-K addresses pandemic-related danger only in broad, forward-looking terms.  The filing clusters a “widespread outbreak of an illness, pandemic” with other disruptive events and states such an outbreak could weaken demand, disrupt operations, and impair the supply chain.  It also cites cybersecurity exposure tied to the sharp rise in remote work.  Because the document was filed roughly three years after COVID-19 was declared a pandemic, the Time Decay Principle still allows moderate scoring (0-3 years window).  However, the wording is generic (“any widespread outbreak… could”) and provides no quantitative or retrospective discussion of COVID-19’s actual impact on IBM.  The risk therefore remains potential rather than confirmed, and mitigating language is minimal but the lack of specificity tempers severity.  Overall, the evidence supports low-to-moderate risk scores—acknowledging relevance yet reflecting the abstract nature of the disclosures.

The 2024 IBM filing addresses the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, potential disruptor rather than as a recently realised, quantified loss. The single explicit mention groups a “pandemic” with other large-scale hazards and states it *could* harm customer demand, operations, supply chains and IBM’s ability to deliver products. This wording is generic and forward-looking, offering no numerical impact or historical loss disclosure, which dampens severity. Nevertheless, the risk remains relevant—COVID-19-related pressures on supply chains, labour availability and remote-work security are still evident less than four years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic (borderline between “recent” and “medium-term”). Applying the Time Decay Principle, evidence can merit a moderate score (upper mid-range, 4-6) because the pandemic’s effects are not yet stale, but the disclosure’s breadth and lack of detail prevent a higher rating. Secondary language about the cybersecurity challenges from widespread remote work provides a weak, indirect pandemic link and therefore scores low.

ICE’s 2024 filing continues to flag the COVID-19 pandemic as a material, though now medium-term, enterprise risk.  The company frames the virus in two ways: (1) a historic shock that already caused global economic disruption, supply-chain delays and office closures; and (2) a continuing threat, especially if new, vaccine-resistant variants or other pandemics emerge.  Language is forward-looking but rooted in concrete operational channels—labour shortages, hardware lead-times, vendor force-majeure claims, and reduced customer trading activity.  While no quantified dollar impacts are provided, the disclosures tie the pandemic directly to potential “material adverse” effects on revenues, operations and liquidity.  Given the four-year gap between the WHO declaration (March 2020) and the filing date (Feb 2024), the Time-Decay Principle caps severity in the moderate band (4-6).  Nonetheless, several sentences describe recently-observed supply-chain problems during 2022-2023, warranting scores at the upper end of that medium range, whereas more generic cautionary sentences score slightly lower.

COVID-19 is presented in the filing as an immediate, enterprise-wide hazard that is already disrupting IDEXX’s operations and could materially worsen.  The company details concrete, current impacts—remote-work shifts, facility access limits, supply-chain stress, slower veterinary clinic traffic—and ties these to potential revenue losses in product lines that collectively account for almost all sales (e.g., CAG at 88 % of 2020 revenue).  Management also warns that weakened macro-conditions have already reduced demand in Water and LPD segments and could impede liquidity, margin and share price.  The discussion mixes present-tense effects (“has increased economic uncertainty… disrupted business activity”) with forward-looking contingencies (“may be material”) and repeatedly labels the downside as “material adverse,” showing high severity but limited quantification.  Because the 10-K is dated February 2021—less than one year after the WHO declaration—the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (up to 10).  Overall, the narrative signals a high-probability, high-impact, multi-vector risk that is still evolving; therefore, individual snippets receive scores in the 5-9 range depending on specificity, scope and any mitigating language.

IDEXX’s 2022 Form 10-K squarely positions COVID-19 as a continuing, high-severity, multi-faceted risk.  The filing, which comes less than two years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic (a 0-3-year window), repeatedly links the ongoing outbreak and its variants to potential and already-experienced disruptions in supply chains, logistics, labour availability, customer demand and internal operations.  The company discloses concrete historical impacts (e.g., reduced 2020 water-testing demand, labour-force shortages already driving higher costs) while warning that future public-health directives could materially dent its core Companion Animal Group (CAG) revenues, which constitute 90 % of consolidated sales.  The narrative blends retrospective evidence (actual declines in certain segments) with forward-looking caution and stresses that most determinants are beyond management’s control, underscoring residual exposure. The evidence therefore earns mid-to-high severity micro-scores (4-7) where impacts are specific and current, moderate scores (3-4) for forward-looking uncertainty, and near-zero/negative where mitigating statements appear.

IRM’s February 2023 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily through two disclosures.  First, management states that the shift to sustained remote-work arrangements “following the COVID-19 pandemic” has already increased – and may continue to increase – the company’s cybersecurity risk profile.  This is framed as a present, operational impact that could worsen, indicating that pandemic-driven changes in the working model have materially altered IRM’s threat surface.  Second, within the catalogue of international-operations risks, IRM cites “global pandemics” alongside trade wars and political instability as events that could compound cross-border‐data and operational complexity.  This second reference is forward-looking and generic, signalling awareness but offering no detail.  Taken together, the pandemic is treated more as an amplifying factor (cybersecurity and global mobility) than as a direct financial shock; there is no quantified impact, supply-chain cost estimate or labour shortfall discussion.  Given the filing date (Feb-2023) is less than three years after the WHO declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows elevated scores.  However, because disclosures lack quantification and mitigation detail, overall severity is moderate rather than extreme.

IRM’s 2024 filing contains almost no direct discussion of the COVID-19 pandemic.  The only reference is a single, illustrative clause inside a broader bullet list of geopolitical risks: the company lists “global pandemics” (alongside trade wars) as examples of events that could heighten risk for its worldwide operations.  The wording is generic, forward-looking and not tied to any quantified impact, operational disruption, or mitigation plan.  Because the statement is made four years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time Decay Principle pushes any residual severity into the moderate band (scores ≈ 4-6).  Given the lack of specificity, the evidence supports the lower end of that band.  Overall, IRM acknowledges pandemic risk in name only; the disclosure signals awareness but provides no meaningful insight into actual COVID-19 impacts or preparedness, yielding a modest risk score.

IR’s 2021 filing presents a dense, multi-faceted discussion of COVID-19-related risk that blends (a) retrospective impacts already absorbed in 2020 and (b) forward-looking contingencies that could further erode revenue, liquidity and operations.  The company discloses realised hits—lower product demand, energy-sector contraction, customer credit stress, temporary plant shutdowns and higher health-safety costs—thus demonstrating that the pandemic is not merely a hypothetical threat but an existing drag on earnings and cash-flow.  At the same time, management flags second-order exposures such as supply-chain breakdowns, remote-work cyber-risk, potential loss of “essential” status, and a cascade scenario in which reduced cash generation imperils debt service and even triggers bankruptcy.  The language is specific (“decrease in demand,” “significant volatility in oil and gas prices,” “increased costs … daily fitness-for-duty assessments”) and explicitly links each effect to COVID-19.  Because the filing date (26-Feb-2021) is within one year of the WHO pandemic declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores (7-10) for the most direct, quantified impacts, and moderate scores (2-6) for unquantified or conditional statements.  Mitigating elements—plants now reopened, proactive cost controls—are noted, but they do not outweigh the breadth and immediacy of the disclosed risks.  Overall, the pandemic constitutes a high-level, ongoing enterprise risk for IR, with evidence spanning demand shock, supply-chain fragility, labour health, cybersecurity, and capital-structure pressure.

Ingersoll Rand’s 2022-02-25 Form 10-K presents a broad, recent-event risk profile tied to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The filing repeatedly links the pandemic to concrete, already-realised consequences—lower product demand, higher operating costs, and supply-chain shortfalls—while also outlining forward-looking exposures such as customer credit stress, labour disruption, cyber-security threats from remote work, and potential loss of ‘essential’ status under government lockdowns.  The language is mostly qualitative (few dollar figures) but uses strong modifiers like “material adverse effect,” indicating management sees the threat as significant and continuing.  Because the pandemic is within the 0-3-year “recent” band, Time-Decay allows elevated scoring.  Statements that cite impacts already experienced (e.g., demand declines, increased PPE costs, real supply delays) justifiably earn higher scores, whereas purely precautionary or mitigated statements receive moderate or low scores.  Overall, the risk level is high but unquantified: the company acknowledges both immediate hits to operations and a wide set of contingent vulnerabilities that could intensify if the pandemic persists.

IR’s 2023 filing makes it clear that management still views COVID-19 as a live, multi-faceted threat that touches every layer of the enterprise.  The text repeatedly links the pandemic to concrete operational pain-points that have already occurred—temporary plant shutdowns in China, component shortages, cost overruns for PPE and sanitation, and distribution bottlenecks—while also flagging forward-looking uncertainties such as demand volatility, customer liquidity problems, and the risk that ‘essential-business’ exemptions could be withdrawn.  Most statements are couched in cautionary language (“could,” “may”), but several describe impacts that have already materialised (e.g., increased costs, supply-delivery disruptions).  Because the event window (2020-present) is well within the 0–3-year “recent” band, high scores are permissible under the Time-Decay Principle, yet the absence of hard dollar quantification tempers the severity.  Overall, the disclosure set depicts a high-impact, still-unfolding risk, warranting upper-mid scores (4–8) across individual snippets depending on how direct, specific and realised each impact is, net of any mitigating context.

Ingersoll Rand’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 as a live, enterprise-level hazard, but the language has clearly shifted from the acute crisis phase to a medium-term, manageable risk.  The company acknowledges two dimensions: (i) it “has experienced” tangible supply-chain interruptions traceable to the pandemic, and (ii) it still “could” face future operational, workforce-availability and demand-fulfilment challenges if pandemic conditions recur or persist.  These statements are moderately specific—pinpointing raw-material delays, labour constraints and production stoppages—but they remain unquantified and largely conditional, signalling a prudent, forward-looking stance rather than a report of current material impairment.  Because the filing date (23 Feb 2024) is nearly four years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle calls for mid-level severity scoring.  Overall, the evidence supports a moderate but non-negligible risk rating: the pandemic is no longer destabilising the firm daily, yet clearly informs ongoing contingency planning around supply chains, labour and customer demand.

ISRG’s 2021-02-10 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-faceted threat that has already disrupted the company’s operations and will likely continue to do so.  The filing moves well beyond boiler-plate language: management cites concrete historical impacts (e.g., 90 % collapse in Chinese procedure volume, U.S. volumes dropping to 30 % of normal, supply-chain slowdowns, facility closures) and details cascading risks—demand collapse, capital-spending deferrals, manufacturing and logistics interruptions, regulatory delays, and macro-economic recessionary pressures.  Most disclosures are framed in both the present perfect (“has had”) and future conditional (“may continue to have”), underscoring that the risk is simultaneously realized and ongoing.  No substantive mitigating measures are offered beyond generic references to monitoring and an inability to forecast impacts, so aggravating factors dominate.  Because the filing date falls squarely within three years of WHO’s 11 Mar 2020 pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Taken together, ISRG’s language signals a high, persisting risk profile with quantified evidence of material financial and operational damage; micro-scores therefore cluster in the upper-middle to high range (4-9), capped by direct quantified losses.

The filing is only eleven months removed from the official declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic, so time-decay is minimal and the statements carry full weight.  ITW discloses that COVID-19 has already produced material, realized damage—lower 2020 revenue, reduced plant capacity, and sector-specific weakness—while simultaneously warning of continuing, difficult-to-quantify threats to liquidity, supply-chain continuity, labour availability, and long-term demand patterns.  Language is concrete ("has adversely affected"), broad in scope (operations, financial condition, liquidity) and forward-looking ("could force customer and supplier bankruptcies").  Although the company lists a roster of mitigating actions (PPE procurement, process redesign, cost management, liquidity preservation), these do not eliminate the underlying exposure.  Considering the recency of the pandemic (0-3-year band), the presence of both realised and prospective impacts, the absence of precise financial quantification, and partial mitigations, individual snippet scores cluster in the 6-9 range for the strongest evidence, with lower scores where the text is mainly uncertainty or mitigation.  Overall, COVID-19 constitutes a high but not maximal risk for ITW at this filing date.

ITW’s 2022-02-11 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a clear, multi-dimensional risk that is both already realized (2020 operational and capacity hits, raw-material cost inflation, supply-chain interruptions) and still highly uncertain going forward (variants, potential facility closures, capital-market dysfunction).  Language is specific and company-focused, citing concrete impacts on 2020 results, raw-material pricing, demand shifts, reduced plant capacity and experienced supply-chain disruptions, while also flagging forward-looking exposures such as liquidity constraints, customer-supplier bankruptcies and inability to access credit.  Mitigating actions (process re-designs, cost management, essential-business designations) are noted but do not eliminate the underlying exposure.  Because the filing date is less than two years after the WHO declaration (recent-event window), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores—especially where impacts are described as already occurring or quantitatively material.  Overall, the risk profile is high: direct, current financial and operational impacts layered on top of significant ongoing uncertainty.

ITW’s 2023 filing portrays COVID-19 as a still-material and multi-dimensional threat.  Almost three years after the WHO declaration, management cites both realised damage (lower plant utilisation, supply-chain interruptions, raw-material inflation) and unresolved exposures (future liquidity pressure, customer-supplier bankruptcies, further demand shifts and border closures).  Language is generally direct—“has adversely affected”, “disrupted”, “negatively impacted”—confirming that actual harm is already embedded in results.  Forward-looking clauses (“continues to have the potential”, “could force bankruptcies”) expand the horizon of concern, showing that management believes the pandemic’s tail-risk remains open-ended.  Despite some mitigating notes (plants stayed open; critical materials still sourced), the balance of discussion skews to aggravation with no quantification that would cap the downside.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is still within the 0-3-year window, so high evidence scores (7-10) are appropriate where impacts are specific and realised, while generic or heavily caveated statements receive moderate or low scores.  Overall, the disclosure signals a significant, ongoing enterprise-level risk that warrants heightened investor attention.

ITW’s 2024 filing continues to treat COVID-19 as both a recently-realised and still-emerging enterprise threat.  The company recounts concrete, already-experienced consequences—“significant disruptions” to global operations, supply-chain disturbance, raw-material scarcity and even the deferral of portfolio actions—showing the risk is not merely hypothetical.  At the same time, language such as “could adversely impact” or “resurgence of COVID-19” reveals a forward-looking dimension, indicating management believes the threat remains active.  Disclosures are largely qualitative; there is no quantified dollar impact, but the breadth of business functions cited (demand, production, working capital, strategy) points to materiality.  Because the pandemic’s onset (March 2020) is fewer than four years before the February 2024 filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows high-moderate scoring (up to 7-8) for direct recent impacts, tapering lower for generic statements.  Overall, the risk evidence profile is meaningful but not catastrophic: specific negative outcomes are acknowledged, yet the narrative lacks granular financial quantification or an outlook that the impacts are worsening.

The filing date of February 24 2021 places the disclosure squarely within the first year of the WHO-declared COVID-19 pandemic, so time-decay is minimal and recent-event scoring can be high.  The company repeatedly states that the pandemic is already producing “material adverse” effects on operations, revenues and customer behaviour; it also identifies multiple operational disruptions—office closures, travel bans, cancelled conferences, remote-work security exposures—and demand-side pressures such as client cost-cutting, delayed purchasing decisions and weakened retention rates.  While some mitigating actions (virtual conferences, remote work, management focus) are noted, they are framed as partial and uncertain offsets, and no hard dollar amounts are provided.  Overall, the risk language is direct, present-tense and multi-faceted, indicating a high but not absolute severity.  Given the immediacy of the pandemic (0-3 years) and the absence of precise quantitative loss figures, individual snippet scores cluster in the 3-7 range, with the most forceful “material adverse impact” statements anchoring the upper end.

The filing occurs less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so time-decay allows high scores.  Gartner repeatedly discloses both realised and prospective impacts: hard-hit revenue streams (especially the Conferences segment), forced global office closures, a wholesale shift to remote and hybrid work, potential attrition and labour shortages, contested insurance recoveries, weakened demand for subscription products, and broad macro-economic volatility.  These statements mix past factual damage (e.g., cancelled events, lower revenue) with forward-looking uncertainty (e.g., variant risk, future client spending).  Language is largely specific—identifying named segments, dollar insurance limits, workforce policies—rather than boiler-plate.  Mitigating factors (virtual events, insurance, cost controls) are mentioned but are either contested or clearly less effective than the losses incurred.  Overall, the pandemic represents a high-severity, continuing enterprise risk with direct financial consequences; snippet scores therefore cluster in the 5-8 range, tempered only when phrasing is generic or when mitigation is credible.

The filing, dated February 16 2023, depicts COVID-19 as an ongoing, high-severity risk that has already produced material adverse effects and continues to cast uncertainty over several business dimensions.  The company discloses concrete, recent impacts—2020 and 2021 conference cancellations, materially lower revenue from virtual substitutes, contested insurance recoveries, and a forced wholesale shift to remote work—which demonstrate realized, not merely hypothetical, harm.  At the same time, multiple forward-looking statements warn of continuing exposure: future conference revenue could fall if public-health restrictions return; insurance policies now exclude communicable-disease claims; hybrid work may erode culture and productivity; office–lease economics and cybersecurity needs remain fluid; and global travel limits could disrupt operations.  These are specific, business-unit-level narratives rather than generic boilerplate, and they rely on metrics (e.g., revenue percentages, insurance limits) that emphasize materiality.  Because the pandemic began less than three years before the filing, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores (7-10) where evidence shows direct, quantified or strategic impact, with moderate scores (4-6) for less quantified but still consequential forward-looking statements, and downward adjustments for disclosed mitigations (virtual events, hybrid model).  Overall, the risk profile remains elevated, situating most evidence in the 6-9 range.

The filing, dated four years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, treats the pandemic primarily as an ongoing but now better-understood operational and financial exposure rather than as an acute crisis. The text shows that the company continues to feel medium-term effects: (i) lingering uncertainty around in-person conferences, (ii) unresolved, high-dollar litigation over event-cancellation insurance for 2020–2021, (iii) an explicit loss of insurance protection for any future disease-related cancellations, and (iv) structural changes such as a hybrid workforce that increases cyber-security risk. These statements are specific—naming COVID-19, dollar limits (up to $170 m and $150 m) and concrete business processes—yet mostly forward-looking or contingent (“could,” “has contested,” “excludes”). Under the Time Decay Principle, the event is four years old, so maximum individual evidence scores should fall in the moderate 4-6 band. Overall, the disclosures reflect a material, continuing risk that is being partially mitigated by prior insurance recoveries and operational adaptations, justifying a moderate aggregate severity assessment.

IVZ’s 2021-02-19 Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and continuing risks across financial performance, operations and infrastructure.  Management discloses that AUM and revenues already “declined significantly” in early 2020 and remain vulnerable to renewed market shocks, demonstrating a direct, contemporaneous impact.  The filing also details multiple operational exposures: large-scale remote-work arrangements for employees and key service providers, possible Internet or supply-chain failures, labour-force illness, and heightened cyber-security threat vectors.  These statements are company-specific, forward-looking and largely unquantified, but they clearly describe material pathways through which the pandemic could further erode earnings, liquidity and business continuity.  Because the filing date is less than one year after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Sentences that confirm actual negative outcomes (e.g., AUM declines) receive the highest scores, while purely contingent or partially mitigated statements earn moderate scores.  Mitigating language (successful remote working to date, absence of widespread employee illness) appropriately reduces some individual scores but does not eliminate the overall high-risk assessment given the immediacy and breadth of the threats.

IVZ’s 2022 filing contains a dedicated COVID-19 risk section that links the pandemic to both realised and still-evolving threats.  The disclosure confirms that during the early stages of COVID-19 the firm’s AUM and revenues “declined significantly,” that market volatility has impaired liquidity in certain funds, and that meaningful additional resources have already been diverted to mitigation efforts.  It then projects multiple forward-looking exposures: renewed market sell-offs tied to variants or waning policy support, persistent hybrid-work vulnerabilities, potential labour-force illness, remote-work disruptions at both IVZ and key vendors, and heightened cyber-risk.  The language is specific (naming AUM/revenue declines, liquidity pressure and operational disruption) and largely event-driven rather than generic.  Because the filing date (18 Feb 2022) is less than two years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), Time-Decay permits high severity scores.  Overall, the risk is assessed as high: the company experienced direct financial impacts, acknowledges ongoing operational strains, and concedes that future shocks could materially damage results of operations and financial condition.  Some mitigating notes—improved markets, successful remote work to date, no mass illness—temper but do not neutralise the threat.

IVZ’s 2023 filing presents COVID-19 as both a realized and an ongoing, forward-looking threat.  The disclosure states that assets under management, revenues and net income “declined significantly” during the early stages of the pandemic and have been “negatively impacted” at various times since, confirming that the risk has already materialised.  Management also warns that renewed waves, new variants, vaccine hesitancy, or withdrawal of governmental support could trigger further market declines, liquidity stress in funds, and operational disruption—especially if illness hits key staff or service-provider workforces.  The company acknowledges structural changes such as a permanent shift to hybrid working and the need for continued, “significant” mitigation spending.  Although IVZ notes some recovery and the absence to date of major workforce illness, these are partial offsets rather than eliminators.  Given the filing date (February 2023) is less than three years after the pandemic’s declared onset, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the wording is specific, cites concrete financial effects already incurred, and outlines multiple forward-looking contingencies, supporting a high but not maximal aggregate risk assessment.

IVZ’s 2024 Form 10-K still treats the COVID-19 pandemic principally as an ongoing, forward-looking operational threat rather than a presently quantified loss.  The company groups pandemics with broader “health crises” and business-continuity hazards and stresses that new variants or future pandemics could materially affect financial performance through human-capital constraints, facility outages and technology disruptions.  Language is largely generic—there are no hard numbers or references to specific supply-chain breakdowns—but it does spell out potential hits to revenues, AUM, net income and reputation.  Because the filing date (Feb 2024) is almost four years after the WHO declaration (Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places the event in the medium window (4-10 yrs), capping snippet scores in a moderate band (≈4-6).  The evidence therefore shows persistent, but un-quantified and largely contingent, risk rather than immediate, measured impact; scores are accordingly mid-range.

JB Hunt’s 2021-02-23 Form 10-K was filed less than a year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle places the disclosure squarely in the “recent-event” window (0-3 years) in which higher risk scores are justified.  The filing demonstrates that COVID-19 is both an existing and a forward-looking threat.  In the Risk Factors section the Company explicitly states that national or international health pandemics—specifically COVID-19—have already disrupted customer freight volumes, created potential bad-debt exposure, and could continue to trigger wide-ranging operational bottlenecks (driver shortages, equipment procurement issues, port restrictions, supply-chain failures and credit-market volatility).  Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) confirms that several of these impacts have materialised: a quantified $12.3 million COVID bonus, higher operating-supply costs, customer-site shutdowns that reduced revenue, and deferred capital expenditure to preserve liquidity.  Although some passages are generic or heavily caveated, the narrative overall combines realised cost hits with a broad catalogue of prospective disruptions, signalling a high but not catastrophic risk profile (i.e., upper-mid range scores rather than a perfect 10).  Mitigating language appears (e.g., adequate credit resources), but it does not outweigh the breadth and immediacy of the exposures.  Therefore, individual snippets generally fall in the 5-8 range, with lower scores for purely contextual or mitigated statements and near-zero scores where risk is effectively neutralised.

JBHT’s 2022 Form 10-K portrays the COVID-19 pandemic as both an already-experienced shock and a continuing, material threat.  Two years after WHO’s March 2020 declaration, management still cites concrete, realised impacts – customer site shutdowns, network inefficiencies, labour shortages, temporary freight-volume declines, cost increases and higher bad-debt exposure – while also highlighting a broad spectrum of forward-looking vulnerabilities such as driver availability, third-party carrier service levels, equipment procurement delays and port restrictions.  The language is mostly specific, uses terms like “have and may continue,” “significantly impacted,” and enumerates multiple operational choke points, indicating that the risk is not merely theoretical.  Mitigating actions are mentioned only tangentially (e.g., productivity gains or revenue growth offsetting some costs), so the net tone remains cautionary.  Because the filing date (25 Feb 2022) is less than three years after the onset of the pandemic, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Overall, COVID-19 constitutes a high-level, ongoing risk for JBHT, warranting elevated but differentiated micro-scores depending on each sentence’s specificity, evidence of actual impact, breadth of effect, and presence (or absence) of mitigating factors.

JBHT’s 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly ties ongoing and prospective operational and financial pressures to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The filing acknowledges both realised impacts (customer freight disruptions, equipment delivery delays, labour shortages) and still-developing uncertainties (future resurgences, macro-economic fallout).  The language is mostly qualitative but specific, naming concrete transmission channels such as procurement of revenue equipment, reserve for bad-debt, driver availability and port restrictions.  Because the pandemic began less than three years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows higher severity scores.  Nonetheless, the absence of hard dollar quantification and the use of conditional verbs (“may,” “could”) warrants some downward adjustment from the maximum possible values.  Overall, the disclosures convey a live, material risk landscape with multiple avenues for adverse impact, justifying mid-to-high snippet scores within the 0-3-year window.

The filing, dated February 23 2024, discusses the continuing threat that large-scale health pandemics pose to J.B. Hunt’s (JBHT’s) operations. Although COVID-19 first emerged four years earlier, the company still frames pandemic exposure as a material, forward-looking risk that could again disrupt freight volumes, labor availability, equipment procurement, credit markets and bad-debt levels. The wording is largely prospective ("can be," "may," "could"), so it is not disclosing a presently quantified impact but rather a scenario analysis of what might recur. Nonetheless, it identifies multiple concrete transmission channels—customer shipping reductions, third-party service limitations, driver shortages, port restrictions, and supply-chain bottlenecks—showing that management still sees pandemic conditions as a meaningful medium-term threat. Applying the Time Decay Principle, evidence scores should sit in the moderate range (4-6) because the event is roughly four years old, the discussion is detailed but unquantified, and mitigation language (uncertainty qualifiers) tempers severity.

Jabil’s 2021 filing presents COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-dimensional threat that is already hitting the company’s income statement and balance sheet, while remaining highly uncertain going forward.  The disclosure contains repeated, specific statements that the pandemic has *had* a “material and adverse” effect on financial condition, details concrete operational strains (factory shutdowns, lower utilisation, labour shortages, supply-chain interruptions, logistics cost inflation, customer-demand volatility and management distraction) and even quantifies a direct cost of about US$142 million in fiscal-year 2020.  The language is neither generic nor hypothetical; it documents realised impacts and anticipates further losses if conditions worsen.  Mitigations (protective measures, government subsidies, remote-work adjustments) are mentioned, but framed with caution (“no assurance these efforts will be successful”).  Because the pandemic is well within the 0-3-year “recent-event” window, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores.  Overall, the risk evidence is strong, specific, and current, warranting elevated severity assessments across most snippets.

Jabil’s 2022-10-25 filing frames COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, high-severity threat that is already inflicting tangible damage on the company’s finances and operations while also presenting significant forward-looking uncertainty.  Nearly three years after the WHO declaration, management reports concrete, realized impacts—higher labour and PPE costs, lower factory utilisation, supplier shutdowns, logistics bottlenecks and demand volatility—while warning that additional plant closures or sourcing shortfalls could trigger further direct costs and lost revenue.  The language is decidedly specific (naming cost categories, capacity constraints and supply-chain delays) and repeatedly labels the effect “material and adverse,” signalling a magnitude well above routine business fluctuations.  Although Jabil lists mitigation efforts, it concedes that these may prove inadequate, so the bulk of the disclosure is aggravating rather than mitigating.  Because the pandemic remains within the 0-3-year “recent event” window, Time Decay imposes little downward pressure; accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the upper-mid range (5-7) with modest deductions for the absence of numeric quantification or for cited mitigations.  Overall, the risk profile justifies an elevated composite severity assessment—roughly the 7-8 zone on a 10-point scale.

Jabil’s 2023 filing repeatedly asserts that the COVID-19 pandemic has already caused, and may again cause, material harm across virtually every layer of its business model—financial performance, supply chain, labor availability, logistics and customer demand.  The wording is explicit and company-specific, describing past factory slow-downs, supplier shutdowns, higher freight costs, employee absenteeism and direct revenue losses.  These references go beyond boiler-plate; they acknowledge historical damage (‘has had’) while maintaining a forward-looking posture (‘may in the future again have’), signalling that the threat remains active.  Although no dollar amounts are disclosed, the consistent use of strong qualifiers such as “material and adverse” elevates severity.  Because the filing date (20-Oct-2023) is only about 3½ years after the WHO pandemic declaration (11-Mar-2020), Time-Decay still permits high—but not maximum—scores.  Accordingly, individual snippets are scored in the upper-mid range (3-9) depending on specificity, immediacy and whether mitigants or conditional language are present.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a significant, recently-experienced and still-unresolved risk for Jabil, warranting a composite high-moderate risk assessment.

Jabil’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to reference the COVID-19 pandemic only in broad, catch-all language, grouping it with other disruptive events such as natural disasters and geopolitical unrest.  The Company discloses that pandemics have already caused component shortages and shipping delays and could again materially harm operations, margins, and supply-chain reliability.  However, the wording is largely generic—no quantitative dollar figures, no discussion of remote-work transitions, labour shortages, or consumer-demand shifts unique to COVID-19.  The references are mostly forward-looking (‘could’, ‘may’) or historical in a non-specific sense (‘in the past there have been pandemics…’).  Because the filing date (28 Oct 2024) is roughly 4½ years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Time-Decay places the event in the medium-term window, capping scores in the mid-range.  Overall, I assess Jabil’s pandemic risk disclosure as moderate: clearly acknowledged, linked to supply-chain and logistics impacts, but unquantified and somewhat boiler-plate, suggesting an overall severity in the 4-6 range for the best evidence sentences.

Johnson Controls International’s 2021-11-15 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as an immediate and multifaceted threat that is already depressing operations and could structurally reshape demand for its building-related products and services.  The company discloses tangible, realised impacts—plant shutdowns, labour shortages, supply-chain delays, cost inflation and earlier demand declines—as well as forward-looking exposures such as vaccine-mandate attrition and the possibility of a lasting drop in commercial-building construction due to remote work.  The language is specific (e.g., references to project cancellations, component shortages, and lost site access) and ties the pandemic directly to margins, cash-flows and potential impairments.  Some mitigating actions (remote-work protocols, vaccination programmes, supplier diversification) are noted, but these are described as costly, disruptive or only partially effective.  Because the filing date is within two years of the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores; the evidence largely merits upper-mid to high ratings (3-7 range) reflecting both realised damage and continuing uncertainty.

COVID-19 remains a live, multi-faceted threat for JCI in the November 2022 filing.  Although more than two years have elapsed since the WHO declaration, the pandemic still falls inside the 0-3-year “recent-event” window, so time-decay does not materially blunt severity scores.  The disclosure set details both realised and prospective impacts: actual lockdown-driven factory and site interruptions (especially in China), labour shortages, vaccine-mandate attrition, supply-chain bottlenecks, and the possibility of a structural fall-off in commercial-building demand because of permanent remote-work habits.  The narrative is operationally specific—identifying delays in project execution, backlog conversion problems, higher costs and margin pressure—yet generally unquantified.  Management also flags uncertainty around variants and public-health measures, underscoring that the risk is ongoing rather than historical.  Mitigating actions (price increases, recruitment, supplier diversification) are mentioned elsewhere, but the COVID paragraphs themselves stress continuing exposure more than mitigation.  Given proximity in time, direct operational evidence, and breadth of affected business drivers, individual sentence scores are clustered in the mid-to-upper range (3-7) under the Time Decay Principle.

COVID-19 is referenced only briefly in JCI’s 2023 Form 10-K, and the language is explicitly forward-looking: the company discusses how a future ‘occurrence or reoccurrence’ of COVID-19-type pandemics could harm operations, liquidity and overall performance.  No quantitative impacts, cost figures, or precise business segments are cited; instead the discussion is framed in conditional verbs ("may", "will depend"), signalling potential–not current–exposure.  Given the filing date (December 2023) is roughly 3¾ years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (March 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places these statements in the 4-10-year “medium-term” bucket where moderate (4-6) scores are appropriate.  The risk is broad in scope—touching operations, finance and macro-economic knock-ons—but the disclosure is generic and lacks quantification or specific mitigation detail, so the evidence is material enough for recognition yet not severe enough for a high score.  Accordingly, individual snippets are scored in the 4-6 range, reflecting a medium residual risk that is acknowledged but not elaborated with concrete data.

JCI’s 2024 Form 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a continuing, forward-looking threat rather than an already-quantified impairment.  The filing appears nearly five years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), so the Time Decay Principle places any pandemic-related disclosure in the medium-term window (4-10 years), capping severity in the mid-single digits.  Within the risk factors, management situates COVID-19 inside broader lists of potential disruptions (pandemics, public-health crises, labor shortages, supply-chain shocks) and calls out one concrete channel—remote and hybrid work—as a vector for elevated cybersecurity exposure.  Language is largely generic (“may adversely affect,” “occurrence or reoccurrence”) and no numerical impact is provided, signalling residual uncertainty rather than present, quantified damage.  Nonetheless, by explicitly naming COVID-19 and tying a renewed outbreak to enterprise-wide effects on operations, liquidity and results, the company admits that pandemic risk remains material.  Given the elapsed time since the acute phase, the lack of dollar figures, and the existence of partial mitigants (e.g., business-continuity planning, insurance), overall evidence merits moderate—but not high—severity scores (≈3-6) under the Time Decay guidelines.

JKHY’s 2021-08-25 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, enterprise-wide threat whose ultimate magnitude remains unpredictable.  Because the filing date falls only ~17 months after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (0-3 years window).  The risk discussion is concentrated in both Item 1A and MD&A. Overall, the risk evidence skews moderately high (unquantified but multi-faceted, ongoing and uncertain) but is tempered by the company’s mitigation narrative and the absence of quantified financial damage.

JNJ’s 2023 Form 10-K explicitly recognizes both the realised and continuing ramifications of the COVID-19 pandemic across sales, supply chain, labour practices and strategic planning. Overall, the risk is both realized and forward-looking, broad in scope (financial, operational, human-capital, supply-chain and strategic), and therefore material to stakeholders’ assessment of Jacobs’ near-term outlook.
