The company cites concrete, present-tense disruptions—higher coronavirus-related costs, supply-chain bottlenecks, workforce absenteeism, production delays and schedule slips—while also warning of future uncertainties tied to new variants, vaccine mandates and long-term impacts on customer budgets.  Although management notes some mitigation steps (e.g., accelerated $2.2 billion supplier payments), these are framed as responses to ongoing stress rather than full risk offsets.  The language is specific (naming production rates, contract milestones and single-source suppliers) and links directly to financial performance.  Overall, the disclosure depicts a broad, continuing and only partially mitigated risk profile, warranting mid-to-upper severity scores for the extracted evidence.

Lockheed Martin’s 2023 filing makes repeated, explicit connections between the COVID-19 pandemic and material business risks that remain current.  The company discloses that COVID-19 has already slowed production rates, disrupted supply chains, caused labour absenteeism, triggered semiconductor shortages and forced large-scale remote-work arrangements.  Management also flags continuing uncertainty tied to new variants, vaccine uptake, government controls and the knock-on effects on defence budgets—demonstrating both realised and forward-looking exposure.  Language such as “adversely affected,” “could continue to be adversely affected,” and references to specific variants (Omicron) show present-tense, concrete impacts, while the absence of hard dollar figures tempers the severity.  The company acknowledges mitigation efforts (supplier pre-payments, hybrid work), but these do not neutralise the broader risk narrative.  Given the filing date (January 2023) is less than three years from the pandemic’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores; nonetheless, lack of precise quantification and some mitigating actions warrant scores mostly in the 5-8 range rather than the maximum.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a significant, ongoing operational and financial risk for LMT.

Lockheed Martin’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to acknowledge the COVID-19 pandemic as an active, though now somewhat aging, source of enterprise risk.  The company frames the pandemic primarily as an ongoing or repeatable public-health threat that can resurface or be mirrored by future outbreaks, rather than as an acute shock that is still driving material year-on-year variances.  The disclosures emphasise potential (forward-looking) adverse effects on labour availability, supply-chain reliability, inflationary cost pressure, production schedules, market volatility, and overall financial performance.  They also highlight a structural change in workforce practices—namely the shift to a long-term hybrid model that originated “beginning with the COVID-19 pandemic.”  No quantified dollar impacts are provided, nor are there statements that the pandemic is currently constraining deliveries; instead, language is largely precautionary and couched in generic “could” or “may” phrasing.  Given the Time-Decay Principle, the event sits just under four years old at the 2024 filing date, placing it in the lower-to-middle of the medium-term band.  Accordingly, evidence items warrant moderate scores (roughly 1-5), reflecting identifiable but unquantified, forward-looking risk without fresh, material impacts or robust mitigation detail.

COVID-19 is portrayed by Alliant Energy (LNT) as a recent, multifaceted threat that is already affecting, and could further erode, virtually every layer of its utility value-chain – from demand swings and customer credit quality to supply-chain blockages, labour availability, construction timetables, liquidity and even cyber-security.  The filing combines backward-looking facts (e.g., 3 % residential demand increase, 4 % C&I decline) with forward-looking cautions (possible pension-plan funding spikes, missed tax-credit deadlines, capital-market access, workforce illness).  Although management repeatedly notes that no “significant issues” have yet materialised and outlines several mitigation steps (regulatory deferrals, liquidity bolstering, cost-cutting, remote-work protocols), the overall tone remains one of heightened vigilance; most statements are framed as credible, near-term contingencies rather than distant hypotheticals.  Applying the Time Decay principle, the pandemic is <3 years old at the filing date, so high per-sentence scores (up to 10) are permissible.  Still, where the company highlights effective offsets or states that impacts are not yet material, scores are scaled down accordingly.  The net result is a risk profile that is acute, broad and only partially mitigated, warranting consistently elevated—but not maximum—snippet scores.

The filing was made in February 2022, less than two years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (March 2020).  Therefore, under the Time Decay Principle the pandemic is a ‘recent’ event and elevated scores (7-10) are permissible where the language demonstrates direct or continuing impacts.  Across both the Risk Factors and MD&A sections, LNT (Alliant Energy, IPL and WPL) describes COVID-19 as an existing and still-evolving threat that is already disrupting supply chains, labour availability, customer demand, capital-market access and large construction timelines.  The wording is mostly specific—e.g., citing customer arrears, supply-chain inflation in the solar market, and potential loss of renewable-tax credits—rather than boiler-plate.  Although management notes some mitigating actions (cost-transformation, modified business practices, active monitoring), these measures are presented as partial and conditional.  On balance, the disclosures reflect a material, ongoing risk with multi-faceted operational and financial exposure.  Given the recency of the pandemic and the concrete linkages to the company’s core utility operations, individual snippet scores predominantly fall in the 4-7 range, with higher scores where quantified or multiple impact vectors are cited, and modest deductions where explicit mitigations are mentioned or the statement is purely uncertain/forward-looking.

LNT’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a continuing external pressure that amplifies existing operational vulnerabilities rather than as a discrete, one-off shock. However, the disclosures remain high-level: there is no quantified revenue, margin or capex impact, and pandemic risk is often bundled with other hazards (weather, geopolitical issues, etc.).  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 falls within the 0-3-year “recent” window, so statements can score in the upper range, but their generic nature and lack of financial specificity temper severity.  Overall, COVID-19 is presented as a moderate-to-high, persistent risk driver—material enough to merit vigilance and contingency planning, yet not evidenced by hard numbers or singularly catastrophic language.

The filing, dated February 16 2024, reflects on the COVID-19 pandemic only in passing but still acknowledges that pandemic-driven disruptions remain a live consideration nearly four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic.  All references are generic—using the plural term “pandemics” rather than naming COVID-19—and they are embedded in broader lists of disruptive forces such as geopolitics, weather, and labor issues.  The company frames the risk as both historical (the global supply chain "has experienced" disruption) and prospective (disruptions are "expected to continue"), indicating management believes pandemic-related volatility has not fully abated.  No quantified dollar impacts, loss estimates, or detailed mitigation plans are provided, signalling an un-measured but still material exposure.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, a 2020 event assessed in early 2024 falls at the edge of the 0-3 versus 4-10-year bands.  Given this borderline timing and the absence of concrete financial metrics, the evidence warrants moderate—not high—severity scores (4-6 range).  The pandemic is portrayed as a contributing factor to supply-chain instability, possible operational outages, and counter-party default rather than as an isolated, overriding threat, which further tempers the overall risk rating.

The filing was prepared roughly one year after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, so the disclosures sit firmly in the ‘recent-event’ window (0-3 years) where high scores are permissible.  Lowe’s text repeatedly stresses that COVID-19 has already disrupted operations (e.g., higher expenses, extraordinary supply-chain strain) while simultaneously warning that future waves, mutations, and macro-economic fallout could further impair revenue, profitability and liquidity.  The language is specific – naming concrete impact channels such as out-of-stocks, higher product costs, labour availability, elevated operating expenses for safety protocols, and the need to re-prioritise capital allocation – yet remains largely qualitative rather than fully quantified.  Because these statements describe both realised impacts (e.g., $1.3 billion spent on pandemic response, supply-chain bottlenecks already producing shortages) and significant continuing uncertainty, the overall risk posture is high.  Applying the Time Decay principle, recent direct impacts with multi-channel exposure merit elevated scores (7-9 range), tempered slightly for the absence of precise dollar-scale loss projections in most sentences.

Lowe’s March 2022 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-dimensional threat that is already distorting the company’s operating environment and will continue to do so for the foreseeable future.  The filing links the pandemic to concrete, present-tense impacts—supply-chain delays, transportation-cost inflation, inventory stock-outs, labour availability issues and volatile consumer-demand patterns—while also flagging prospective hazards such as renewed lockdowns, new variants and a post-pandemic spending shift away from home-improvement.  Although some passages note temporary benefits (e.g., elevated DIY spending) or cost relief (lower pandemic-related expenses), management makes it clear that these positives could reverse quickly and that residual uncertainty remains high.  Because the disclosure (a) is made within two years of the WHO pandemic declaration, (b) describes direct, already-realised financial and operational effects, and (c) highlights ongoing exposure with few definitive mitigants, the Time-Decay Principle permits high risk-severity scores—generally in the 5-9 range depending on specificity, materiality and the presence of mitigating language.

The filing, dated March 27 2023, repeatedly ties Lowe’s risk profile to the ongoing and historical effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company discloses both realized impacts (e.g., higher transportation costs, out-of-stock inventory, port congestion, and a significant hit to 2020-2021 operations) and continuing, forward-looking uncertainties (future supply-chain strain, labor availability, demand shifts, macro-economic drag).  The language is specific—naming concrete operational vectors such as domestic and international supply chains, fulfillment networks, inventory levels, vendor stability, transportation capacity, and overall results of operations—yet largely un-quantified.  Because the pandemic began only three years before the filing, the Time Decay Principle allows high-severity scores.  Taken together, the evidence shows that COVID-19 remains a material, multi-dimensional threat: it has already damaged margins and logistics and could keep doing so if medical, labor, or macro-economic conditions worsen.  No major mitigating language (e.g., definitive recovery trends, quantified cost offsets) is provided, so the aggregate risk level stays elevated, though not maximal because impacts are described qualitatively rather than with hard dollar figures.

LOW’s 2024 Form 10-K still acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic as a material but now-maturing risk driver.  The company frames the pandemic mostly in retrospective language (“placed strains”, “were further exacerbated”), yet also makes clear that ripple-effects—ongoing supply-chain volatility, labour imbalances, port congestion, a larger remote-work attack surface and general macro-economic uncertainty—remain embedded in its risk profile.  No quantified dollar impact is provided, and some statements are folded into broader ‘public-health crises’ catch-alls, signalling a shift from acute crisis management toward longer-term, moderate vigilance.  Applying the Time Decay Principle (event ≈ 4 years old), evidence can earn at most a mid-range severity: direct, specific COVID references merit scores near the upper end of the 4-6 band, while generic pandemic language or indirect remote-work consequences receive lower mid-range values.  No significant mitigating actions are cited in the same sentences, so deductions are minimal.  Overall risk is assessed as moderate but persistent rather than severe or negligible.

Lam Research’s 2021 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic to multiple, already-realised disruptions across the company’s value chain and warns of continuing, potentially “material” impacts.  Because the filing date (August 2021) falls well within three years of the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration (March 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity ratings.  The disclosure is not merely hypothetical: management states that COVID-related restrictions have *already* delayed shipments, raised costs, reduced revenue and profitability, and constrained cash generation, while simultaneously threatening supply-chain continuity, labour availability, facility uptime, and customer demand.  Although the narrative contains some forward-looking language (“could further,” “may continue”), the dominant tone is that of an ongoing, direct impact with few concrete mitigations beyond generic references to business-continuity plans and alternative sourcing.  The statements are mostly qualitative, lacking hard dollar figures, but the breadth and immediacy of effects—combined with use of strong qualifiers such as “material adverse effect”—support elevated risk scores (generally in the 5-8 range) under the recent-event window.

The filing, dated August 24 2022, links the COVID-19 pandemic to multiple, concrete and continuing threats for Lam Research (LRCX).  The text moves well beyond generic boiler-plate: it catalogues specific, already-realised operational disruptions (facility closures, production delays, supply shortages, workforce constraints) and clearly states that these have driven higher costs, shipment delays, lower revenue and profitability—and that such effects "may be material."  It also flags future-looking uncertainty around the duration of the pandemic and the resulting volatility in customer demand and financing markets.  While the company briefly mentions contingency actions (business-continuity plans, alternative sourcing), these mitigants are described as reactive necessities rather than fully effective solutions.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is a very recent event (within three years of the filing), so direct, quantified, or materially adverse statements warrant high scores (7-10).  Less specific or more contextual statements still rate moderate-to-high (4-6) because recency keeps the risk salient.  No evidence merits a score reduction to zero because all statements occur after the WHO declaration date (11 Mar 2020).

COVID-19 appears in LRCX’s 2023 Form 10-K as a still-active, multi-faceted threat.  The company characterises the pandemic as having already caused specific operational interruptions—parts shortages, shipping unpredictability, facility closures—and as an ongoing source of higher costs, lower revenues and potential ‘material’ effects on results.  Statements are mostly qualitative but highly specific to Lam’s supply chain, labour availability, manufacturing throughput and financial metrics.  They are framed both in the past tense (actual impact) and the future tense (continuing exposure), signalling that management views the pandemic as a live, not merely historical, risk.  No meaningful mitigating language (e.g., alternative sourcing successes or permanent cost offsets) is offered in the cited sentences, so aggravating factors dominate.  Because the filing date (15 Aug 2023) is within three years of the pandemic’s declared onset, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores (up to 10).  Overall, the evidence supports a high-but-not-maximum risk assessment: direct impacts are asserted, breadth of business functions is wide, but there are no quantified dollar amounts.

Lam Research’s 2024 Form-10-K squarely links the 2020-onward COVID-19 pandemic to a continuing, though now moderated, set of operational and financial risks. The language is detailed (naming quarantines, travel bans, tele-work transitions, shortages of parts, and material hits to revenue and cash flow) and largely forward-looking, signalling that management still views pandemic after-shocks as a live threat. Overall, the disclosures portray a meaningful, specific, and persisting—but no longer acute—risk profile, warranting moderate individual snippet scores in the 4-6 range, with one generic reference scoring lower.

Lululemon’s 2021 Form-10-K presents COVID-19 as both an already-experienced shock and a persistent, forward-looking threat.  Multiple sentences describe concrete, realized impacts during fiscal 2020—store and distribution-centre shutdowns, a 34 % drop in in-store revenue, negative cash-flow effects, and forced operational changes.  They also outline potential and continuing exposures: renewed lockdowns, supply-chain interruptions, labour shortages, long-term shifts in consumer behaviour, and macro-economic deterioration.  The disclosures are specific (naming closed sites, quantified revenue decline, and cash-flow pressure) and framed as material (“have and will continue to adversely affect”).  Because the filing date (30-Mar-2021) is less than 13 months after the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the pandemic constitutes an acute, enterprise-wide risk with ongoing uncertainty, only partially mitigated by e-commerce growth and liquidity buffers, yielding consistently high—but not always maximum—risk scores across the extracted evidence.

Lululemon’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as a multidimensional, still-evolving threat that has already produced material harm and could continue to do so for at least the medium term.  Management discloses both realised impacts—2020 store shutdowns, shipment delays, higher freight cost—and forward-looking exposures such as renewed store closures, labour shortages, prolonged supply-chain bottlenecks, cybersecurity vulnerabilities tied to remote work, and persistent shifts in consumer buying behaviour from physical stores to e-commerce.  The tone is specific and candid, repeatedly linking the pandemic to concrete operational nodes: retail traffic, staffing, logistics, manufacturing capacity, and liquidity.  Although the filing notes some improvement in 2021, it explicitly states that the duration, magnitude, and secondary effects (e.g., variants, pricing pressures) remain uncertain.  Given the filing date (March 2022) falls well within three years of the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Because most statements describe either (a) actual, recent hits to performance or (b) plausible near-term recurrences with material financial implications, overall risk evidence merits medium-to-high snippet scores (4-8 range), only modestly tempered where the company cites mitigating actions or improvements.

Lululemon’s 2023 Form 10-K shows that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a material but moderating enterprise-wide risk.  Management acknowledges both (a) concrete, historical damage (store closures, weakened traffic, liquidity pressure, supply-chain back-ups) and (b) ongoing exposure to renewed outbreaks that could again disrupt operations, labour availability, consumer demand and sourcing.  The language is largely narrative and unquantified, but it ties the pandemic directly to multi-line impacts—retail, e-commerce, supply chain, labour, and financial health—making it more than a generic disclosure.  Because the filing date is just over three years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle still allows for high but not maximal severity: the event is on the edge of the ‘recent’ window, its acute shocks have eased, yet management still devotes explicit risk-factor space to potential recurrences.  Accordingly, snippets that describe actual past harm score in the upper-mid range (around 7) while purely forward-looking or macro-level statements receive lower marks.  No snippet reaches 9-10 because the company provides no quantified dollar effects or covenant-level distress, and the discussion now mixes mitigation with contingency planning.

Lululemon’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to treat COVID-19 as a material but now-tempered enterprise risk.  The filing acknowledges that the pandemic produced real, historic impacts on revenue, margins, store traffic, labour availability and liquidity, while simultaneously projecting that renewed outbreaks or other public-health crises could again disrupt supply chains, store operations and consumer demand.  The language combines backward-looking facts (e.g., 2021–2022 store closures and margin compression) with forward-looking conditionals (“could”, “may”) that warn of recessionary knock-on effects, labour shortages and factory shutdowns.  Four years have elapsed since the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), placing the event at the front edge of the medium-term band under the Time Decay Principle; therefore individual evidence scores are capped at a moderate 6.  The disclosures remain company-specific, detail multiple impact channels (supply chain, distribution centres, staffing, consumer behaviour), and in several instances concede concrete past damage, supporting mid-level severity scores despite slightly diminishing immediacy.

Southwest’s 2021-02-08 Form 10-K depicts COVID-19 as a recent, acute, and multi-faceted threat that has already caused severe, quantified damage and is expected to remain a dominant source of uncertainty.  The filing enumerates direct financial hits (e.g., a 59.7 % revenue collapse, $934 million in 2020 cash refunds) and operational shocks ranging from schedule cuts and workforce infections to supply-chain fragility and the need for mass remote work.  It also stresses forward-looking hazards—variant outbreaks, lingering travel fear, continued government restrictions, and deteriorated capital-market access—making clear that the risk is both current and prospective.  The language is highly specific and repeatedly uses forceful qualifiers such as “materially and adversely,” reflecting a high severity level.  Because the filing date is less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (7-10) where disclosures are direct, quantified, and materially impactful, while moderate scores (4-6) apply to secondary or unquantified impacts, and lower scores (≤3) are reserved for ancillary or mitigated items.  The evidence below itemises every sentence in the filing that squarely discusses pandemic-related impacts on demand, liquidity, operations, labour, supply chain, remote work, and cyber risk.

The narrative is recent (2020-22), highly specific (naming revenue lines, liquidity, Boeing dependence, vendor bankruptcies, fuel-pipeline bottlenecks, credit-rating downgrades, health-safety perception, vaccination mandates, cyber-risk, etc.) and mostly aggravating, with only occasional mitigating references (e.g., partial employee-vaccination progress, remote-work controls). Overall, the risk profile is high because impacts are already realised, multi-dimensional, and future outcomes remain “highly uncertain,” supporting snippet scores largely in the 6-9 range, with minor downward adjustments where mitigating language appears.

Southwest (LUV) positions COVID-19 as both an historic shock and an ongoing, forward-looking risk across virtually every core dimension of its business model—demand, labour, supply chain, liquidity, cybersecurity, and regulatory flexibility. COVID-19 is no longer an acute shock for Southwest, yet the Form 10-K shows the virus’ after-effects are still embedded in the Company’s risk profile. Because the pandemic’s onset is roughly four years before the 2024 filing date, the Time Decay Principle places the evidence in the medium-term category: risks are still material but no longer peak-crisis.  Accordingly, individual snippet scores are capped in the moderate band (4-6 for the most acute continuing exposures, lower when references are more generic or partially mitigated).

Minor downward adjustments are applied where statements are purely forward-looking or lack financial quantification, but the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scoring given the extreme immediacy of the risk.

Accordingly, snippet scores cluster in the 4-6 range, reflecting meaningful but moderating risk consistent with the nearly-four-year age of the event.

The disclosure moves well beyond boiler-plate: management cites concrete, quantified hits (e.g., a 40–50 % PO/TBA cost over-run and a $582 million refinery impairment) and identifies specific channels of vulnerability such as supply-chain dislocation, fuel-demand collapse, and potential amplification of other risk factors. Because the pandemic began less than a year before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores; the mix of hard numbers, segment-level impacts, and forward-looking uncertainty supports elevated (but not maximal) ratings for the strongest excerpts, with moderate scores for contextual or less company-specific statements.

The filing, dated February 24 2022, discusses COVID-19 in the dedicated risk-factor section and also embeds a quantified project-level impact elsewhere in the document. The language confirms that the pandemic has already affected LYB (e.g., a 40-50 % cost overrun on the PO/TBA plant) and could "continue to materially adversely affect" the company. The statements blend backward-looking evidence (economic disruption already experienced) with forward-looking uncertainty (variants, supply-chain stress, liquidity pressure), so the risk is both existing and prospective. Most disclosures are qualitative but one is specifically quantified, strengthening the materiality assessment. Because the event is recent (within two years of the filing), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores. No meaningful mitigating language offsets the core risk beyond a brief reference to stakeholder collaboration. Overall, the pandemic represents a high, sustained enterprise-wide risk with demonstrated financial consequences, justifying elevated scores, especially for the quantified cost overrun snippet.

LYB’s 2023 filing continues to frame COVID-19 as a live, enterprise-level threat even though the initial outbreak occurred three years ago.  The disclosure mixes (i) concrete, realized impacts – higher project costs and schedule delays, historic demand destruction, supply-chain volatility – with (ii) forward-looking warnings that further waves or policy responses could still materially disrupt operations, liquidity, and profitability.  The language is mostly qualitative; only one sentence provides a numerical data point (a 4 % revenue lift from post-COVID demand recovery).  Nonetheless, several passages explicitly tie incremental cost overruns, supply-chain risks and broad macroeconomic uncertainty to the pandemic.  Given the filing date (Feb 2023) the event is within the 0-3-year “recent” window, so time-decay allows scores toward the upper range.  However, most statements are not quantified and some blend COVID with other factors, so individual snippet scores cluster in the mid-to-upper single digits rather than the maximum 10.

The filing is dated February 2024, almost four years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic in March 2020, so the Time-Decay Principle places COVID-19 within the early edge of the medium-term window (4 – 10 years).  Within the risk-factor section, LYB does not describe any concrete, historical impact from COVID-19—no discussion of shutdowns, labour shortages, remote-work transitions or quantified financial effects is provided.  Instead, the company folds “epidemics, pandemics” into a broad catalogue of geopolitical and logistical threats that could disrupt international operations.  The language is forward-looking and highly generic; it acknowledges that pandemics can create transportation delays and wider instability, but supplies no data and no mitigation plan.  Consequently, the overall pandemic disclosure signals only a moderate, prospective risk.  Given the medium-term timing and the generic nature of the wording, individual snippet scores must be kept in the middle of the scale (≈ 4-5) and cannot approach the maximum reserved for specific, near-term, quantified impacts.

LYV’s 2021-03-01 Form 10-K paints an unambiguous picture: the COVID-19 pandemic is the single largest and most immediate enterprise-level threat the company has ever faced.  Because LYV’s economic model is based almost entirely on mass gatherings (concerts, festivals, ticketing and in-venue sponsorships), the global shutdown of live events that began in mid-March 2020 created an already-realised, catastrophic revenue collapse (-84 % top-line and a swing from +$325 m operating profit to ‑$1.7 bn loss).  Management discloses that revenue will remain “minimal” until large-scale events return, but it cannot forecast timing, capacity limits, incremental safety costs, consumer demand shifts or future regulatory waves.  The filing details knock-on effects—liquidity strain, credit downgrades, leverage covenant pressure, litigation risk, labour disruption, supply constraints and potential structural change in consumer preferences.  Although the company cites cost-cutting, liquidity raises and eventual vaccine roll-outs as mitigants, those measures are explicitly framed as uncertain bridges, not solutions.  Given that the filing date (Mar-2021) falls within one year of the event’s onset (Mar-2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits scores at the very top of the scale.  Most evidence sentences describe direct, already-material impacts with quantified magnitudes, so they gravitate toward 7-10 severity; more speculative or mitigated statements score lower.  No evidence predates the event, so no score is time-decayed to zero.

Live Nation Entertainment (LYV) describes COVID-19 as both an already-realised shock and an ongoing, open-ended threat to its live-events-centred business model.  The company discloses that the pandemic forced a full shutdown of tours and venues in March 2020, cutting cash inflows and triggering liquidity-management measures—evidence of direct, historical impact.  Equally important, LYV warns that revenue will remain depressed until global events can return to full capacity, and that successive viral waves, changing government restrictions, labour shortages, supply-chain bottlenecks, and shifts in consumer behaviour could prolong or worsen the damage.  The language is specific (“ceased all Live Nation tours…”, “tightening labor markets… continuing supply chain issues…”) and repeatedly labels the impact “material,” but the filing stops short of quantifying dollar amounts.  Because the 2022 filing date falls within three years of the event’s onset, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, direct, multi-faceted and only partially mitigated (e.g., liquidity actions), leading to a generally high-risk assessment across the extracted snippets.

LYV’s 2023-02-23 filing presents COVID-19 as both an historical shock and an ongoing strategic hazard.  The company discloses that the pandemic caused an immediate, material shutdown of tours and venue operations beginning in March 2020, severely depressing cash flow and triggering emergency liquidity measures—including new debt.  Although most venues have since reopened, management stresses that any resurgence, even if localized, could again halt shows, restrict capacity, disrupt labour and supply chains, and erode profitability.  Detailed bullets enumerate knock-on effects: tightening labour markets, supply-chain delays, lower artist willingness to tour, shifting consumer demand, lost ticketing clients, sponsor withdrawal, litigation exposure, rising compliance costs and leverage-related credit risks.  The language is largely specific (e.g., “ceased all Live Nation tours”, “material negative impact”, “negative credit actions”) and forward-looking where appropriate, signalling both realised damage and potential recurrence.  Because the event is recent (≤3 years) under the Time Decay Principle, elevated scores (7-10) are possible for direct, material impacts, while forward-looking or partially mitigated statements merit moderate scores.  This contextual narrative underpins the micro-scores that follow.

Live Nation Entertainment’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 as both a historically material shock and an ongoing, though attenuated, strategic risk.  Management explicitly recalls the 2020-2021 shutdowns—cancelling all tours and closing venues—and labels the impact on operating results as “material.”  Four years on, the company acknowledges that operations have “largely returned to normal,” yet highlights that any resurgence of COVID-19 or similar outbreaks could quickly force renewed closures, reinstate government restrictions, and erode consumer demand.  The narrative therefore blends retrospective certainty of large losses with forward-looking contingency language (“would adversely affect,” “cannot assure”), signalling that pandemic-related disruptions remain embedded in the live-events risk profile.  Because the original event is now in the medium-term window (≈4 years), the Time Decay Principle caps individual sentence scores at the moderate level (4-6).  The disclosures are specific—naming complete tour cessations, venue shutdowns, and direct hits to business, financial condition, and results—but they are qualitative and unquantified, keeping severity below maximum.  Overall, the risk evidence warrants mid-range severity assessments, reflecting lingering vulnerability without the acute crisis intensity of 2020-2021.

All three principal operating subsidiaries—CNA (insurance), Boardwalk Pipelines (mid-stream energy) and Loews Hotels & Co (hospitality)—explicitly link the COVID-19 pandemic to material, enterprise-wide threats that are already eroding revenues, inflating costs and creating legal / regulatory exposures.  The disclosures mix backward-looking facts (e.g., hotel closures, premium and occupancy declines, litigation already filed, staff furloughs) with forward-looking warnings (additional catastrophe losses, supply-chain interruptions, workforce outages, financing constraints).  Language is strong (“material adverse impacts,” “significant risk,” “could be material”) and repeatedly stresses uncertainty about duration and magnitude.  Because the Form 10-K was filed in February 2021—less than one year after the WHO declared the pandemic—a high severity range (7-10) is warranted under the Time Decay Principle.  None of the snippets offer meaningful quantitative mitigation; where actions are noted (e.g., cost controls, resumed hotel operations) they are partial and do not offset the scale of the stated risks.  Accordingly, the individual micro-scores cluster toward the upper mid-range, with the largest scores reserved for sentences that (1) explicitly tie COVID-19 to “material” financial harm, (2) describe concrete operational disruptions such as hotel shutdowns or workforce outages, or (3) enumerate multiple balance-sheet risks (e.g., mortgage default, liquidity crunch).

Loews Corporation’s 2022 filing repeatedly flags the COVID-19 pandemic as both an already-realised and still-evolving source of material risk across its diversified holdings.  CNA (the insurance arm) discloses concrete, incurred losses, a spike in claim submissions and an ongoing wave of coverage litigation – evidence that the pandemic has already crystallised into hard costs while still carrying forward-looking uncertainty.  Boardwalk Pipelines discusses potential labour interruptions, cost overruns and customer-payment delays tied to COVID-19, framing these as contingencies that could materially weaken operations if outbreaks or quarantines persist.  Loews Hotels & Co provides the most granular operational narrative: whole-property shutdowns, structurally lower occupancy, higher safety-protocol expenses and balance-sheet strains linked to heavy property ownership.  At the parent level the company also notes systemic remote-work and vendor-productivity challenges.  All statements are recent (within two years of the March 2020 WHO declaration) and therefore score high under the Time Decay Principle, yet they vary in specificity and quantification.  CNA’s acknowledgements of booked losses and litigation costs warrant the severest marks, while broader cautionary language at Boardwalk and corporate level earns moderate scores.  On balance, the evidence portrays COVID-19 as an enterprise-wide, multi-year threat that has already dented earnings and could further erode cash flow, margins and operating resilience.

COVID-19 remains a live, high-severity risk for Loews Corporation nearly three years after the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration (11 March 2020).  The 7 February 2023 Form 10-K shows that every major subsidiary – CNA (insurance), Boardwalk Pipelines (mid-stream energy) and Loews Hotels & Co (hospitality) – continues to face meaningful, and in some cases already realised, financial and operational pressure from the pandemic.  CNA discloses that the pandemic has already triggered ‘significant losses’ (mostly IBNR), an up-surge in claim submissions, heightened litigation, and “substantial expenses”, all of which may persist and remain “material”.  Boardwalk Pipelines warns that future waves could impede contract performance, raise costs, and disrupt customers’ cash-flows.  The hospitality arm provides the most concrete operating evidence: temporary hotel closures, markedly lower occupancy, revenue compression and cost inflation, plus lingering labour shortages.  These statements are recent (within the 0–3-year window) and combine backward-looking impact with forward-looking uncertainty, thereby justifying high but differentiated severity scores under the Time Decay Principle.  No significant mitigating language (e.g., firm quantification of recovery, insurance offsets, or completed restructuring) is offered, so net risk remains acute across the group.

Loews Corporation’s 2024-02-06 10-K demonstrates that COVID-19 remains a live, financially meaningful threat across the group even four years after the WHO declaration.  Disclosures span CNA’s insurance arm, Boardwalk Pipelines’ mid-stream operations and the lodging segment.  CNA reports that it already absorbed “significant losses” and still carries sizeable IBNR reserves tied to pandemic-era claims, while continuing to confront elevated claim frequency, litigation expenses and the prospect of further long-tail emergence.  Boardwalk Pipelines warns that pandemic-driven labour shortages, customer payment delays and supply-chain stress could still disrupt an “essential infrastructure” business with limited ability to pass through incremental costs.  Loews Hotels & Co supplies the most vivid, backward-looking impact narrative: 2020 shutdowns slashed revenue while fixed costs remained high, and management concedes that similar or worse outcomes could recur.  Language is mostly qualitative but repeatedly uses “material,” “substantial” and “significant” to flag magnitude, and cites concrete operational vectors (claims spikes, lower occupancy, workforce illness).  Because the filing date is within roughly four years of the initial event, the Time Decay Principle calls for moderate—but still meaningful—severity scores.  Statements describing realised losses/litigation receive the upper end of the medium band (≈6); forward-looking but unquantified risk references sit mid-band (≈4-5); generic contingency language scores lower (≈3-4).  No excerpt is pre-event, so no evidence is forced to zero.

MAA’s 2021 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a clear, near-term, enterprise-level threat.  The filing date (18-Feb-2021) sits less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration, so any disclosed impacts carry maximum temporal relevance under the Time Decay Principle.  Management discloses both realised damage (lower 2020 rent collections, disrupted capital-market access) and forward-looking exposures (future rent pressure, uncertain reopening, possible renewed lockdowns).  Language is consistently strong—“materially impacted,” “significant adverse impacts,” “material risks and uncertainties.”  The risks are direct and fundamental: reduced tenant ability to pay, suppressed demand, and heightened macro-economic volatility that could cascade into financing constraints and amplify other risk factors.  Mitigating statements (e.g., resumed bond-market access, resident assistance programmes) are mentioned but do not neutralise the overarching severity.  Given the recency of the pandemic and the specificity of the described impacts, individual snippet scores concentrate in the 3-8 range, with downward adjustments where mitigation or generic wording tempers severity.

MAA’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as a recent (within two years) and ongoing source of material risk that spans virtually every facet of the company’s multifamily-housing business.  The narrative is neither hypothetical nor generic: management states the pandemic “has materially impacted” results to date and details forward-looking exposures—including eviction moratoria, rent-collection pressure, supply-chain disruptions, labor shortages, construction delays, inflation in materials pricing, remote-work driven demand shifts, and possible workforce attrition from vaccine mandates.  Most impacts are framed as continuing or escalating, amplified by new variants (Delta and Omicron).  Because the event window (2020-present) is well inside the 0-3-year “recent” band of the Time Decay Principle, high severity scores (up to 10) are supportable where language is direct and material.  The disclosure is largely aggravating; only a few passages introduce uncertainty or acknowledge mitigation, so downward adjustments are limited.  Overall, the risk evidence points to a high residual exposure profile for COVID-19 across operations, development, capital costs and cash flow.

MAA’s 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as both an historic and continuing source of material risk.  Management states that the pandemic has already "materially impacted" the company and then presents a granular catalogue of ways a renewed outbreak or lingering after-effects could hit revenues, cash flow, capital projects, labour availability, supply chains and access to capital.  The language is mostly forward-looking, but repeatedly anchored in past, realised disruption (e.g., lockdowns, eviction moratoria, winter-storm repair delays).  No quantified dollar amounts are supplied, yet the discussion is unusually specific—linking the pandemic to rent collection risk, social-distancing limits on leasing, construction delays, supply-chain inflation and workforce attrition from vaccine mandates.  Because the filing date (14-Feb-2023) is less than three years after the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits elevated severity scores.  Overall, the disclosures reveal a high, multi-faceted risk that is recognised as ongoing, with only limited mitigation (easing restrictions); therefore evidence snippets cluster in the upper–mid severity band (scores 2-8), with the lead statement receiving the highest mark.

MAA’s 2024 Form 10-K situates the COVID-19 pandemic as a medium-term, still-salient risk.  Management acknowledges that the most disruptive government mandates peaked in 2020-2021, but the filing highlights enduring knock-on effects—rent-collection friction from eviction moratoria, lingering social-distancing constraints, workforce vaccination mandates, supply-chain bottlenecks, inflationary cost spikes, and debt-market volatility.  All references are qualitative and largely scenario-based, yet the document also cites concrete, historical impacts (e.g., temporary closure of amenities and suspension of redevelopment) that directly reduced leasing activity and cash collection.  Because nearly four years have elapsed since the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle caps per-snippet severity in the moderate range (4-6).  Overall, the risk is framed as ongoing and multifaceted rather than acute, with no quantified dollar figures, so aggregate evidence supports mid-level severity but not a maximum score.

MAS’s 2021 Form 10-K squarely integrates COVID-19 into its core risk narrative.  The filing describes both realized impacts in 2020 (facility shutdowns of up to eight weeks, reduced capacity from social-distancing rules, and supply-chain interruptions) and ongoing, forward-looking uncertainties (potential future closures, dampened consumer demand, forecasting difficulty, and heightened liquidity pressure on customers and suppliers).  The language is mostly specific and operational, citing concrete disruptions in production, logistics, labour availability and remote-work transitions, while still acknowledging that the full financial magnitude cannot yet be estimated.  Because the filing date (9 Feb 2021) is less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Overall, the risk is assessed as high: the company has already been hit, sees material threats to revenue, cost structure and liquidity, and concedes that mitigation efforts may prove insufficient.  The evidence therefore earns upper-mid to very high micro-scores (4–8 range), moderated where statements are more generic or mention mitigating actions.

MAS’s 2022 filing presents COVID-19 as a clear, ongoing, and multi-dimensional enterprise risk.  The discussion moves well beyond boiler-plate language: management affirms that the pandemic “has” already disrupted its facilities, workforce, supply chain, logistics and cost structure, and warns that it “may continue” to do so.  The company cites concrete operational stressors—plant closures, shortages of raw materials, shipping congestion, labour constraints and inflationary pressures—and ties them explicitly to potential or actual impacts on results of operations and financial condition.  Although no dollar amounts are quantified, the wording (“materially and adversely affect,” “significantly disrupted”) is strong and the timeframe is immediate (event < 2 years old), so Time Decay does not meaningfully diminish severity.  Management also acknowledges heightened uncertainty and limited visibility, which amplifies risk.  A single sentence outlines mitigation (productivity initiatives), but this is high-level and does not offset the breadth of stated exposures.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, specific, and descriptive of actual impacts, meriting high—but not maximum—scores for the strongest snippets, with moderate scores where discussion is more forward-looking or generic.

MAS’s 2023 filing treats COVID-19 as an active, continuing threat that has already disrupted operations and may further erode financial performance.  The company discloses concrete operational impacts—facility shutdowns, supply-chain delays, cost inflation, logistics constraints and labor shortages—while also warning that future waves could materially harm results and intensify other risk factors.  These statements are recent (within three years of the pandemic’s declaration) and mostly describe realised or still-unfolding effects, which pushes the risk level toward the higher end of the 0-10 scale.  However, the narrative remains largely qualitative; no dollar figures or probability estimates are supplied, and some language is hedged (“may,” “could”).  Applying the Time Decay Principle (recent event) and discounting for the absence of quantification, the strongest sentences merit scores near 9, while generic list-style references receive only minimal points.

MAS’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to reference pandemics – implicitly the COVID-19 outbreak – as one of several macro-hazards that can disrupt demand and supply.  All three instances are housed in the generic “Risk Factors” section and treat the threat largely as an ongoing possibility rather than a currently quantifiable drag.  Only one sentence concedes that the company’s suppliers “have been” affected, providing slight evidence that COVID-19 already stressed the supply chain; otherwise the language is broad, un-quantified and bundled with other catastrophes (weather, wars, terrorism).  Given that COVID-19’s declaration as a global pandemic occurred in March 2020, the disclosure date of February 2024 sits just under four years later—borderline between the “recent” and “medium-term” Time–Decay buckets.  Because the wording is generic and forward-looking, but the elapsed time is still fairly short, the overall risk evidence merits low-to-moderate severity scores (3–5).

Mastercard’s 2020 Form 10-K was filed eleven months after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, placing the disclosure well inside the 0-3-year “recent-event” window of the Time-Decay Principle.  The filing repeatedly states that the Company has already suffered measurable, material harm—flat gross dollar volume, sharply lower cross-border volume, and weaker switched-transaction growth—while also warning that the breadth, duration and intensity of future impacts remain highly uncertain.  Risk language is concrete and specific: it enumerates operating disruptions (remote-work shift, employee travel curtailment), demand shocks (collapse of global travel, lower consumer spending), and ecosystem strain (supplier, customer and partner impacts).  At the same time, the Company acknowledges that mitigation actions (monitoring, policy compliance, modified business practices) may prove insufficient.  Because the disclosures detail both realized financial detriment and the potential for prolonged or deepening effects, the overall risk profile is high and forward-looking, justifying elevated snippet scores (7-9 range) under the Time-Decay framework.

Mastercard’s 2021 Form 10-K, filed in February 2022, provides a layered discussion of COVID-19.  The company acknowledges that the pandemic has ALREADY produced material, adverse effects on its business, operations and financial condition, while also stressing that the magnitude and duration of future impacts remain highly uncertain.  The disclosures identify concrete operational changes—remote/hybrid work, curtailed travel—and link them to knock-on threats such as heightened cyber-security risk.  They also reference broad economic headwinds, potential recessions, and continued volatility tied to new virus variants and vaccination progress.  The language is largely qualitative but explicitly uses terms such as “adversely impacted,” “materially adverse,” and “significant rise,” signalling a high-severity, ongoing risk.  Because the filing date falls less than two years after the WHO’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scores (up to 10).  Nonetheless, the absence of quantified dollar amounts and the mention of mitigating actions (business practice modifications, monitoring) temper the risk scoring.  Overall, the pandemic is framed as a recent, direct and continuing threat with multiple vectors—financial, operational, workforce and cyber—warranting moderately high but not maximal severity scores across the extracted evidence.

Mastercard’s 2022 Form 10-K, filed 14 Feb 2023, contains an explicit risk subsection devoted to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company states that the pandemic has already ‘adversely impacted’ revenues, operations and financial condition and stresses that those impacts could persist or worsen.  The language is largely qualitative but it is concrete: it links COVID-19 to reduced travel, supply-chain stress, impacts on consumers, customers, suppliers, partners and the workforce, as well as security vulnerabilities created by a remote-work environment.  The risk is framed as both realised (historic adverse impacts) and prospective (future variants, border restrictions, lingering recessionary effects).  Although no dollar figures are supplied, the statements are recent (within three years of the March 2020 WHO declaration) and tie directly to multiple operational drivers (cross-border volumes, staffing, cyber-security).  Under the Time-Decay Principle, evidence this fresh can attract high scores—up to 10—because the event is still unfolding and materially relevant.  Mitigating language is minimal (no claims that impacts are fully resolved), so most snippets warrant moderately high severity scores in the 4-8 range, with deductions where the wording is generic or lacks specificity.

The Form 10-K makes only scattered and largely generic references to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The most explicit mention appears in a bulleted list under cross-border risks, where Mastercard states that the global COVID-19 pandemic has already affected, and could continue to affect, cross-border volumes.  This is framed as one of several macro-level factors (alongside wars, terrorism and weather) and is not quantified.  Elsewhere, the company links the rise of cyber-security threats to its workforce’s hybrid (part-remote) operating model – a structural shift that traces back to the pandemic, although COVID-19 is not named.  There is no discussion of supply-chain disruption, labour shortages or consumer-demand shocks attributable to the pandemic.  Because the filing date (February 2024) is almost four years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time Decay Principle places the pandemic at the start of the medium-term window; therefore, even strong evidence should be moderated toward the 4–6 range.  Given the limited, high-level language and absence of financial quantification, the overall risk signal is modest.  The disclosures recognise that COVID-19 did hurt cross-border spending and that pandemic-driven hybrid work arrangements elevate cyber-risk, but they neither assign dollar values nor identify specific operational constraints.  Consequently, the evidence supports only moderate severity, consistent with a residual, forward-looking risk rather than an immediate, material threat.

The 2021-05-18 Form 10-K shows that Microchip (MCHP) frames COVID-19 as both an already-experienced shock and an ongoing, forward-looking threat.  Numerous passages move beyond boiler-plate language: they describe concrete disruptions in Q1-FY21 (factory slow-downs in the Philippines, Malaysia and China; customer order cancellations; subcontractor stop-work orders) and continuing supply-chain constraints expected into calendar 2022.  These statements demonstrate direct operational, demand-side and supply-side impacts that have already materialised, while also warning of future capacity, labour and logistics risks should infection rates rise again.  No quantified dollar amounts are provided, but the company repeatedly labels the effects as “adverse,” “material” and affecting “operating results,” signalling financial significance.  Because the filing date is within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (up to 10) for strong, specific evidence; generic or purely contingent statements are scored lower.  The evidence set therefore ranges from severe, realised impacts (scores 6-7) to generic, anticipatory clauses (scores 2-3).

Microchip’s 2022 Form-10-K repeatedly frames COVID-19 as a multi-faceted, continuing risk that is already affecting—and could further disrupt—its operations.  The filing describes (1) concrete, realized impacts in fiscal-2022 such as plant slow-downs, subcontractor stoppages, Chinese lockdown effects and logistics bottlenecks; (2) on-going supply-chain inflation, labour shortages and foundry capacity limits that management explicitly links to the pandemic; and (3) forward-looking exposures, including the possibility of renewed government shutdowns, mandatory-vaccine mandates and demand volatility.  Although many statements are still cast in the conditional tense, several passages acknowledge measurable adverse consequences that have already occurred.  Because the filing date (20-May-2022) is barely two years after the WHO pandemic declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Nonetheless, individual snippets vary: direct, quantified or operationally specific impacts merit higher marks, while generic boiler-plate or partially-mitigated disclosures score lower.  Overall, the tenor is one of heightened and persistent risk, but with limited quantification and some mitigating notes (e.g., “no significant impact”).

MCHP’s 2023-05-25 Form 10-K reveals that COVID-19 remains a material, multi-dimension risk affecting the company’s operations, supply chain, labour markets, logistics, customer demand and governmental contract performance.  The filing contains both backward-looking evidence (actual factory slow-downs, logistics bottlenecks, order cancellations, stop–work orders and labour shortages that occurred during fiscal 2022-2023) and forward-looking statements warning that renewed outbreaks or governmental mandates could again constrain production, shipping and demand.  The disclosures are largely qualitative but describe concrete operational disruptions across multiple geographies (U.S., Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia, Taiwan, China) and functional areas (manufacturing, logistics, government sub-contracts).  No specific dollar amounts are cited; however, the statements confirm real adverse impacts within the past three fiscal years, satisfying the high-relevance “recent-event” window (0-3 years).  Mitigating language is minimal—largely limited to generic statements that the company “has taken steps to mitigate” impacts—so most snippets tilt toward aggravating factors.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, scores can range up to the high end (7-10) for direct, recent impacts, and mid-range (4-6) for forward-looking or indirect references.  Older impacts from early 2020 are still within the three-year window but receive slightly lower weight as they are less immediate.  Overall, COVID-19 represents an ongoing, non-trivial operational and financial risk for MCHP as portrayed in the filing.

Microchip’s 10-K shows that the company still sees COVID-19 as a meaningful, though now largely operational and supply-chain focused, risk.  Statements span three categories: (1) historical, quantified impacts (factory slow-downs, order cancellations, stop-work notices); (2) forward-looking warnings that renewed outbreaks could again disrupt production, logistics and customer demand; and (3) second-order effects such as tight labour markets created by remote-work practices.  Although the pandemic outbreak itself is now more than four years old, many of the cited impacts occurred as recently as fiscal-year 2023, so Time-Decay permits mid-level scores.  The language is mostly qualitative—no dollar figures—but it links COVID-19 directly to manufacturing downtime, supply-chain bottlenecks, government-contract suspensions and potential future shocks.  Because most disclosures are specific, recent, and describe enterprise-wide disruption, individual snippet scores cluster in the 4-7 range, reflecting moderate-to-heightened ongoing risk consistent with a medium-term event.

McKesson’s 2021 Form 10-K repeatedly describes COVID-19 as an immediate and material enterprise-wide threat.  The language is not hypothetical; it states that the pandemic “has disrupted” operations, distorted supply-and-demand patterns, triggered labour and logistics pressures, intensified foreign-exchange volatility, and forced a large-scale remote-work transition.  These statements therefore evidence direct, already-occurring impacts, not merely possible future contingencies.  In addition, the disclosure links COVID-19 to numerous specific risk vectors—supply-chain shortages, allocation decisions that could damage customer relationships, workforce absenteeism, lower product demand, and macro-economic recessionary pressure—making the narrative highly event-focused and granular rather than boiler-plate.  Although the Company outlines some mitigating actions (e.g., remote work, sanitation, participation in vaccine programmes), the text explicitly concedes that such steps “might not fully mitigate” pandemic risks.  Given the filing date (May 2021) falls well within three years of the pandemic’s declared start (March 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high-severity scoring (up to 10).  Overall, the evidence supports elevated but not maximum scores—mostly in the 5-8 range—because the disclosures are detailed and confirm realised impacts, yet stop short of providing hard quantitative loss figures.

MCK’s 2022 filing describes COVID-19 as an ongoing, material enterprise-wide risk that is still within the recent-event window (<3 years).  The company links the pandemic to direct disruptions in product availability, manufacturing, transportation, and forecasting precision, and even notes already-observed shortages of COVID-19 tests.  Several disclosures acknowledge concrete operational consequences such as inventory allocation, delivery delays, and volatility in future economic trends.  Although some statements are couched in broader multi-factor lists, the overall narrative is specific, forward-looking, and identifies real impacts that have already manifested.  No quantification is provided, and only limited mitigating actions (e.g., monitoring supply chains) are mentioned, so the risk evidence remains significant but not maximal.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, individual snippet scores can reach high single digits because the pandemic is current; however, scores are tempered when language is generic or bundled with other risks, or when partial mitigation is evident.  The final micro-scores therefore range from 4 to 7, reflecting varying degrees of severity and specificity across the extracted sentences.

McKesson’s 2023 Form 10-K discloses a multi-layered, still-active risk landscape linked to the COVID-19 pandemic.  Because the filing date (9 May 2023) is only three years after the WHO’s pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  The company describes both backward-looking impacts (actual supply-chain impairments, volatility in vaccine demand, variability in operating results) and forward-looking exposures (future pandemics, regulatory oversight, dependence on government funding).  The language is largely specific: it cites concrete operational areas—vaccine distribution scope, ancillary-kit logistics, labour and transport availability, consumer-demand shifts—and repeatedly uses “materially adverse” to characterise potential financial damage.  Although the firm mentions some mitigating actions (e.g., alternate sourcing, extraordinary procedures), these are not framed as fully offsetting; rather they illustrate the breadth of contingency planning still required.  Overall, the disclosures evidence a continuing, direct, and material pandemic risk with potential to swing earnings, constrain supply chains, and damage reputation.  Accordingly, individual snippets drawn from Item 1A and the General Risks section merit high but differentiated scores (7-10 for quantified or ‘materially adverse’ statements; moderate scores where wording is more generic or mitigated).

McKesson’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to acknowledge the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a medium-term, external risk factor rather than an immediate, quantified threat. Moody’s 2020 Form 10-K, filed 22 Feb 2021, conveys a broad, recent-period assessment of COVID-19-related risks that cut across every material dimension of the firm’s business model. This narrative underpins the individual snippet scores below.

MDLZ’s 2021-02-05 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a pervasive, recently-manifested threat that is already diminishing revenues in specific channels (travel retail, traditional trade, food-service) while simultaneously stressing supply chains, labour availability, commodity costs, currency exposure and liquidity. Taken together, the language shows an event that is both current and forward-looking, with direct operational and financial consequences, justifying elevated risk scores for the extracted evidence.
