MTD’s 2021 filing repeatedly links the recent COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective damage across its operations.  Management discloses direct, already-incurred impacts on 2020 sales and customer demand, while simultaneously warning that the virus is still evolving and may further disrupt supply chains, workforce availability, production sites, and receivable collections.  Language such as “has negatively affected,” “will likely continue,” and “could be material” reflects a mixture of current losses and forward-looking uncertainty.  The statements are specific— citing reduced global customer demand, potential employee quarantines, stay-at-home orders, and possible supply-chain interruptions—rather than boiler-plate.  Because the 10-K was filed less than one year after WHO’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle places these disclosures in the 0-3-year window, allowing high severity scores.  Overall, the risk profile is elevated (typical snippet scores 7–9) with only limited mitigating language (e.g., adequate inventories, remote-work adaptations) that slightly tempers but does not neutralise the threat.

The filing, dated February 11 2022, discusses the COVID-19 pandemic in a recent-event window (<3 years), so the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  MTD expressly states that COVID-19 has already harmed its workforce, supply chain, sales volumes and overall financial condition, and that these pressures are likely to persist and could become “material.”  The language is largely specific—detailing supply-chain shortages, transportation cost inflation, labor shortages, customer payment risk, lockdown-driven manufacturing interruptions, and Omicron-related volatility—rather than boiler-plate.  Although a few mitigating references (e.g., meeting most delivery commitments) appear, they are minor compared with the breadth and immediacy of the risks described.  No hard dollar figures are provided, so the evidence is un-quantified but still points to a clear, continuing and multifaceted threat.  Accordingly, the individual snippet scores cluster in the 4-8 range, reflecting significant but not maximum severity for a very recent, still-evolving event.

COVID-19 is repeatedly referenced throughout the 2023-02-10 MTD filing as an event that has already produced tangible harm and is expected to remain a material threat.  The disclosure palette spans past, present, and forward-looking language: management cites supply-chain breakdowns, labour shortages, higher logistics costs, Chinese lockdown volatility, customer demand swings and inflationary after-shocks.  The company explicitly states that effects on sales, margins, and financial condition ‘could be material,’ underscoring severity.  Virtually every mention stresses that disruptions ‘continue’ or ‘may continue,’ signalling persistence rather than a one-off shock.  Because the pandemic window (2020-present) is less than three years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores when impacts are direct, quantified, or designated as material.  Mitigating detail is scarce; there are no quantified offsets or definitive remediation strategies.  Consequently, most sentences warrant upper-mid to high risk scores (6-8), with a few reduced for generic phrasing or dilution by other concurrent risks.  Overall, COVID-19 remains one of MTD’s most acute operational and financial risk factors.

MTD’s 2024 filing continues to portray COVID-19 as both an historical shock and a still-relevant, forward-looking threat.  The company acknowledges that the pandemic has already hurt workforce availability, supply chains, customer demand and overall economic conditions, while warning that any resurgence could again depress sales, inflate costs and disrupt logistics.  Although the immediate health crisis has “diminished,” MTD explicitly lists multiple pathways through which lingering or renewed outbreaks could impair operations—labour shortages, material shortages, transportation delays, rising freight costs and shifts in pharmaceutical demand.  These disclosures are mostly qualitative and not quantified, but they are company-specific and tie to core revenue drivers (pharma/biopharma, China production, and global supply chain).  Because the event’s onset is now about four years old, the Time Decay Principle moderates maximum snippet scores into the mid-range; nevertheless, the persistence of supply-chain and demand risks keeps overall severity in the moderate-to-high band.  No strong mitigating language (e.g., permanent fixes, insurance coverage) is offered beyond noting that impacts have reduced, so net risk remains meaningful.

Micron’s 2021-10-08 Form 10-K devotes extensive, detailed language to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company frames the virus as a RECENT (≈18 months old) but still-evolving threat that has ALREADY caused concrete, measured disruptions—factory slow-downs in Malaysia, higher logistics costs, lower workforce density, and customer demand adjustments—while also remaining a forward-looking uncertainty (vaccine uptake, future outbreaks).  The risk disclosures are unusually granular: they enumerate impacts on supply chains, labour availability, construction projects, credit markets and even employee morale via a mandated vaccination policy.  Many of the statements reference historical impacts (“we reduced output levels”) as well as continuing or potential future impacts; therefore, both realised and prospective risk exist.  Given the Time Decay Principle, evidence from 2020-21 qualifies as ‘recent’, so high snippet scores (7-9) are permissible when language shows direct, material, or already-realised effects; moderate scores (4-6) are used for generic or conditional language; minimal deductions are applied for any noted mitigation (e.g., operations now normal).  Collectively, the filing signals a significant, multi-faceted exposure to the pandemic across demand, supply, labour, and finance, warranting an overall elevated risk assessment.

MU’s 10-K squarely identifies the COVID-19 pandemic as an active, enterprise-wide threat that is still playing out in real time.  Because the filing date (October 2022) falls well within three years of the World Health Organization’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  The company blends backward-looking language ("have included") with forward-looking cautions ("may continue to include"), signalling both realized and potential damage.  The disclosure catalogues multiple concrete pressure points—supply-chain breakdowns, demand destruction, price erosion, labour/operational shutdowns, cost inflation, and construction delays—yet provides no numerical sizing or mitigation plan beyond generic references to “measures” it is taking.  Taken together, the evidence portrays a recent, broad, and only partially quantified risk that remains largely unmitigated; therefore most snippets merit mid-to-high severity scores (4-7), tempered slightly for lack of dollar-level quantification or strong counter-measures.

Micron’s 2023 Form 10-K still flags public-health disruptions as a live strategic threat, but the discussion has clearly moved from the emergency footing of 2020-2021 to a more generic, forward-looking posture.  Most references appear in the Risk Factors section and speak in conditional language (“may,” “could”) that bundles ‘public health crises’ with other macro shocks such as inflation or geopolitics.  Nevertheless, the company acknowledges that such crises have already harmed its business and could again trigger supply-chain interruptions, quarantines, factory closures, labour and travel constraints, and demand shocks— classic pandemic-era pain points.  Because the filing date (6 Oct 2023) is roughly 3 years and 7 months after the WHO declaration, the Time-Decay Principle pushes evidentiary scores into the medium tier: the pandemic is neither brand-new nor forgotten, and Micron supplies no fresh, quantified impact figures.  Overall, the residual pandemic risk is assessed as moderate: material enough to merit board-level disclosure but expressed largely in broad, un-quantified terms, warranting snippet scores in the 4-6 range.

Micron’s 2024-10-04 Form 10-K no longer singles out COVID-19 by name, yet multiple sentences still frame “public health crises” and “outbreaks of contagious diseases” as material threats to operations, supply chains, labour availability and macro-demand. The disclosures are forward-looking, largely qualitative and lack fresh, quantified impacts, indicating that management views pandemic fallout as an ongoing but now background-level risk rather than an acute crisis. Because the filing date is roughly 4½ years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time Decay Principle caps individual evidence scores in the moderate range (4-6). Overall, the company acknowledges enduring vulnerabilities—factory shutdowns, shipping delays, hiring constraints and demand shocks—but couches them in broad language without new financial metrics or remedial detail, resulting in mid-level severity assessments.

NCLH’s 2021-02-26 filing portrays COVID-19 as an immediate, enterprise-threatening event whose effects permeate every core function—revenue generation, fleet operations, supply chain, labor logistics, liquidity and consumer demand.  The risk is overwhelmingly current rather than merely hypothetical: voyages have been fully suspended since March 2020, cash burn is ongoing, credit ratings have been downgraded and shipyard delays are already occurring.  Language is consistently strong (“significant negative impacts”, “severe and prolonged effect”), signalling materiality and persistence.  Although the company references future relaunch plans and cost-containment initiatives, these mitigants are tentative and highly conditional on external factors such as regulators, vaccine roll-outs and port availability.  Given the filing date is less than one year after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7-10).  Statements that describe realised losses or hard operational shutdowns score at the top of the range; those that are forward-looking but still concrete (e.g., uncertain demand, crew staffing constraints) score slightly lower, while passages that contain partial mitigations receive modest downward adjustments.  Overall, the disclosure evidences a near-term, high-severity risk landscape for NCLH.

NCLH’s 2022-03-01 filing paints COVID-19 as the single most acute enterprise-wide threat.  The text repeatedly moves beyond boiler-plate to describe concrete, realised losses (full fleet suspension, billions in lost revenue, $1.2 bn collateral posted, delayed ship deliveries) and operational dislocations (supply-chain shortages, crew transport bottlenecks, labour-vaccination issues).  It also stresses persistence and uncertainty—demand weakness, potential reinstatement of suspensions, and exposure to new variants—making the risk both current and forward-looking.  Because the pandemic began less than three years before the filing, the Time-Decay Principle permits high scores.  Most sentences provide direct causal language (“has had”, “resulted in”) and reference materiality (“significant impact”, “net loss”), warranting severe ratings, although a few include mitigating efforts (phased relaunch, health protocols) that temper—but do not erase—the risk.  Overall, the disclosure evidences a high, ongoing severity level (7-8/10) consistent with a recent, still-unfolding global crisis.

NCLH’s 2023 Form 10-K paints a picture of a company still wrestling with very direct, recently-experienced fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic while conceding that many of those shocks could flare up again.  Multiple disclosures confirm that the pandemic produced immediate, material hits—full fleet suspensions, sizeable lost revenues, added health-safety costs, liquidity strains, covenant pressure and credit-rating downgrades.  The language is largely specific (e.g., complete voyage suspension, collateral holds by credit-card processors) and is framed both as realized losses (“has resulted in significant costs and lost revenue”) and as continuing threats (“may continue to have,” “could be further downgraded”).  Because the filing date (28 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores; however, statements that are purely generic or already partially mitigated (e.g., easing protocols) temper some scores.  Overall, the risk level remains elevated: liquidity buffers rely on amended debt terms, demand recovery is not yet complete, supply-chain/air-travel disturbances persist, and legal or regulatory exposures remain open-ended.  Consequently, COVID-19 remains one of the most consequential, actively monitored risks in the company’s risk taxonomy.

NCLH’s 2024 Form 10-K shows the COVID-19 pandemic remains a material, albeit moderating, enterprise-wide risk.  The filing chronicles large, realized losses (fleet-wide shutdown, impairment charges, travel-agency failures) and identifies continuing second-order effects—crew-transport bottlenecks, airline capacity shortages, fuel-supply distortions, and possible litigation.  Although the most acute disruption occurred four years ago (March 2020), management still frames the pandemic as both an historical shock and an ongoing, forward-looking exposure: future variants or public-health crises could again trigger port closures, government bans, supply-chain interruptions and demand destruction.  The language is largely specific (detailing cost increases, operational prohibitions and geographic restrictions) rather than boiler-plate, but only rarely quantified.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic now falls into the 4-to-10-year window, which caps individual snippet scores in the mid-range.  Overall, the company’s disclosures warrant moderate severity: the event is no longer existential, yet its legacy and potential recurrence still materially threaten liquidity, margins and strategic flexibility.

Nasdaq’s 2021 Form 10-K ties the still-unfolding COVID-19 pandemic to numerous operational, financial and strategic vulnerabilities.  The disclosure mixes descriptions of impacts already felt (elevated trading volumes, mandatory remote-work, delayed technology projects) with forward-looking warnings (possible revenue declines, cyber-risk expansion, credit defaults and asset impairments).  Most statements are recent (within 12 months of the WHO declaration) and refer directly to pandemic-specific disruptions such as virtual trading floors, employee illness, customer spending cuts and sales-pipeline delays.  Although a few mitigating actions are noted (e.g., added network capacity, SEC proposal for virtual trading), the overall tone emphasises heightened uncertainty and material downside potential.  Under the Time Decay Principle the event is well inside the 0-3-year window, so individual snippet scores can legitimately fall in the upper range.  Nevertheless, language that is purely conditional, generic or accompanied by concrete mitigants receives modest deductions.  Collectively, the evidence indicates a high but not yet crystallised risk profile—Nasdaq acknowledges serious exposures yet stops short of quantifying a definitive financial hit—placing most sentences in the 4-7 severity band, with none warranting the absolute maximum because impacts are largely prospective and un-quantified.

Nasdaq’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat rather than a closed historical episode.  Statements span actual impacts (remote-work shift, trading-volume volatility) and forward-looking uncertainties (future office closures, stakeholder illness, defaults).  Language identifies multiple vectors—cyber-security, employee health, regulatory fines, liquidity, market volumes—showing pervasive operational and financial exposure.  Most disclosures are qualitative and use modal verbs (“may,” “could”), so they stop short of hard quantification, yet the narrative concedes that 2020-21 trading volumes “fluctuated significantly” because of the pandemic, signalling real, observed effects.  Given the filing date (Feb-2022) is less than three years after WHO’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  Mitigating references (e.g., remote-work arrangements, monitoring, safety protocols) temper but do not eliminate risk since management admits these measures might fail.  Overall, the evidence reflects a high but primarily unquantified current-period risk, warranting mid-to-high snippet scores (3-7) rather than extreme scores reserved for quantified dollar impacts.

Nasdaq’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a broad macro-economic and operational hazard rather than a currently quantified loss.  Across the risk-factor section the company repeatedly classifies pandemics—citing COVID-19 by name—as exogenous drivers that can weaken economic conditions, disrupt operations, heighten cybersecurity exposure through prolonged remote-work, and even trigger accounting impairments.  The statements are largely forward-looking and qualitative; they warn that COVID-19 could continue to depress trading activity, impair goodwill, or generate other losses but provide no numerical estimates.  Because the filing date (Feb-2023) is less than three years after the WHO declaration (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows moderately high scores, yet the lack of specificity, quantification, or demonstrated direct losses tempers severity.  Overall, the company presents pandemic risk as real and ongoing but in generic, catch-all language, warranting mid-range risk scores rather than maximum severity.

Nasdaq’s 2024 Form 10-K still cites the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a broad macro-economic hazard rather than a currently quantified hit to revenue.  The filing places ‘pandemics’ in a list of global factors that could weaken trading volumes, impair goodwill, or disrupt operations, and also describes a permanent shift to a hybrid-work model that introduces fresh cyber-security and operational risks—an indirect legacy of COVID-19.  All statements are forward-looking or continuing-impact in nature; none provide dollar figures or point to a concrete loss already incurred.  Because nearly four years have passed since the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time-Decay Principle caps individual severity at a moderate level.  Overall, the disclosures acknowledge that pandemic conditions could still erode market demand, trigger asset-impairment charges, and complicate workforce and technology posture, but the language is largely generic and unquantified, warranting mid-range risk scores (≈3-5) rather than the high scores appropriate for fresh, quantified impacts.

Nordson’s 2021 Form 10-K provides an extensive, contemporaneous discussion of COVID-19 as both an already-realised and still-evolving enterprise risk.  The company discloses concrete, realised impacts—manufacturing inefficiencies, cost inflation from supply-chain disruptions, labour shortages, currency volatility, and broad economic slow-downs—which have negatively affected operations, liquidity and capital investments since the March 2020 outbreak.  At the same time, management emphasises uncertainty about future variants, government restrictions and customer demand, projecting that these conditions could materially impair revenues, asset values and strategic spending for an ‘unknown period of time.’  While some mitigating actions are noted (continued operations as “critical infrastructure,” safety investments, diversification efforts), the language remains predominantly aggravating, acknowledging both current damage and the prospect of further material harm.  Because the filing date (17-Dec-2021) is within two years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, direct, multi-faceted and only partially mitigated—warranting upper-tier but sub-maximum scores across the extracted sentences.

Nordson’s 2022 filing shows that COVID-19 remains a live, material and multi-dimensional risk.  Nearly three years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic, management still describes direct, realized impacts (e.g., lower Asia-Pacific revenue, reduced manufacturing efficiencies, higher input costs, labour disruptions) while simultaneously warning of continued uncertainty around government lockdowns, infection waves and supply-chain constraints.  The language is largely specific and event-linked, not boiler-plate: it cites concrete examples (Q2-22 China lockdowns, raw-material shortages) and ties them to financial metrics (revenue growth, results of operations).  Although the company notes some mitigating actions (health-safety protocols, ongoing monitoring), these are outweighed by the breadth of exposures across supply chains, labour, demand and FX volatility.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic is well within the recent 0-3-year window, so the evidence justifies generally high snippet scores (upper-mid to high single digits), tempered only where impacts are less specific or share attribution with other macro events.

Nordson’s 2023 Form 10-K still acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic as a live source of risk even though the initial outbreak is nearly four years old.  Management concedes that the pandemic has already produced adverse macro-economic effects (volatility in financial markets) and continues to be grouped with other disruptive geopolitical events.  At the company level, the filing frames pandemic exposure primarily as an operational threat: possible shutdowns of facilities, supply-chain interruptions, distribution bottlenecks and demand shocks.  The language is largely qualitative and forward-looking (frequent use of “may”), and it lacks any quantified, company-specific loss data, suggesting the impact has been manageable to date.  Nevertheless, because the pandemic remains within the recent 0-to-4-year window and is tied to critical functions such as supply continuity and production, the overall risk is best characterised as moderate-high under the Time Decay principle.

The filing, dated December 18 2024, discusses the COVID-19 pandemic in a section on broad macro–economic risks.  Because the first wave of the pandemic began in March 2020, the reference event is now roughly four years old—squarely in the Time-Decay “medium-term” window (4-10 years), which caps individual evidence scores at a moderate level (≈4-6).  The disclosure provides a single, explicit sentence acknowledging that the pandemic has already produced negative macro-economic effects and may continue to generate volatility going forward.  However, the company neither quantifies the specific financial hit nor details operational counter-measures (e.g., remote-work policies, supply-chain redesign, labour management).  Additional language elsewhere in the filing refers to “pandemics or other public health crises” only generically, positioning them alongside other possible disruptions such as armed conflict or severe weather; these statements are purely contingent and do not confirm an existing impact.  Overall, the pandemic is framed as an external, ongoing threat rather than an acute, company-specific crisis.  Given the elapsed time since the initial outbreak, the absence of quantified loss data, and the largely generic tone of the risk language, the overall evidentiary weight is moderate and fully consistent with a medium-term Time-Decay ceiling.

The filing was made in February 2021, less than a year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle allows relatively high scores (0-3-year window).  The risk language appears in a dedicated subsection of Item 1A and stresses that COVID-19 and similar public-health crises could create “material adverse impacts” across liquidity, operations, workforce, supply chain and capital-market access.  The discussion is primarily forward-looking—management states that, so far, no material harm has been felt—but it still frames the threat as ongoing, wide-ranging and difficult to quantify.  Multiple aggravating elements are present: acknowledgement of exposure to government-mandated restrictions, dependence on vaccine roll-out, and the inability to predict severity or duration.  Mitigating language is limited to the facts that the company is “closely monitoring” the outbreak and has not yet suffered material harm, which slightly tempers (but does not eliminate) the risk assessment.  Overall, I assess the pandemic-related disclosures as presenting a moderately high level of persisting risk (average snippet scores in the 5–6 range), with no hard numbers but strong assertions of potential materiality, uncertainty and multi-faceted impact.

The filing—dated February 18 2022, less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic—places the pandemic squarely in the “recent-event” window, so any related disclosure carries high potential severity under the Time Decay Principle.  NEE couches the pandemic primarily as an ongoing, forward-looking risk rather than reporting quantified, realized damages.  The language repeatedly uses strong qualifiers such as “material adverse impacts” and extends the threat across multiple business dimensions: operations, liquidity, markets, supply chain, workforce and regulatory response.  However, the discussion remains generic; it does not cite dollar amounts, timeline scenarios, or specific mitigation programs.  Consequently, the overall risk remains significant but un-quantified: high enough to merit elevated scores (largely 6-8) because of recency, breadth, and intensity of wording, yet tempered by the absence of concrete impact figures or evidence of current impairments.  The disclosure therefore signals meaningful exposure that management cannot yet measure, emphasizing uncertainty about duration, vaccine efficacy, and governmental actions—factors that could quickly amplify or prolong financial strain.

NEE’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges the continuing threat of the COVID-19 pandemic—but does so in broad, largely boiler-plate language. The company groups COVID-19 with other “public health crises” and frames the effects as potential rather than currently quantifiable losses. The narrative identifies multiple exposure channels (workforce disruption, supply-chain stress via suppliers, capital-market volatility, government counter-measures), and repeatedly uses the phrase “material adverse impact,” signalling that management sees real downside. Yet there are no concrete figures, no description of actual 2020–2022 hit-to-earnings, and no new mitigation steps beyond generic uncertainty clauses. Because the pandemic remains within the 0-3-year “recent” window, the Time Decay Principle allows for elevated scores; however, the absence of specificity, quantification, or evidence of realised harm tempers severity. Overall, the disclosure indicates a live but only moderately articulated risk rather than an acute, measured impact.

The filing addresses pandemic exposure in one compact, forward-looking subsection that treats COVID-19 and similar health crises as a continuing, enterprise-wide hazard.  The company frames the risk in generic terms – it does not cite any 2020-23 revenue loss, supply-chain shortfall or staffing disruption – but it does warn that public-health events can materially damage virtually every financial metric (business, liquidity, results of operations, prospects).  The language is prospective ("may have"), signalling management views the pandemic as an ongoing possibility rather than a currently quantified loss.  Because the Form 10-K is dated February 2024 – roughly four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic – the Time-Decay Principle places the disclosure in the early “medium-term” window (4 years).  That requires middle-tier severity scores (≈4-6) when evidence shows a broad but un-quantified threat.  Overall, the risk appears significant but un-measured, and the tone is cautionary rather than crisis-driven, justifying moderate per-snippet scores.

All cited language comes from Netflix’s 2021 Form 10-K, filed roughly ten months after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic.  Because the filing date is well inside the 0-3-year “recent-event” window, the Time-Decay principle allows high scores when disclosures show material, direct or continuing impacts.  The company repeatedly links COVID-19 to concrete operational disruptions (production halts, vendor failures, remote-work shifts), supply-chain constraints, labour limitations, customer-service degradation, liquidity pressure and unpredictable swings in subscriber growth.  Much of the wording is specific (e.g., “many of our productions continue to experience disruption,” “vendors go out of business,” “content asset impairments”) and largely forward-looking, signalling that management sees the threat as ongoing rather than a one-off historical event.  Although a few sentences mention partial resumptions of activity, the overall tone stresses uncertainty and potential downside.  Accordingly, most individual snippets warrant mid-to-high risk scores (5-9) after modest deductions where mitigation is mentioned.  No sentence merits the absolute maximum of 10 because quantitative dollar impacts are absent, yet several sentences still reach the severe range by detailing critical operational and financial exposures in the current time frame.

COVID-19 is treated in the 2022 Netflix Form 10-K as an active, still-evolving threat that already has concrete, negative consequences for the company and could further erode performance.  The filing lists direct, realized effects—business disruption, higher production costs, and delayed content releases—as well as second-order impacts such as weakened consumer demand and partner instability.  It also stresses continued uncertainty, noting that future outcomes hinge on factors outside management’s control.  The disclosures are company-specific (production pauses, margin distortion, content-cash timing) rather than boiler-plate and they admit both historical damage and ongoing exposure.  Because the filing date (January 2022) is less than two years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7-10) when evidence shows current, material harm; moderate scores (4-6) for broad but unquantified or partially mitigated risks; and lower scores (0-3) where statements are largely cautionary or cite offsetting measures.  This framework drives the micro-scores below.

NFLX’s 2023 Form 10-K openly acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic has produced both realized and continuing risks across multiple operational fronts.  The wording is largely direct and contemporaneous: management cites concrete past impacts such as business disruption, higher costs, delayed content releases, and an observable rise in content amortization.  At the same time, it frames the pandemic as an ongoing, forward-looking hazard—highlighting potential future stoppages, cost inflation, and demand weakness should new waves occur.  Mitigation language (e.g., active monitoring, possible operational adjustments) appears but is modest and non-quantified, so it only partially offsets the threat level.  Because the filing date (January 26 2023) sits less than three years after the WHO’s pandemic declaration (March 11 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  Overall, the disclosures describe a recent, materially adverse set of circumstances with lingering uncertainty, warranting medium-to-high risk scores for the strongest evidence and lower scores where the company emphasizes mitigation or offers only generic statements.

Netflix’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only a brief, generic reference to pandemics. Management groups “public health issues such as pandemics or epidemics” with other disaster scenarios that could interrupt its computer systems. No sentence quantifies COVID-19’s historical effects, and there is no discussion of supply-chain constraints, production shutdowns, remote-work transitions, or lasting shifts in consumer demand. The language is purely forward-looking, framed with the conditional “may,” which signals potential rather than present exposure. Nearly four years have passed since the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle tempers the severity from “recent” to “medium-term.” Nonetheless, dependable IT infrastructure is mission-critical for a streaming service; any pandemic-driven outage could still materially harm operations. Accordingly, the overall evidentiary weight is moderate—acknowledging a continuing but unquantified risk—and individual snippet scores fall in the 4-6 range.

NI’s 2021-02-17 filing contains a concentrated cluster of Risk Factor paragraphs dedicated to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The language spans both backward-looking impacts (e.g., lower 2020 revenue, higher PPE expense, rising bad-debt) and forward-looking contingencies (supply-chain disruption, labor shortages, demand erosion, regulatory moratoria).  These statements are recent (within one year of the WHO declaration) and describe multiple operational and financial pressure points—commercial & industrial load loss, customer bankruptcies, employee availability, and credit-collection impairment—showing the pandemic is already hurting cash flow while simultaneously threatening future performance.  Although the disclosure rarely quantifies the dollar impact, the breadth of affected areas (revenue, liquidity, compliance, workforce, supply chain) and the admission of continuing uncertainty elevate overall severity.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, a post-event filing less than three years after onset allows high scores (7-10) where impacts are direct and realized; forward-looking but specific items merit mid-range scores (4-6); generic caveats get low scores (1-3).  Mitigating references (residential demand offsets, regulatory deferrals) are factored as negative points within each micro-scorecard.  On balance, the filing portrays a material, ongoing, multi-dimensional risk, justifying an overall elevated risk assessment.

NI’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic (declared March 2020) to both realised and prospective financial, operational and workforce risks.  Management discloses concrete, already-incurred impacts in 2020 – lower revenues, extra PPE costs and higher bad-debt expense – and warns that many of those pressures could persist or recur as variants spread.  The filing details multiple risk channels that match the requested focus: depressed commercial/industrial demand, late-fee moratoria, elevated customer bankruptcies, labour shortages tied to vaccine mandates or illness, and potential compliance gaps caused by remote-work restrictions.  While most statements remain qualitative and unquantified, they are recent (within two years of the event) and explicitly acknowledge that the pandemic “has adversely impacted and may continue to adversely impact” almost every key financial metric.  Mitigating references—regulatory deferrals, customer-assistance programmes, an incident-command structure—temper but do not eliminate the severity because NI still faces material uncertainty about duration, variants and regulatory responses.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, evidence dated February 2022 about an ongoing event that began in 2020 remains in the high-severity window (0-3 years), so top-scoring snippets can reach the 7-10 range, with modest downward adjustments where impacts are generic or partially offset by mitigation.

NI’s 2023-02-22 Form 10-K shows that COVID-19 is treated as an active, continuing threat rather than a closed historical matter.  Management discloses that the pandemic has already had adverse effects on operations, liquidity and cash-flows, and that these effects may persist given unknown variables such as future variants, labour constraints and possible regulatory cost disallowances.  The language is largely qualitative—there is no dollar quantification—but it is explicit that impacts have been felt and could worsen.  Because the filing date is within three years of the WHO declaration (Time-Decay window for “recent events”), high but not maximum severity scores are warranted where the company cites direct, enterprise-wide exposure; lower scores apply where discussion is generic or merely lists pandemics among many catastrophes.  No strong mitigating controls (e.g., insurance recovery, quantified hedging, or pandemic-specific contingency plans) are offered, so little offset is taken.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a material, near-term risk driver for NI, especially through workforce availability, supply-chain stress and potential regulatory push-back on cost recovery.

NI’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only limited but still noteworthy discussion of pandemic-related risks.  Four years have elapsed since the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, moving the issue out of the “recent” window and into the medium-term (4-10 years) band under the Time Decay Principle.  The filing no longer treats COVID-19 as an acute crisis, yet management still recognises persistent second-order effects: (1) lingering economic damage that elevated customer bankruptcies and depressed revenue, and (2) the possibility that a future public-health emergency could disrupt field operations and customer service.  The first disclosure is framed as an existing, measurable impact (“results of operations are negatively impacted”), while the second is a forward-looking contingency folded into a broad catalogue of catastrophic events.  Neither passage quantifies dollar impacts or outlines detailed mitigation programmes; therefore they are more qualitative than numerical.  Considering both the moderate vintage of the pandemic and the generic tone of much of the language, the overall severity of the risk evidence is assessed as moderate.  Individual snippet scores are therefore capped in the 2-6 range to comply with the Time Decay Principle.

Nike’s 2021-07-20 Form 10-K openly acknowledges that COVID-19 has already harmed—and may continue to harm—the company across every major risk vector the prompt highlights.  The filing repeatedly states that fiscal-year results were directly hit by store closures, supply-chain bottlenecks, higher logistics costs and changing consumer demand, and it lays out a granular catalogue of forward-looking threats: labour shortages at factories and distribution centres, remote-work cyber-risks, incremental health-protocol costs, retailer bankruptcies, and potential inventory overhang.  The language is largely specific (naming container shortages, U.S. port congestion, increased freight costs, etc.) and often retrospective, confirming realised impacts, which raises severity.  Because the filing date is less than 18 months after the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (7-10) for direct, current impacts; moderate scores (4-6) for general or highly uncertain statements; and small deductions where the wording is purely precautionary or unquantified.  Overall, the risk profile is high: Nike concedes both material past damage and meaningful exposure going forward, especially in supply-chain resilience, consumer demand shifts and operational continuity under remote-work models.

NIKE’s 2023-07-20 10-K makes it clear that COVID-19 remains a live, material risk only a little more than three years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic. Northrop Grumman’s January 28 2021 Form 10-K embeds an extensive, dedicated disclosure to the COVID-19 pandemic that blends (1) concrete impacts already felt during 2020 and (2) a broad set of forward-looking uncertainties. ServiceNow’s 2021-02-12 filing repeatedly links the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and prospective risks across virtually every operational dimension: customer demand, revenue visibility, collections, competitive pressure, office closures, labour health-and-safety, data-centre and hardware supply chains, cyber-security, and capital-market volatility. The filing acknowledges COVID-19 primarily as a historical but still-relevant disruptor. Northern Trust’s 2021 Form 10-K describes COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-faceted threat rather than a distant possibility. Given the filing date (February 2022) is less than two years after the WHO declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  Because the language combines hard evidence of past harm with specific, plausible future pathways of disruption, the overall COVID-19 risk profile for OTIS is assessed as high-to-very-high, tempered slightly by the lone liquidity-comfort note.

The filing is dated February 3 2023, making the COVID-19 pandemic a very recent, still-evolving event. OTIS explicitly discloses both realised and prospective impacts across operations, supply chain, customer demand, liquidity and capital resources. Several sentences confirm that COVID-19 has already disrupted factory operations, installations, maintenance access and customer payment behaviour—clear evidence of a direct, existing impact. Others project future uncertainty tied to new variants, potential renewed lockdowns, and supplier distress, demonstrating forward-looking risk. Although one sentence states that management does not currently expect a significant impact on capital resources, this is a narrow mitigation that only partially offsets the broader operational and demand-side threats. Given the recency (0-3 years) and the specificity of the disruptions cited, the overall risk level is high; most snippets score in the 7-9 range, with modest deductions where statements are generic or contain internal mitigations.

COVID-19 appears in the 2024 Form 10-K only inside the Risk Factors section and always in a forward-looking, contingency style.  The company states that pandemic health issues, including COVID-19, could disrupt macro-economic conditions and, more narrowly, that remote-work trends tied to the pandemic could dampen demand for construction and commercial real-estate projects, thereby hurting Otis’s sales pipeline.  There is no disclosure of any quantified 2023 impact, no description of actual supply-chain or labour shortages, and no discussion of ongoing mitigation programmes specific to COVID-19.  Accordingly, the references are generic, un-quantified and framed with conditional verbs such as “may” and “could.”  Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is now almost four years old, placing it in the early medium-term bracket: residual risk remains, but severity scores must be moderated.  The net result is a moderate aggregate risk signal—material enough to warrant disclosure, yet clearly more attenuated and speculative than in filings from 2020-2022.

The filing was made nearly one year after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the disclosures capture both the real-time damage already felt and the still-evolving uncertainty.  Realty Income describes multiple direct impacts—lower rent collections, actual impairment charges, tenant bankruptcies and reserve buildups—indicating the risk has already crystallised. The language is largely company-specific (e.g., 5.6 % exposure to theatres, recorded reserves, quantified impairments) rather than boiler-plate, which heightens severity.  Because the pandemic is a very recent event (well within the 0-3-year Time Decay window) and the statements reveal concrete financial consequences with potential to worsen, individual snippets can legitimately score into the upper range, though any mitigating language (e.g., precautionary measures) earns deductions.  Overall, the risk profile is acute and multi-faceted, warranting generally high micro-scores consistent with current-period materiality.

COVID-19 is framed by Realty Income (Company O) as both an already-manifest and a still-evolving threat that permeates virtually every dimension of its REIT business model.  The filing, dated February 23 2022—less than two years after the WHO declared the pandemic—contains language showing that the pandemic has (i) directly disrupted operations, (ii) weakened rent collections, (iii) triggered impairment charges, (iv) complicated capital-raising and covenant compliance, (v) created supply-chain delays, and (vi) forced internal continuity measures such as large-scale remote work.  The statements are largely factual and present-tense (e.g., “has disrupted,” “have adversely impacted”) with forward-looking concern about further material damage. Under the Time Decay Principle, with the filing less than two years after the onset date, scores can legitimately occupy the upper range.  I therefore weight aggravating factors—operational shutdowns, rent non-payment, capital-market constraints—more heavily than mitigants (cautionary language, internal precautions), producing snippet scores mostly between 6 and 9 and reflecting a persistent, material, near-term risk profile.

The filing, dated February 22, 2023, squarely places COVID-19 within the recent-event window (less than three years since WHO’s pandemic declaration).  Realty Income acknowledges both realised and prospective damage from the pandemic across virtually every driver of its business model: tenant operations, rent collections, property valuations, capital-markets access, and supply-chain functionality.  The language is primarily present-tense or forward-looking (“has disrupted”, “expected to continue”), confirming that impacts are current and ongoing rather than hypothetical.  Several passages disclose concrete consequences—e.g., recognised impairment charges—and describe specific transmission channels such as government lockdowns, retail-traffic collapse, and supply-chain bottlenecks.  Because the company is a net-lease REIT that depends on retail tenants (the sector most affected by COVID-19), concentration risk magnifies the severity.  Mitigations (e.g., net-lease structure, diversified client base) are mentioned elsewhere in the filing but not in the cited sentences, so the extracted evidence is largely unmitigated.  Applying the Time Decay Principle for a recent event, individual snippet scores justifiably range from 4 to 9, clustering toward the higher end where the disclosure is direct, proven and multi-faceted.

The filing acknowledges that, nearly four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Realty Income still sees pandemic-related pressures as a live, albeit moderating, threat.  Management frames the risk primarily as an indirect exposure: epidemics can weaken tenants’ businesses, disrupt supply chains and consumer behaviour, and ultimately impair rent collections, property values and the company’s ability to service debt or pay dividends.  The language is largely forward-looking and qualitative—there are no quantified dollar impacts—yet it recognises that COVID-19 has already caused downturns in certain industries (e.g., theatres) and could trigger further tenant distress.  Because the event falls just inside the 4-year “medium-term” window, the Time-Decay principle limits severity scores to a mid-range.  Overall, the narrative depicts a real but un-quantified exposure that could amplify financial stress if tenant credit deteriorates, justifying moderate risk scores (4-6) for the individual statements.

PANW’s September 2021 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad set of operational, financial and strategic risks.  The disclosures state that the virus has already caused identifiable harm—e.g., global economic slowdown, supply-chain delays, remote-work complications—and that these effects are expected to persist.  The language is current-period and forward-looking, emphasising continuing uncertainty (“fluid and uncertain”) and the possibility of “material” adverse impacts on cash-flows, sales cycles, manufacturing, customer demand and credit risk.  Some mitigating steps (work-from-home transition, ongoing monitoring, vaccination progress) are noted, but they are described as incomplete and themselves potentially harmful (e.g., longer sales cycles).  Given the filing date (Sept 2021) falls well within three years of the WHO 11-Mar-2020 declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the company presents COVID-19 as an active, multi-dimensional threat with both realised and potential future impacts; consequently most evidence snippets receive high (6-9) scores, moderated slightly where mitigation or conditional language appears.

PANW’s 2022-09-06 filing repeatedly and explicitly connects the COVID-19 pandemic to a spectrum of material business risks that are still unfolding.  The language is forward-looking but also cites concrete, already-felt impacts—extended component lead-times, higher input costs, disrupted sales cycles, and remote-work operational challenges.  The disclosures are specific to supply-chain shortages, labour constraints, customer demand shifts, liquidity pressures, work-from-home transitions, and forecasting difficulty, all of which map directly to the requested pandemic-risk indicators.  No dollar figures are given, so the statements are qualitative rather than quantified, yet they are detailed and cover multiple functional areas (workforce, supply chain, sales, R&D roadmap, credit risk).  Given that the event window (2020-03-11 onward) is within three years of the filing date, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7–10) for the strongest evidence and mid-high scores (5–8) for less granular or partially mitigated statements.  Where the company describes concrete mitigation (e.g., FLEXWORK, hygiene measures) or frames impacts as merely “could” occur, some downward adjustment is applied.  Overall, the document paints a picture of an ongoing, multi-faceted, and materially adverse risk environment driven by COVID-19, warranting elevated but not maximum scores for most snippets.

PANW’s 2023-09-01 Form 10-K continues to frame the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, forward-looking operational hazard rather than a source of already-quantified financial damage. References to “epidemics and pandemics such as COVID-19” appear in multiple risk-factor sections—international sales, supply-chain/manufacturing, and general catastrophe planning—underscoring management’s view that future outbreaks or lingering after-effects could disrupt production, logistics, customer demand and on-the-ground sales execution. The language is still largely generic and bundled with other macro threats, showing no event-specific metrics or past hit to revenue or costs; however, the company does articulate clear transmission channels (e.g., factory shutdowns, shipment delays, international-trade uncertainty). Because the filing date is within three years of the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores, yet the absence of quantified impacts or uniquely tailored mitigation keeps the risk assessment in the moderate—not extreme—range. Overall, COVID-19 remains a live, non-trivial but un-quantified risk factor for PANW, meriting mid-level evidence scores of roughly 6/10 for each substantive disclosure.

PANW’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only brief, largely generic references to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company frames the pandemic primarily as one of several exogenous hazards (alongside wars, natural disasters, inflation, etc.) that could disrupt supply chains, manufacturing, or global demand.  There is no quantification of historical losses, nor any assertion that COVID-19 is currently depressing results; the disclosures are forward-looking and precautionary.  Because the pandemic’s onset is now more than four years old, the Time Decay Principle moderates severity: the risk remains relevant (e.g., supply-chain shocks or future waves) but is no longer acute.  Overall, the filing signals a medium-level, un-quantified, potential risk rather than an active, material impairment.  Accordingly, individual sentence scores fall in the mid-range (4–5), with slight deductions for generic language and lack of specific impact, and a very low score for a purely generic “health risks” citation.

The filing, dated February 24 2021—well within three years of the March 2020 World Health Organization declaration—provides both backward-looking evidence of actual damages and forward-looking warnings that COVID-19 can continue to reshape Paramount Global’s (PARA) economics.  Management discloses concrete, already-realised hits to advertising, theatrical, and content-licensing revenues, plus incremental production-safety costs, thereby establishing that the pandemic is not merely a hypothetical risk but a present, material impact.  At the same time, the text projects multiple future stress points—uncertain sports schedules, potential affiliate-fee pressure, debt-finance constraints, and even cyber-fraud exposure—showing that the threat profile remains open-ended.  The language mixes precise causal chains (e.g., cancelled NCAA games → lost ad revenue) with broader “could” statements.  Because the event is recent, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Statements that quantify impact as “material” or detail operational disruptions receive elevated scores (7-10).  Generic or mitigated comments are scored lower (2-5).  Overall, the document evidences a high-severity, multi-faceted risk environment, only partially offset by limited mitigation (e.g., film rescheduling, streaming migration).

PARA’s 2022-02-15 filing presents COVID-19 as a recent, multi-faceted threat that is already depressing revenue streams (advertising, licensing, theatrical) and could continue to do so through persistent macro-economic weakness, supply-chain disruption and lasting shifts in consumer behaviour.  The discussion blends backward-looking facts (e.g., “material negative impact” in 2020) with forward-looking uncertainty (inability to predict future theatre attendance, production delays, or advertising demand).  The language is largely specific to PARA’s core businesses (content production, distribution and advertising) and repeatedly characterises the impact as “material” or “negative,” signalling a high severity profile.  Because the pandemic began only two years before the filing, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores (up to 10).  Nevertheless, where statements are conditional, generic, or mention partial recovery, scores are tempered.  Direct, quantified or already-incurred impacts receive the highest micro-scores, while generic or mitigated statements are scored modestly.  Overall, the evidence points to a significant, ongoing risk that is both realised and still evolving.

Paramount’s 2023 filing contains an explicit, stand-alone pandemic risk factor that blends backward-looking evidence of actual damage with forward-looking warnings. The company states that COVID-19 directly reduced advertising, licensing and theatrical revenues because of event cancellations, production shutdowns and cinema closures—clear, realized financial harm that is still less than three years old.  Although no dollar amounts are disclosed, the narrative expressly ties multiple revenue lines to pandemic disruptions, signalling materiality.  Paramount also highlights macro-level knock-ons (supply-chain bottlenecks, labour and consumer-behaviour shifts, inflation), describes continuing uncertainty around variants, and concedes an inability to quantify full future impacts.  Mitigating actions are notably absent; instead, the language is predominantly cautionary, using “material adverse effect” and “continues to negatively impact,” which elevates severity.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the March 2023 filing date is well within three years of the March 2020 WHO declaration, so high scores (up to 10) are permissible.  However, lack of numerical detail and some generic phrasing temper the evidence.  Overall, the risk is assessed as high-to-moderate: the company has already suffered identifiable revenue hits and sees ongoing exposure, but the disclosure remains qualitative rather than quantified.

COVID-19 is no longer an acute, day-to-day emergency for PARA, yet the 2024 filing shows the pandemic still shapes both historical performance and forward-looking risk.  Management discloses (i) material, quantified operating losses from 2020-2023 caused by travel shutdowns, (ii) lingering structural exposure—especially to any future ‘health outbreaks or pandemics similar to COVID-19’ that could again halt content production or depress advertising demand, and (iii) a recognition that most government restrictions were lifted only in 2023.  The language is partly backward-looking (describing the damage already experienced in Macao and Singapore), but the Risk Factors section also treats pandemics as an ongoing macro threat that could quickly recur and disrupt programming, supply of content, and advertiser spending.  Because the initial COVID shock occurred almost four years ago, the Time-Decay principle moderates the severity from “acute” to “medium”; however, PARA’s direct operational history and explicit warning of renewed disruption justify a moderate-high residual risk posture.  Overall, the evidence supports snippet-level scores in the 4-6 range, reflecting a still-meaningful but no longer extreme pandemic risk profile.

PAYC’s 2021-02-18 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a recent, material and ongoing threat that is already depressing revenue drivers (per-employee billing, interest-income float) and introducing operational frictions (remote-work cyber-risk, virtualised sales cycles).  The wording moves well beyond boiler-plate: management cites concrete mechanisms such as client lay-offs, CARES-Act tax deferrals shrinking ‘funds-held-for-clients’, lower Fed rates, delayed implementations, and a 96 % remote workforce.  These disclosures show both realised impacts (2020 revenue drag, higher expenses) and forward-looking exposure (“will continue”, “may experience”), indicating the risk is active rather than merely prospective.  Mitigations (remote transition, virtual sales, internal controls) are mentioned but are not framed as fully offsetting the financial headwinds.  Because the filing date is less than one year after the WHO declaration (within the 0-3-year “recent event” window), Time-Decay permits high severity scores; nevertheless, each snippet’s score is calibrated for the specificity of impact, materiality wording, and any embedded mitigants.  Overall, PAYC’s pandemic risk disclosure is significant, specific, and current, warranting high—but not maximal—scores on the extracted evidence.

PAYC’s 2022-02-17 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, enterprise-wide hazard.  The filing blends backward-looking evidence of actual damage—lower recurring revenue from client head-count cuts and lost interest income—with forward-looking warnings about prolonged client disruption, tighter labor markets, possible recession, vaccination mandates and cyber-risk from an extended remote-work model.  While management highlights certain offsets (robust product demand, virtual-sales efficiencies), the dominant tone is caution: the pandemic has already compressed top-line growth and may continue to do so through macro-economic weakness, regulatory uncertainty and operational frictions.  Because the disclosure date is less than three years after the WHO declaration (Time Decay window 0-3 years), high severity scores are warranted when PAYC cites concrete, realized financial impacts; generic or primarily mitigative statements receive lower—or negative—scores.

PAYC’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 primarily as a continuing, forward-looking operational and regulatory hazard rather than as a source of already-incurred, quantified losses.  References cluster around four themes: (1) possible constraints on physical expansion and staffing, (2) the proliferation of pandemic-driven legislation that could raise compliance costs, (3) generic warnings that public-health crises can disrupt business operations, and (4) the potential for the pandemic to amplify broader macro-economic slowdowns.  None of the disclosures provide dollar figures or cite an observable hit to revenue or margins; all are phrased with conditional language (“may,” “could”).  Because the filing date (16 Feb 2023) is within three years of the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits higher scores, yet the generic, un-quantified nature of the statements warrants only moderate severity.  Overall, the pandemic is framed as an ongoing but manageable risk that management continues to monitor, assigning it a medium-low impact profile in the firm’s risk universe.

PAYC’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only passing, largely generic references to pandemic-related risk.  The filing does not describe specific operational disruptions, supply-chain blockages, labour shortages or quantified financial impacts from COVID-19.  Instead, it frames a potential pandemic as one of many macro-economic or geopolitical headwinds that could amplify an economic downturn, and it cites “outbreak of disease” in a long risk laundry-list for international expansion.  One sentence implicitly links the pandemic to changing office expectations (remote or hybrid work), but again without detail.  All statements are forward-looking or hypothetical, signalling awareness rather than reporting current damage.  Because the filing date is about four years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time-Decay Principle caps evidence at a moderate level.  Overall, the company acknowledges the pandemic as a continuing external uncertainty, but the disclosures are brief, non-quantified and generic; therefore the risk evidence merits only a mid- to low-level severity assessment.

PAYX’s 2021-07-16 Form 10-K repeatedly links the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic to material, multi-dimensional risks.  Management treats the pandemic as a current, continuing threat that has already disrupted the business (e.g., labour shortages, client bankruptcies) and may further depress revenue, margins, and service delivery.  The disclosure mixes backward-looking facts (actual supply-chain disruptions, labour shortages, added compliance costs) with forward-looking uncertainty (potential new lockdowns, variant surges, unpredictable duration).  Several statements explicitly use “materially adverse” language and quantify broad macro-economic channels—client attrition, pricing pressure, cyber-fraud exposure, regulatory burdens—indicating that the threat is not merely hypothetical.  Because the filing date is within 16 months of the WHO pandemic declaration (inside the 0-3 year “recent” window), the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores where the company provides concrete, specific, or already-realised impacts, while more generic catch-all references warrant only moderate scores.  Overall, the risk profile is elevated: PAYX faces live operational, financial, and regulatory hazards that could intensify as variants emerge and clients struggle.  The evidence therefore skews toward the upper half of the 1-10 scale, tempered only when language is generic or unquantified.

PAYX’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly links the company’s operating and financial outlook to continuing risks from the 2020-present COVID-19 pandemic.  The filing emphasises that, although business conditions improved versus the depths of 2020, the pandemic still produces realised impacts (extra compliance costs, client demand fluctuations and direct spending on support services) as well as forward-looking uncertainties (uneven recovery, labour shortages, supply-chain disruption, inflation and a fast-changing regulatory environment).  These statements are largely qualitative but they are recent (within 0-3 years of the event) and frequently describe concrete operational stressors rather than remote hypotheticals—for example citing actual additional costs and enumerating specific macro-economic knock-ons (unemployment, credit-market instability, etc.).  Because the pandemic is ongoing, Time-Decay allows high severity scores.  However, the disclosures are not quantified and occasionally include mitigating language (PAYX “remains committed” and is “supporting clients”), tempering the maximum severity.  Overall, the risk evidence is current, direct and multi-faceted, warranting upper-mid scores across snippets.

PAYX’s 2023 Form 10-K contains only a brief, catch-all reference to a “public health emergency, pandemic” as one of several events that could severely disrupt operations. Instead, management frames it as a forward-looking contingency: if a pandemic strikes (or re-escalates), infrastructure failures and service interruptions could occur.  Although the COVID-19 pandemic is still within the recent-event window (≤3 years) under the Time-Decay Principle, the disclosure is generic and largely precautionary, providing minimal detail on exposure or mitigation beyond an acknowledgement that a business-continuity plan exists but might fail.  Consequently, the overall risk evidence is assessed as moderate-to-low severity; the recency of the pandemic keeps the score from dropping further, but the lack of specificity prevents a high score.

The filing discusses the COVID-19 pandemic only once, folded into a broader list of potential catastrophes.  The company frames a pandemic as a future-oriented, contingency risk that could "significantly disrupt" operations if its infrastructure were damaged or inaccessible.  There is no disclosure of actual historical impact (e.g., supply-chain constraints, labour shortages, or permanent remote-work changes) nor any quantified financial effect.  Thus, while the reference confirms that Paychex still recognises pandemics as a material threat four years after the outbreak (placing it inside the 4-to-10-year medium window of the Time Decay Principle), the language is generic and un-differentiated.  Overall, the evidence supports a moderate but not high COVID-19 risk assessment: the company acknowledges the hazard but provides little specificity or measurement and cites no new mitigation steps beyond its ordinary business-continuity planning.

The filing, dated February 17, 2021, discusses COVID-19 less than one year after the WHO declared the pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle allows high-severity scores (0–3 yrs window).  The 10-K combines forward-looking warnings (possible facility shutdowns, supplier failures, demand shocks) with retrospective evidence of material impacts that already occurred in 2020 (global production suspension, reduced truck deliveries, higher credit-loss provisions, incremental costs). Quantification is mostly qualitative, but breadth and immediacy of effects elevate risk.  Mitigants (essential-business status, re-start of plants, cost-saving measures) temper but do not eliminate the exposure.  Overall, COVID-19 represents a high, currently-manifesting risk to PACCAR, meriting high individual snippet scores (7–9) where concrete operational or financial impacts are described, and moderate scores (3–5) where risks are more generic or contingent.  Purely mitigating statements receive zero or low scores, consistent with the point-addition/subtraction method and the recent-event time-decay window.

PACCAR’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective risks across operations, supply chain, workforce, demand and financing activities. PACCAR’s 2022 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and potential operational and financial threats.  Disclosures range from generic “pandemic” language in the general risk catalogue to a dedicated COVID-19 subsection that details continuing supply-chain shortages of components and semiconductors, and warns of renewed strains forcing supplier capacity constraints or plant shutdowns.  The filing recognises that, although the acute phase of the pandemic eased during 2022, residual impacts (e.g., parts undersupply) are still present and are expected to influence 2023 deliveries.  The company concedes that it cannot yet quantify COVID-19–related effects in its results of operations, underscoring ongoing uncertainty.  Because the filing date (22 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  Nonetheless, most statements are qualitative and only one cites an actual continuing impact (component shortages), so the highest evidence merits a strong but not maximum score.  Overall, the pandemic risk is current, partially realized (supply chain disruptions), and remains material but largely un-quantified, warranting a spectrum of snippet scores between 2 and 7.

PACCAR’s 2024 Form 10-K only references the COVID-19 pandemic in the generic, forward-looking portions of its risk factor discussion. Scores therefore land in the 3-4 range—enough to reflect acknowledged exposure, but tempered by generic wording, lack of quantification, and time decay since the height of COVID-19 impacts.

The filing, dated February 25 2021, was written less than a year after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  PG&E describes both realised and prospective impacts.  Several passages record concrete, quantified deteriorations – a US $478 million jump in overdue customer receivables, a US $430 million fall in billed revenues, and 2 % drops in electric and gas load – demonstrating that COVID-19 is materially eroding cash-flow and demand.  Other sentences flag operational pressures: workforce shortages, remote-work protocols, supply-chain lags and the need to re-sequence capital projects, all of which raise execution risk.  The company also warns of possible future financing strain through wider credit spreads.  Taken together, the disclosures show a blend of present damage and ongoing vulnerability.  Because the effects are already quantifiable and hit multiple risk dimensions (liquidity, operations, supply chain, financing), I assess the overall pandemic risk for PG&E as high-to-severe (upper-mid of the 0-10 spectrum).

COVID-19 is depicted in PG&E’s 2021 Form 10-K as a still-evolving, multi-faceted threat that is already depressing cash collections, swelling customer arrears, straining supply chains, and up-shifting operating costs.  The company cites concrete, near-term financial harm – e.g., an $832 million jump in >30-day receivables – while also flagging prospective pressures such as labour attrition, materials shortages and higher credit-market spreads.  These disclosures are recent (less than three years after the WHO declaration on 11 March 2020) and describe both realised impacts (historical cash shortfalls, material delays already felt) and forward-looking uncertainties (future PSPS execution, capital-project slippage, unpredictable demand).  Language is mostly qualitative, but one key metric is quantified, underscoring materiality.  No definitive mitigation offsets are offered beyond regulatory tracking accounts, so risk remains largely un-hedged.  Under the Time Decay Principle, evidence tied to a current, ongoing pandemic can attract high scores; accordingly, quantified, realised impacts are scored highest, while generic or hypothetical statements receive moderate or low scores.

PCG’s Form 10-K makes clear that COVID-19 remains a high-severity, near-term risk to the company’s financial condition, operations and liquidity.  The filing—dated February 23 2023, well within three years of the March 2020 WHO declaration—describes both realised and prospective impacts: sharp growth in overdue customer receivables, continuing uncertainty in collections and demand, supply-chain bottlenecks that threaten timely maintenance and capital projects, labour shortages driven by health mandates, and potential increases in financing costs.  Some mitigating steps are noted (regulatory tracking accounts, ongoing evaluations) but recovery timing is “uncertain,” meaning cash-flow pressure persists.  The disclosures combine hard, quantified data (e.g., $890 million rise in arrears) with directional statements of sustained adverse effects.  Because the pandemic is recent and impacts are already material—and in several cases numerically specified—the individual evidence snippets merit high scores (7-9) under the Time Decay Principle, with modest downward adjustments where language is conditional or mitigation is cited.

Across the almost-600-page filing, COVID-19 is mentioned only in passing and almost always in the same breath as ‘other pandemics’ or an array of natural-disaster scenarios.  The company no longer treats the pandemic as an acute emergency but as a residual, forward-looking operational risk that could trigger labour shortages or require customer-protection spending.  The disclosures are mostly qualitative, use conditional language ("could experience", "may continue"), and provide no new quantified impact metrics.  The only concrete reference is to two memorandum accounts (CPPMA and RUBA) that tracked pandemic-related customer-protection costs—signalling that any material cash outflows have already been isolated for future regulatory recovery.  Because the event is now four years old, the Time Decay Principle points to moderate scoring: the risk is neither fresh enough for high severity nor distant enough to be negligible.  Overall, pandemic risk for PG&E is assessed as low-to-moderate, largely mitigated by existing cost-recovery mechanisms and by the fact that pandemic-induced disruptions are now folded into the company’s standard business-continuity planning rather than driving unique, material exposures.

PEG’s 2024 filing still treats COVID-19 as a live, medium-term enterprise risk.  Although the initial outbreak occurred nearly four years ago, management links the pandemic to both realized and continuing exposures: (i) operational disruption (labour shortages, service delays, remote-work continuity); (ii) regulatory interventions (state-mandated shut-off moratoria) that impaired cash collection; and (iii) lingering balance-sheet stress through elevated accounts-receivable and potential bad-debt write-offs.  The language is moderately specific—identifying concrete consequences such as ‘elevated aged accounts-receivable’—yet largely un-quantified and couched in conditional ‘could’ phrasing for forward-looking elements.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 now sits in the 4-to-10-year window, so maximum snippet severity is capped at a mid-range level.  Evidence that reflects actual, historical financial impact (e.g., collections shortfall) is scored toward the upper end of this medium band (5–6), while broad, hypothetical references to pandemics receive lower mid-range scores (3-4).  No mitigating controls strong enough to materially offset the risk are disclosed, so deductions are minimal.

PepsiCo’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an acute, multi-dimensional threat that is still unfolding less than two years after the WHO declared the pandemic.  The narrative blends backward-looking evidence of realised harm (higher operating costs, negative profitability effects, volatility in capital markets) with forward-looking uncertainty about variants, labour availability and supply-chain congestion.  The filing ties the pandemic to core value-drivers — consumer demand, channel mix, manufacturing continuity, logistics capacity and financing access — and repeatedly states that these factors have already *negatively impacted* results and could do so further.  Although the company cites mitigation efforts (health protocols, continuity planning), it stresses that outcomes remain “uncertain” and “cannot be accurately predicted.”  Given the filing date (Feb 2022) the Time-Decay window is 0-3 years, allowing for high severity scores.  Each selected sentence therefore earns between 7 and 9 points, with minor deductions where language is more speculative or notes partial controls.  Overall, COVID-19 is presented as a live, enterprise-wide risk with tangible financial and operational consequences, warranting a high composite risk assessment.

PepsiCo’s 2023 filing presents COVID-19 chiefly as a still-unfolding, enterprise-wide risk that has already affected – and can continue to affect – demand patterns, supply-chain continuity, commodity costs and labour availability. Accordingly, individual snippets merit mid-to-upper-range scores (5-7) rather than the maximum, reflecting clear, recent, multi-faceted impact acknowledgement without quantified materiality.

COVID-19 is acknowledged throughout PEP’s 2024 Form 10-K as a continuing, though now longer-dated, enterprise-wide risk.  The company links the pandemic to past and potential future impacts on consumer demand, supply-chain stability, labor availability (e.g., truck-driver shortages) and remote-work related cyber-exposure.  The language is partly backward-looking (“have impacted”) and partly forward-looking (“could continue”), confirming that COVID-19 already affected financial performance and still represents an uncertainty factor.  The disclosures are moderately specific: they cite concrete operational pinch-points (availability of raw materials, transportation, labor) and behavioural shifts (consumer preferences) rather than generic boiler-plate.  No quantified dollar exposures are given and mitigation efforts (crisis-management plans) are briefly referenced, tempering severity.  Under the Time-Decay Principle the pandemic now sits just beyond the 3-year ‘recent’ window (March 2020 to Feb 2024 ≈ 3 years 11 months), so evidence scores should fall in the medium band (4-6).  Overall, COVID-19 remains a material but partially mitigated, medium-term risk for PepsiCo.

Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K frames the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that has already produced tangible financial harm (e.g., 2023 inventory write-offs) and could continue to disrupt operations, supply chains, third-party collaborations and product demand.  The filing mixes backward-looking evidence of realized impacts—revenue declines, excess inventory and supply-chain shocks—with forward-looking disclaimers that such effects ‘may’ continue. Applying the Time Decay Principle, these disclosures warrant mid-range severity scores (4-6): the event is slightly beyond the 0-3-year “recent” window, yet the company still reports live impairments and detailed operational vulnerabilities, raising the risk above a merely historic concern but below a near-crisis maximum.

PFG’s February 12 2021 Form 10-K squarely acknowledges COVID-19 as a material, ongoing risk across the enterprise. Because the filing date is inside the first year of the pandemic, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores. The disclosure moves from a brief catalog reference (generic flag) to a dedicated, multi-sentence paragraph that details concrete channels of impact: higher mortality and disability claims, customer withdrawals, liquidity strain, increased credit defaults, workforce health threats and large-scale remote-work disruption, as well as demand-side pressure tied to rising unemployment. These statements are forward-looking but also recognise existing adverse effects (e.g., volatility already experienced in 2020).
