Mitigating actions are only briefly referenced (contingency plans), so they do little to offset severity. Overall, the filing presents a high-level, specific and timely warning, warranting elevated risk scores for the evidence sentences that follow.

The filing repeatedly flags COVID-19 as an immediate, enterprise-wide threat that has already altered economic conditions and could further erode profitability, capital and liquidity.  The discussion moves beyond a boiler-plate reference, describing concrete channels through which the pandemic is affecting or could affect PFG—higher life and disability claims, customer withdrawals, elevated credit defaults, operational disruptions, workforce health issues, lower sales tied to unemployment, and stressed capital-market access.  Language such as “have led to significant economic disruption” shows that some impacts are current, while phrases like “may include” keep much of the disclosure forward-looking.  No explicit dollar amounts are provided, so the evidence is qualitative, but the breadth and immediacy of the risks, combined with the filing date falling inside the 0-3-year window of the Time Decay Principle, justify moderately high severity scores (generally 5-7).  Generic, list-style mentions of pandemic risk are given minimal weight, whereas sentences that enumerate specific operational or financial channels receive higher scores.

PFG’s 2023 filing offers only brief, generic references to a ‘pandemic’ within a broader litany of catastrophic events.  The wording is entirely forward-looking (e.g., ‘could adversely affect’) and does not cite COVID-19 by name, quantify impacts, or describe concrete operational responses such as supply-chain changes or remote-work protocols.  While the pandemic remains within the 0-3-year ‘recent’ window of the Time Decay Principle—allowing for potentially high scores—the company’s language is high-level and purely hypothetical, so each individual sentence carries limited aggravating weight.  Consequently, the overall risk evidence is assessed as moderate-to-low: PFG acknowledges that a pandemic could hurt operations, claims experience, capital markets and workforce availability, but provides no data or specificity indicating direct, material COVID-19 consequences already realized.

PFG’s 2024 Form 10-K still treats COVID-19—and pandemics in general—as a broad, forward-looking catastrophe risk rather than a discrete, quantified impact. Because the filing date is almost four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places the event at the front edge of the 4-to-10-year “medium-term” window; therefore, maximum individual-snippet scores should fall in the moderate range (≈ 4-6).  Given the absence of specificity or quantified impact, the actual evidentiary weight of each sentence is low-to-moderate.  Overall, the company acknowledges pandemic risk but only in the most sweeping terms, indicating continued vigilance yet minimal current strategic or financial exposure.

PGR’s March 1 2021 Form 10-K was filed less than one year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the disclosure is contemporaneous with an unfolding, still-uncertain crisis; under the Time Decay Principle, any well-supported evidence can merit a high score.  The company positions the pandemic chiefly as a forward-looking, enterprise-wide threat that could materially affect underwriting volumes, pricing accuracy, claims severity, staffing, technology resilience, vendor performance and regulatory burden.  Although most language is framed with conditional verbs ("could" or "may"), the narrative is highly specific—linking the virus to reduced driving, lower policy demand, supply-chain-driven repair delays, legislative mandates, employee illness, and cascading effects on liquidity, capital and cyber-security.  No quantified dollar impacts are offered, and mitigation strategies are largely absent, which keeps the emphasis squarely on downside exposure.  Given the recency of the event, the breadth of operational touch-points, and the repeated use of "material" qualifiers, the overall pandemic risk evidentiary weight is assessed as high (upper-mid single-digit scores), with no Time-Decay discount necessary beyond the acknowledgement that most statements remain scenario-based rather than reporting realized losses.

Progressive’s 2022 filing presents a multi-layered, still-unfolding exposure to the COVID-19 pandemic.  Because the filing date (February 2022) is well within three years of the WHO’s March 2020 declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores. Although most statements are qualitative and use conditional verbs (“could,” “may”), many employ strong modifiers such as “materially adversely affect,” signalling severity.  There are also broader, more generic references to “pandemics” embedded in other risk sections (pricing, catastrophe modelling, talent retention).  We therefore see a spectrum: centerpiece COVID-19 section scores high (7-9) for direct, recent, enterprise-wide danger, while generic or indirect pandemic mentions score moderate (3-5).

Progressive’s 2023 filing embeds pandemic-related commentary across multiple risk sections, indicating that COVID-19 remains an active, cross-functional threat.  The text spans underwriting assumptions, catastrophe modelling, litigation exposure, regulatory rebate pressure, labour availability, remote-work continuity and broad macro-economic demand shifts. Progressive’s 2024 Form 10-K embeds pandemic language in several risk categories, but the tone has shifted from describing an acute, on-going crisis to treating COVID-19 as a background factor that could re-emerge or amplify other risks. Most references are forward-looking and qualitative—no dollar figures or quantified margin impacts are supplied—indicating that management now views pandemic exposure as an uncertain but manageable scenario rather than a present, material drag. Overall, the residual pandemic risk for PGR is moderate: specific enough to warrant monitoring (supply–demand shifts, regulatory credits, sustained remote-work vulnerabilities), but tempered by management’s assertion that current impacts are “not material.”

PG’s 2021-08-06 Form 10-K draws a clear, multi-dimensional link between the COVID-19 pandemic (declared March 2020) and material corporate risks that persist into the filing year. Given that the pandemic is within the 0-3-year “recent” window, Time-Decay allows high severity scores when the text shows concrete or probable adverse effects; purely generic statements receive moderate marks, while expressed mitigants subtract points.  The evidence shows a balanced but still elevated risk posture, justifying snippet scores ranging from moderate (2-5) to high (7-8).

Procter & Gamble’s 2022-08-05 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that could still materially disrupt operations, even though the company has so far weathered the crisis relatively well.  The disclosed language spans supply-chain fragility, workforce constraints, volatility in consumer demand (including pantry loading and subsequent destocking), risks from governmental restrictions, liquidity pressures, and knock-on macro-economic slowdowns. Taken together, the risk profile is high but not catastrophic: the probability of further disruption remains significant, while the magnitude is potentially material but partially offset by strong past performance and mitigation efforts such as supplier engagement and employee-safety programs.

COVID-19 falls squarely within the 0-3-year “recent” window, so any current-period disclosure can command a high score under the Time-Decay Principle. Overall, the evidence supports a moderately high risk posture in the 6–7 range for the strongest snippets, with lower scores for generic list items.  All scores respect the Time-Decay limits for a recent event.

PG’s 2024-08-05 Form 10-K continues to frame the COVID-19 pandemic principally as a medium-term, forward-looking enterprise-wide risk that spans demand volatility, supply-chain continuity, workforce availability and governmental restrictions. Because the pandemic’s inception (March 2020) is roughly four years prior to the filing date, the Time Decay Principle caps individual evidence scores in the moderate range (≈4-6). PHM’s 2021-02-02 Form 10-K weaves a dense, highly specific narrative linking COVID-19 to both realised and prospective risks across virtually every facet of its operations. Overall, the pandemic is positioned as an ongoing, material, multi-dimensional threat whose duration and magnitude remain unknowable. PHM’s 2022 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, high-severity risk that has already produced material, quantifiable consequences and could generate even more acute impacts going forward. Because the filing date (February 2022) is less than two years after the March 2020 pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores (7-10) where the text shows direct, realised, enterprise-wide effects; moderately high scores (5-7) are assigned where impact is prospective or partially mitigated.  No pre-event discount applies, and there are no distant-event statements requiring suppression.  Overall, PHM presents COVID-19 as a dominant, near-term driver of cost, capacity and demand risk, with limited offsets and highly uncertain duration, justifying elevated severity scores across most snippets.

PHM’s 2023-02-06 10-K demonstrates that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a high-severity, present-day risk driver for the company even though the initial outbreak began almost three years earlier.  The filing repeatedly ties ongoing inflation, labour scarcity, and supply-chain bottlenecks directly to pandemic-era disruptions and explicitly states that these conditions are still lengthening build cycles and squeezing margins.  Management admits that certain cost pressures and material shortages that started in 2020 are ‘continuing,’ and that future resurgences or new variants could again materially impair operations, financial performance and cash flows.  Although the narrative also notes some recovery in demand and the company being ‘fully functioning,’ those statements serve mainly as partial mitigants rather than eliminating the risk.  Because the event window (2020-03-11 to the filing date) falls squarely inside the 0-3-year “recent” band of the Time Decay Principle, evidence that shows direct, ongoing, or potentially recurring pandemic impacts receives high scores (7-10), while purely forward-looking or mitigated statements score in the mid-range, and recovery-focused language produces negative (risk-reducing) points.  This blended approach yields an overall high pandemic-risk profile for PHM, tempered only slightly by signs of operational adaptation and market recovery.

PHM’s 2024 Form 10-K still treats COVID-19 as a live, multi-vector threat: past waves depressed demand and margins, but lingering supply-chain knots, labor shortages, cost inflation and mortgage-rate spikes continue to influence operations, while management warns that any new resurgence could again stall construction or sales.  The language is largely qualitative—no single dollar figure is attached—but it expressly ties elevated material-and-labor costs, production delays, pricing pressure and consumer-affordability issues to the pandemic’s direct and indirect after-effects.  Because the filing date is almost four years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic, Time-Decay tempers severity; risks are neither brand-new nor fully abated.  They remain meaningful but now co-exist with mitigating trends (e.g., partial supply-chain recovery).  Accordingly, individual sentence scores fall in the moderate band (≈1-6), reflecting continuing but decaying materiality rather than peak-crisis urgency.

PKG’s 2021 Form 10-K depicts COVID-19 as an event with both realized and still-emerging consequences. The evidence therefore spans a spectrum—from high-impact, quantified losses (scores near 7-8) to purely mitigating language (zero or negative scores)—all calibrated for minimal time-decay because the pandemic remains within the 0-3-year “recent event” window.

PKG’s 2022 filing presents a multifaceted portrayal of COVID-19-related risk.  Although the company’s core packaging operations stayed largely open, the disclosure acknowledges a cascade of direct, already-realised impacts—labour shortages, elevated freight and supply-chain costs, sharp demand destruction in the Paper segment, machine idling, and a goodwill impairment—alongside forward-looking threats from future variants and regulatory mandates. Overall, the risk is recent, partially quantified, and already altering strategy (machine conversion), placing the pandemic squarely in the high-severity zone, albeit moderated by PKG’s ability so far to keep most facilities running and benefit from strong containerboard demand.

PKG’s 2022 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 as both an historical and continuing risk across multiple operational dimensions. Because these effects occurred between 2020 and mid-2022 and management still flags tight labour conditions “exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic,” the overall risk remains material and current, but not existential, yielding mid-to-upper severity scores (5–8) for individual sentences.  Generic, purely hypothetical references earn lower scores, while direct statements of realized disruption receive higher scores.  No meaningful mitigating actions or offsets are disclosed in the cited sentences, so deductions for mitigation are limited.

PKG’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only a single, brief reference to the COVID-19 pandemic. Because the pandemic began almost four years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle also moderates the severity that can be assigned. PLD explicitly acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, material threat that could adversely affect virtually every aspect of its business model—from capital-market access and real-estate valuations to customer solvency and day-to-day operations. Overall, the pandemic is portrayed as an active, un-mitigated threat with potentially severe financial consequences, justifying elevated snippet scores.

PLD’s 2023 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 and future pandemics primarily as an ongoing, enterprise-wide hazard that could materially disrupt operations, value, and liquidity, yet the language remains high-level and largely unquantified. PLD’s 2024 filing still frames COVID-19 and future pandemic conditions as a material, though now longer-tail, enterprise risk. Palantir’s 2021 Form 10-K contains extensive, recent-period discussion of COVID-19. Palantir’s 2022-02-24 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as an active, ongoing threat that has already produced tangible operational effects and that could further erode future performance. Palantir’s 2023-02-21 Form 10-K repeatedly frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, material and multi-dimensional threat. Philip Morris International’s 2021-02-09 Form 10-K embeds a concentrated block of disclosures under “Risks Related to the Impact of COVID-19 on our Business,” supplemented by pandemic references scattered elsewhere in the filing. PMI’s 2022 filing describes COVID-19 as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat that has already produced direct operational disruptions and could materially alter future performance.
