Multiple sentences document realised impacts (temporary factory suspensions, duty-free volume collapse) as well as forward-looking vulnerabilities (supply-chain fragility, labour shortages, credit-market access, regulatory setbacks and demand erosion).  The company stresses that business-continuity plans ‘may not be effective,’ signalling limited mitigation.  Although a few clauses note past resilience (e.g., suspensions “did not materially affect” operations to date), the balance of disclosure is heavily weighted toward significant, multi-channel downside, implying a medium-to-high risk profile.  Given the recency, breadth and potential materiality, individual snippets can justifiably reach upper-range scores (7-8) unless tempered by explicit mitigating language, which the micro-scorecards reflect.

Philip Morris International’s 2023 Form 10-K places the COVID-19 pandemic squarely among its most significant contemporary risk drivers.  Nearly three years after the WHO declared the pandemic, the filing (dated 10 Feb 2023) still frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, material threat rather than a fully historical event.  The company links the pandemic to concrete and prospective impacts: (i) actual operational disruptions (factory, store and office closures; travel and distribution restrictions); (ii) supply-chain fragility, especially shortages of key electronic-device components sourced from single or limited suppliers; (iii) potential demand shifts away from mid- and premium-price brands; and (iv) doubts about the adequacy of existing business-continuity plans.  These statements are mostly forward-looking but anchored in real experience accrued since 2020, and several use strong qualifiers such as “materially adversely impacted.”  Because the filing date falls inside the 0-3-year “recent event” window, Time-Decay allows high severity scores.  However, some snippets carry partial mitigation (e.g., the company notes it has so far secured adequate component supply), which tempers individual scores.  Overall, the extracted evidence paints a picture of a live, multi-faceted risk with direct operational and financial implications that remain unresolved, warranting high—but not maximum—severity ratings across the cited sentences.

Philip Morris International’s 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 primarily as an operational and cost risk that, although originating in 2020, remains relevant four years later.  Management links past pandemic-driven disruptions (mandatory shutdowns, mobility restrictions and acute supply-chain shocks) to present-day vulnerabilities: higher logistics and material costs, the possibility of renewed outbreaks that could idle factories (notably the critical ZYN plant), and potential pricing pressure on agricultural inputs.  All disclosures are couched as ‘could’ or ‘may’ occur, reflecting forward-looking uncertainty rather than an already-quantified hit to 2023 results.  Given the filing date of February 2024, the Time Decay Principle caps severity in the middle range; risks are no longer acute but are still material enough to influence contingency planning and cost structures.  Overall, the language is moderately specific—identifying concrete channels such as supply-chain expense, facility downtime and raw-material inflation—yet lacks fresh quantification or evidence of current impairment.  Accordingly, individual snippets merit medium scores (4-6), consistent with a four-year-old but continuing global-pandemic risk.

PNC’s 2021 Form 10-K discloses extensive, concrete and contemporaneous impacts from COVID-19 across virtually every dimension of the bank’s operations.  Management describes both realised damage – e.g., a “substantial decrease in economic activity,” branch closures, work-from-home execution problems and rising credit-loss volatility – and an explicit expectation that these pressures will “continue” and could be “material.”  The language is largely specific, tied to measurable operational levers (staffing levels, branch formats, deposit flows, fee waivers, credit costs) and to well-defined macro shocks (unemployment spike, Fed policy at the zero lower bound).  Because the filing date (26 Feb 2021) is less than one year after the WHO declaration of a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores: the risk is recent, ongoing, and already affecting earnings and capital planning.  No meaningful mitigating language offsets these statements; most caveats are conditional (“may,” “likely”) but are overwhelmed by the multitude of concrete impacts already recognised.  Taken together, the evidence signals a high, persistent risk profile directly attributable to the global pandemic.

PNC’s 2021 Form 10-K, filed on 25 February 2022—well within three years of the WHO’s declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic—contains an extensive, dedicated risk factor describing both the realised and prospective impacts of the pandemic on the bank.  The language is direct, repeatedly linking COVID-19 to material adverse effects on PNC’s business, credit quality, liquidity, labour force and customers.  The disclosure mixes backward-looking evidence (e.g., actual declines in travel-related sectors, Fed rate cuts) with forward-looking uncertainty, emphasising that many impacts are ‘likely to continue’ or ‘persist after the pandemic.’  It cites concrete transmission channels that regulators care about—demand destruction, supply-chain disruptions, labour shortages, remote-work effects on commercial real estate, and sector-specific credit risk.  Although the filing notes some offsets (e.g., deposit growth, macro improvement), these are portrayed as fragile or uncertain.  Given the recency of the pandemic, the explicit statement of possible ‘material’ damage, and the breadth of operational and credit channels identified, the overall severity is high.  Applying the Time-Decay Principle for a 0-3-year-old event, the most persuasive sentences merit scores in the upper mid-to-high range (7-10) while moderating for any mitigating language.

PNC’s 2023 Form 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 as a live, enterprise-wide risk driver.  Although the initial shock is almost three years old, management still attributes current macro-economic uncertainty, supply-chain bottlenecks, labour-market tightness and the persistence of remote-work patterns to pandemic after-effects.  The filing highlights several forward-looking pathways through which these conditions could erode credit quality, squeeze profitability, alter capital-return flexibility and raise operating costs (e.g., through new legislation and digital-acceleration spend).  The language is mostly qualitative—there are no hard dollar figures—but it repeatedly links specific business lines (commercial real-estate, credit portfolios, technology spend, capital distributions) to potential downside outcomes that could be “material.”  Because the disclosure is recent (Feb-2023) and the pandemic period lies well within the 0-3-year high-relevance window, time-decay is minimal.  Nevertheless, the absence of quantified impacts or explicit stress metrics tempers severity.  Overall, the pandemic remains a significant, ongoing risk for PNC, warranting upper-mid scores (5–8) for the strongest statements and lower scores where impacts are more indirect or generic.

PNC’s 2023 Form 10-K filings reference COVID-19 mostly in the context of lingering, structural after-effects rather than acute, company-specific shocks.  The bank frames the pandemic as a catalyst for secular changes—most notably the persistence of remote work and the resulting weakness in certain commercial-real-estate segments—and as a precedent for possible future regulatory constraints on capital distributions.  The language is primarily forward-looking, stressing uncertainty and potential vulnerability rather than disclosing quantified, realised losses.  Because the filing date (February 2024) is just under four years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places the evidence in a medium-term window: risks remain relevant but should not receive the highest severity scores.  Overall, the statements are moderately specific (they single out commercial real-estate demand and reference prior Fed dividend restrictions) yet still largely qualitative, so individual snippet scores cluster in the 4-6 range, reflecting material but unquantified, medium-term risk.

PNR’s 2021-02-16 Form 10-K provides an unusually detailed, forward-looking and backward-looking discussion of COVID-19.  The filing date is within 12 months of the WHO pandemic declaration (11 March 2020), so Time-Decay permits high severity scores (0-3 years bucket).  Management discloses both realised impacts – factory shutdowns, absenteeism, $10.4 million in incremental safety costs, supply-chain delays, higher freight and labour – and still-uncertain but probable future harms such as persistent demand reductions in multiple end-markets, potential liquidity strain and further regulatory lockdowns.  The language is specific (“material”, “significantly impacted”, names end-markets, quantifies costs) and ties each operational vector (demand, supply chain, labour, capital markets) directly to the pandemic.  Although the company notes mitigation efforts (remote work, alternate suppliers, cost-cutting), these are outweighed by the breadth, immediacy and materiality of the threats.  Therefore, individual snippets generally warrant high risk scores (7-10).  Mitigating components reduce some scores slightly, but none of the evidence is older than three years, so no Time-Decay cap is triggered below the recent-event ceiling of 10.

The filing, dated February 22 2022—well within three years of the WHO’s March 11 2020 pandemic declaration—devotes an extensive, highly specific risk-factor section to COVID-19.  The company states that it has already suffered material disruptions (e.g., lower demand in certain end-markets, facility absenteeism, supply-chain bottlenecks, inflationary cost spikes) and warns these impacts could intensify or recur.  The language is mostly concrete and backward-looking ("have experienced") with quantified operational channels such as logistics, labor attrition, regulatory vaccine mandates, and inability to meet backlog, but also contains forward-looking uncertainty about unknown duration, variants, and macro-economic deterioration.  There are virtually no strong mitigating statements beyond generic efforts (monitoring suppliers, price increases).  Under the Time Decay Principle the event is classified as “recent,” so high scores (7-10) are permissible.  Where the text discloses realised, continuing, and potentially material impacts, snippets are scored at the upper end; where risk is contingent or generic, mid-high scores are used; and modest mitigants result in small point deductions.  No snippet exceeds 10 because none provides a specific quantified dollar figure, yet the breadth and seriousness of impacts justify scores largely between 6 and 9.

PNR’s 2023 Form 10-K repeatedly describes COVID-19 as both an historical and continuing driver of adverse outcomes across demand, labour availability, manufacturing continuity and supply-chain logistics.  The company states that it has already experienced revenue declines, facility absenteeism and supply delays in 2020–2022, and warns that government restrictions, future outbreaks or variant waves could once again shut plants, slow shipping and erode margins.  Although no precise dollar amounts are disclosed, the language is concrete (“have been and may continue to be negatively impacted”, “material negative impact”, “significantly impacted economic activity”) and ties the pandemic to multiple operational vectors (customer demand, workforce, logistics, liquidity).  Because the filing date (21 Feb 2023) is within three years of the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores (7-10).  However, the absence of quantified losses or specific forward guidance tempers each individual snippet.  Overall, the pandemic remains an elevated, current-period threat with persistent uncertainty, justifying high-moderate scores across the extracted evidence.

Pentair’s 2024 filing references the COVID-19 pandemic only in broad, precautionary language embedded within general supply-chain and business-interruption risk factors. The company frames pandemics as one of several uncontrollable events that *could* impede production, delay deliveries, raise logistics costs, and erode profitability. No quantified dollar impact, historical loss, or specific operational change (e.g., remote-work protocols) is provided. These statements therefore represent forward-looking, hypothetical risks rather than current impairments. Because the pandemic’s onset is now just under four years old, the Time Decay Principle dictates that evidence be scored in the “medium-term” band (4-6 maximum). Taken together, the sentences show continuing—but unquantified—exposure to pandemic-driven supply-chain shocks, warranting a moderate overall risk assessment.

The filing was made in February 2022—well within the 0-3-year ‘recent-event’ window for the COVID-19 pandemic that began in March 2020—so Time Decay allows relatively high risk scores.  PNW (through its subsidiary APS) discloses both realized and prospective impacts.  The company cites concrete historical effects (shifts in load profile, higher bad-debt expense, liquidity actions, and incremental O&M costs for PPE) alongside a broad catalogue of forward-looking vulnerabilities (demand destruction, supply-chain disruption, labour shortages tied to vaccine mandates, project delays, capital-market volatility, etc.).  Most statements are specific to the utility’s operations, although only a few give hard numbers; therefore they warrant mid-to-high single-digit scores rather than a maximum 10.  Mitigating language is limited (e.g., revolver repaid, continued access to CP market), so deductions are modest.  Overall, COVID-19 presents a material, multi-faceted, and continuing risk to PNW’s revenues, costs, liquidity and workforce, justifying cumulative evidentiary scores skewed toward the higher end of the recent-event scale.

The filing, dated February 27 2023, discusses COVID-19 expressly in the risk-factor section, framing the pandemic as an ongoing, still-evolving threat.  Because the first U.S. outbreak and WHO declaration occurred in March 2020, the event is well within the 0-3-year ‘recent’ window; therefore, elevated severity scores are permissible under the Time Decay Principle.  Management’s language is predominantly forward-looking ("could" and "may") rather than citing hard numbers, yet it goes beyond boiler-plate by enumerating concrete channels of exposure: diminished electricity demand, supply-chain interruptions, higher operating costs, labour constraints, capital-market volatility affecting financing, project delays, and increased credit losses.  These disclosures indicate a multifaceted risk profile that is material to both operations and cash-flow.  No meaningful mitigating controls are offered in the cited sentences, so little downward adjustment is warranted.  Overall, I assess the COVID-19 pandemic risk to PNW as high but unquantified; individual snippets earn scores ranging from 2 (headline-level statement) to 8 (detailed catalogue of potential adverse effects), consistent with a recent, specific yet largely qualitative risk narrative.

The filing does not explicitly mention COVID-19 or a pandemic, yet it still reflects lingering, systemic issues that first surfaced during the pandemic era—most notably global supply-chain fragility.  The company warns that constrained supply chains are delaying projects and raising equipment costs, and concedes that nationwide supply-chain impacts have already produced cost inflation.  These statements are prospective (they describe exposure that ‘may be exacerbated’) and contemporaneous (they acknowledge current delays and added costs), but they remain generic: no dollar figures, no direct causal tie to COVID-19, and no discussion of labour shortages or remote-work challenges.  Because the pandemic began four years before the 27-Feb-2024 filing, the Time Decay Principle places the event in the “medium-term” window where maximum scores should be moderate (≈4-6).  Given the absence of explicit pandemic language and any quantification, the evidentiary strength is modest; the disclosures confirm continuing exposure to supply-chain disruption but do not rise to the level of a severe, quantified pandemic impact.  Overall, the risk evidence merits low-to-moderate scores that reflect indirect, ongoing vulnerability rather than direct, material shock.

PODD’s February 2021 Form 10-K contains a concentrated block of disclosures that tie the COVID-19 pandemic to multiple, material risk vectors: (i) an already-felt drag on financial performance; (ii) prospective erosion of demand as unemployment and loss of insurance squeeze consumers; (iii) acute and chronic supply-chain fragility linked to factory shutdowns, worker shortages, logistics interruptions and China-centric manufacturing concentration; (iv) operational re-engineering to remote work that spawns cyber-security exposure; and (v) regulatory-process delays that could defer future product launches.  All of these statements are recent (within one year of the 11 March 2020 pandemic declaration), largely company-specific, and many acknowledge impacts that are occurring now, not merely hypothetical.  Although no dollar amounts are offered, the language repeatedly references “material adverse effect,” underscoring severity.  Taking Time Decay into account, the evidence warrants upper-mid scores (4-7 range): high because the event is current and multifaceted, but not maximal because impacts are described qualitatively rather than quantitatively and a few mitigating notes (e.g., China back to pre-COVID levels) appear.

PODD’s 2022 Form-10-K provides a recent-event (within 0-3 years) discussion of the COVID-19 pandemic that is both backward-looking (actual impacts) and forward-looking (continuing exposure).  The filing discloses realised negatives such as delayed FDA clearance of Omnipod 5, weaker new-customer starts, supply-chain volatility and labour shortages, while also warning of further threats to production capacity in China, logistics, consumer demand, cyber-security and clinical-trial timelines.  These statements are largely qualitative and un-quantified, yet they are explicit, company-specific and reference potentially “material adverse” effects on revenue, operations and financial condition, thus meriting medium-to-high risk scores under the Time Decay Principle.  Mitigating language appears in several places (e.g., current manufacturing back at pre-COVID levels, recurring-revenue model, successful supply-chain mitigation, pandemic-driven increase in Drug-Delivery revenue), tempering some of the severity.  Overall, the pandemic remains a multifaceted, active threat and, despite partial mitigation, represents a significant ongoing risk (aggregate severity impression ≈7/10).

PODD’s 2023 Form 10-K embeds a relatively rich, recent-vintage discussion of COVID-19.  The company expressly states that the pandemic has already affected results and may continue to do so, enumerating concrete impact channels—supply-chain interruptions, labor shortages, demand contraction, remote-work cyber-risk, regulatory delays, and potential manufacturing stoppages in China.  Most of the language is framed in the present-to-near-term tense (e.g., “have been and may continue,” “are continuing to cause”), confirming that management views the threat as ongoing rather than purely hypothetical.  While a few mitigating notes appear (e.g., production back to pre-COVID levels in China; successful inventory builds), they do not eliminate exposure; they merely temper it.  Because the filing date (24-Feb-2023) sits less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits high per-sentence scores (up to 10).  Overall, the disclosures reveal a material, multi-faceted risk that is partly realized and still forward-looking, justifying mid-to-high snippet scores depending on specificity, immediacy, and the presence of mitigants.

PODD’s 2024 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 as both a historical and continuing risk driver across several operational dimensions—supply-chain resilience, labor practices, cybersecurity, regulatory timelines and overall business demand.  Nearly four years have passed since the WHO declaration (March 2020), placing the disclosure at the cusp between the “recent” and “medium-term” Time-Decay buckets.  The language therefore mixes concrete, backward-looking impacts (e.g., FDA approval delays, forced remote-work shift) with forward-looking contingency statements (“may”, “could”).  No new quantified dollar impact is provided, but the company still flags material exposure (“significantly impact”, “materially disrupt”), showing the threat remains strategically relevant.  Given the absence of fresh, quantified losses but the presence of specific operational examples, the overall COVID-19 risk profile is assessed as moderate—serious enough to warrant attention (scores in the 3-6 range), yet somewhat attenuated by the passage of time and by the forward-looking, contingency-style phrasing that dominates several passages.

POOL’s 2021 10-K places the COVID-19 pandemic squarely in the category of an active, near-term enterprise risk.  The filing explicitly documents (a) realized, quantified financial damage in early 2020 (a $6.9 million impairment and sales declines), (b) operational disruptions such as temporary facility closures in Europe and sporadic U.S. shutdowns, and (c) forward-looking exposures ranging from renewed stay-at-home mandates to supply-chain strain and potential reversal of the pandemic-generated demand surge.  Although the company benefited from “home-centric” trends in the short run, management stresses that these gains may be unsustainable and that future impacts “may be worse than we anticipate.”  The language is therefore both backward-looking (realized impacts) and forward-looking (persistent uncertainty), and it spans multiple risk vectors—demand volatility, supply-chain interruptions, labor / facility availability, and financial impairment.  Because the filing date (Feb-2021) is within one year of the WHO declaration (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Quantified impairments and specific operational effects warrant the highest micro-scores, while more generic or mitigated statements receive lower or even negative scores to reflect offsetting factors such as the “essential business” designation or temporary nature of some closures.

POOL’s 2022 filing discusses COVID-19 almost entirely in the Risk Factors and MD&A sections, framing the pandemic as a still-unfolding, multi-dimensional threat that sits squarely within the 0-3-year ‘recent’ window of the Time-Decay Principle.  Management acknowledges both realised effects (government lockdowns, store-hour limitations, unprecedented demand swings) and forward-looking exposures (future variants, supply-chain fragility, labour-market pressure and the possibility that home-centric demand will reverse).  The language is moderately specific—detailing supply-chain bottlenecks, essential-business status, and the need for sanitation protocols—but stops short of quantifying dollar impacts.  Several mitigating statements appear (e.g., “thus far supply chain not materially impacted,” essential-business designation), but these are hedged with caveats (“no assurances”).  Overall, the narrative portrays a material but manageable risk whose severity is amplified by uncertainty and potential volatility in consumer demand and sourcing, justifying mid-to-upper single-digit snippet scores under the recent-event category.

POOL’s 2023 filing presents COVID-19 risk as both a recently-realised operational shock and a still-unfolding strategic uncertainty.  Management acknowledges that the pandemic initially lifted demand (home-centric spending) but simultaneously strained the company’s global supply chain, squeezed product availability, and complicated labour markets.  The narrative combines concrete historical impacts (e.g., 2021–2022 sourcing problems) with forward-looking language that future variants or other public-health crises could be “worse than we anticipate.”  These disclosures are largely company-specific (supply chain, labour, profitability) and fall within the 0-to-3-year window, so the Time Decay Principle permits high per-snippet scores.  Mitigating factors—recent supply-chain improvements, vaccination progress, and prior sales gains—temper but do not erase the residual risk because management repeatedly stresses continuing uncertainty and the possibility of renewed disruptions.  Overall, the risk profile is assessed as moderately high: material impacts have already occurred, structural vulnerabilities (supplier concentration, labour expectations) remain, and the ultimate trajectory of consumer demand and variant outbreaks is unresolved.

POOL’s 2024 filing treats COVID-19 as an event whose acute phase has passed but whose after-effects still shape operating risk. Management acknowledges that the pandemic initially boosted demand (a mitigating historical fact) yet now frames the issue as a forward-looking, multi-faceted threat: potential fresh outbreaks, long-tail supply-chain fragility, labour-market pressures, and volatility in discretionary consumer spending on pools and backyard products. All references are qualitative—no dollar figures or probability weights—so the evidence is less severe than a quantified impairment but stronger than boiler-plate because it cites concrete transmission channels (workforce, supply chain, pricing, consumer demand). Applying the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is now four years old; therefore, individual snippet scores must sit in the moderate band (4-6) unless the language is heavily mitigated or merely historical. Overall, the risk profile is assessed as ‘moderate but persistent’, warranting mid-range scoring across the extracted sentences.

PPG’s 2020 Form 10-K leaves little doubt that the COVID-19 pandemic is both an already-realised and still-evolving threat to the company.  The filing, dated February 2021—well within one year of the WHO declaration—contains multiple, explicit statements that the pandemic has materially hurt net sales, disrupted supply chains, depressed demand across key end-markets (automotive OEM, aerospace, protective & marine), and forced the company to launch a $176 million restructuring.  These impacts are described as current (“have negatively impacted”), continuing (“will continue to adversely impact”) and open-ended (“cannot predict the duration or scope”).  The language is specific—citing shutdowns, reduced ability to supply product, mid-digit to double-digit volume declines and a 15 % drop in automotive OEM sales—yet generally unquantified at the total-company level, which tempers severity somewhat.  Mitigating references (cost-savings, higher selling prices, restructuring, and expected volume rebounds) offset but do not neutralise the risk, because the adverse factors are already embedded in 2020 financials and management still forecasts inflationary and demand pressures.  Under the Time Decay Principle, a February 2021 filing discussing a 2020 event qualifies for high potential scores (7-10) when impacts are direct and quantified; moderately lower scores (3-6) are warranted where impacts are generic, forward-looking or partially mitigated.  The micro-scorecards below apply this framework sentence-by-sentence.

PPG’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an immediate and continuing threat that has already impaired the company’s operations, supply chain and financial performance, while also warning of material, unquantifiable future damage.  The narrative repeatedly links the pandemic to concrete cost inflation, supply constraints, labor shortfalls and diminished demand, demonstrating that impacts are not hypothetical but realized and ongoing.  Language such as “have been and will continue,” “significantly impacted,” and “cannot be reasonably estimated, but could be material” underscores both current harm and high residual uncertainty.  Because the filing date (Feb 2022) falls less than two years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores (upper-mid to high single digits).  No sentences provide meaningful mitigation beyond generic price-increase efforts, so most evidence remains strongly aggravating.  Overall, the risk profile is high, recent, and company-specific, justifying robust—but sub-maximum—scores across the extracted evidence.

PPG’s 2023-02-16 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as an immediate and still-evolving threat that has already damaged—and is expected to keep pressuring—the company’s finances, operations and supply chain.  Nearly three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, management continues to cite specific, realised impacts: lower sales, supply chain and logistics interruptions, labour shortages and region-specific demand weakness (notably China and Europe).  The disclosures emphasise persistency ("have been and will continue"), breadth (suppliers, customers, distribution channels) and potential materiality, while admitting that the ultimate magnitude and duration remain unpredictable.  Although some mitigating actions are noted (price increases, geographical diversification), these are framed mostly as partial offsets rather than full remedies.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is a “recent” event (0-3 years), so high severity scores (7-10) are appropriate where statements show direct, quantified or continuing impacts; moderate scores (2-6) apply to generic or partly-mitigated references.  No snippet predates the event, so no score is forced to zero by timing alone.

The filing explicitly recognises COVID-19 as both a past and continuing source of operational and financial stress for PPG.  Management recounts concrete historical damage to liquidity, supply continuity, labour availability and customer demand, while also warning that similar conditions could recur in future public-health crises.  The language is largely qualitative—no dollar figures are provided—but it is detailed, naming specific impact channels such as business shutdowns, workforce shortages and reduced demand.  Because the pandemic’s outbreak is now roughly four years old, the Time-Decay Principle caps individual sentence scores in the mid-range; the risk is still clearly live (PPG cites lingering demand deficits and Q1-2023 disruptions in China), but it is no longer at peak severity.  Overall, the disclosures paint a moderate yet persistent risk profile that justifies mid-band scores (4-6) for each piece of evidence.

PRU’s 2021 filing portrays COVID-19 as a pervasive, still-unfolding threat that cuts across every major risk category the company tracks.  The disclosures are forward-looking as well as backward-looking – they cite the very real disruptions experienced in 2020 (market volatility, interest-rate collapse, operational upheaval, liquidity draws) and stress that these pressures ‘may continue’ or ‘may worsen’.  The language is specific, linking the pandemic to sharply higher mortality, potential disability spikes, derailment of ALM and hedging tactics, pressure on solvency ratios, remote-work vulnerabilities, and reduced product demand.  Although quantitative figures are scarce, the company repeatedly uses strong qualifiers such as ‘materially adversely affect’, ‘elevated’, ‘significant reduction’, signalling management’s judgment that the impacts could be severe.  Because the 2021-02-19 filing date is less than one year after the WHO declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Mitigating language (e.g., descriptions of liquidity actions already taken) is present but does not dominate; most statements emphasise residual or future risk.  Taken together, the evidence indicates a high, continuing risk profile directly tied to the global pandemic, warranting snippet scores mostly in the 8-10 range.

PRU’s 2022 10-K ties the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic to multiple core risk pillars—investment, insurance, market, liquidity and operational.  The language is largely contemporaneous (reflecting experience in 2020-2021 and explicitly projecting future effects) and identifies concrete negative mechanisms: defaults in the asset portfolio, excess mortality, higher disability claims, market volatility, liquidity strain, and operational fragility from prolonged remote work.  These are not remote hypotheticals; the filing affirms that COVID-19 has already produced elevated losses and stresses and states it "may continue" to do so.  The disclosures are company-specific (e.g., Group Insurance morbidity, liquidity draws, hedging constraints) rather than boiler-plate, yet they remain largely unquantified.  Given the filing date (February 2022—well within three years of the March 2020 World Health Organization declaration), the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Overall, the pandemic is portrayed as an active, multi-year threat with limited mitigation discussion, justifying upper-tier snippet scores (7-9) for direct financial impacts and mid-tier scores (5-6) where wording is broader or partly mitigated.

PRU’s 2023 filing treats the COVID-19 pandemic as a still-material, enterprise-wide threat whose ramifications span underwriting losses, capital-markets stress, operational disruption and mortality volatility.  Management discloses that the pandemic has already produced a “significant net negative impact” on underwriting, especially in Group Insurance, Individual Life and International lines, while only partially offset by gains in certain pension-transfer products.  The text also underscores that COVID-19 continues to shape forward-looking actuarial assumptions and could re-emerge through new variants, thereby keeping future results at risk.  Although some mitigating language appears—e.g., embedding pandemic assumptions into pricing models and noting vaccine efficacy—these steps do not eliminate the exposure.  Given the filing date (February 2023) and the event window (since March 2020), the disclosures fall inside the 0-to-3-year “recent” band, so snippet scores may range as high as 10.  Most sentences provide qualitative (not quantified) evidence of ongoing or realised impacts, so severity scores cluster in the mid-to-high range (5-7) when direct financial harm is cited, and lower (0-4) when the wording is generic or heavily caveated by mitigations.

The filing acknowledges pandemic risk primarily through two lenses: (i) direct insurance exposure to excess mortality and morbidity and (ii) enterprise-wide operational disruption.  Statements are forward-looking—there is no historic COVID-19 loss disclosure—but they explicitly link a pandemic to earnings erosion, capital strain, forced asset sales and business-continuity breakdowns.  Because the Form 10-K is dated February 2024, COVID-19 remains a recent (≤ 4 years) event under the Time-Decay Principle, so evidence can score toward the higher end of the scale.  Nevertheless, the narrative is largely qualitative and un-quantified; it outlines potential, not realised, impacts and offers no new mitigation steps beyond the generic risk framework.  Accordingly, the overall evidence weight is “high-moderate”: material risk is clearly identified, but without hard numbers or fresh COVID-specific disclosures.  The extracted snippets therefore earn mid-to-upper single-digit scores—significant, but not the maximum severity that a quantified, realised loss would command.

Public Storage’s 2022 Form 10-K devotes an explicit subsection of Item 1A to the “COVID Pandemic,” signalling that management still views the virus as a live, material threat less than two years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  The language is forward-looking but grounded in experience: the company recounts concrete operational constraints already imposed (rent caps, eviction moratoria, delayed construction) while warning that future variants (Delta, Omicron) or new pathogens could re-impose or widen those limits.  Multiple demand-side channels are identified—economic contraction, unemployment, remote-work–driven population shifts—and supply-side pressures such as labour health risks and capital-market dislocation are also flagged.  Although no dollar amounts are assigned, the filing repeatedly uses high-salience phrases such as “material impact,” “negative impacts,” and “could lead to lower occupancies,” reinforcing severity.  Because the filing date (22 Feb 2022) falls well within the 0-3-year “recent event” window, Time Decay allows elevated scores.  Mitigation language is minimal (little about vaccines or contingency planning), so most statements remain aggravating.  Overall, the COVID-19 discussion presents a high but unquantified residual risk that warrants upper-mid scores (5-8) for individual sentences, depending on their specificity and evidence of realised impact.

PSA’s 2024 filing contains a discrete subsection devoted to “public health and other crises,” with COVID-19 cited as the exemplar.  The company expressly states that the pandemic has already ‘adversely impacted’ operations and enumerates six operational and financial vectors—health and safety, demand destruction, population migration, regulatory curbs, customer-mix deterioration, and capital-market stress.  Elsewhere, the filing documents concrete historical government restrictions during COVID-19 that limited facility use, rent increases, rent collection, evictions and completion of development projects, while warning that comparable measures could recur.  Although no hard dollar figures are provided, the language is specific, multi-dimensional, and acknowledges both realised and continuing exposure.  Because the pandemic onset is now roughly four years old, the Time Decay Principle places the event in the medium-term category (4-10 years), capping individual snippet severity at a moderate level (approximately 4-6).  Overall, the risk evidence is forward-looking but grounded in past disruption, warranting mid-range scores that reflect persistent, material—but not fresh—threats.

Phillips 66’s 2021 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic directly to both realized and potential future harm across virtually every line of business.  The company discloses that the pandemic has already produced materially adverse effects—such as collapsed product demand, negative oil prices, reduced refinery utilization, $4 billion of losses and impairments—and it warns that these impacts are expected to persist as long as travel restrictions and economic weakness continue.  The language is recent, specific and framed in operational, financial‐statement and counterparty terms, not merely hypothetical.  Because the filing date (24-Feb-2021) falls well within three years of the WHO’s 11-Mar-2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  While the text does note cost-cutting and liquidity actions, the thrust is overwhelmingly on ongoing exposure and uncertainty, so mitigating factors are limited.  Accordingly, individual sentences earn scores predominately in the 5–9 range, reflecting fresh, concrete and enterprise-wide risk with only modest offsets.

COVID-19 is treated by PSX as a recent, already-materialised risk that continues to cast a shadow over future performance.  The filing cites factual 2020 demand collapses, identifies specific business lines most hurt (especially Refining) and repeatedly uses high-severity language such as “material adverse effect.”  While no dollar figures are offered, the company makes clear that the pandemic lowered earnings in 2020–2021 and could do so again if new variants or government restrictions re-emerge.  Management also flags second-order effects—supply-chain tension, customer default risk, labour availability—that COVID-19 could amplify.  Mitigating elements (vaccine roll-out, demand recovery) are mentioned only briefly and speculatively, so they do little to offset the risk narrative.  Because the event is within the 0-3-year “recent” window, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores; however, the absence of quantified dollar impacts and acknowledgement of some recovery restrain most sentences to the 6-9 range rather than a maximum 10.

Phillips 66 frames the COVID-19 pandemic as both a realized and continuing enterprise-wide hazard.  The filing, dated February 2023—less than three years after the WHO declaration—places the discussion squarely in the ‘recent-event’ window, so Time Decay is minimal.  Management discloses that the pandemic already caused a “serious adverse impact” by sharply reducing demand for core products such as gasoline, jet fuel and diesel.  They also warn that renewed outbreaks or even the *perception* of health risk could again depress volumes, magnify other risk factors (e.g., supply-chain fragility, customer default and utilization rates) and generate material but presently un-quantifiable financial losses.  Language is strong (“material adverse effect,” “significantly reduced”), global in scope, tied directly to demand destruction and operational disruption, and forward-looking about residual uncertainty (duration, vaccine rollout, containment measures).  No meaningful mitigations or offsets are offered beyond general uncertainty statements.  Accordingly, the overall COVID-19 risk profile remains high—consistent with 7-10 range scores under the Time Decay Principle—with individual snippets graded according to specificity, directness, materiality and any mitigating caveats.

Phillips 66 frames COVID-19 primarily as a recently experienced shock that produced a “serious” and “material” decline in product demand, while also cautioning that future pandemics (or resurgences) could replicate or amplify those effects.  The company links the pandemic directly to reduced demand for crude oil and refined products, signalling that revenue and margin compression already occurred.  At the same time, management positions the threat as ongoing and multifaceted—able to reignite supply-chain interruptions, depress capacity utilisation, raise logistics costs and cascade into other risk categories.  The language is specific about causal mechanisms (e.g., travel restrictions, vaccine timing, perceived infection risk), but it stops short of providing hard numbers.  Because the filing date (Feb 2024) is roughly four years after the WHO declaration (Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places this evidence in the 4-10 year “medium-term” bracket, capping appropriate severity in the mid-range.  Overall, the disclosures reflect a meaningful, but not current-year-acute, risk; historical impacts are confirmed, and persistence is deemed plausible but uncertain.  Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster between 4 and 6, reflecting moderate residual risk without quantified forward losses or imminent crisis language.

PTC’s 2021 Form 10-K ties the still-unfolding COVID-19 pandemic directly to multiple, material pressure points across its value chain.  The filing moves beyond generic boiler-plate by citing concrete, already-experienced impacts—declines in software demand, customer plant shutdowns, and impediments to in-person sales work—while also flagging forward-looking scenarios such as increased churn and reduced renewals.  The company acknowledges that, although its own transition to remote work was smooth, the larger ecosystem of manufacturers and prospects remains disrupted, creating macro-economic uncertainty that could ‘materially adversely affect’ results.  These statements are recent (within 0-3 years of the pandemic’s onset) and emphasize direct operational and financial consequences, so the Time Decay Principle permits elevated risk scores.  Mitigating language does appear (e.g., smooth internal remote transition, potential upside for remote-work software), but it is outweighed by the breadth and immediacy of the identified threats.  Overall, the disclosure signals a high, ongoing risk profile that is actively influencing revenue, ARR growth, sales execution and customer renewal behavior.

PTC’s 2022-11-15 filing discusses COVID-19 primarily as a catalyst for a structural shift toward remote work among its global customer base and as a source of tangible revenue disruption to its own professional-services operations. The disclosure blends backward-looking evidence of actual harm (lower FY’21 services revenue) with forward-looking uncertainty about whether remote-work patterns will persist and whether PTC’s product mix can fully address that demand. The language is event-specific (explicitly naming the pandemic), recent (within three years), and acknowledges both operational and competitive exposures, yet it stops short of quantifying dollar amounts or citing supply-chain or labor-shortage impacts. Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 remains a “recent” event, so high—but not maximum—severity scores are warranted. Overall, the risk is material and continuing, but partially mitigated by PTC’s existing SaaS/remote-work capabilities and its ongoing platform transition, yielding moderate-to-high risk scores for the extracted evidence.

A thorough review of the November 20 2023 PTC filing shows that the company does not explicitly reference “COVID-19,” “coronavirus,” or “pandemic.”  Instead, the only language that tangentially overlaps with pandemic-era concerns is a single, general statement about “earlier and ongoing supply chain disruptions.”  Because the company neither attributes those disruptions to the pandemic nor discusses related issues such as remote-work transitions, employee illness, or demand shocks, the disclosure is generic and indirect.  Consequently, any connection to the COVID-19 Pandemic is weak and highly inferential.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic is now in the 3-to-4-year window, so even strong, explicit disclosures would merit only moderate scores (4-6).  Given the absence of a direct link, the residual risk signal is minimal, and the overall severity assessment is low.

The 2024-11-14 filing contains only indirect, residual references to pandemic-type pressures—principally ‘earlier and ongoing supply-chain disruptions’ and knock-on demand uncertainty. PTC does not expressly cite COVID-19, nor does it quantify any related financial hit. Instead, management bundles supply-chain turbulence into a broader macroeconomic risk set that could still dampen manufacturer spending. Because the pandemic began more than four years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle caps any individual snippet at a moderate level (roughly 4-6) even when the language is aggravating. The absence of explicit pandemic attribution and the use of conditional verbs (“could,” “may”) further dilute severity. Overall, the company acknowledges lingering, global operational headwinds consistent with the COVID-19 aftermath, but the disclosures remain generic and forward-looking rather than reporting concrete, current damage. Accordingly, the available evidence supports only modest risk scores.

PWR’s 2021-03-01 filing discusses COVID-19 as a live, multi-faceted threat that is already eroding operations and profitability while remaining highly unpredictable.  Statements repeatedly use strong qualifiers such as “materially affected,” “negatively impacted,” “suspensions and delays,” and “uncertain duration,” showing that the risk is both current and prospective.  The company cites concrete transmission paths—shelter-in-place orders, permitting delays, labour availability, supply-chain bottlenecks, customer financial distress, and reduced downstream energy demand—indicating broad exposure across revenue streams.  No dollar figures are given, but the language conveys enterprise-level severity and acknowledges that mitigation is limited and outcomes remain indeterminate.  Because the 2020 pandemic is well within the 0-3-year window, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  Overall risk is assessed as high: direct, already realised impacts with continuing downside potential and only generic or nascent mitigation described.

PWR’s 2022 filing describes COVID-19 as both an already-realized shock and an ongoing, hard-to-quantify threat that permeates nearly every part of the company’s value chain.  Management discloses that the pandemic has “materially affected” operations, naming concrete disruptions to Canadian, Australian, U.S. metro and Latin-American units, regulatory and permitting delays, labour attrition tied to vaccination mandates, and suspended or delayed high-pressure turnaround services.  Although no dollar amounts are supplied, the language is unmistakably strong—“material adverse,” “significant,” “continues to impact”—and spans supply-chain, workforce, customer-demand and compliance dimensions.  These statements combine backward-looking evidence (actual business impacts in 2020-2021) with forward-looking uncertainty (duration, future cash-flow effects, potential penalties, cyber-attack exposure).  Under the Time Decay principle, COVID-19 is a recent, still-unfolding event (within 0-3 years of the 2022 filing), so high severity scores are warranted.  No meaningful mitigating language (e.g., insurance recovery, hedging, or fully executed contingency plans) appears.  Overall, the disclosure signals a high-level, multi-faceted risk that remains active and could further erode margins, liquidity or strategic execution.

The filing, dated February 23 2023, references COVID-19 chiefly as an external shock that has already produced tangible impacts (e.g., lost industrial‐services demand in 2020–2021 and current cross-border labor delays) while also framing the virus as an ongoing macro-level uncertainty that could weaken future demand, disrupt supply chains and constrain workforce mobility.  Because the pandemic is still within the 0–3-year “recent-event” window, the Time Decay Principle allows higher severity scores where the company cites concrete, realized effects.  Only one sentence delivers a clearly realized operational impact, while several others discuss continuing or potential impacts in broader, less specific terms, often bundled with other risks.  Accordingly, evidence showing direct, dated consequences receives upper-mid scores (6–7), whereas generic, catch-all listings receive very low scores (0–2).  The overall risk posture is therefore assessed as moderate-to-elevated: the company has experienced measurable disruptions but largely treats COVID-19 as one of many external variables rather than an existential threat.

The filing, dated four years after WHO’s declaration of COVID-19 as a pandemic, frames pandemic exposure primarily as an ongoing but generalized risk factor.  References to “public-health crises (e.g., pandemics)” appear repetitively in multi-factor bullet lists that discuss quarterly earnings volatility, project delays, contract claims, and international demand.  Only one sentence explicitly names “COVID-19,” and it does so in a retrospective context—customer spending that had been deferred is now resuming—suggesting that the most acute operational impacts have largely worked through the system.  No language quantifies current financial exposure, nor does management identify material supply-chain or labour disruptions attributable to COVID-19 that remain unresolved.  Accordingly, the disclosures are forward-looking, largely generic, and serve more as standard risk boiler-plate than as evidence of a present, material drag on performance.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, a 2020 event evaluated in a 2024 filing falls into the 4-to-10-year “medium-term” window, implying moderate severity scores (roughly 4-6).  Because the statements are mostly unquantified, broad and partially mitigated by recovery in customer spending, each snippet receives a mid-range score, with no item exceeding 5.

PayPal’s 2021-02-05 Form 10-K embeds an extensive, multi-faceted discussion of the COVID-19 pandemic.  The filing repeatedly acknowledges that the pandemic is already producing concrete, material effects (e.g., merchant failures, higher credit losses, remote-work disruption) while also flagging substantial forward-looking uncertainty tied to public-health measures and behaviour shifts.  The language goes far beyond boiler-plate: it itemises specific operational vectors (employee remote-work, customer-service strain, site lock-downs), financial exposures (charge-backs, defaulting credit portfolios, inaccurate loss allowances), and macro channels (collapse in travel & events, cross-border trade curbs).  Because the filing date is less than a year after the WHO’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores (7–10).  Statements that report present, quantified or clearly described impacts score toward the upper end, whereas broader caveats or partially offsetting positives (e-commerce tail-winds) lower the score slightly.  No material mitigating actions are asserted to neutralise the risk; even the noted growth in digital payments is framed as potentially reversible, keeping overall pandemic risk at an elevated level.

PayPal’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as a still-unfolding, enterprise-wide threat with both realized and prospective consequences.  The company discloses that it has already suffered operational and financial impacts—ranging from heightened charge-backs and credit defaults to direct supply-chain disruptions—and warns that these pressures are likely to persist or intensify as the pandemic evolves.  The language is largely qualitative, but it repeatedly uses strong material-adverse wording and cites concrete impact channels: cross-border commerce restrictions, remote-work operational stresses, and fundamental shifts in consumer payment behaviour.  While management acknowledges temporary pandemic-driven tailwinds (e-commerce acceleration), those benefits are presented as potentially reversible.  Because the filing date (3 Feb 2022) falls well within three years of the WHO’s March 2020 declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores.  Overall, the disclosure signals a high, ongoing risk profile with limited quantification but detailed narrative specificity, justifying upper-mid to high micro-scores for the strongest sentences and lower scores where statements are more conditional or generic.

PayPal’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 primarily as an external, continuing threat rather than a discrete shock with already-quantified consequences. The company frames the pandemic in two ways: (1) as a potential trigger of operational outages—grouped with other catastrophes such as natural disasters—and (2) as a macro-economic wildcard that can suppress consumer spending and merchant solvency. These discussions are largely qualitative and bundled with numerous other uncertainties, showing management views the pandemic as an enduring but diffuse risk rather than a dominant, isolated driver. Because the filing date (Feb-2023) is within three years of the WHO declaration (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores; however, the generic language and absence of quantified impact or specific mitigation limit severity. Overall, COVID-19 appears as a material but moderately articulated risk, warranting mid-range evidence scores.

PayPal’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only a single, high-level reference to pandemics. The company folds “public health crises (including pandemics)” into a long list of possible causes of business interruption for its own and third-party systems. The language is forward-looking and generic, offering no COVID-19-specific data, no quantified impacts, and no discussion of supply-chain, labour, remote-work, or demand-shift issues. Although the sentence concedes that PayPal and its partners "have experienced" interruptions in the past, it does not tie those incidents directly to the COVID-19 pandemic. Given the filing date (February 2024) the pandemic is now four years old, placing it in the medium-term window under the Time Decay Principle. The evidence therefore merits only a moderate severity score: it acknowledges an ongoing potential threat but provides minimal detail and no fresh, material disclosure.

Qualcomm’s 2021 filing acknowledges COVID-19 as both an historic and an ongoing enterprise-wide risk.  The company discloses that the pandemic already produced concrete adverse impacts in 2020-2021 – notably lower handset demand, reduced royalty revenue and a forced shift to large-scale remote work.  It also lays out multiple forward-looking threat vectors: prolonged demand volatility, supply-chain delays, potential insolvency of partners, labour shortages, cyber-security exposure, manufacturing shutdowns and even adverse tax legislation to fund stimulus programmes.  These statements are recent (within 0-3 years of the WHO declaration) and are mostly specific to Qualcomm’s cost structure, revenue streams and operational model rather than generic boiler-plate.  No material mitigating language (e.g., insured losses, full recovery, or quantified offsets) is offered beyond noting partial rebounds and remote-work adaptations.  Under the Time Decay Principle, evidence can be scored aggressively (7-10) because the pandemic is still unfolding and the impacts described are direct and material.  Sentences that merely note uncertainty or minor secondary effects receive lower weights, while those detailing realised revenue declines or critical-function risks receive higher scores.

Qualcomm’s 2022 filing shows that COVID-19 remains both a realised and an ongoing source of material risk.  The company cites concrete past impacts – e.g., remote-work transitions, supply-chain interruptions and measurable drops in demand that hurt royalties – while also flagging forward-looking vulnerabilities (factory closures, employee illness, Chinese lockdowns, delayed 5G roll-outs, etc.).  Language is fairly specific, naming particular geographies (China), business lines (integrated circuits, licensing) and operational nodes (third-party suppliers, in-house fabs, critical staff).  Although most statements are qualitative, they link directly to revenue, cash-flow and manufacturing continuity.  Given the filing date (Nov-2022) the pandemic is still within the 0-3-year “recent” window, so Time Decay does not materially dilute severity.  Overall, the disclosed pandemic risks are moderate-to-high: they are not fully quantified, but they are explicitly tied to realised financial hits and to critical future exposures across supply chain, labour and end-market demand.

Qualcomm’s 2023 Form 10-K continues to acknowledge the COVID-19 pandemic as a material, though now moderating, enterprise-wide risk.  Statements span supply chain fragility, manufacturing interruptions, workforce management and delayed market roll-outs.  Most references are forward-looking (“could,” “may”) yet they are anchored by past, realized impacts such as mandatory remote work and deferrals of 5G network launches.  Because the filing date (Nov-2023) is roughly 3 years 8 months after the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration, the evidence falls just beyond the ‘recent’ band and is therefore scored under the Time Decay Principle’s medium-term bracket, capping snippet scores at 6.  None of the disclosures provide quantified dollar effects, but they do specify operational mechanisms—quarantines, factory closures, supplier stoppages and talent retention challenges—demonstrating more than generic boiler-plate.  Overall, the pandemic remains a live, multi-faceted risk with moderate severity for Qualcomm’s supply continuity, production capacity and strategic 5G roadmap, warranting mid-range scores.

Qualcomm’s 2024 filing continues to frame COVID-19 — and broader pandemic-scale health crises — as an important, though now medium-term, enterprise risk.  References occur in multiple Risk Factor sections and consistently associate pandemics with supply-chain interruptions, factory shutdowns, quarantine-driven labor unavailability and macro-economic demand shocks.  The language is predominantly forward-looking (“could affect,” “could disrupt”), signalling potential rather than presently quantified losses, and is delivered in generic legal-safe-harbor style rather than with data or dollar figures.  Nevertheless, the company explicitly ties pandemics to core operational levers: ability of third-party foundries to manufacture chips, continuity of its own RF facilities, and end-market demand for smartphones and IoT devices.  Given that the pandemic’s onset is four-plus years old, the Time Decay Principle caps severity in the mid-range; there is no fresh, quantified impact, but the disclosures still highlight non-trivial, enterprise-wide exposure.  Overall, the risk profile merits moderate scores (4-5 for the most detailed statements, 2-3 for broad boiler-plate) reflecting persistent, supply-chain-centric vulnerability without immediate financial distress.

RCL’s 2024 Form 10-K presents the COVID-19 pandemic as both a historical shock and a continuing operational threat.  The filing explicitly recalls that governmental responses to COVID-19 forced a complete shutdown of global cruise operations in March-2020 and acknowledges enduring vulnerabilities: renewed outbreaks could again halt sailings, depress demand, disrupt supply of crew, food and other inputs, and impose costly health-protocol upgrades.  The language is specific—linking COVID-19 to a prior ‘voluntary suspension,’ to possible future cruise cancellations, and to ‘material adverse’ financial effects—so the disclosure is stronger than generic boiler-plate.  Because the suspension began four years before the 2024 filing, the Time Decay Principle shifts the evidence from “acute/recent” toward “medium-term,” capping individual sentence scores in the mid-range.  Nevertheless, the risk remains live: the company concedes there is ‘‘no assurance’’ operations will remain uninterrupted and that additional costs and reputational damage could follow.  Consequently, I assess the overall pandemic risk level as moderate-to-elevated (scores 4-6), reflecting tangible past impacts coupled with still-credible forward-looking threats, tempered by time elapsed since the 2020 shutdown and by partial mitigants such as resumption of sailing and protocol development.

The filing, dated February 8 2021, addresses the COVID-19 pandemic in a dedicated risk-factor section that is both extensive and recent (well within the 0-3-year “high-impact” window).  The company links the pandemic to virtually every layer of its value chain: (1) operations—manufacturing, supply-chain, and R&D; (2) human capital—remote-work productivity and potential loss of key staff; (3) commercial execution—sales-force curtailment, product-demand erosion, and inventory obsolescence; (4) financial markets—capital-access constraints; and (5) regulatory processes—trial delays and FDA review slow-downs.  Importantly, REGN cites a realised revenue decline for its flagship product EYLEA in Q2-2020, providing concrete evidence of material impact.  Most statements are forward-looking (“may,” “could”) but are grounded in already-experienced effects, indicating that risk is both present and ongoing.  No significant mitigating language (e.g., insurance, diversified suppliers) offsets the disclosures.  Given the immediacy (event is current), breadth (enterprise-wide), and partial quantification (actual sales drop), the excerpts merit upper-tier severity scores (7-9 range), fully consistent with the Time Decay Principle for recent events.

The filing, dated February 7 2022—less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic—contains an extensive, dedicated risk-factor subsection detailing both realised and continuing threats from COVID-19.  REGN describes concrete, already-experienced impacts (e.g., a fall in U.S. EYLEA sales, supply-chain strains, regulatory slow-downs) and forward-looking exposures (labour shortages, remote-work productivity losses, inventory write-offs, financing constraints).  The language is specific, touches all major operational pillars—manufacturing, R&D, clinical trials, sales & marketing, workforce, and capital markets—and in several instances cites materiality or quantifies past damage.  Because the disclosure period is well within the 0-3-year “recent-event” window, the Time-Decay Principle permits elevated severity scores.  Nonetheless, some statements remain conditional (“may,” “could”), which tempers scores where appropriate.  Overall, the risk is pervasive, direct, and ongoing, justifying high but differentiated snippet ratings.

Regeneron’s 2023 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a still-active, multi-dimensional threat.  The company intertwines descriptions of *actual past harm* (e.g., the 2020 EYLEA sales dip, previous inventory write-offs, earlier clinical-trial delays) with *forward-looking* language that the pandemic "may" or "could" inflict further damage.  The filing highlights virtually every canonical pandemic risk vector: manufacturing and supply-chain strain, labour and key-person loss, remote-work productivity drag, regulatory and clinical-trial delays, sales-force disruptions, diminished patient demand, and macro-market volatility.  These statements are specific to business functions, sometimes illustrated with concrete evidence (e.g., the Q2-20 EYLEA sales decline) and therefore go well beyond boilerplate.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, COVID-19 is a recent event (occurring < 3 years before the 2023 filing date and still evolving), so high severity scores (7-10) are justified for strong, direct, and quantified impacts, while merely potential or un-quantified impacts receive moderate-high scores (5-7).  Mitigating language is sparse; the tone is predominantly cautionary.  Overall, the pandemic remains a material, elevated risk to REGN’s operations and financials.

Regeneron’s 2024 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 mostly as an environmental, continuing risk rather than an acute, quantified shock.  References to the pandemic sit inside broad “public-health-outbreak” language, but the company still cites concrete historical disruption (inventory imbalances, supply-chain strain, workforce impacts) and warns that similar effects could recur.  All statements are forward-looking and largely qualitative—no dollar amounts, explicit probability figures or scenario modelling appear.  Because the filing date is almost four years after the WHO declaration (March 2020) yet within ten years, the Time Decay Principle prescribes a mid-range severity ceiling (roughly 4-6).  Taken together, the disclosures depict a material but now-managed risk profile: COVID-19 amplified prior vulnerabilities (manufacturing capacity limits, supply-chain dependence) and remains a potential drag on operations, but the language is generic and bundled with other outbreaks, signalling reduced immediacy.  Therefore each snippet is micro-scored in the moderate band, with aggravating points for citing past adverse impact and enterprise-wide exposure, and minor mitigating deductions for the absence of quantitative details and the broad framing.

REG’s 2021 filing paints COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-faceted threat that is already depressing revenue and could further damage liquidity, development timetables and portfolio value.  Unlike a purely forward-looking disclosure, the document cites concrete 2020 impacts—tenant bankruptcies, a 132 million-dollar goodwill impairment, stalled projects, supply-chain delays and material drops in cash collections—while still warning of additional future deterioration.  The language is generally specific (“labor shortages,” “significant declines in customer traffic,” “$132.1 million goodwill impairment”) and repeatedly uses ‘material adverse effect,’ signalling high severity.  Given the filing date (Feb 2021) is less than a year after the WHO declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high scoring (up to 10).  Mitigating references (e.g., grocery anchors still operating) are sparse and do not offset the pervasive, quantified downside.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, direct and already crystallising, warranting strong per-sentence scores that cluster in the 5–10 range, with the largest score reserved for the quantified impairment charge.

REG’s 2022 filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to a broad suite of operational, financial and strategic risks that are both current and forward-looking.  The company discloses immediate, quantified impacts (e.g., $132.1 million goodwill impairment and $117 million of uncollectible lease income in 2020) and continuing pressure on rent collections, leasing velocity, property sales, supply-chain timing and tenant credit health.  The narrative demonstrates that while collections have improved to 99 % in Q4-21, management still anticipates lower-than-normal collections over the next year and acknowledges lingering uncertainty about variants, governmental restrictions and consumer behaviour shifts (including accelerated e-commerce adoption).  The risk language is mostly specific and supported by concrete examples such as eviction moratoria, tenant rent concessions, construction delays and geographic hot spots (e.g., California).  Coupled with explicit statements that the pandemic can “materially impact” results of operations, cash flow and access to capital, the disclosures warrant elevated severity scores.  Under the Time Decay Principle the event is recent (≤ 3 years), so high scores (7-10) are permitted where evidence is direct and quantified; more generic or partially mitigated statements are scored in the mid-range.  Mitigating references (near-pre-pandemic collections, demand rebound, liquidity strength) temper but do not eliminate the overall high-risk posture.

The filing, dated February 17 2023, describes COVID-19 as both an historical shock that has already damaged Regency Centers (REG) and an ongoing, forward-looking threat that could further erode rent collections, occupancy, development timelines and even capital-market access.  The disclosures are concentrated in a dedicated pandemic risk subsection, signalling management’s recognition that the issue remains material less than three years after the WHO declaration (time-decay window 0-3 yrs).  The language mixes concrete, backward-looking impacts (e.g., rent concessions granted, tenants that never reopened, legal moratoria that blocked rent enforcement) with hypotheticals about future lockdowns, online-shopping shifts and supply-chain delays.  While no dollar amounts are provided, the text repeatedly references ‘material adverse effect,’ ‘lower occupancy,’ and ‘higher levels of uncollectible lease income,’ indicating severity.  Because most statements are qualitative and unquantified, the risk evidence scores trend toward the middle-to-upper range (3-7), not the absolute maximum.  Overall, REG’s pandemic exposure remains moderate-to-high, warranting sustained investor attention.

REG’s 2024 filing positions the COVID-19 pandemic as a still-salient, multi-faceted threat that has already produced measurable harm (rent concessions, store closures, legal moratoria) and could recur or morph (new virus strains, future lockdowns).  The narrative mixes backward-looking evidence of realized impacts with forward-looking warnings that similar conditions could re-emerge, depress occupancy, delay construction, or shift demand permanently toward e-commerce.  The company repeatedly labels the risk as “material” and ties it to concrete value drivers—tenant credit, lease collectability, supply-chain timing and ultimately cash flow.  Because the filing date (February 2024) is roughly four years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle caps individual scores in the mid-range: the event is no longer “recent,” yet it remains within the medium window where persistent operational and behavioral overhangs justify moderate severity.  The evidence is unquantified but specific, describing actual concessions, shutdowns, and legal barriers; therefore, most snippets earn scores between 4-6, reflecting a credible, ongoing but not freshly acute risk profile.

The filing, dated February 24 2022, portrays COVID-19 as a recent, still-unfolding threat that is already depressing Regions Financial’s performance and could further destabilise it.  Management acknowledges concrete, present-day effects on “business, financial condition, liquidity, capital and results of operations,” and details forward-looking exposures such as supply-chain disruptions, labour shortages, heightened credit losses, and altered consumer behaviour.  The discussion is specific, not boiler-plate: it quantifies a lingering $748 million PPP loan exposure, predicts possible large draws on credit lines, and links pandemic conditions to higher operating costs and reduced investment.  Because the pandemic began less than three years before the filing, the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores (up to 10).  Nonetheless, most statements remain qualitative and un-quantified, and the company cites no catastrophic losses to date; therefore individual snippet scores mainly fall in the 4-8 range.  Overall, the risk is assessed as high, immediate and multi-dimensional, warranting elevated but not maximal scores.

Regions Financial’s 2023 Form 10-K places the COVID-19 pandemic squarely in the category of a recently-experienced, still-unfolding threat.  The filing states that COVID-19 has already hurt the company’s business, financial condition, liquidity, capital and results of operations and is expected to continue doing so, demonstrating that the risk is both current and forward-looking.  Management goes beyond generic wording, identifying concrete transmission channels—supply-chain disruption, labour shortages, market volatility, credit deterioration, liquidity draws and higher business-continuity costs—which map directly to the requested focal areas of this review.  The company also flags secondary operational effects such as cyber-resilience and remote-work fragility.  Although the disclosures stop short of quantifying dollar impacts, the language is explicit, broad in scope and framed in terms of adverse consequences already being felt.  Because the filing date (24 Feb 2023) is within three years of the WHO’s pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Taken together, the evidence signals a significant, multi-faceted risk that remains material to the firm’s outlook, meriting upper-tier but not maximum scores due to the absence of hard numbers and some use of qualifying words such as “may” and “likely.”

RF’s 2024 filing addresses the COVID-19 pandemic only in broad, forward-looking language.  References to “pandemics” appear in general risk lists that group the hazard with weather events, cyber-attacks and other disasters, and do not quantify past or expected financial impacts.  The company highlights that a pandemic could disrupt operations, impair systems, and strain staffing, and it notes that continued remote-work arrangements can amplify operational risks.  It also flags potential workforce-health issues that could hamper its own and vendors’ ability to remain appropriately staffed.  These statements show management still views global health shocks as a relevant exogenous threat, but the discussion is highly generic and framed as a contingency rather than an observed loss.  Because the first wave of COVID-19 occurred almost four years before the 2024 filing, the Time Decay Principle tempers severity to a mid-range level: the risk is neither urgent nor dismissed, but acknowledged as an ongoing possibility whose magnitude is not yet measurable.  Overall, the disclosure supports a moderate aggregate severity assessment (≈4/10).

RJF’s November 2021 Form 10-K places the COVID-19 pandemic squarely in the centre of its risk narrative.  Because the filing date falls less than two years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  The disclosure acknowledges both realised impacts (e.g., near-zero rates already depressing net-interest income, heightened credit losses, brokerage and investment-banking volatility) and forward-looking exposures (labour-force attrition, OSHA vaccine mandates, digital-investment spend, potential goodwill impairments and capital-market constraints).  Language is specific – it cites particular revenue lines, cost items, and vulnerable industry cohorts – yet generally un-quantified.  Importantly, the company admits the risks are continuing, highly uncertain, and tied to evolving variants such as Delta.  While the firm references contingency planning, those mitigants are modest compared with the breadth of identified threats.  Consequently, individual snippets merit high but sub-maximal scores (7-9) reflecting recent timing, concrete operating channels, and the absence of hard dollar figures or catastrophic claims.

RJF’s 2022 filing couches pandemic matters largely in the context of macro-level uncertainty but still concedes a concrete, on-going operational hit: an unusually tight post-COVID labour market that is affecting every part of the business.
