The text therefore presents the pandemic primarily as a forward-looking, hypothetical threat (“could have,” “may be affected”) with no quantified or historical financial hits.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, evidence from this 2024 document referring to a 2020 event falls in the 4-to-10-year window, warranting moderate—not maximal—severity scores.  The most material statement links infectious-disease outbreaks to potential plant shutdowns and “material adverse effect,” justifying mid-range scoring, while more generic listings of pandemics among many hazards merit only minimal weight.  Overall, the risk is acknowledged, unquantified, and mitigated by its conditional framing, so individual snippet scores peak at the mid-scale level (≤6), consistent with a medium-term, non-specific disclosure.

The filing, dated December 12, 2022, discusses COVID-19 less than three years after the WHO declared the pandemic, so any risk evidence should be treated as a recent event under the Time-Decay Principle and can merit scores toward the upper range.  Synopsys repeatedly links the pandemic to supply-chain delays, hardware logistics, customer spending slow-downs, and potential material hits to financial condition.  The language is mostly forward-looking and conditional (“could,” “may”) but is anchored by concrete examples of prior minor disruptions and limited supply-chain issues.  Thus, the company acknowledges both realised and prospective impacts.  Mitigating language—“minor disruptions,” “limited impact,” “navigate … with minimal disruptions”— tempers the severity, suggesting the firm has managed the crisis so far, but uncertainty about duration, vaccines, partner performance and continued supply of hardware keeps overall risk elevated.  Given this mix of modest realised impact and material future exposure, the individual sentence scores generally fall in the 4-7 range, consistent with recent-event guidance.

Synopsys’ 2023 Form 10-K contains only brief, largely boiler-plate references to the COVID-19 pandemic.  All mentions are in the general ‘Risk Factors’ section and are framed as potential or continuing uncertainties rather than detailing any quantified or presently-observed damage.  The company groups COVID-19 with other broad disruptive forces (natural disasters, wars, climate events) and offers no hard numbers on revenue, supply chain delays, head-count impacts, or costs.  Nonetheless, it does acknowledge that government-imposed restrictions during the pandemic curtailed global economic activity and introduces the idea that such measures could again affect its sales, infrastructure and overall operating results.  Because the filing date (December 2023) is less than four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (March 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows moderate scoring—but the generic tone and lack of concrete metrics keep the severity modest.  Overall, COVID-19 is portrayed as an ongoing but not transformational risk, warranting mid-single-digit scores for the most informative sentence and very low scores for the purely ‘laundry-list’ references.

The 2024-12-19 SNPS 10-K discusses pandemic exposure primarily in a consolidated ‘Catastrophic events’ risk factor.  The language frames COVID-19 as part of a broader class of events that can disrupt global operations, affect sales infrastructure, and create macro-market volatility.  Most statements are forward-looking and couched in conditional verbs (“may”, “could”), signalling potential rather than quantified, realised loss.  One sentence, however, explicitly recalls the government-imposed restrictions and financial-market turmoil experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrating that the company has already observed concrete business-environment impacts.  Because the pandemic’s onset is now roughly four years old, the Time-Decay Principle places the event in the medium-term bucket; accordingly, even the strongest evidence is capped at a moderate severity score.  Overall, the filing indicates continuing vigilance but no acute, quantified damage, so individual snippet scores fall in the 3-6 range, reflecting generic disclosure, operational vulnerability, and limited specificity.

The filing, dated February 9 2021, was prepared less than one year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time-Decay Principle classifies the disclosure window as “recent.”  SPGI devotes a dedicated risk-factor section to COVID-19, repeatedly warning that the pandemic has already affected operations and could exert further "material adverse" pressure on revenue, productivity, client demand and overall economic conditions.  The language is largely qualitative but quite explicit: it cites recessionary fallout, subscription pricing pressure, remote-work operational risks, heightened cyber-threat exposure and possible knock-on effects if the bond-issuance surge that temporarily lifted 2020 results reverses.  Those statements raise the risk from a hypothetical to an ongoing, direct impact.  Mitigating language exists—e.g., the firm’s continuity program “has been effective to date” and vaccines are becoming available—but these caveats are overshadowed by acknowledgements of uncertainty and potential material harm.  Accordingly, most snippets merit high but not maximum scores (7-9), reflecting significant, near-term, yet largely unquantified exposure; sentences that emphasise operational success or other offsets receive small downward adjustments.  All scoring honours the 0-10 scale and the recent-event allowance for up to 10 points.

SPGI’s 2021 Form 10-K, filed in February 2022, presents COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat rather than a historical footnote.  The risk language is forward-looking but anchored in already-experienced disruption: the company acknowledges concrete operational impacts (remote-only workforce since March 2020, higher cyber-threat volumes, pressure on client spending) while warning that these effects “may ultimately have a material adverse impact” on future results.  The disclosure repeatedly ties pandemic dynamics to revenue erosion (pricing pressure, delayed renewals), productivity loss, and macro-volatility in the capital and commodities markets that underpin SPGI’s core businesses.  Although SPGI notes some mitigating developments (vaccine rollout, functioning business-continuity programme), the text stresses uncertainty around new variants, prolonged remote work, and clients’ financial health.  Given the filing date falls inside the 0-to-3-year “recent event” window and the company uses strong, materiality-based wording without providing numerical impact, the overall risk evidence merits high—but not maximal—scores (7-9 range).

SPGI’s 2023 Form 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat rather than as a closed historical episode.  The company catalogues multiple transmission channels—mobility restrictions, supply-chain and customer-side disruption, market volatility, revenue pressure, and demand weakness in its Commodity Insights segment—showing an appreciation of both operational and macro-financial exposure.  Most statements remain forward-looking and conditional ("may," "could"), signalling potential rather than booked losses, yet one sentence notes that COVID-related uncertainty "has" already slowed demand for certain subscriptions, providing evidence of an existing impact.  No dollar amounts are supplied, and the company also discloses that, so far, the pandemic "has not had a material adverse effect," partially mitigating overall severity.  Given the February 2023 filing date—well within three years of the WHO declaration—the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scores, but the absence of quantified damage keeps individual snippet scores in the mid-to-upper range rather than at the maximum.  Overall risk exposure is assessed as moderately high because the disclosures acknowledge concrete pressure points and the possibility of material adverse effects, while concurrently noting limited realized damage to date.

SPGI’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to frame COVID-19 primarily as a forward-looking, enterprise-wide threat rather than as a source of currently quantified losses.  The pandemic is grouped with other “public-health crises,” but the filing repeatedly names COVID-19 and details pathways through which another wave—or a similar infectious-disease emergency—could damage the company: government-mandated travel bans, social-distancing requirements, quarantines, supply-chain and customer-operation disruptions, pricing pressure, delayed renewals, and depressed demand that would erode revenue.  The company also warns of macro-level knock-on effects such as capital-market volatility and prolonged global recessions.  Language such as “material adverse effect” and “materially and adversely affected” indicates management views the risk as potentially severe, but all statements are couched in conditional (“may,” “could”) phrasing and no dollar figures or probability estimates are provided.  Given the filing date (February 2024) is just under four years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle places COVID-19 in the early portion of the 4--10-year “medium-term” window; therefore individual evidence scores should fall in the moderate band (4-6) unless the sentence is highly generic (lower) or contains unusually strong aggravating or mitigating factors.  Overall, the disclosures reflect a live but unquantified risk with clearly articulated operational and financial impact channels, meriting a moderate aggregate severity assessment.

SPG’s 2021-02-25 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and prospective harms across every core metric—rent collections, occupancy, liquidity, tenant solvency and long-term demand for physical retail.  The disclosure is largely contemporaneous (within one year of WHO’s 11-Mar-2020 declaration), so under the Time Decay Principle the evidentiary weight can be high.  The filing contains numerous concrete facts: a complete nationwide shutdown of properties, 13,500 lost shopping days, rent abatements covering <16 % of contractual rents for three quarters, and continuing cash-rent shortfalls.  It also warns of future reinstated lockdowns, accelerated e-commerce substitution and persistent tenant bankruptcies.  Mitigating language (e.g., curb-side pickup, gradual re-openings) is minimal and largely speculative, so most snippets warrant elevated scores (7-9).  Statements that are forward-looking but less quantified receive mid-range scores (4-6).  No snippet predates the pandemic, hence no zero-scores are required.

Simon Property Group (SPG) is a mall-focused REIT whose cash flow depends almost entirely on in-person retail traffic.  In this 2022 filing—just two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic—the company describes both realised damage and continuing uncertainty.  Management discloses quantifiable losses (e.g., 13,500 shopping days lost; >$940 million lease-income shortfall; $224 million drop in JV earnings) and highlights structural, longer-term threats such as persistent shifts to e-commerce and the possibility that consumer foot-traffic never fully recovers.  The language is emphatic (“material negative impact,” “significant negative impact,” “no guarantee that retail will return to pre-pandemic levels”), indicating that COVID-19 is not merely a hypothetical concern but an ongoing, enterprise-wide risk.  Mitigating references (curb-side pickup, cost reductions, lifted restrictions) appear, yet they are tentative and outweighed by the magnitude of the disclosed impacts.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic falls in the 0-3-year window, so high scores (7-10) are permissible for direct, quantified effects; forward-looking but un-quantified statements merit mid-range scores (4-6); and passages tempered by mitigation receive lower values.  Overall, the COVID-19 pandemic constitutes a high-severity, still-evolving risk for SPG.

Simon Property Group’s 2023 filing links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and prospective risks across virtually every driver of the Company’s cash-flow model: tenant viability, traffic levels, rent collections, asset values, capital-market access and leverage metrics.  Statements span (i) hard, historic impacts—e.g., the loss of 13,500 shopping days and recognised revenue-collection issues, (ii) continuing operational headwinds—e.g., elevated vacancies, accelerated bankruptcies and e-commerce substitution that ‘significantly increased’ during the pandemic, and (iii) forward-looking exposure—e.g., the possibility that renewed government restrictions or consumer-behaviour shifts could again depress demand.  The language is largely specific (naming lost trading days, cash-flow effects and discrete operational adaptations) and repeatedly characterises the impact as ‘material’ or ‘significant.’  Given the filing date (Feb-2023), the pandemic sits within the 0-3-year “recent event” window; the Time Decay Principle therefore allows high severity scores.  Mitigants (e.g., recovery to “more normalised” cost levels and management cost-cutting) are noted but do not override the breadth and depth of remaining risk.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a major, partially quantified, still-evolving threat for SPG, justifying elevated evidence scores in the 7-10 range.

SPG’s 2024 Form 10-K reiterates that COVID-19 remains a consequential, though now primarily forward-looking, threat to its retail-centric real-estate model. The company acknowledges that the pandemic already demonstrated its ability to shut properties, depress foot-traffic and accelerate e-commerce substitution, while warning that renewed outbreaks or other public-health crises could again trigger governmental lockdowns, travel bans and consumer avoidance.  The language is specific—detailing possible stay-at-home orders, border closings, vaccine uptake uncertainty, and tourism declines—yet remains unquantified and largely conditional, signalling that management views the hazard as significant but not currently crippling.  Because the first global wave peaked roughly four years ago, the Time-Decay Principle caps the evidentiary severity at a moderate level: the risks are not stale, but neither are they as acute as during 2020-2021.  Overall, the disclosures depict a medium-term, systemic exposure that could amplify many existing vulnerabilities (occupancy rates, capital-market access, tenant solvency) without offering meaningful mitigating offsets, justifying mid-range snippet scores (4-6) and lower scores (1-3) for more generic or heavily qualified statements.

The filing, dated February 25 2021, sits less than 12 months after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so any referenced impacts or forward-looking risks fall into the “recent-event” band of the Time-Decay Principle (scores potentially as high as 10).  Sempra Energy acknowledges both actual and potential consequences across multiple vectors: (1) immediate, already-realized effects—project delays, supply-chain strain, customer payment shortfalls, and the need to modify working arrangements; (2) quantified or clearly sign-posted financial exposures—rising uncollectible accounts, liquidity pressure, and higher operating costs; and (3) broad strategic threats—capital-market disruption, hindered capital spending, workforce productivity loss and heightened cyber-risk.  While one sentence states the pandemic has not yet materially hit results of operations, most language is emphatic (“materially impacting”, “material adverse effect”) and often links impacts to cash flow, liquidity and project timing, demonstrating high severity and specificity.  Because the pandemic is ongoing and the issuer reports fresh, concrete impacts plus credible future downside, individual snippet scores cluster in the 6-9 range; weaker or mitigating statements are scored lower.  No score exceeds 9, leaving room below the absolute maximum for truly quantified dollar-based impacts, which are absent here.

Sempra’s February 25 2022 filing discusses COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, enterprise-wide source of operational and financial uncertainty.  Although management explicitly states that the pandemic has not yet produced a material hit to results, the risk language moves beyond boiler-plate by cataloguing concrete pressure points: altered work practices and the associated productivity drag, labour turnover, customer-protection measures that have already driven up bad-debt expense, and capital-markets volatility that has slowed spending plans.  These disclosures show both realised impacts (higher uncollectibles, market disruptions) and forward-looking threats (supply-chain strain, liquidity risk, compliance jeopardy).  Because the event window (March 2020-present) is well inside the 0-3-year “recent” band, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores.  Nevertheless, management’s statement that COVID-19 has not materially affected results to date, coupled with references to mitigation protocols, tempers the overall risk assessment.  Netting these factors, the pandemic constitutes a live, moderate-to-high emerging risk—significant enough to monitor closely, but not yet existential for Sempra.

Sempra’s 2023 Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic primarily to prospective risks rather than already-incurred losses.  Management states that the pandemic has not materially hurt 2022 operating results, yet immediately lists several ways it has already strained supply chains and customer collections and may continue to do so.  The disclosure is forward-looking, qualitative, and only partially company-specific: it cites tangible stressors—supply-chain disruption, capital-market volatility, liquidity exposure, slower capital spending, and rising uncollectible accounts at the California utilities—without quantifying dollar amounts.  Because the filing date (28 Feb 2023) is within three years of the event onset (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows relatively high severity scores.  Nevertheless, severity is tempered by management’s explicit statement that COVID-19 has "not had a material impact" to date and by on-going mitigation (customer-protection measures, active monitoring).  Overall, the pandemic represents a medium-to-high forward risk (mostly potential, with early signs of impact on cash-collections), warranting snippet scores in the 4-7 range, with a single mitigating snippet scored lower.

A line-by-line review of the 2023 Form 10-K excerpt reveals no direct or even indirect acknowledgement of the COVID-19 pandemic, its lingering effects, or any explicit discussion of pandemic-driven supply-chain disruption, labour shortages, remote work, or altered customer-demand patterns.  The risk-factor and MD&A sections instead reference general ‘supply-chain constraints’ and ‘tight labour-market conditions’ without attributing them to COVID-19 or any other public-health emergency.  Because the filing date (27 Feb 2024) falls well within three years of the height of the COVID-19 shock, an explicit disclosure would normally merit a high risk score under the Time Decay Principle.  However, the company’s silence on the topic means that, in effect, SRE is providing the market with no COVID-specific transparency.  The absence of language is itself a governance signal, yet strictly under the scoring framework there is no extractable sentence to which a positive or negative risk weight can be attached.  Consequently, there is no evidence to score, and the overall pandemic-related risk evidence level is assessed as non-existent for this document.

COVID-19 is treated by STE as an ongoing, high-priority enterprise risk with both retrospective and forward-looking dimensions.  The filing, dated May 31 2022 (within 3 years of the WHO declaration), repeatedly cites actual disruptions that have already occurred—mandatory plant shutdowns, reduced product demand from deferred medical procedures, higher supply-chain costs, and regulatory slow-downs—as well as the possibility that these impacts could intensify.  The language is specific (e.g., facility closures, stay-at-home orders, rising logistics costs) and is framed as potentially “material” to operations, cash-flow and financial condition; therefore the baseline severity is elevated.  Some mitigating language appears (e.g., management believes impacts were not material to date and has implemented safety protocols), but these caveats are outweighed by the breadth of identified vulnerability (operations, customers, labour, cyber-security, regulation).  Applying the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic is still recent, so scores can legitimately reach the upper range.  Overall, the risk is assessed as high but with modest downward adjustments where the company cites successful counter-measures or uncertainty about duration or magnitude.

STE’s 2023 Form 10-K continues to treat COVID-19 as a live, enterprise-wide threat that has already impaired the company’s operations and could do so again.  The filing moves beyond generic boiler-plate: it states that the pandemic caused mandatory and voluntary plant closures, suppressed procedural-volume-driven demand, inflated labour and freight costs, disrupted supply chains, and triggered remote-work cyber-exposure.  It also flags secondary knock-on effects—government budget constraints, customer liquidity issues, potential trade barriers, and staffing shortages—thereby linking COVID-19 to credit risk, revenue risk and cost inflation.  Although STE lists certain mitigations (essential-business exemptions, tele-work policies, modified practices), these are portrayed as tentative and possibly insufficient.  Because the disclosed impacts are both historical (actual closures, demand declines) and forward-looking (“could have a material adverse effect if further disruptions occur”), and the event occurred within the last three years, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  The overall risk profile is therefore assessed as high-to-very-high, with individual snippet scores in the 5-9 range depending on specificity, breadth of impact, and presence of mitigating language.

STE’s 2024-05-29 filing describes COVID-19 as both a historical shock and a continuing, forward-looking threat.  Management cites concrete, already-incurred impacts—mandatory facility closures, reduced procedure volumes, labour and supply-chain cost spikes—showing the pandemic materially disrupted operations between 2020 and 2023.  At the same time, the disclosure stresses that residual effects remain difficult to forecast and could still pressure demand, staffing, cyber-security and overall financial health.  The language is largely qualitative (no dollar figures) but ties risks explicitly to specific operational areas that matter for STE’s business model: hospitals’ capital purchases, sterilisation capacity, staffing and logistics.  Because the pandemic’s peak is now four years old, the Time Decay Principle caps severity in the mid-range; nevertheless, the persistence of supply-chain challenges, customer spending uncertainty and elevated costs justifies moderate scores (4-6) for the strongest sentences, with lower scores for broader or more speculative points.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a meaningful but no longer acute enterprise risk, warranting a moderate aggregate assessment.

STLD’s 10-K, filed only eleven months after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, devotes a full, dedicated subsection of Item 1A to the virus.  The company repeatedly states that COVID-19 “has and may continue” to harm sales volumes, supply-chain robustness, project-execution timetables, labor productivity and even the firm’s share price.  Language is neither hypothetical nor generic: it combines backward-looking evidence (second-quarter shutdowns, steel-demand collapse, scrap-flow reductions) with forward-looking uncertainties (vaccine efficacy, further government lockdowns, credit-market volatility).  Multiple risk vectors are flagged: (i) demand destruction among key end-markets such as automotive and energy; (ii) supply-chain and construction delays (e.g., Sinton mill); (iii) labor-force and workplace disruptions; (iv) capital-market and liquidity shocks.  Mitigations are also disclosed—essential-industry status, variable-compensation flexibility, and extensive safety protocols—moderating some individual sentence scores.  Given the recency of the pandemic (<3 years) and the direct, already-experienced financial impacts, Time-Decay allows high severity ratings (7–10) for the most concrete disclosures, with lower scores (0–3) for purely mitigative or generic statements.  Overall, the filing reveals a material, continuing, multi-dimensional risk landscape tied to COVID-19, justifying elevated risk scores across numerous excerpts.

The filing was made in February 2022, less than two years after WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  STLD devotes an entire subsection of Item 1A to pandemic risk, combining backward-looking evidence of actual disruption in 2020 with forward-looking warnings about ongoing supply-chain fragility, labor restrictions, demand volatility and capital-market turbulence.  Most statements are qualitative rather than quantified, but they explicitly connect the virus to core financial metrics (volumes, margins, cash-flows, liquidity, stock price) and to operational levers (productivity, working conditions, supply of raw materials).  No meaningful mitigating language (e.g., insurance, hedging) is offered beyond noting that operations have not yet been curtailed, so the overall risk tone is elevated. Because the event is recent and the company acknowledges both realised and potential impacts across multiple dimensions, individual snippet scores cluster in the mid-to-upper range (3-6), with the highest scores reserved for sentences that link specific government measures or historical performance hits directly to STLD’s results.  None reach the absolute maximum because there is no quantified dollar figure or percentage loss.

The filing, dated February 28 2023, discusses the COVID-19 pandemic primarily in the Risk Factors section. The company frames the pandemic as both an event that HAS ALREADY HAD tangible effects (e.g., demand shocks, supply-chain interruptions, labour shortages, inflationary pressures) and as a CONTINUING, forward-looking threat (e.g., potential resurgences and more severe variants). Language ranges from concrete acknowledgements (“have impacted”) to conditional wording (“could” or “may”), but several statements explicitly confirm adverse impacts that have already materialised. Because the event is well within the 0-3-year “recent” window, the Time-Decay Principle allows relatively high severity scores where warranted. Overall, the pandemic remains a significant operational and financial risk for STLD, with no clear quantitative dollar figure but with multiple operational dimensions (demand, supply chain, workforce) already affected and potentially worsening. Mitigating language is minimal (only one sentence notes operations have not yet been curtailed), so the risk profile is assessed as moderate-to-high in the current environment.

The 2024-02-29 filing places the discussion roughly four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the event now sits at the front edge of the Time-Decay “medium-term” band (4-10 years). In this 10-K, Steel Dynamics (STLD) no longer reports acute, quantified COVID impacts, but it still highlights pandemics as a material, recurring threat capable of disrupting demand, supply chains, labour availability and overall financial performance. The language remains largely forward-looking ("may adversely affect") and is grouped with other macro hazards, signalling management sees the pandemic primarily as an ongoing contingency rather than an immediate crisis. Nevertheless, the text explicitly links government pandemic responses to historical impacts on product demand, supply chains, workforce and inflation—affirming lived experience from 2020-2022. Because the statements are broad, un-quantified and partly historic, the residual severity is moderate: significant enough to remain in the Risk Factors section, but tempered by elapsed time and lack of fresh, specific damage. Under the Time Decay Principle, snippet scores therefore fall in the 4-6 range for direct, descriptive sentences and lower (≈2-3) for generic list references.

State Street’s 2021 filing presents the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, near-term (inside the 0-3-year window) threat that is already disrupting operations and earnings and could further erode capital, liquidity and strategic flexibility.  The disclosure moves well beyond generic caution: management details concrete stress points—spikes in transaction-processing volumes, heightened FX and asset-management volatility, elevated credit-loss provisions, work-from-home cyber-risks, impediments to capital return and direct pressure on NII/NIM from policy-driven rate declines.  These statements make clear that the risk is both current and forward-looking: tangible impacts were experienced in 2020 (e.g., suspension of share repurchases, higher credit provisions), while uncertainty about duration, market behaviour, staff availability and regulatory responses could amplify losses in 2021 and beyond.  The language is unequivocal (“significant risks”, “material adverse impact”) and ties the pandemic to specific financial metrics, giving the evidence high severity scores.  Because the filing date (19 Feb 2021) is less than a year after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores—up to 10—for direct, quantified or operationally acute impacts; mitigation actions (e.g., authorised resumption of dividends, remote-work adaptations) temper but do not eliminate severity.  Overall, the pandemic constitutes a strategically important, multifaceted risk with elevated severity for State Street.

State Street’s 2022 filing devotes a discrete, multi-sentence passage to the ongoing effects of COVID-19.  The language states that the pandemic is not a historical footnote but a *continuing* source of “significant risks and uncertainties,” explicitly naming potential damage to revenue, capital, liquidity ratios, staffing, cybersecurity, transaction-processing capacity and client service levels.  The risk is framed as forward-looking and conditional— management stresses that the ultimate scale of impact “cannot be predicted.”  Nevertheless, the text lists concrete transmission channels (remote-work dependence, labor shortages, return-to-office challenges, supply-chain disruptions, volatility in equity and fixed-income markets) that clearly map to the requested themes (supply chain, labour, remote work, demand shifts).  Because the 10-K was filed only two years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time-Decay principle permits high severity scores.  Mitigating factors are minimal—there is no quantification of losses or disclosure of offsets—so the overall risk tone remains acute and recent.  Accordingly, individual sentences that deliver specific mechanisms or business-line exposures are scored in the upper half of the 0-10 scale, with minor deductions where the text is general, caveated or un-quantified.

After a meticulous review of the provided 2023-02-16 STT 10-K excerpt, no sentences explicitly or implicitly address the continuing impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on the company’s operations, supply chain, labour force, remote-work arrangements or demand patterns.  The text discusses numerous other macro-economic, geopolitical, market-volatility and technology-related risks, yet it never references the pandemic, public-health measures, or disease-related disruptions.  Consequently, there is no basis on which to evaluate pandemic-related risk severity, likelihood, or materiality.  In line with the methodology, when a filing post-dates the triggering event but contains no qualifying disclosure, the overall assessment is that pandemic-specific risk is either deemed immaterial by the issuer or omitted altogether; therefore, the evidentiary score is zero and no micro-scorecards are generated.

The filing contains only high-level, precautionary language regarding the COVID-19 pandemic.  References to a "pandemic" are bundled with other extreme but unspecified events, signalling that management now views COVID-19 primarily as a generic, forward-looking threat rather than a currently-material issue.  No sentence discloses dollar impacts, supply-chain problems, or explicit operational disruptions; instead, the company warns that a pandemic could create losses or heighten operational risk.  One workforce-related sentence hints at lasting changes in employee expectations for hybrid work—an indirect legacy of the pandemic—but still lacks specificity.  Because the disclosure is generic, unquantified and occurs nearly four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the overall severity is assessed as moderate under the Time Decay Principle, warranting mid-range micro-scores (≈3-4) rather than the high scores (7-10) typical of acute, quantified impacts.

STX’s 2021-08-06 Form 10-K embeds a dense, multi-layered discussion of COVID-19. Narrative language repeatedly uses present-tense (“has impacted”, “continue to incur”) and forward-looking qualifiers (“may adversely impact”, “unable to predict”), signalling both realised losses and future uncertainty.  Numerous granular risk vectors are enumerated: factory shutdowns, component shortages, labour unavailability, elevated expenses, customer payment delays, remote-work cyber-exposure and broad macro-economic deterioration.  No quantified dollar figures are given, but the breadth and immediacy of the impacts, coupled with management’s admission that they could be “material and adverse”, warrant high severity scores.  Because the filing date (August 2021) falls well inside three years of the 11 March 2020 pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scores (up to 10).  Mitigating language is minimal; the company offers no concrete offsets besides monitoring and cost-control efforts.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, specific and already partially realised, justifying strong but sub-maximal snippet scores in the 3-9 range.

STX’s 2022-08-05 10-K paints COVID-19 as a still-active, multi-dimensional threat.  The filing repeatedly confirms that the pandemic has ALREADY hurt the company—citing FY-2022 supply-chain bottlenecks, component shortages that throttled non-HDD sales, higher logistics and material costs, and variable customer demand.  It then layers forward-looking uncertainty, warning that further mutations, lockdowns or economic malaise could trigger manufacturing shutdowns, labour shortfalls, inventory imbalances, margin compression and even heightened cyber-exposure from remote work.  Only limited mitigating language appears (e.g., cost-control initiatives), and no quantified dollar figures are given, so risk remains high but not maximal.  Because the event is well within the 0-3-year ‘recent’ window, the Time Decay principle allows elevated scores (up to 10).  Sentences that describe concrete, already-realised impacts score toward the upper band (6-9), while purely contingent statements or those coupled with mitigation are tempered to mid-range (2-5).

STX’s 2023-08-04 10-K squarely links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and continuing operational and financial pressure.  The filing describes concrete, first-order disruptions—labour shortages, factory shutdowns, supply-chain bottlenecks, higher mitigation costs, elongated sales cycles and weaker customer demand—plus second-order impacts such as tighter credit markets and lingering recovery delays.  All references are company-specific (not merely macro commentary) and confirm that losses have already occurred ("negatively impacted") while flagging the risk as still active ("may, in the future").  No dollar figures are provided and the text is largely qualitative, but the breadth of functions affected (manufacturing, logistics, expenses, revenue, liquidity) signals a material threat.  Because the pandemic began in March 2020 and the filing date is August 2023, the event sits just beyond the 3-year “recent” window; therefore, the Time Decay Principle caps individual snippet scores in the moderate-to-high band (4-6 for the strongest statements).  Mitigations are sparse—limited mainly to “monitoring”—so most aggravating factors remain unreduced.  Overall, the disclosure evidences a significant but not peak-level risk profile that justifies mid-range severity scores across the extracted sentences.

COVID-19 is no longer a brand-new shock for STX, yet the filing still links the pandemic to both realized and prospective operational threats.  The text contains (i) a backward-looking quantified cost ($7 million lockdown charge in FY-23) showing that COVID-related factory stoppages have already hit gross margin, and (ii) several forward-looking statements that pandemics can disrupt supply chains, logistics, labour mobility and demand.  These disclosures are generally qualitative and embedded in broader ‘public-health-issues’ risk language, but they nevertheless acknowledge that pandemics have ‘materially impacted’ component availability and could do so again.  Because the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020—roughly 4-½ years before the 2 Aug 2024 filing date—the Time Decay Principle places the event in the medium-term window (4-10 years), capping reasonably supportable snippet scores in the mid-range.  The company’s language is moderately specific (naming supply chain delays, freight costs, travel restrictions and factory lockdowns) without offering large, quantified, ongoing financial impacts.  Overall, the risk evidence is assessed as material but managed, warranting mid-level severity scores (4-6) for the extracted sentences.

The filing reflects that, four years after the official declaration of COVID-19 as a global pandemic, STZ continues to view health-crisis-related disruptions as a live, but now medium-term, enterprise-wide risk.  The company discloses both historical impacts ("have resulted") and forward-looking exposures ("could result") across consumer demand, supply-chain logistics, workforce availability, and financial markets.  Language is largely qualitative—no dollar amounts or quantified volume impacts are provided—but it is still specific, citing venue closures, quarantines, border shutdowns, and uninsured losses.  Severity is underlined by repeated references to "material adverse effect," yet the text offers little in the way of concrete mitigations beyond general awareness.  Applying the Time-Decay Principle, the pandemic sits at the 4-year mark, so evidence scores must be moderated (4-6 range for the strongest sentences, tapering downward for ancillary mentions).  Overall, the pandemic remains a meaningful, but no longer acute, risk driver for STZ.

SWKS’s 2021-11-24 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as a clear, multi-faceted, and still-evolving threat.  Because the pandemic erupted only eighteen months before fiscal year-end, Time-Decay is minimal and the filing is replete with both historical damage (plant shutdowns, supply-chain delays, higher logistics costs, inventory builds, efficiency loss) and forward-looking warnings (continued supply constraints, labor attrition from vaccination mandates, demand volatility, macro-economic drag).  The narrative is specific—naming a two-week factory closure, discrete cost inflation and capacity shortfalls—yet largely un-quantified in dollars.  Management repeatedly acknowledges that many effects “continue” or “may continue,” underscoring an active, not hypothetical, risk posture.  Although the company lists certain mitigation steps (remote work, safety protocols, supplier engagement), these are framed as costly and only partially effective.  Taken together, the disclosures signal a high-severity, contemporaneous operational and financial risk consistent with 0-3-year recency, justifying upper-mid score levels on the micro-scorecards.

Skyworks Solutions (SWKS) portrays COVID-19 as an immediate, multi-faceted and still-evolving threat.  The company moves beyond boilerplate phrasing and cites concrete, already-experienced impacts – supply-chain interruptions, higher input costs, factory shutdowns, labour attrition, transportation bottlenecks and demand volatility.  While some sentences are forward-looking, many describe current or historical disruptions, confirming that the risk is not merely hypothetical.  No material quantitative dollar figure is disclosed, but the narrative repeatedly links the pandemic to reduced profitability, manufacturing inefficiencies and potential inability to meet customer demand.  Mitigations (inventory builds, employee-protection measures) are acknowledged yet framed as cost-increasing or only partially effective.  Because the filing date (23-Nov-2022) is less than three years after the event’s onset (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores; most excerpts merit 6-9 points, reflecting directness, specificity and recency, with modest downward adjustments where the company emphasises limited impact or mitigation.

SWKS’s 2023 filing continues to portray the COVID-19 pandemic as a live, multi-faceted threat that has already hurt the company’s supply chain and cost structure and could still erode demand and margins.  The language blends backward-looking statements (e.g., supply constraints and higher costs that have already been felt) with forward-looking cautions about new variants, lingering macro-economic drag, and possible order reductions from key customers.  Although the pandemic began more than three years ago, management describes current disruptions (materials shortages, logistics delays) and expressly warns that problems ‘may continue’ or even emerge ‘after the pandemic has subsided.’  The disclosures are therefore more than generic boiler-plate; they cite concrete operational pinch-points—materials, assembly/test services, shipping—and identify potential revenue risk from large customers.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic now falls just inside the medium-term window (≈3.5 years after onset), so individual sentence scores are capped at a moderate 6, but the persistence and breadth of impacts keep the risk profile toward the upper end of that band.

The filing, completed almost five years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, still contains multiple references that link the outbreak to tangible operational stresses for Skyworks (SWKS).  The company discloses both realised impacts (e.g., supply-chain shortages that lengthened lead-times and inflated costs) and continuing, forward-looking vulnerabilities (employee turnover linked to remote-work trends, possible lockdowns or quarantines, and broad ‘global health crisis’ disruptions).  These statements are moderately specific—naming concrete effects such as production delays and higher material costs—but they stop short of quantifying dollar values or margin erosion.  Because the pandemic is now a medium-term event (≈4½ years old at the 2024-11-15 filing date), the Time-Decay Principle warrants mid-range severity scores: the risks are still live and material yet no longer at their 2020–2021 peak intensity.  Overall, the evidence supports a medium risk posture, with individual snippet scores clustered in the 3-6 range.

The filing, dated February 18 2021, was prepared less than twelve months after the WHO-declared start of the COVID-19 pandemic and therefore falls squarely in the 0-3-year “recent-event” window.  SWK devotes extensive, specific disclosure to pandemic-related disruptions, repeatedly flagging material threats to liquidity, supply-chain continuity, labour availability, demand volatility and strategic execution.  The narrative contains both backward-looking evidence (actual cost-saving actions; $500 million realised in 2020) and forward-looking warnings (possible impairments, capital-market constraints, demand declines once lockdown spending fades).  Although some mitigating actions are cited—large cost-reduction programmes, capital flexibility—the overall tone stresses uncertainty and the possibility of further adverse shocks.  Because the statements are explicit, contemporaneous with the pandemic and at times quantify financial effects, they merit high but not maximum severity: typically in the 6-9 range.  Time-decay does not require any discount because the event is ongoing and the filing is recent.  Scores are moderated when language is more generic or when management describes effective counter-measures; they are elevated when the text notes ‘material’ impacts, quantified savings or critical operational impairments.

SWK’s 2022 Form 10-K explicitly links the COVID-19 pandemic to concrete, ongoing and potentially material threats across virtually every facet of its operations—supply-chain visibility, factory access, labour availability, customer demand, liquidity, strategic execution and capital markets volatility.  The disclosures are largely contemporaneous, describing both impacts already realised (e.g., supply-chain delays, modified work practices, heightened freight costs) and forward-looking uncertainties (e.g., vaccine-mandate attrition, demand contraction once home-improvement tailwinds fade).  Language such as “materially negative impact,” “adversely affected,” and “highly uncertain” elevates severity, while very few mitigating specifics are offered beyond generic cost-savings programmes and vaccination protocols.  Because the filing date (22-Feb-2022) falls inside three years of the World Health Organization’s 11-Mar-2020 pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high per-sentence scores (up to 10).  Nevertheless, scores are tapered when statements are broad, lack quantification, or mention mitigation.  Overall, the documentary evidence signals a significant, still-evolving risk profile warranting upper-medium to high micro-scores (3-7 range), with no snippet meriting the absolute maximum since none quantifies financial impact.

SWK’s 2023 Form 10-K ties the COVID-19 pandemic to both historical and forward-looking risks across virtually every operational dimension.  Management acknowledges concrete, already-experienced impacts—supply-chain bottlenecks, freight inflation, temporary plant access limits, labour adjustments, and atypical demand spikes—and warns that new variants or policy responses could reignite or prolong these pressures.  Language such as “materially negative impact,” “have adversely affected,” and “may continue to disrupt” elevates the risk from hypothetical to demonstrably real.  Although the Company notes some easing of constraints in late 2022, it offers no assurance of permanence, repeatedly stressing uncertainty and dependency on uncontrollable external developments.  Because the filing date (Feb 2023) is less than three years after the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Overall, the disclosures present specific, multi-faceted, still-unfolding threats rather than boiler-plate cautions, justifying a generally high—but not maximal—risk assessment with some mitigation reflected where improvements are acknowledged.

SWK’s 2024 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 primarily as a medium-term, background risk rather than an acute, ongoing crisis.  References to the pandemic appear only twice: once folded into a long catalogue of potential business disruptions and once as a historical example of why the company might withdraw earnings guidance.  No sentence quantifies impact or cites current operational constraints tied to COVID-19; instead, the language is cautionary and forward-looking, signalling that management now views the pandemic alongside other generic threat categories (natural disasters, cyber-attacks, geopolitical events).  Because the filing date is four years after the World Health Organization’s declaration of the pandemic, the Time Decay Principle dictates that severity scores should be moderate.  Still, the disclosures acknowledge that COVID-19 previously forced withdrawal of guidance and could again disrupt manufacturing, supply chains and financial performance, so a non-trivial risk rating is justified.  Overall, the documentary evidence supports medium-level concern with scores clustered in the 4-6 range.

The filing, dated less than a year after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, contains extensive, highly specific language linking the outbreak to both realised and still-evolving threats.  Stryker repeatedly discloses that COVID-19 has already ‘materially adversely affected’ core functions—manufacturing, supply chain, distribution, sales—and quantifies the impact where data are available (e.g., suspension of elective procedures driving a 3.6 % sales decline).  The text also details forward-looking exposures: continuing labour shortages, remote-work cyber-risk, liquidity strain on customers, regulatory uncertainties and government commandeering of capacity.  These statements are direct, recent and operationally granular, so the Time Decay Principle allows high per-sentence severity scores (7-10).  Mitigating elements—such as references to progressive improvement or company actions to adjust operations—temper but do not outweigh the immediacy and breadth of the disclosed harms.  Overall, COVID-19 represents a high-severity, multi-faceted and ongoing risk for Stryker.

Stryker’s 2021 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as both a realized and an ongoing enterprise-level hazard.  Disclosures span every major risk vector requested—supply-chain choke points (electronic component shortages, transportation cost spikes), labour dislocation (tight labour markets, absenteeism, remote-work cyber exposure), abrupt demand swings (elective-procedure suspensions and unpredictable surges), and regulatory / liability overhang (accelerated product approvals, EUA products).  The language is specific, repeatedly states that impacts have already been “material”, and cites concrete operational and financial consequences recorded through Q4 2021.  Because the filing date (11 Feb 2022) is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Mitigating language is minimal and largely speculative; most passages emphasise continuing uncertainty and the possibility of further deterioration.  Overall, the risk profile is acute and pervasive, justifying consistently elevated snippet scores that cluster in the 6-9 range, with modest downward adjustments where impacts are merely potential or heavily conditional.

Stryker’s 2023-02-10 Form 10-K shows that COVID-19 remains a highly consequential, multi-dimensional risk that is both historical (already causing material harm) and forward-looking (likely to persist or recur).  Sentences throughout the Risk Factors section describe concrete, realised impacts – supply-chain delays, component shortages, labour attrition, elective-procedure suspensions – as well as continuing uncertainty tied to resurgences, variants and macro-economic knock-on effects such as inflation.  The language is specific (“materially adversely affected”, “unable to retain employees”, “delays and shortages”) and repeatedly links the pandemic to core business drivers: manufacturing throughput, customer demand, profitability and even cybersecurity posture via remote work.  Because the filing date is within three years of the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7–10) where impacts are direct and material, moderate scores (4–6) when impacts are unquantified or conditional, and lower scores (≤3) where discussion is largely speculative or mitigated.  The following micro-scorecards apply this rubric sentence by sentence.

Stryker’s 2024 Form 10-K makes clear that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a prominent, multifaceted risk driver nearly four years after the World Health Organization declared the outbreak a global pandemic.  The filing moves beyond boiler-plate language and cites both realized impacts (e.g., elective-procedure suspensions, manufacturing delays, inflationary cost spikes) and forward-looking exposures (possible renewed shutdowns, labour shortages, remote-work cyber-risk).  The company explicitly characterises these effects as having materially impacted past results and as capable of materially impacting future performance across supply chain reliability, demand patterns, pricing power and operational continuity.  Although the original outbreak is approaching the 4-year mark, many of the described consequences are still unfolding, keeping the severity in the upper-mid range under the Time Decay Principle.  Accordingly, most individual sentences earn moderate-to-high scores (5-8), reflecting specific, recent and continuing exposures, while statements that note offsetting demand or are more generic earn lower scores.  Overall, COVID-19 remains a live, systemic risk for Stryker rather than a fully historical footnote.

Sysco’s 2021-08-30 Form 10-K provides an unusually detailed, near-term discussion of COVID-19 risks.  The filing was made roughly 18 months after the WHO pandemic declaration, so the statements concern an event squarely within the 0-3-year “recent” window, meaning high scores (7-10) are permissible under the Time Decay Principle.  The company describes both (a) direct, already-incurred harms (e.g., lost food-service demand, higher bad-debt, labour shortages, supply-chain bottlenecks) and (b) continuing or escalating exposures (new variants, future shutdowns, credit-market access).  Several passages explicitly quantify the breadth of affected operating levers—growth, product cost, logistics, collections, liquidity—signalling enterprise-wide materiality.  Language is concrete (“have adversely affected”, “customer demand is outpacing supply”, “experienced an increase in past-due receivables”) rather than boiler-plate.  Mitigations (safety protocols, community donations) are mentioned but do not materially offset the severity, keeping most sentence-level scores high.  Taken together, the evidence shows Sysco facing an active, systemic threat with multi-year persistence, warranting elevated risk ratings in the upper‐mid range of the 0-10 scale for each snippet.

Sysco’s 2022 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as a still-acute, multi-dimensional threat that spans immediate operating impacts and forward-looking uncertainties. Nearly two and a half years after the WHO declaration, management states that the pandemic “continues” to hurt revenues, supply-chain fluidity, labour availability, consumer behaviour and even cyber-risk. The language is largely qualitative but repeatedly describes real, ongoing adverse effects (e.g., demand destruction in restaurants, supplier shortfalls, higher wage costs). Because the filing date is August 2022—well within the 0-3-year “recent-event” window—Time-Decay allows elevated severity scores. None of the cited passages quantify dollar impacts, which tempers scoring versus a fully quantified disclosure, yet the breadth of operational areas affected, plus explicit acknowledgement that COVID may magnify other risks (e.g., leverage, stock price), keeps overall materiality high. Taken together, the evidence supports a consolidated risk severity in the upper-middle range (roughly 7-8/10), reflecting a direct, ongoing, but largely un-quantified exposure that permeates Sysco’s core business model.

Sysco’s 2023 Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic to both historical damage and continuing vulnerability across three major vectors: (1) demand destruction in the food-away-from-home channel, (2) supply-chain and labor dislocations, and (3) macro-economic uncertainty that can amplify other risk factors.  The filing confirms that the pandemic materially “adversely impacted” operations in prior periods and explicitly warns that lingering or renewed outbreaks, including aggressive variants, could re-impose government restrictions, depress consumer confidence, and strain suppliers.  Although management notes that operations have “generally stabilized,” they concede an inability to “predict with certainty” future effects, signalling unresolved exposure.  The language is mostly qualitative—no dollar figures or probability metrics—but it is specific to Sysco’s business model (restaurants, schools, hotels, cruise lines) and directly references supply shortages and consumer behaviour shifts.  Because the filing date (Aug-2023) is roughly 3½ years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle moderates but does not neutralise severity; evidence sits on the cusp of the 0-3 and 4-10-year bands, so scores are weighted in the upper-middle range (4-7).  Mitigating references to business “stabilisation” and the absence of fresh quantitative losses temper some scores, but the continued emphasis on potential future disruptions keeps overall risk assessment at a meaningful level.

Sysco’s 2024 Form 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to material business risks.  The filing cites (a) concrete, already-realised harm—lower demand, operational disruption, and financial hits—and (b) persisting, forward-looking uncertainties such as new variants, renewed government shutdowns, labour squeezes and supply-chain strain.  Language is largely qualitative but unequivocal, stressing vulnerability in core revenue drivers (food-away-from-home demand, restaurant traffic) and in logistical dependencies (suppliers, transportation, workforce).  Although management notes that operations have "generally stabilised," it simultaneously concedes it "cannot predict with certainty" future impacts, so mitigation is partial at best.  Because the initial pandemic shock occurred in March 2020—roughly 4-½ years before the 28 Aug 2024 filing—the Time Decay Principle places the evidence in the medium-term band (4-10 years).  Accordingly, individual snippet scores are capped in the moderate 4-6 range: high enough to reflect genuine, continuing exposure but tempered to recognise elapsed time and some recovery momentum.

TAP’s February 2021 filing presents an unambiguous, near-term risk profile tied to the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company discloses both realised 2020 impacts (lower sales, net-sales reductions, incremental costs, supply-chain bottlenecks and specific write-downs) and forward-looking threats (continued on-premise shutdowns, labour interruptions, collection risk, packaging shortages and macro-economic weakness).  Language is highly specific—naming channels (on-premise vs. off-premise), geographies (North America, Europe), financial line items (net sales, liquidity, dividends), and quantified charges—demonstrating that the threat is not hypothetical but already material.  Because the filing date (11-Feb-2021) is within one year of the core event start (11-Mar-2020), the Time-Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  Still, a few mitigating notes (shift to off-premise demand, ongoing cost-savings plan, amended credit covenant) slightly temper extreme ratings.  Overall, the risk evidence is recent, direct, specific, and financially consequential, warranting high micro-scores in the 7-10 range for each extracted sentence.

COVID-19 is portrayed by TAP (Molson Coors Beverage Company) as a recent, still-evolving threat that has already produced concrete, material damage to almost every facet of the enterprise—top-line demand, on-premise channel closure, supply-chain continuity, labour availability, packaging shortages, working-capital collection, and overall liquidity.  The company repeatedly cites 2020-2021 actual negative results while warning that 2022 could also be ‘significantly adversely affected,’ reflecting an unmistakable direct-impact posture rather than a purely precautionary outlook.  Language such as ‘material adverse effect,’ ‘significantly adversely affected,’ and detailed operational pinch-points (e.g., freight inflation, package-mix shifts, workforce disruptions from vaccine mandates) confirms high severity.  Because the filing date (23 Feb 2022) falls only two years after the official WHO pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), Time-Decay allows high per-snippet scores (up to 10).  Mitigating references (e.g., phased re-openings, remote work, employee safety protocols) appear but do not outweigh the breadth and depth of continuing risk.  Overall, COVID-19 constitutes an elevated, ongoing enterprise risk with multi-year financial repercussions, warranting high evidence scores in the 7-9 range.

TAP’s 2023 filing portrays COVID-19 as an active, multi-dimensional threat that has already produced measurable harm and is expected to persist.  The company cites concrete, realized impacts – disrupted operations, higher freight and material costs, reduced on-premise demand, labour shortages and heightened cybersecurity exposure from remote work – while also stressing that these pressures could "continue" or worsen depending on uncertain future developments (variants, regulation, vaccine efficacy).  Language is frequently strong (“material adverse effect,” “negative impact to our financial results”) and attaches the pandemic to core value drivers such as supply-chain resilience, consumer demand and margin performance.  Because the pandemic’s start (March 2020) is within the 0-3-year “recent” window, Time Decay allows high scores.  Most statements are specific to COVID-19, acknowledge both historic and forward-looking risk, but remain largely unquantified.  Overall, the evidence signals elevated, continuing risk at the company-wide level, justifying high—though not maximum—severity scores.

TAP’s 2024 Form 10-K still flags the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a medium-term, enterprise-wide operational hazard rather than an acute crisis.  The company frames pandemics alongside other catastrophic events that can disrupt brewery operations, inflate input costs and constrain logistics.  Most language is forward-looking and generic, yet the filing does acknowledge that TAP «experienced» losses during the coronavirus pandemic—evidence of an already-realised impact.  No dollar figures are supplied, so the disclosure is unquantified, but it ties the event to supply-chain reliability, production continuity, labour availability, remote-work cyber-exposure and potential margin pressure.  Given the filing date is almost four years after the WHO declaration (March 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places COVID-19 in the medium-term window (4-10 years), capping scores in the 4-6 range even when impact is described as material.  Consequently, the sentences below are scored as moderate but still meaningful risk indicators.

TDG’s 2021-11-16 filing discusses the COVID-19 pandemic as an acute, ongoing enterprise-wide threat.  The disclosures blend backward-looking evidence of realised harm (e.g., depressed travel demand, lower OEM sales, supply shortages, labour disruptions) with forward-looking statements that the company “expects” continued adverse effects on net sales, net income and EBITDA into fiscal-2022 and that longer-term outcomes remain impossible to forecast.  The language is highly specific—naming concrete operational pinch-points such as global supply-chain breakdowns, electronic-part shortages, employee health impacts, and government travel restrictions—and repeatedly labels the impact “material” or “significant.”  Because the filing date is less than two years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores (7-10).  Mitigating language is scarce and largely speculative (e.g., “could identify alternative suppliers”), so reductions for mitigation are minimal.  Collectively, the evidence portrays a high-severity, still-evolving risk environment with direct hits to revenue, margins, cash flow and strategic flexibility.  Therefore, individual snippets generally score in the 6-9 range, with the most quantified, financially oriented sentences earning the upper end of that band.

TDG’s 2022-11-10 filing portrays COVID-19 as an active, multi-faceted threat that is still shaping the firm’s financial and operational landscape nearly three years after the WHO declaration.  The language is predominantly present-tense (“is continuing to cause”, “currently experiencing”), confirming a direct and ongoing impact rather than a purely speculative, forward-looking risk.  TDG names concrete pressure points: depressed air-travel demand, commercial OEM production cuts, supply-chain blockages for electronic parts, freight and labour cost inflation, workforce reductions and rehiring challenges, and uncertainty about future government actions or virus variants.  In several places the company concedes that the magnitude and duration of the damage are “unknown” and “difficult to forecast,” amplifying severity.  While the disclosure does mention incremental recovery in domestic traffic and the ability to find alternative suppliers, those mitigating notes are outweighed by extensive evidence of persistent headwinds and by explicit statements that EBITDA, net sales and cash flow remain below pre-pandemic levels.  Because the filing date is within three years of the event’s onset, the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  Overall, the pandemic constitutes a high but not existential risk (high-single-digit scores), moderated slightly where TDG cites partial recovery or substitution strategies.

TDG’s 2023-11-09 filing frames COVID-19 as both an already-realized and still-evolving enterprise risk.  Management confirms that the pandemic materially impaired sales, cash flow and supply-chain performance during 2020-2021 and notes that lingering supply shortages and labor pressures persisted through fiscal-year 2023.  Although domestic air-traffic demand is rebounding, the company concedes that international recovery remains incomplete and that long-term behavioural or regulatory shifts could produce further material disruption.  The disclosures are mostly qualitative—no dollar amounts are provided—but they are specific, multifaceted (demand shock, supply chain, production cut-backs) and explicitly labelled “material.”  Because the first pandemic impacts occurred just over three and a half years ago, Time Decay tempers maximum severity; nevertheless, the combination of proven historical damage and acknowledged future uncertainty sustains a moderate–high risk profile (roughly mid-range on a 0-10 scale).

TDG’s filing acknowledges that the COVID-19 pandemic created both realized and continuing risks that are highly relevant to its narrow aerospace-centric business model.  The company discloses a history of materially negative impacts—lower sales, supply-chain interruptions, labor and raw-material constraints—while also warning that future public-health crises could again be ‘material’.  Although management notes that domestic and international traffic has largely rebounded, it concedes that long-term behavioural and operational shifts may still disrupt demand patterns and margins.  Overall, the disclosures blend backward-looking evidence of actual harm with forward-looking cautions, providing moderately specific descriptions but limited quantification.  Because the pandemic’s onset is now more than four years old, the Time Decay Principle caps severity at a mid-level range; yet the persistence of supply-chain fragility, potential long-term effects, and TDG’s concentrated exposure keep the risk material.  Accordingly, individual sentence scores fall chiefly in the 4-6 range, reflecting medium-term but still significant risk, with modest deductions where the company cites recovery or diversification mitigants.

Teledyne’s 2021 Form 10-K treats COVID-19 as an ongoing, high-severity threat that is already reshaping demand, capital markets and internal operations while simultaneously posing forward-looking uncertainties.  Multiple sections acknowledge concrete impacts that have already materialised—slower growth in China, market volatility, head-count reductions—and warn of further exposure to supply-chain interruptions and acquisition delays.  The language is generally specific (naming supply-chain risk, labour-force actions, capital-market turbulence and financial-statement volatility) yet mostly qualitative, with only one quantified data-point (9.8 % workforce reduction).  Mitigating disclosures (essential-business status, hygiene protocols) slightly temper but do not neutralise the risk narrative.  Because the filing date (26 Feb 2021) is less than a year after the WHO declared the pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits elevated scores.  Overall, Teledyne frames COVID-19 as a near-term, enterprise-wide hazard that could materially disrupt operations, finances and strategic transactions, justifying moderate-to-high snippet scores with occasional deductions for mitigation wording.

TDY’s 2022 filing contains numerous, concrete references to the COVID-19 pandemic that reveal both present-day impacts and forward-looking uncertainties.  Management explicitly states that the pandemic has already interrupted global supply chains, driven component shortages, delayed shipments and elevated costs, thereby squeezing revenue, margins and cash-flow.  They also concede that COVID-related labour shortages—made worse by quarantine rules and vaccine mandates—are limiting production capacity and could raise wage expense.  In addition, demand-side pressures are flagged: commercial-air-travel weakness, a China growth slowdown and volatile capital markets are all traced to the pandemic.  While the company notes some mitigation (e.g., “limited disruptions” in 2021, contingency planning), most language is definitive (“is being impacted,” “have experienced”) and extends into 2022, keeping risk levels high under the Time-Decay Principle (event < 3 yrs).  Overall, COVID-19 constitutes an acute, multi-faceted risk with enterprise-wide financial consequences, warranting high but not maximum severity scores (7–9) for the strongest passages, and moderate deductions where impacts are less quantified or partly offset by mitigating actions.

TDY’s 2023-02-24 Form 10-K links the still-unfolding COVID-19 pandemic to a range of concrete, near-term operational and financial risks.  The filing acknowledges direct, ongoing impacts—supply-chain bottlenecks, component shortages, inflationary input costs, and labour deficits triggered by infections, quarantines and government lockdowns (especially in China).  Management further warns that a resurgence of the virus could materially impair manufacturing throughput, revenue and margins, while admitting it cannot yet quantify all financial consequences.  Although the company notes some mitigation—contingency planning, expectations of improvement in 2023, and the fact that 2022 disruptions were “limited”—these caveats do not eliminate the core exposure.  Because the pandemic is within three years of the filing date, the Time Decay Principle permits higher scores.  Evidence sentences that show direct, present-tense impacts or invoke material financial/labour consequences score toward the upper range (7-9).  Statements that are generic, historical, or heavily caveated receive moderate-to-low scores, and explicit mitigating language deducts points.  The aggregated disclosures portray a material, active risk that, while somewhat stabilising, remains strategically significant for TDY.

TDY’s 2024 filing treats COVID-19 primarily as an event that triggered earlier operational pain but still casts a medium-term shadow.  The company cites two concrete vectors: (1) a pandemic-related slowdown in Chinese economic growth that could dampen demand for its instrumentation and imaging products, and (2) supply-chain interruptions that already reduced its ability to manufacture and ship, with some constraints still lingering.  These references confirm that COVID-19 produced direct impacts (supply-chain delays) and indirect impacts (macro-economic softness) that remain relevant four years on, though the language shifts from acute crisis to managed, improving conditions.  The disclosure is therefore partly retrospective and partly forward-looking, contains no quantified dollar figures, and includes only limited mitigating language.  Under the Time Decay Principle (event ≈ 4 years old), the pandemic risks merit moderate—not maximal—severity scores.  No sentences describe remote-work transitions or labour shortages explicitly tied to COVID-19, so the evidence set is confined to the cited impacts.

TECH’s 2021-08-25 filing was written roughly eighteen months after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so the Time-Decay principle allows high severity scores (0-3 year window).  The disclosure package shows both retrospective and forward-looking impacts: the company explicitly states that COVID-19 has already harmed employees, supply chains, commercial operations and revenue, and that these effects are expected to continue and could be “material.”  The discussion is relatively specific – it names concrete disruption channels (stay-at-home orders, travel bans, remote-work frictions, site closures, uncertain demand, potential border closures, labour-market retention issues, and supply-chain shocks).  However, there is little hard quantification (no dollar amounts); several passages also outline mitigations (new product launches, safety protocols, supply-chain monitoring, full operational continuity), which temper—but do not eliminate—the risk.  Overall, the evidence portrays a high but not catastrophic risk profile: real, multi-faceted impacts are already occurring and could intensify, yet management is actively adapting.  Therefore, the strongest snippets approach the upper band (8-9/10), while statements dominated by mitigations or generic wording fall in the low range (0-3/10).

TECH’s 10-K, filed in August 2022, squarely links the recent COVID-19 pandemic (now roughly two years old at filing) to multiple operational and financial threats.  The disclosures move beyond boiler-plate: management cites concrete, already-experienced effects (e.g., Chinese lockdowns that have “significantly impacted … our business”), details a multi-pronged list of observed and potential consequences (demand shocks, supply-chain blockages, labour constraints, price inflation, credit risk, market-size contraction) and warns that many of these pressures could recur or intensify.  Most statements are forward-looking as well as retrospective, stressing that restrictions “likely will continue” and “could be materially impacted” if renewed.  No hard dollar figures are given, but the language is strong (“materially impacted,” “significantly impacted”) and broad in scope.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, COVID-19 remains a recent, ongoing crisis (<3 years), so the evidence can command upper-tier severity scores.  Overall, I assess the pandemic risk level for TECH as high-to-severe, driven by credible first-hand impacts, explicit supply-chain and labour disruptions, and the absence of substantive mitigations or offsets.

TECH’s 10-K repeatedly links the COVID-19 pandemic to concrete, already-felt disruptions and to continuing uncertainty.  The company says it has “experienced” demand reductions, supply-chain blockages, price inflation and labour constraints, while also warning that renewed government lockdowns could again “materially impact” results.  The discussion is neither hypothetical nor remote—the impacts span the last three fiscal years and remain possible going forward—yet most statements are qualitative and un-quantified.  Because the filing date (23 Aug 2023) is roughly 3.5 years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle moderates scores into the mid-range (4-6) rather than the very high band reserved for events <3 years old.  Overall, the disclosures evidence a live, moderately severe risk that continues to influence demand, supply chains, workforce stability and cost structure, without citing specific dollar amounts or irreversible damage, justifying medium-level severity ratings for individual snippets.

TECH’s 2024-08-22 filing frames the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as a continuing, economy-wide hazard that can still ripple through its supply chain, workforce, demand profile and operational infrastructure even four-plus years after the World Health Organization declared the outbreak a pandemic.  The risk language is largely prospective ("may in the future"), but the Company also acknowledges that it has already "experienced" many of these disruptions, signalling that the threat is both historical and ongoing.  None of the disclosures quantify dollar impacts, and COVID-19 is discussed together with other macro shocks, making the wording somewhat generic.  Nevertheless, the statements cover the four key pandemic vectors requested—demand volatility, supply-chain blockages, labour constraints and broad operational exposure to public-health emergencies—so they remain materially relevant.
