Several sentences tie the pandemic to multiple risk channels (demand shifts, labour/field-work constraints, and vendor failures) and to traditional risk factors (credit losses, financing).  Although Verizon describes mitigation actions (business-continuity plans, store re-openings, repayment programs), these do not eliminate the fundamental exposure.  Because the event is recent (0-3 years) and the filing discloses both realised financial harm and ongoing potential impact across critical corporate functions, most evidence snippets merit upper-mid scores (6-8), with modest deductions where language is purely cautionary or heavily caveated by uncertainty.

Verizon’s 2022-02-11 Form 10-K links COVID-19 to both realized and prospective risks across revenue, cost structure, supply‐chain continuity, workforce deployment and customer demand.  Management discloses that 2020 results were already hit by lower revenue, higher costs and reduced EPS, demonstrating a direct historical impact that remains relevant because the pandemic is still less than three years old.  Forward-looking language stresses that the crisis could “materially adversely affect” operations by altering how customers pay, how employees work, and how suppliers deliver, while also compounding ordinary-course risks such as financing and regulatory exposure.  Several passages highlight continuing uncertainty from new variants and the unknown duration of the crisis, providing only limited mitigation (“no material impact from the new variants thus far”).  Verizon also flags pandemic-driven global supply-chain disruption that could delay equipment and network builds.  Given the recency (0-3 years) and the mix of realized financial harm plus ongoing, potentially compounding threats, the overall risk profile is elevated; most evidence snippets warrant high scores (7-8) with modest downward adjustments where the company cites uncertainty or current immateriality.  Time-decay therefore does not materially reduce severity, but minor mitigation language prevents a blanket maximum score.

Verizon’s 2023 filing confirms that the COVID-19 pandemic remains a live, high-severity risk just three years after the World Health Organization declaration.  The company explicitly recognises both historical damage (lower revenue, higher costs and reduced EPS in 2020) and a continuing threat that a renewed or prolonged public-health crisis could disrupt customer demand, employee availability, supplier performance and overall financial health.  Although the language is largely qualitative, it clearly attributes past financial harm to COVID-19, outlines multiple transmission channels (supply-chain disruption, labour issues, customer payment capacity and macro-financing stress) and labels the potential future impact as “materially adverse.”  Because the filing date (2023-02-10) is within three years of the key event date (2020-03-11), the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scores.  No detailed quantitative forward guidance or new mitigation plan is provided, so risk remains significant rather than fully managed.  Overall, the disclosures warrant moderate-to-high severity micro-scores, with the strongest evidence being the sentence that chronicles concrete 2020 financial impacts linked directly to COVID-19.

Verizon’s 2024 Form 10-K still portrays the COVID-19 pandemic as a meaningful—though now primarily prospective—risk driver.  Management reminds investors that the pandemic caused tangible harm in 2020 (lower revenue, higher costs and lower EPS) and that similar public-health shocks could once again disrupt the company’s three critical dependency chains: customers (demand/collections), labour (employee availability and safety) and suppliers (equipment and service delivery).  The language is partly backward-looking (citing 2020 impact) but mostly forward-looking and conditional (“could materially adversely affect”).  While no fresh dollar figures are offered, the narrative links a single global event to multiple enterprise-wide vulnerabilities, signalling a non-trivial exposure.  Because the original outbreak is now nearly four years old, the Time Decay Principle tempers maximum severity; nevertheless, COVID-19 remains within the medium-term window (4-10 years) and the filing expressly ties past losses to the same underlying hazard, justifying mid-range snippet scores (roughly 2-6) rather than extreme values.  Overall, the risk is assessed as moderate-to-high and still relevant, but not at crisis-level intensity.

Visa’s 2021 filing connects COVID-19 to a spectrum of still-unfolding threats that touch every part of its business model.  Because cross-border travel drives a meaningful share of Visa’s fees, any pandemic-induced slump in international spending immediately depresses revenue—an impact the company cites directly.  Management further details cascading second-order risks: supply-chain and third-party outages that could interrupt processing; higher charge-backs and fraud as commerce migrates online; workforce challenges tied to prolonged remote work; and, critically, emergency government actions such as temporary caps on interchange that are already in force and could become permanent.  The narrative is largely forward-looking (“may,” “could”) but is anchored by several instances of realised impact (e.g., actual fee caps in multiple countries).  Given the filing date (Nov-2021) falls well inside the 0-3-year “recent event” window, and given the breadth, immediacy and partial realisation of the threats, the overall pandemic-related risk profile is high.  The evidence therefore earns generally elevated micro-scores, tempered only where language is purely precautionary or mitigation steps (e.g., phased office re-openings) are emphasised.

Visa’s 2022-11-16 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-vector risk that still actively shapes the company’s operating environment almost three years after the WHO declaration.  The filing ties the pandemic to macro-level revenue pressure (cross-border travel collapse, fee-cap regulation), operational exposures (remote-work cyber-attacks, talent retention under shifting health protocols) and potential future regulatory headwinds that could revive fee caps.  All references are forward-looking and emphasize continuing uncertainty rather than legacy impacts, underscoring that management views the pandemic as a live, materially adverse factor rather than a historical footnote.  Although the disclosure stops short of precise dollar quantification, it supplies several concrete channels—interchange limits, travel-related volumes, cyber-fraud upticks, and labor market friction—through which earnings could be hit.  Given the filing date (late 2022), the Time Decay Principle treats COVID-19 as a very recent event; high but not maximum snippet scores (5-8 range) are therefore appropriate.  No substantial mitigating language (e.g., robust counter-measures or full recovery) offsets the risk, so net severity remains elevated.

Visa’s 2023-11-15 filing continues to tie the COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and prospective business risks. Although more than three years have passed since the World Health Organization first declared the pandemic, Visa still describes concrete, ongoing impacts—e.g., negative effects on operations, suppliers, cross-border travel, and heightened cyber-fraud exposure driven by remote-work patterns. The disclosures mainly reference broad operational and regulatory consequences (interchange-fee caps, lingering travel uncertainty) rather than quantified dollar figures, but they use definitive language such as “have negatively impacted” and “we continue to see,” indicating that the threat is not merely hypothetical. Because the pandemic event window (2020-03-11 onward) is less than four years before the filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows relatively elevated scores; however, the absence of hard financial metrics and the inclusion of mitigating context (e.g., formal end of the health emergency) temper the severity. Overall, COVID-19 remains a material, recently experienced risk for Visa, but the company frames it in mainly qualitative terms and alongside other macro threats, warranting moderate-to-high evidence scores rather than the maximum levels.

Visa’s 2024 Form 10-K contains only a brief, catch-all reference to “pandemics like COVID-19” within a broader list of macro-level disruptors.  The company frames COVID-19 as one of several health, geopolitical, and environmental shocks that have already “negatively impacted” operations, suppliers, and cross-border travel and spend.  The disclosure is therefore backward- and contemporaneously-looking: it acknowledges observable impacts rather than providing quantified forward guidance, and it offers no detail on supply-chain fragility, labour shortages, remote-work arrangements, or demand shifts.  Because the pandemic began more than four years before the 2024 Filing Date, the Time Decay Principle moderates any severity score into a mid-range band (4-6).  The language nevertheless concedes direct operational harm, keeping the risk material enough to warrant a moderate score, but its generic phrasing and lack of financial quantification prevent a higher rating.

WAB’s 2024 filing acknowledges COVID-19 as both a recently experienced shock and a continuing source of operational uncertainty.  The company cites concrete, realized impacts—order deferrals and backlog delays during the 2020-2022 slowdown—as well as persistent after-effects on global supply chains, labour availability and component shortages that are still depressing revenue timing today.  These disclosures show that the pandemic is not merely historical; it remains embedded in current cost structures and delivery schedules.  At the same time, management notes that operations have “generally stabilised,” signalling partial mitigation, and frames most forward-looking language in probabilistic terms (e.g., “could,” “may”).  Because the event occurred less than four years ago, the Time Decay Principle allows elevated scores, but the presence of mitigation and generic phrasing in several sentences moderates the severity.  Overall, the risk profile is mixed: tangible past impacts and ongoing supply-chain friction drive higher scores for direct statements, while broad, catch-all references to ‘disease outbreaks’ or hypothetical future pandemics score lower.

WAT’s 2022 filing links COVID-19 to a broad spectrum of acute operational and financial threats. The language is largely present-tense and backed by recent empirical experience, confirming that the pandemic is not merely a hypothetical future risk but an ongoing, realised pressure point. Core exposures identified include supply-chain breakdowns, logistics cost spikes, labour shortages, cybersecurity vulnerabilities stemming from remote work, and potential demand shocks that could trigger sizeable balance-sheet write-downs. While the company notes some successful mitigations (e.g., no material factory shutdowns to date and completed 2020 cost-saving actions), it simultaneously concedes uncertainty about the adequacy of these measures and the possibility of “material impact” going forward. Under the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic falls within the 0-3-year window, so evidence can be scored as high as 10. Given the filing’s frank acknowledgment of actual disruptions, continuing volatility, and explicitly “material” downside scenarios—balanced only partially by mitigation claims—the overall risk profile is elevated but not catastrophic. Most individual sentences therefore cluster in the 6-9 range, with downward adjustments where the company cites mitigating facts, and higher scores where it describes concrete or potentially material adverse effects.

Waters Corporation’s 2024 filing positions the COVID-19 pandemic as an ongoing, but now medium-term, enterprise-wide risk. The language combines retrospective acknowledgement—e.g., a concrete hit to China sales in 2022—with forward-looking caution that future public-health crises could again disrupt operations, demand and cash flow. While the company stops short of providing hard dollar figures or detailed scenario modelling, it explicitly cites past negative impacts, worldwide economic volatility, and exposure stemming from its globally distributed workforce and facilities. Mitigating language (“could,” “highly uncertain”) and references to recovering demand temper the severity. Applying the Time Decay Principle, four years have elapsed since the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, so direct pandemic disclosures warrant moderate (not maximal) scores. Overall, the evidence supports a mid-range risk rating: the threat is still material, recently realized in certain geographies, but increasingly framed as a manageable uncertainty rather than a current crisis.

Walgreens Boots Alliance’s 2021 filing contains extensive, event-specific language linking the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and prospective risks across virtually every facet of the enterprise.  Because the disclosure comes just 18-19 months after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (0-3 year window).  The company states that COVID-19 has already cut store traffic, raised operating costs, triggered supply-chain bottlenecks, created labour shortfalls, forced a large-scale shift to remote work and heightened cyber-security exposure.  It further warns that these disruptions may persist or worsen as new variants emerge and as government restrictions ebb and flow.  The language is concrete (e.g., “have adversely impacted” and “we have incurred additional costs”), forward-looking (“may continue to severely impact”), and covers multiple core value drivers—revenue, margins, liquidity and strategic execution—without offering commensurate mitigations beyond ongoing monitoring.  Collectively, these passages depict a high, multi-dimensional risk profile with immediate financial consequences, justifying elevated snippet scores in the 6-9 range, well within the upper band permitted for a recent event.

Walgreens Boots Alliance’s 2022 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as both an already-realized shock and an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat.  Management states that the pandemic has “adversely impacted” past results while explicitly warning that many of those impacts “may continue,” demonstrating that risk is current and forward-looking.  The discussion is highly specific: it references store-traffic collapses, supply-chain disruptions, labor shortages, remote-work productivity drag, incremental IT and safety costs, potential store closures, volatility in liquidity and capital-market access, and inflationary pressures tied to global logistics.  This granularity, combined with multiple acknowledgements of materiality, indicates a meaningful, multi-vector risk rather than boiler-plate language.  Because the filing date (Oct-2022) is within three years of the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high scores.  However, the text offers no quantified dollar amounts and only limited mention of mitigation, so individual sentence scores peak in the 7–8 range rather than a maximum 10.  Overall, the filing portrays COVID-19 as a severe, persistent operational and financial hazard with broad reach across WBA’s value chain.

Walgreens Boots Alliance’s 2023-10-12 filing still treats COVID-19 as a live, multi-faceted threat.  Although the first global shock occurred in March 2020, the company describes *continuing* and *potentially escalating* impacts on consumer demand, input-price inflation, supply-chain continuity, labour availability, cybersecurity posture (because of remote work) and the accelerated shift to omni-channel retail.  The language is mostly forward-looking ("may continue" / "could"), but it is anchored in concrete experience – the firm notes that prior-year earnings were materially influenced by vaccination revenues and that pandemic-related disruptions have already affected operations.  Phrases such as “material adverse impact” and “severely impacted” indicate high management concern.  Applying the Time-Decay Principle, the event sits just beyond the 3-year “recent” window (≈3.6 years), so raw risk indications are slightly tempered; nevertheless, the disclosures remain specific, multi-dimensional and unmitigated by any strong offsetting actions.  Overall, I assess a moderately high residual severity (upper-mid band scores around 5-7) rather than the peak 8-10 that would have applied in 2021-22.

Walgreens Boots Alliance’s 2024 Form 10-K still frames COVID-19 as a live, though now moderating, enterprise-wide threat.  Nearly five years after the World Health Organization declared a pandemic, management links COVID-19 to multiple risk vectors: weakened consumer confidence, persistent supply-chain fragility, lasting shifts to e-commerce, an uptick in cyber-exposure due to remote work, and continuing volatility in vaccine-related demand.  The wording combines backward-looking impacts (e.g., lower 2023–24 vaccine volumes) with forward-looking cautions (e.g., ‘material adverse impact’ on operations if new disruptions arise).  The disclosures are mostly qualitative and unquantified, but they do acknowledge tangible financial effects (such as the “significant” 2022 vaccination contribution that has since faded).  Applying the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic sits in the medium-term window (4–5 years old), so individual sentence scores must fall in the moderate range (4-6 maximum for the strongest evidence).  Overall, COVID-19 remains a material but decaying risk: no longer existential, yet still capable of pressuring margins, supply logistics and consumer behaviour if new waves or long-tail disruptions emerge.

COVID-19 is presented in the filing as an acute, enterprise-wide threat that is already eroding core revenue streams and could intensify.  Because the 10-K is dated February 22 2021—well within the 0-3-year recency window—the Time Decay principle allows high severity scores where warranted.  The disclosure language blends (1) concrete, realized impacts (e.g., Q2 2020 advertising declines, Olympic postponement, $500 million liquidity draw-down, extra production-safety costs) with (2) forward-looking exposures (continued advertiser pull-backs, recession-driven subscriber losses, remote-work frictions).  Risks are framed as material and specific—52 % of total 2020 revenue derives from advertising that is now vulnerable—rather than boiler-plate.  While management cites mitigation (cost-cutting, remote work, liquidity buffers), those steps are portrayed as partial offsets, not neutralizers.  Taken together, the pandemic risk is immediate, directly linked to cash flow, and only partially controllable; therefore individual snippets receive scores clustered in the 6-9 range, tempered downward when the text highlights offsets such as cost-savings or successful remote operations.

WBD’s 2022 Form 10-K delivers an extensive, mostly qualitative discussion of how the COVID-19 pandemic has already affected—and may continue to affect—the company.  Because the filing date (24 Feb 2022) falls less than two years after the WHO declaration (11 Mar 2020), the disclosures sit in the “recent-event” window of the Time-Decay Principle, so elevated risk scores are justified.  The text cites concrete, realized impacts (production shutdowns, advertising‐demand declines, cancelled sporting events, incremental safety costs) alongside forward-looking uncertainties (continued supply-chain and labor interruptions, covenant-compliance risk, unpredictable shifts in consumer viewing).  Although management notes some recovery in 2021 and highlights acceleration of digital consumption—which could be viewed as partially mitigating—the overall tone remains cautionary: many effects are ongoing or could re-emerge, and management concedes that its counter-measures may fail.  Taken together, the pandemic represents a material, multi-faceted risk touching operations, revenues, liquidity and strategic direction.  My sentence-level scoring therefore leans high (5-7 range) where direct, current impacts are cited, moderate (3-4) where risks are prospective or less quantified, and negative where text expressly downplays impact, all consistent with the Time-Decay thresholds for a recent global event.

WBD’s 2023 Form 10-K explicitly acknowledges that COVID-19 remains a material, recent (≤3-year) risk with both realized and forward-looking dimensions.  The filing describes concrete, adverse impacts that have already occurred—e.g., theater shutdowns, production delays, reductions in studio and theme-park revenues—and it also stresses continuing uncertainty around consumer behaviour, advertising demand, goodwill impairment triggers and macro-economic spill-overs.  Most statements are qualitative rather than dollar-quantified, but they are specific to business lines (Studios, Networks, DTC) and reference identifiable mechanisms (government shutdowns, labor interruptions, depressed attendance).  Because the pandemic is well within the 0-3-year “recent-event” window, the Time Decay Principle permits relatively high severity scores.  Nevertheless, absence of hard numbers and some mitigating language (monitoring, expectations of trend continuation, absence of assurance) temper individual sentence scores to the mid-to-upper range rather than the maximum possible.  Overall, the document portrays COVID-19 as an ongoing, strategically significant risk whose ultimate financial toll remains uncertain.

COVID-19 is treated in WBD’s 2024 Form 10-K as a lingering, but diminishing, enterprise-wide risk. Management frames the pandemic mostly in medium-term, forward-looking terms: while lockdown-driven disruptions have largely subsided, advertising budgets, box-office demand and other revenue lines are still vulnerable to renewed outbreaks or to permanent behavioural shifts that the pandemic accelerated. The filing cites both historical, realised impacts (lost advertising sales, postponed live events, reduced theatre attendance) and potential future impacts (slower theatrical rebound, advertising pull-backs if another pandemic emerges). Language is largely qualitative and couched in contingency words (“could,” “may”), with no precise dollar amounts, supply-chain statistics or labour-force metrics. Given the four-year gap between the WHO pandemic declaration (March 2020) and the filing date (Feb 2024), the Time Decay Principle places the event in the medium-term window: residual effects remain material but are no longer acute. Consequently, individual evidence snippets earn moderate scores; none exceed 6 because impacts are either historic or hypothetical, not quantified, and tempered by acknowledgements that many COVID-related restrictions have “largely lifted.” Overall, the risk is real but receding, warranting a portfolio of medium-level severity scores across the extracted sentences.

Workday’s 2021-03-02 10-K presents COVID-19 as a near-term (“ongoing”) threat with both realized and potential impacts across operations, demand, workforce management, infrastructure, and financial performance.  Numerous passages disclose concrete disruptions already felt (e.g., delayed purchasing decisions, reduced renewals, cancelled in-person events, and margin effects) while simultaneously warning of uncertain, possibly worsening, future consequences.  Language such as “materially and adversely affect” signals high severity, and several statements specify channels of impact: supply-chain issues for data-centres, labour-force health risks, remote-work real-estate pressures, competitor price concessions, and volatility in revenue growth.  Because the filing date sits well within three years of the WHO pandemic declaration (Time Decay window for high scores), evidence can warrant elevated ratings (7–9) when direct effects are acknowledged, with slightly lower (4–6) scores where impacts remain only hypothetical or mitigated (e.g., predictable subscription model).  Overall, COVID-19 is framed as Workday’s most pervasive recent risk, touching nearly every corporate function and amplifying other risk factors.

The filing, dated February 28 2022, was prepared nearly two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, so the risk is both current and observable.  Workday repeatedly characterises COVID-19 as a material threat that has already produced concrete effects—office closures, remote-work mandates, delayed sales cycles, lower renewal rates, labour-market tightness, supply-chain interruptions for data-centre equipment, cost inflation, and volatility in the company’s share price.  Most disclosures are forward-looking as to duration and magnitude, but they are rooted in direct experience (e.g., demand slowdown in travel & hospitality vertical, reduced renewal rates among SMB customers).  Language such as “materially and adversely affect,” “could have a material adverse effect,” and “highly uncertain and difficult to predict” underscores severity while acknowledging uncertainty.  Mitigating statements (vaccine roll-outs, subscription-based revenue predictability, gradual office re-openings) appear, but they are tentative and do not neutralise the overarching risk narrative.  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 is a recent, ongoing event (0-3 years), so individual sentence scores can range near the upper bound when warranted.  Overall, the pandemic is depicted as a high-impact, multi-faceted risk touching operations, finance, workforce, customers, brand, and supply chain—justifying high micro-scores with only modest downward adjustments where mitigating language exists.

Workday’s 2023 Form 10-K explicitly links the COVID-19 pandemic to several ongoing enterprise-wide risk vectors.  Although three years have passed since the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Workday still sees it as a live, material driver of macro-economic volatility, supply-chain disruption, labour-market dislocation and operational uncertainty.  The filing emphasises that pandemic-related upheaval has already affected the global economy and supply chains, and that future ‘measures taken in response’ remain highly unpredictable, leaving a lingering cloud over forecasting, renewals and productivity.  At the micro-operational level, pandemic-accelerated remote and hybrid working models are flagged as catalysts for heightened talent-competition, potential productivity drag and elevated cybersecurity exposure.  None of the statements provide precise, quantified dollar impacts, but they are forward-looking, un-mitigated and clearly tie the pandemic to continuing adverse conditions.  Given the recency window (0-3 years) established by the Time-Decay Principle, these disclosures warrant moderate-to-high severity scores: the threats are direct and current, yet largely qualitative and macro rather than company-specific and quantified.

Workday’s 2024 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 and broader pandemic threats as part of a constellation of macro-risk factors that can still materially disrupt the business even four years after the World Health Organization’s declaration. The language remains largely forward-looking—phrases such as “may negatively affect” or “may be unable to continue operations” dominate—indicating that management now treats COVID-19 as an ongoing contingency rather than an acute crisis. The filing highlights three residual vectors of exposure: (1) macro-demand uncertainty arising from future global health crises; (2) operational fragility should another pandemic-scale event occur, with the potential for outright service outages and data loss; and (3) the enduring cybersecurity vulnerabilities created by a hybrid/remote workforce that originated in the pandemic period. There is no quantified dollar impact, no discussion of specific supply-chain constraints, and only indirect reference to labour challenges. Consequently, while the disclosures acknowledge meaningful risk, they are generic and un-quantified, consistent with a medium-term (four-year-old) event. Applying the Time Decay Principle, overall severity is moderate rather than acute, which guides individual snippet scores into the 4-6 range.

WDC’s August 2021 Form 10-K squarely links the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic to both realized and potential future harms across nearly every facet of its business.  The filing discloses concrete, already-booked financial impacts (e.g., $127 million in incremental logistics charges) while also detailing forward-looking exposures such as supply-chain disruptions, factory shutdowns, cybersecurity vulnerabilities caused by remote work, labor‐force infections, and demand volatility.  The language is largely specific—naming cost categories, operational choke-points, and even quantifying charges—rather than boiler-plate.  Because the filing date is within two years of the WHO’s pandemic declaration, the Time Decay Principle allows high risk scores.  Overall, the risk profile is elevated: there are proven, material cash outflows and the company warns that conditions could deteriorate further if variants emerge or governmental restrictions tighten.  Some mitigating statements (current factory uptime, solid revenue trends) temper—but do not outweigh—the severity.  Consequently, evidence snippets receive scores ranging from mild negative (mitigation) to the maximum for a quantified, realized hit, with the aggregate picture reflecting a high-severity, recently realized risk environment.

WDC’s 2022 Form 10-K contains an extensive, multi-layered discussion of COVID-19 and broader pandemic-related risk.  The company confirms that the virus has already caused concrete, material impacts—ranging from temporary plant shutdowns to $248 million of incremental logistics and factory charges—and warns that similar or larger effects may persist.  The disclosure spans direct operational hits (labour safety measures, under-absorbed overhead, component shortages), knock-on financial pressures (credit-market deterioration, higher borrowing costs, margin compression) and systemic vulnerabilities (remote-work cyber-risk, supply-chain fragility).  While certain passages strike a cautious tone by stressing uncertainty or highlighting mitigation (e.g., sanitation protocols, facilities currently open), the bulk of language is specific, recent and linked to measured dollar figures, signalling a live, high-severity risk well within the 0-3-year window of the Time Decay Principle.  Taken together, the document portrays COVID-19 as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat with both realised and potential future costs, warranting overall elevated risk scores despite partial offsets from mitigation efforts.

Western Digital’s 2023 Form 10-K discloses both retrospective and forward-looking consequences from the COVID-19 pandemic.  The company confirms that it already suffered concrete operational harm—factory shutdowns, under-absorbed overhead, higher logistics and component costs, and weakened product demand—yet stresses that similar or expanded disruptions could re-emerge with future waves.  The language is moderately specific, naming particular cost buckets and operational choke-points (supply chain, labor availability, remote-work security, credit-market stress).  No dollar figures are cited, so the magnitude is qualitative rather than quantified, but the impacts described (plant closures, demand contraction) are inherently material to a high-fixed-cost manufacturer.  Because the filing date (22 Aug 2023) is just over three years after the pandemic’s official declaration (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle shifts the evidence from a “recent” to an “early-medium” horizon, capping extreme scores yet still allowing for elevated risk ratings given the company’s acknowledgement of continuing and possibly recurring effects.  Overall, the disclosures warrant a moderate-to-high risk assessment—significant enough to influence strategy and finances, but tempered by the passage of time and the absence of quantified damage.

The filing places COVID-19 within a broader category of “public health crises” but still provides several direct references to how the 2020-2022 pandemic affected Western Digital (WDC).  The company discloses concrete, historical consequences—temporary plant shutdowns, under-absorbed overhead, higher logistics costs, and falling product demand—showing that the pandemic was not merely hypothetical.  At the same time, management frames many statements in the conditional tense (e.g., “may in the future negatively impact”), signalling that the residual exposure is now viewed as an ongoing, forward-looking risk rather than an acute emergency.  Because the filing date (Aug-2024) is roughly four years after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (Mar-2020), the Time-Decay Principle limits maximum severity to the “medium-term” band (4-10 years), suggesting individual snippet scores should fall in the moderate 4-6 range unless materially mitigated.  Where the language is generic or heavily caveated, scores are further discounted.  Conversely, where the company lists specific operational impacts attributable to COVID-19, the evidence receives the higher end of the medium-term band.  No snippet is scored above 6, and mitigating statements (e.g., uncertainty or future tense) reduce scores accordingly.

WEC’s 2021-02-25 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as an active, materially adverse event whose effects were already being felt throughout 2020 and could intensify in subsequent years.  The disclosure moves well beyond boiler-plate: management specifies concrete channels of impact – supply-chain interruption, labour shortages, capital-market volatility, construction delays (e.g. Badger Hollow I), rising bad-debt and liquidity strain – and links them directly to lower energy demand from commercial and industrial customers.  Although no precise dollar amounts are provided, the narrative makes clear that the pandemic has both realised and prospective consequences for operations, liquidity and earnings.  Mitigating actions (remote-work protocols, hygiene measures, a $340 m term-loan back-stop, suspension of customer disconnections) are noted, but they do not neutralise the breadth of exposure.  Given that the filing date falls well within three years of the WHO declaration (Time-Decay window for high severity), recent factual impacts and the forward-looking warnings together warrant elevated snippet scores, typically in the 4-8 range, with the highest marks reserved for sentences enumerating multiple direct financial and operational threats.  Statements limited to mitigation or generic uncertainty receive lower scores to reflect partial offset or weaker signalling.

Because the 10-K was filed in February 2022 – less than two years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic – time-decay is minimal and recent facts carry full weight.  WEC discloses both realised and prospective impacts.  Realised impacts include project delays (Badger Hollow I), higher uncollectible receivables, and temporary stress in commercial-paper markets.  Forward-looking language warns of further revenue erosion, liquidity strain, supply-chain cost inflation, labour shortages, and construction slow-downs if new public-health orders arise.  The wording is generally specific (naming supply-chain disruptions, bad-debt spikes, labour attrition, capital-market access), although no dollar amounts are provided.  Mitigations – hygiene protocols, remote-work policies, employee surcharges, monitoring efforts – are noted but do not fully offset the breadth of exposure.  Overall, the pandemic remains a material, multi-dimensional risk with medium-to-high severity; snippet scores therefore cluster in the 3-8 range, consistent with the Time Decay Principle for a very recent event.

WEC’s 2023 filing presents COVID-19 (referred to generically as “public health crises, including epidemics and pandemics”) as an ongoing, enterprise-wide threat that can depress revenues, raise bad-debt expense, strain liquidity, disrupt capital-market access, and hinder construction programmes.  The risk is framed largely in forward-looking terms—management emphasises that future pandemics or variants may still impair supply chains, raise inflationary pressure on labour / materials, and trigger workforce shortages—yet it is anchored in experience from 2020-2022, establishing that these effects are not hypothetical.  The language is company-specific (e.g., implementation of the corporate strategy, development of facilities) but remains unquantified and lacks a discussion of actual dollar impacts.  Given the recency of the pandemic (within three years of the filing date), the Time-Decay Principle allows relatively high scoring, although the absence of hard numbers and presence of generic contingency phrasing (“could,” “may”) temper individual snippet scores.  Overall, the disclosures indicate a material, still-present threat whose severity is mitigated only by its largely speculative wording and the lack of concrete financial metrics.

WEC’s 2024 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 (and future pandemics) chiefly as an ongoing, enterprise-wide hazard rather than a past, fully-realised shock.  The risk language is forward-looking and largely qualitative, emphasising potential—not yet fully quantified—financial, operational and strategic impacts: lost revenue, higher bad-debt, capital-market access problems, supply-chain inflation, project delays, and workforce disruptions.  The company also concedes substantial uncertainty around magnitude and duration, signalling limited visibility into residual effects four years after the World Health Organization declaration.  Under the Time Decay Principle, COVID-19 sits at the edge of the 0-3-year “recent” band and in the early stage of the 4-10-year “medium-term” window; consequently, individual evidence snippets merit moderate scores (4-6) unless tempered by mitigating language such as acknowledgements of uncertainty or management efforts.  No sentence provides hard dollar figures or cites realised losses, so scores do not reach the highest tier.  Overall, the disclosure points to a material but still largely contingent risk that could hinder WEC’s strategy execution and financial performance if another severe wave or comparable public-health crisis emerges.

Welltower’s 2021-02-10 filing provides a detailed, contemporaneous picture of COVID-19 risk, written only eleven months after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic.  The text stitches together both realized impacts—sharp occupancy declines, higher operating costs, staff dislocation, supply-chain disruption, rent-collection stress—and forward-looking uncertainties such as capital-market access and dividend capacity.  Many statements quantify the damage (e.g., occupancy falling from 85.8 % to 74.4 %), anchoring the risk as material and already embedded in financial performance, while other passages acknowledge that management cannot yet bound the ultimate effect.  Mitigations (government relief funds, high historical rent collections) are mentioned but framed as insufficient. Although no dollar figures are supplied and mitigation plans are sparse, the language is specific to core revenue drivers, geographically focused on Macau (the Company’s largest profit centre) and cascades into broader liquidity-and-leverage concerns.  Under the Time Decay Principle, the recency and immediacy of these disclosures justify upper-mid to high micro-scores (generally 3-6), tempered slightly for the absence of exact quantification and the presence of conditional phrasing.

WYNN’s 2024 filing continues to link the COVID-19 pandemic to material business risk.  The company recalls a sharp visitation collapse beginning in 2020, notes that lingering testing and entry rules remained in place through early-2023, and concedes that Macau demand has not yet rebounded to pre-pandemic levels.  Management explicitly warns that it cannot predict when – or even if – full recovery will occur, and cites the pandemic as a direct reason for suspending dividends at its Macau subsidiary.  These disclosures show that COVID-19 is both an historic loss driver (steep revenue drop, dividend suspension) and an ongoing, forward-looking uncertainty (slow recovery, potential future outbreaks).  While some mitigation exists (most restrictions lifted, improving volumes), the risk remains live, especially given WYNN’s heavy dependence on inbound travel to Macau.  Applying the Time Decay Principle, the pandemic sits at the four-year mark: not brand-new but still recent enough that direct effects persist.  Therefore, individual sentence scores gravitate toward the middle-upper of the medium-term band (roughly 3-6), with upward weight for concrete past impacts and downward weight where mitigation or generic wording appears.

Xcel Energy’s 2021 Form 10-K squarely acknowledges COVID-19 as a fresh, still-unfolding threat that could alter virtually every aspect of its utility business.  The risk discussion combines (i) factual statements that the pandemic is already depressing sales and heightening bad-debt exposure, (ii) forward-looking uncertainty about employee health, supply-chain reliability and the pace of economic recovery, and (iii) descriptions of contingency or regulatory mechanisms that partially cushion the blow (e.g., decoupling, true-ups and expense deferrals).  The language is mostly qualitative, but it does include one quantified data point (-$0.15 EPS headwind from lower sales) and multiple references to potentially “material” impacts, indicating that management sees the threat as significant.  Because the filing date (17 Feb 2021) is less than one year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores.  Nonetheless, the evidence is moderated by the company’s cost-recovery mechanisms, mitigation plans and the fact that 2020 results were “largely mitigated.”  Overall, the pandemic represents a live, near-term risk with moderate-to-high severity for Xcel Energy, warranting per-sentence scores that cluster in the 3-6 range, with a few higher where concrete financial effects or large magnitudes are cited and lower where only generic uncertainty or explicit mitigations are noted.

Xcel Energy’s 2022 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 as an active, multifaceted threat that is still unfolding less than two years after the formal WHO pandemic declaration.  The filing places the virus squarely within the company’s top-level risk taxonomy, citing supply-chain dislocations, labour shortages, sales-mix volatility, and the possibility that COVID-19 could magnify other risk categories.  The language is largely present-tense (e.g., “continues to impact,” “may continue to experience”) and therefore evidences existing — not merely hypothetical — exposure.  Several mitigating measures (decoupling, sales true-ups) are discussed, but these are either geographically limited, have expired, or are only in the proposal stage, which tempers but does not eliminate residual risk.  No hard dollar amounts are provided, so the disclosures remain qualitative, yet the repeated use of phrases such as “material effect” and explicit references to supply-chain and workforce disruptions elevate the severity assessment.  Because the filing date (Feb 2022) lies inside the 0-3-year “recent event” window, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores where warranted.  Overall, the narrative supports a moderate-to-high residual pandemic risk, punctuated by pockets of mitigation that partially offset but do not neutralise the threat.

The filing, dated February 2023, squarely falls within three years of the WHO’s March 2020 declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic, so Time-Decay allows relatively high scores.  Xcel Energy frames pandemic exposure chiefly as an ongoing, enterprise-wide risk that could materially affect cash flow, liquidity, supply-chain reliability and labour availability.  The language is forward-looking but acknowledges continuing impacts (e.g., on supply chains and markets), indicating the risk is not merely hypothetical.  However, the disclosures remain largely qualitative: there are no quantified dollar amounts, no explicit discussion of remote-work adaptations, and only broad references to potential shutdowns and workforce shortages.  Mitigations or concrete response plans are absent, and the company repeatedly states it “cannot predict” the ultimate impact, which tempers severity.  Overall, the pandemic is presented as a real, continuing threat with multiple operational vectors, but the absence of specific financial metrics or incidents keeps the evidence from the highest severity tier.  Consequently, individual snippet scores cluster in the mid-single digits, reflecting recent timing and identifiable operational links, moderated by generic wording and uncertainty disclaimers.

The filing discusses pandemic exposure primarily in a forward-looking, qualitative manner.  COVID-19 is now four years old, placing it in the early edge of the “medium-term” window under the Time Decay Principle; therefore, evidence can receive moderate—but not peak—severity scores.  Xcel Energy does not quantify any historical losses, but it explicitly states that epidemics could be “material,” and it specifies operational vectors such as supply-chain disruption, labor shortages, shutdowns and transportation bottlenecks.  At the same time, the company repeatedly hedges with uncertainty language (“cannot ultimately predict”), signalling that impacts remain contingent rather than already realised.  Taken together, the disclosures indicate a live, but not yet crystallised, enterprise-wide risk.  Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the 1-5 range, reflecting meaningful but unquantified pandemic exposure, tempered by generic caveats and the moderating effect of time since the initial 2020 outbreak.

The filing, dated February 24 2021, falls well inside the first twelve months after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic on 11 March 2020, so disclosures are evaluated under the “recent event” bracket of the Time Decay Principle (0-3 years).  ExxonMobil explicitly links the pandemic to both realised and prospective financial harm. One sentence states that demand destruction caused by COVID-19 has already resulted in a “significant decrease” in commodity prices and margins—evidence of an immediate, material impact rather than a mere possibility.  A follow-on sentence broadens the discussion to forward-looking consequences, warning that future cash flows, financing needs, and overall business results will hinge on how long pandemic conditions persist and on the success of response measures such as cost cuts and global vaccination efforts.  Elsewhere, the company also lists “public health issues and responses” as a factor that can weaken macro-economic conditions and thus energy demand; this reference is far more generic and therefore carries only minor risk weight.  Taken together, the narrative contains both concrete, present-day impacts and unresolved uncertainties, with no numerical quantification but with strong directional language (“significant decrease,” “will be affected”).  Because the pandemic was ongoing at the filing date, these statements merit high-to-moderate scores, unmitigated by time decay, although partial offsets are applied where the company notes potential mitigating actions (cost-cutting, vaccine roll-out).

The filing, dated February 23, 2022, addresses the COVID-19 pandemic both retrospectively and prospectively. The company explicitly states that the initial phase of the pandemic produced a rapid, material collapse in demand that eroded commodity prices and margins – evidence of a realised, quantified (though not numerically disclosed) impact. It then projects that future outbreaks, government counter-measures, and lasting shifts in consumer behaviour could continue to influence cash flows, financing needs, and overall demand. These statements are recent (within two years of the March 2020 WHO declaration) so the Time Decay Principle permits high scores. However, the disclosures remain qualitative – they speak of “significant decreases” but do not provide dollar figures – and they mention some internal mitigating actions (protecting employee safety). Consequently, while the risk is clearly elevated and ongoing, the absence of precise numbers or unique vulnerabilities keeps the evidence just below the maximum severity threshold.

The filing, dated February 22 2023, addresses the continuing ramifications of the March 2020 outbreak of COVID-19 primarily as an ongoing, forward-looking risk that could still influence ExxonMobil’s cash flows, financing needs, and overall market conditions. Because the discussion occurs less than three years after the World Health Organization declared the pandemic, the Time Decay Principle permits relatively high severity scores. The language is mostly qualitative and anticipatory—linking future business results to the speed of recovery, possible new outbreaks, government responses, and knock-on economic effects—rather than providing quantified impacts. Additional references to ‘public health issues,’ ‘supply-chain disruptions,’ and other operational bottlenecks broaden the pandemic-related risk context, although these are framed generically rather than tied directly to COVID-19. Overall, the evidence portrays a material but unquantified, still-current threat that can hamper demand, disrupt logistics, and raise costs, warranting moderately high scores for explicit COVID-19 references and lower but still positive scores for indirect pandemic-related factors.

The filing mentions the COVID-19 pandemic only in a broad, forward-looking context. ExxonMobil does not quantify a past hit to earnings or describe specific operational shutdowns; instead it warns that future epidemics or pandemics—together with government counter-measures—could again influence demand, supply chains, financing needs and global economic conditions. The disclosure therefore represents an existing but largely prospective risk rather than a description of a crystallised loss. Given the February 2024 filing date, the pandemic is still within roughly four years of onset, so the Time Decay principle allows for moderately high scores. However, the language is generic and bundled with other macro factors, and the company pairs some of the risks with its own ability to manage or mitigate them. Consequently, the overall severity reflected in individual snippets is moderate (not severe), generally scoring in the 2-7 range.

XYL’s 2021-02-26 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that is already eroding revenue and operations while remaining highly unpredictable going forward.  The filing is entirely post-event (within 12 months of the WHO declaration on 2020-03-11) so Time-Decay permits elevated severity scores.  Disclosures move well beyond boiler-plate: management cites concrete, realised impacts (facility slow-downs, global volume reductions, elevated logistics costs, supply-chain bottlenecks, remote-work dependency, customer project delays, restructuring actions, financial-market volatility) and explicitly labels them “material adverse.”  Although no single, quantified dollar figure is provided, the company ties the pandemic to multiple core value drivers—sales, production, supply chain continuity, labour deployment, liquidity and capital access—making the risk systemic and enterprise-wide.  Forward-looking language (“may continue,” “could worsen,” “uncertain how materially…throughout 2021 and beyond”) confirms that management expects persistence rather than rapid dissipation, consistent with minimal time decay.  Some mitigating steps (supplier redundancy, remote-work infrastructure, special pay programmes, restructuring) are acknowledged but portrayed as partial buffers rather than definitive solutions.  Taken together, the evidence supports high but not maximum snippet scores (7-9) reflecting severe, current impacts tempered by the absence of precise quantitative loss figures and the presence of limited mitigations.

XYL’s 2022 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, multifaceted enterprise-level threat that is already material and could intensify.  The company discloses concrete, realized impacts—plant slow-downs, revenue pressure, supply-chain breakdowns (especially semiconductor shortages), higher freight and inflation—that have ‘had, and continue to have, a material adverse effect.’  It also warns of forward-looking exposures: future sales declines, backlog execution risk, labour scarcity, capital-market volatility, weakened internal controls, and uncertainty around virus mutations and vaccine efficacy.  The language is specific (naming cost categories, operations halted in 2020-21, quantified backlog risk) rather than boiler-plate and repeatedly uses high-severity qualifiers such as “material adverse.”  Because the filing date (25 Feb 2022) is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration (11 Mar 2020), Time-Decay allows high severity scores.  Overall, the risk is active, direct and pervasive across operations, finance and strategy, so individual snippets score predominantly in the 6-9 range, with modest downward adjustments where mitigation or uncertainty is emphasised.

XYL’s 2023 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted threat that is already depressing performance and could further destabilise the company.  The narrative is skewed toward direct, present-tense impacts—especially supply-chain shortages (notably semiconductors), freight and logistics congestion, tight labour markets, cost inflation and disruptions linked to China’s shifting COVID policy.  Management states these factors "have had, and continue to have, a material adverse effect" on business and results, signalling that the risk has already crystallised.  Although no dollar amounts are provided, the language (“material adverse effect”, “significant volatility”, “unable to predict the full extent”) is strong, specific and operationally detailed.  Because the filing date (24 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO pandemic declaration, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Evidence therefore receives upper-mid to high scores when it (a) directly attributes material harm to COVID-19, (b) enumerates concrete operational pinch-points (chips, freight, labour, China lockdowns), or (c) extends the threat to liquidity and capital markets.  Generic statements of uncertainty or unquantified forward-looking caution are scored lower.  Overall, the pandemic remains an acute, pervasive enterprise risk for XYL, warranting elevated but not maximum scores due to the absence of precise financial quantification.

XYL’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to reference pandemic risk, but frames it mostly as an ongoing, broad contingency rather than a currently quantified drag on performance.  COVID-19 is not singled-out by name; instead, the filing folds “epidemics, global health crises or pandemics” into longer lists of geopolitical and supply-chain hazards.  The company does acknowledge that (1) its Chinese operations and suppliers “have been in the past” adversely affected by public-health crises and (2) supply-chain and facility operations could again be disrupted by future outbreaks.  These statements show the risk is both experiential (past impacts) and forward-looking, but they remain qualitative and un-quantified.  Given that the original COVID-19 shock is now four years old (medium-term under the Time Decay Principle) and that the text provides no fresh, specific financial metrics, the overall evidence merits only a moderate severity rating.  The risk is real—especially through global supply-chain sensitivity and geographic concentration in China—but is conveyed in generic, catch-all language that dilutes immediacy.  Accordingly, individual snippet scores cluster in the 2-4 range, comfortably within the 4-10-year ‘medium-term’ band, and the aggregate narrative supports a moderate but not high risk profile.

YUM’s 2021-02-22 Form 10-K portrays COVID-19 as a severe, multi-faceted, still-unfolding threat that is materially affecting every layer of the company’s global restaurant system.  The filing makes clear that the pandemic is not merely a hypothetical future concern but an event that has already reduced revenues, forced permanent store closures, caused goodwill and asset impairments, raised operating costs (PPE, cleaning, labour premiums), interrupted supplies, and driven franchisees into financial distress.  Management repeatedly states that these pressures will “continue,” underscoring that the risk horizon extends well beyond the 2020 financial year.  The disclosures are specific—naming lost revenues, dine-in bans, labour shortages, and potential liquidity strain—rather than boiler-plate, and they establish direct causal links to COVID-19.  Because the filing date is within one year of the World Health Organization’s pandemic declaration (March 2020), the Time Decay Principle permits high severity scores (7-10).  I therefore weight sentences that show realised, quantified, or system-wide impacts most heavily, while forward-looking or partially mitigated statements receive moderate scores.  Sentences that describe upside (e.g., drive-thru sales gains) are treated as mitigating factors and scored lower.  Collectively, the evidence supports an overall risk level near the top of the scale for a recent event with ongoing, material consequences.

COVID-19 is portrayed by YUM as a current, multi-faceted, and still-unfolding risk that touches virtually every operational lever of the business—from sales volatility and margin pressure to supply-chain fragility, labour availability, franchisee solvency, capital-market access and even heightened cyber-security exposure due to remote work.  The text is largely forward-looking but anchored in concrete experience: it cites revenue losses from 2020-21 closures, continuing outbreaks in Asia, elevated operating costs and ongoing supply and labour disruptions.  Although some mitigating factors are mentioned (e.g., drive-thru/delivery sales gains and precautionary measures), the narrative stresses uncertainty, potential erosion of recent sales tail-winds, and the possibility of systemic financial stress for both YUM and its franchise network.  Because the filing date (February 2022) is less than two years after the pandemic’s declared onset, the Time-Decay principle allows high severity scores.  Given the breadth of impacts, the persistent uncertainty and the strategic dependence on franchisees and external capital, the evidence collectively supports high (but sub-maximal) risk scores, generally in the 6-9 range, tempered only where explicit mitigating factors are disclosed.

YUM’s 2023 Form 10-K depicts COVID-19 as both a recently-experienced shock and a continuing threat.  Management acknowledges concrete impacts already suffered—store closures, reduced operating hours, mobility restrictions, supply-chain bottlenecks, and labour shortages—and notes that these effects persisted through 2022 (especially in China).  The wording repeatedly stresses materiality (“has had, and may continue to have, an adverse effect”) and emphasises that some government mandates remain in force.  Although no hard dollar figures are supplied, the company links the pandemic to revenue pressure, cost inflation, and operational disruption across its global franchise network.  Statements are forward-looking as well, citing uncertainty about future outbreaks, vaccine efficacy, and evolving regulations; thus risk is framed as both realised and prospective.  Because the filing date (27 Feb 2023) is less than three years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, the Time-Decay Principle allows elevated severity scores.  Overall, the disclosures indicate a high but not catastrophic risk—specific impacts are enumerated, yet no quantified loss is provided and some mitigation (vaccines, reopening trends) is implicit—warranting mid-to-upper‐range micro-scores for individual sentences.

YUM’s 2024 Form 10-K continues to flag the COVID-19 pandemic as a live, enterprise-level threat.  The language is forward-looking—describing what “may” or “could” happen if public-health conditions deteriorate again—yet it explicitly connects pandemic dynamics to material hits on sales, unit traffic, labour availability, mandatory closures, and supply-chain continuity.  No hard dollar figures are supplied, but the company stresses that worsening conditions would directly disrupt operations and growth prospects worldwide.  Because the filing date (20 Feb 2024) is roughly four years after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic (11 Mar 2020), the Time-Decay Principle places these disclosures in the early “medium-term” band; therefore, individual evidence scores should cluster around 4-6.  The statements are moderately specific (naming store closures, quarantines, guest-traffic declines, etc.) and emphasise pervasive, global exposure, but they remain largely conditional and unquantified.  Accordingly, each snippet earns a mid-level severity score—significant enough to warrant attention, yet tempered because impacts are described as potential rather than already realised.

Zimmer Biomet’s 2021 Form 10-K presents COVID-19 as an acute and continuing enterprise-level threat.  Most disclosures are framed in the present tense (“continues to pose risks,” “we expect it to continue”) and cite specific, already-realised impacts—steep declines in elective surgeries, supply-chain and manufacturing interruptions, remote-work cyber-exposures, and two multi-hundred-million-dollar impairment charges.  In addition, several passages are forward-looking, warning that new variants and hospital labour shortages will prolong revenue pressure through 2022.  The language is concrete (e.g., ‘net sales decreased dramatically’, ‘$612 million goodwill impairment’) and repeatedly links the pandemic to material financial harm.  Because the event began less than three years before the 2022 filing date, the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores (up to 10).  Overall, the risk profile is high: existing, quantified impacts have already eroded earnings and cash flow, while variant-driven uncertainty and operational bottlenecks threaten further downside.

ZBH’s 2024 Form 10-K shows that COVID-19 remains a live but moderating enterprise risk.  The filing repeatedly connects the pandemic to earlier deferrals of elective procedures, supply-chain strain, labor shortages and the company’s continuing reliance on hybrid/remote work—each of which can still translate into margin pressure, cyber-exposure and operational volatility.  The disclosures are largely backward-looking (e.g., 2022 Omicron disruptions) or framed as conditional (“there can be no assurance we will successfully manage…”) rather than presenting fresh, quantified damage.  Because the pandemic’s peak shock is now about four years old, the Time-Decay principle requires us to temper severity scores; residual impacts are meaningful but no longer existential.  Overall, the risk evidence is specific enough (referring to procedure deferrals, staffing shortages, remote work and cyber-threat amplification) to merit moderate scoring, but the mitigants (recovery in volumes, fewer disruptions, management adaptations) prevent the highest ratings.

Zebra’s 2021 Form 10-K was filed less than a year after the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a global pandemic, so the Time-Decay Principle allows high scores for recent evidence.  The filing contains an extensive, largely risk-factor-oriented discussion that makes three things clear: (i) COVID-19 has already produced tangible, material impacts (lower customer demand, higher fulfilment costs, supply-chain interruptions, and a measurable hit to 2020 net sales and profitability); (ii) management views those impacts as continuing and highly uncertain, explicitly tying future performance to variables such as vaccine roll-out, government restrictions, and labour availability; and (iii) although Zebra is taking mitigation actions (remote work, safety protocols, alternative logistics, hazard pay, etc.), the Company still warns of potentially pronounced future disruptions, liquidity pressure, and compound effects on existing risks.  The language is specific and event-linked, but most sentences remain qualitative rather than quantified, and several include partial mitigants, tempering—but not eliminating—the overall severity.  Given the proximity to the event date, the breadth of operational and financial exposure described, and the blend of realised and forward-looking elements, individual sentences range from moderate to high severity (3–8 points).  No snippet reaches a maximum 10 because there is no exact dollar quantification, but many exceed mid-range scores due to direct, current adverse impacts and acknowledgement of ongoing uncertainty.

Zebra Technologies’ 2022 Form 10-K anchors COVID-19 as a recent, still-evolving risk with both realised and prospective impacts across virtually every dimension of the business.  The filing documents concrete, already-incurred consequences – lower 2020 net sales, supply-chain bottlenecks, higher freight and component costs, and labour shortages – and warns that these pressures persist through 2022.  It also layers forward-looking uncertainty around new virus variants, shifting government mandates (OSHA ETS, global vaccine rules), and possible attrition of critical talent.  Management acknowledges extensive mitigation steps (remote work, office protocols, pricing actions) but concedes they may be insufficient, and that the pandemic could amplify other strategic and operational risks.  Because the filing date (February 2022) is within two years of the World Health Organization’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle places these statements in the “recent” category, permitting high severity scores when disclosures describe direct, material or continuing effects.  Overall, the narrative portrays COVID-19 as an active, multi-faceted threat that is only partially under management’s control, justifying above-median risk scores while granting modest deductions where the company describes effective counter-measures or improving trends.

Zebra’s 2023 filing presents COVID-19 as an ongoing, multi-faceted risk that is both retrospective (it has already reduced sales, raised costs and strained labour and supply chains) and prospective (future variants, renewed lockdowns and structural shifts in demand could intensify the impact).  The language is largely specific, citing concrete channels of exposure: component shortages, premium freight, longer lead times, labour constraints, remote-work protocols, decelerating customer demand and higher input costs.  While certain passages describe mitigation (remote work arrangements, health protocols, price increases), the overall tone concedes material, continuing vulnerability.  Because the pandemic window (March 2020-2023) is within the 0-3-year “recent” band, the Time Decay Principle permits high scores, especially where the filing admits realised financial damage (e.g., significant 2020 declines) or still-unquantified but ‘material adverse’ possibilities.  Accordingly, strongest snippets receive 7-8 points, moderate forward-looking or partially mitigated disclosures sit in the 4-6 range, and generic or heavily mitigated statements fall to 1-3.  No evidence predates the event, so no snippet is forced to zero.

Zebra Technologies (ZBRA) acknowledges the COVID-19 pandemic primarily as an ongoing, medium-term operational hazard that has already affected its supply chain and may continue to disrupt manufacturing, logistics, labour availability and overall financial performance. The disclosure is forward-looking but anchored by a concrete admission that the pandemic "has had an impact on our supply chain," indicating an existing, direct exposure. Nevertheless, the narrative remains largely qualitative—there is no quantified dollar impact, no explicit reference to permanent demand shifts, and several statements are bundled with other generic disaster risks, diluting severity. Because the filing date (15 Feb 2024) is roughly four years after the WHO’s March 2020 declaration, the Time Decay Principle caps scores in the mid-range. Overall, the company’s language depicts a material yet un-quantified threat that persists through evolving variants, potential supply-chain bottlenecks and regulatory health orders, warranting moderate—not extreme—risk scores.

Zoetis’ 2020 Form 10-K links the COVID-19 pandemic to both realised and prospective risks across virtually every facet of its business.  The filing—made less than a year after the WHO declared a pandemic—contains specific language that the company has already suffered revenue reductions (especially in livestock), supply-chain interruptions, remote-work inefficiencies and higher financing needs.  It also projects further threats: future government restrictions could choke manufacturing or logistics capacity, dampen R&D progress and prolong demand weakness.  The disclosures move well beyond boiler-plate by citing concrete operating effects (e.g., livestock revenue declines, debt issuance for liquidity) and by flagging multiple risk channels—supply chain, labour, capital markets, cyber-security and litigation.  Because the filing date (16 Feb 2021) falls squarely within three years of the pandemic’s onset, the Time-Decay Principle allows high severity scoring.  Most sentences warrant scores in the 6-10 range: they either confirm current financial harm or outline highly plausible, near-term adverse scenarios.  Minor mitigating comments (e.g., ‘essential-business’ status) slightly temper—but do not negate—the weight of the evidence.

The filing—dated February 15 2022, i.e., within two years of the WHO’s March 11 2020 pandemic declaration—contains an extensive, dedicated COVID-19 risk discussion.  The language is mostly recent-impact and forward-looking, not hypothetical: management cites concrete disruptions already experienced (lower demand, supply-chain delays, remote-work complications) and explicitly warns of material adverse effects on revenue, cash-flows and operations if conditions persist or worsen.  The disclosures also detail sector-specific pressures (livestock plant shutdowns, labor shortages, vaccination-mandate uncertainty) that could structurally affect Zoetis’ markets.  Although no hard dollar figure is provided, the statements are highly specific, cover multiple operational vectors (supply, demand, workforce, regulation), and acknowledge continuing uncertainty through 2022.  Under the Time-Decay Principle, a pandemic still unfolding (0-3 years) justifies high severity scores (7-9) where direct impacts are described, with moderate scores (3-6) for secondary or less-quantified effects, and minor deductions where mitigation or uncertainty is emphasised.

Zoetis’ 2022 Form 10-K makes it clear that the COVID-19 pandemic is both a realised and an evolving risk.  Numerous passages document concrete, already-incurred impacts—such as supply-chain delays, product shortages, labour constraints and reduced demand from livestock customers—while also flagging forward-looking uncertainties tied to new variants, changing government restrictions and knock-on economic weakness.  The company repeatedly uses material-adverse-effect language, links the pandemic to specific business lines (e.g., Simparica Trio, livestock vaccines) and details operational counter-measures (remote work, controlled launches).  Because the filing date (14-Feb-2023) falls within three years of the WHO’s pandemic declaration (11-Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores where disclosures show direct, quantified or continuing impacts.  Overall, the narrative portrays COVID-19 as a high-priority risk driver that simultaneously depresses demand, constrains supply, strains labour and amplifies other risk factors; therefore, individual snippets that evidence tangible disruptions or material language warrant scores in the upper range (7-9), while more generic or forward-looking references merit moderate scores (2-6).

The filing situates COVID-19 primarily as a still-relevant but now maturing risk factor.  Nearly four years after the WHO pandemic declaration, Zoetis frames the virus less as an acute shock and more as one of several macro disruptors that can impair operations, finances, and supply chains.  Language oscillates between forward-looking caution ("could have a material adverse effect") and backward-looking evidence of actual impact—most notably the manufacturing shortfalls for Simparica Trio, Librela and Solensia and the pandemic-accelerated migration of flea-and-tick sales to e-commerce.  These disclosures demonstrate that COVID-19 continues to influence distribution channels, manufacturing capacity, labour availability and customer demand, but with fewer quantified numbers and no fresh, dramatic losses.  Under the Time Decay Principle the event now falls into the early "medium-term" window (≈4 years old), warranting moderate scores.  Sentences that document concrete, historical disruptions score toward the upper end of the 4-6 band, while broad, speculative or highly generic statements receive lower, but still non-zero, marks.  Mitigating factors include the absence of precise financial figures and the company’s emphasis on “could” rather than “has” in many passages.  Collectively, the evidence shows persistent, multi-faceted pandemic risk, but one that is stabilising rather than escalating.
